parts.overview: Ostra is a local server that runs an engineering pipeline: research, spec, plan, implement, review, test, and documentation. Developers use it from a browser console. A code-driven engine folds each session's event log into a state, a pure planner chooses the next steps, and a runner performs them. Leaf agents run on a native API-key executor or inside an installed harness CLI (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Antigravity). A policy engine and an OS sandbox contain every tool call. The Rust workspace has 14 crates, one per concern. The React console in `web/` uses the design system in `design/`.

sections.title: Ostra at a glance
sections.summary: What Ostra does, its main parts, the 15 Rust crates with their dependency direction, and the path of one request from the browser to a finished session.
sections.body:
Ostra is a local server that runs an engineering pipeline for you: research, spec, plan, implement, review, test, and documentation. You use it from a browser console. This page names the parts, shows how the crates depend on each other, and follows one request from the console to a finished session. Each part has its own page, and this page links to it.

## The problem Ostra solves

A single agent that reads a request and edits code has no fixed process. It can skip the research, ignore the review, run a command that harms the machine, or stop in the middle of a task and lose its state. Ostra puts a fixed process around the agents and keeps the control in code, not in a prompt.

Ostra makes these rules:

- **The code decides the next step.** A pure function, `next_steps` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs), reads the session state and returns the steps to run. No agent decides what happens next.
- **A model decides only where judgment is needed.** A judge call answers one question with a JSON schema, for example the category of a request.
- **Each agent has one job.** A leaf agent such as `explore`, `plan`, or `implementer` does one task and ends with a structured `submit_<agent>` call.
- **Every session is a log.** The engine stores each change as an event. After a restart, the engine rebuilds the state from the events and continues.
- **A person can stop and steer.** A gate pauses the session until a person answers, unless the session runs in YOLO mode.
- **Every tool call is checked.** The policy engine judges each call, and a sandbox limits what a command can reach.

## The main parts

Ostra has six parts. Each part is a group of crates or folders.

| Part | What it does | Owner page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Server | Starts the `ostra` binary, signs in the browser, serves the REST API, the `/ws` socket, and the web build. | [Server, REST API, and WebSocket](server-and-api.md) |
| Engine | Folds events into `SessionState`, plans steps, calls judges, and runs steps. | [Sessions and the pipeline](sessions-and-pipeline.md), [The engine runner, recovery, and control](engine-runner.md) |
| Agents | Holds the prompts, judges, and references, and renders a spawn for an executor. | [Agents, prompts, and the spawn contract](agents-and-prompts.md) |
| Executors | Run one agent. The native executor calls a model API. The harness executor runs an installed CLI. | [Executors: native loop and harness CLIs](executors.md) |
| Safety | The policy engine checks tool calls. The sandbox limits commands. The auth layer checks the browser. | [Policy engine](policy.md), [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md), [Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md) |
| Console | A React app in `web/`, built on the design system in `design/`. | [The web console](web-console.md), [The design system](design-system.md) |

The other pages cover the data and the support areas: [Storage](storage.md), [Configuration reference](configuration.md), [Workspaces, projects, and approvals](workspaces-and-trust.md), [Project init, skills, and lesson memory](project-init-and-memory.md), [Documentation books](documentation-books.md), [Code navigation](code-navigation.md), and [MCP servers and Web Push](mcp-and-notifications.md). To install and start Ostra, read [Install, run, and the command line](install-and-run.md).

## The pipeline in one view

A session has a category. The `Category` enum in [`crates/ostra-core/src/pipeline.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/pipeline.rs) has 10 values: `Research`, `Spec`, `Plan`, `Implement`, `Verify`, `Test`, `Docs`, `Prompt`, `QuickChange`, and `QuickAnswer`. The category decides which stages run.

A stage is one node of the pipeline. The `StageKind` enum names the nodes, for example `Explore`, `Spec`, `Plan`, `Implement`, `Review`, and `ClosingGate`. The `StageKind::lane` function maps each stage to one of 9 board lanes: `Research`, `Requirements`, `Verification`, `Design`, `Build`, `Review`, `Test`, `Docs`, and `Done`. The console draws these lanes on the session board.

An `Implement` request has two tracks. The light track goes from research straight to reviewed phases. The full track adds the spec, its fact-check, the plan, and the approvals. The `Track` judge starts on the light track and escalates to the full track when the evidence needs it. [Sessions and the pipeline](sessions-and-pipeline.md) owns the stages, the tracks, and the loops.

## Crate map and dependency direction

The Rust workspace in [`Cargo.toml`](Cargo.toml) has the members `crates/*`. That is 15 crates, and each crate has one concern. The `ostra-server` crate builds the single binary `ostra`. Its `[[bin]]` entry names the binary, and `main.rs` parses the command line.

An arrow in the next diagram points from a crate to a crate that it uses. Every crate also depends on `ostra-core`, so the diagram shows only some of those arrows. `ostra-core` has no dependency on another Ostra crate.

### Diagram: crate dependencies

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  server["ostra-server"]
  workspace["ostra-workspace"]
  engine["ostra-engine"]
  native["ostra-exec-native"]
  harness["ostra-exec-harness"]
  code["ostra-code"]
  mcp["ostra-mcp"]
  notify["ostra-notify"]
  agents["ostra-agents"]
  providers["ostra-providers"]
  tools["ostra-tools"]
  policy["ostra-policy"]
  store["ostra-store"]
  sandbox["ostra-sandbox"]
  core["ostra-core"]
  server --> workspace
  server --> engine
  server --> native
  server --> harness
  server --> code
  server --> mcp
  server --> notify
  workspace --> engine
  engine --> agents
  engine --> store
  native --> providers
  native --> tools
  native --> policy
  tools --> store
  engine --> sandbox
  harness --> sandbox
  tools --> sandbox
  code --> sandbox
  sandbox --> core
  agents --> core
  store --> core
```

### What each crate owns

| Crate | Concern | Depends on (besides `ostra-core`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ostra-core` | Shared types: ids, agents, config, events, pipeline enums, API messages, and the `Executor` trait. | none |
| `ostra-engine` | Sessions as event-sourced state, the planner, the judge calls, and the runner. | `ostra-sandbox`, `ostra-store`, `ostra-agents` |
| `ostra-agents` | Agent assets, the spawn contract, and the repo brief. | none |
| `ostra-store` | SQLite: the workspace database, the registry, and the lesson memory. | none |
| `ostra-workspace` | Workspace settings, projects, trust approvals, and `WorkspaceRt`. | `ostra-sandbox`, `ostra-store`, `ostra-engine`, `ostra-agents`, `ostra-policy` |
| `ostra-exec-native` | The native agent loop on an API key. | `ostra-sandbox`, `ostra-providers`, `ostra-tools`, `ostra-policy`, `ostra-store` |
| `ostra-exec-harness` | The harness executor: a CLI under a PTY, with a hook bridge. | `ostra-sandbox` |
| `ostra-providers` | The Anthropic and OpenAI streaming clients and the scripted provider. | none |
| `ostra-tools` | The native tool implementations. | `ostra-sandbox`, `ostra-store` |
| `ostra-policy` | Guards (layer 1) and permissions (layer 2). | none |
| `ostra-sandbox` | The kernel boundary under agent commands, and the egress proxy. | none |
| `ostra-code` | Code navigation: the index, outlines, the graph, and LSP servers. | `ostra-sandbox` |
| `ostra-mcp` | The MCP client for external MCP servers. | none |
| `ostra-notify` | Web Push encryption and VAPID. | none |
| `ostra-server` | The binary, auth, the REST API, the socket, and the embedded web build. | every crate above |

Two folders sit outside the crate map. The `web/` folder holds the React console. The `design/` folder holds the design system that `web/` imports. The `assets/` folder holds the prompts that `ostra-agents` renders: `assets/agents/<name>/`, `assets/judges/`, `assets/refs/`, and `assets/skills/`. The `tests/` folder holds the browser, conformance, eval, and Windows probe tests.

## Why the engine does not depend on the executors

The `ostra-engine` crate does not depend on `ostra-exec-native`, `ostra-exec-harness`, `ostra-providers`, `ostra-policy`, or `ostra-tools`. It reaches them only through the `Services` trait in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/services.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/services.rs). The doc comment says that the server implements the trait and that tests use fakes.

The `Services` trait gives the engine these functions:

- `global` and `workspace` return the settings.
- `executor` returns the `Executor` for an `ExecutorKind`.
- `factory` returns the `SpawnFactory` that renders a spawn.
- `judge` makes one structured model call.
- `notify` sends a Web Push notice.
- `protected_paths`, `command_approved`, and `add_allow_rule` serve the policy and trust rules.

The server implements the trait as `ServerServices` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs). This split has one result: the engine tests run with fake executors and fake judges, with no model call and no sandbox. Only the server crate knows every other crate, because it connects them.

## Path of one request from the console to a finished session

The next steps follow one `Implement` request. The route names, the types, and the functions are the real ones.

### Step 1: the browser sends the request

The New task screen calls `api.createSession` in [`web/src/screens/workspace/NewTask.tsx`](web/src/screens/workspace/NewTask.tsx). This call sends `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/sessions` with a `CreateSession` body: the request text, the pinned projects, the files, the uploads, the options, and an optional documentation book.

The `guard` middleware in [`crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs) runs before the handler. It makes these checks in order:

1. The `Host` header must be in the allowlist. If not, the guard returns status 421.
2. The `Origin` header must be allowed, the `Sec-Fetch-Site` header must not be `cross-site` or `same-site`, and `Sec-Fetch-Dest` must be `empty`, `websocket`, or `document`. If not, the guard returns status 403.
3. The request must carry a valid session cookie, except for `/api/auth/exchange`. If not, the guard returns status 401.

The handler `create_session` then calls `start_work`, which holds a read lock so that a workspace removal cannot run at the same time. It calls `Engine::create_session`. [Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md) owns these checks.

### Step 2: the engine creates the session

`Engine::create_session` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs) refuses an empty request and a bad book id. It then calls `start_session`, which does these actions:

1. Keep only the projects that have an inventory file. If no project has one, return the error that tells the user to initialize a project first.
2. Check the context files and the uploads.
3. Create a `SessionId`, the session folder, and a folder for each project.
4. Insert the session row with `WorkspaceDb::create_session`.
5. Append the first event, `SessionEvent::SessionCreated`.
6. Call `ensure_driver`, which starts one driver task for the session.

The handler returns a `SessionSummary` at once. The work continues in the driver task. The browser does not wait for the pipeline.

### Step 3: the driver plans and runs steps

The `drive` loop reads the state, calls `next_steps`, and starts each new step in its own task. The `Step::key` function gives each step an identity, so the loop never starts the same step twice. After a step ends, the loop wakes and plans again.

The first plan has one step. The session has no category yet, so `next_steps` returns `Step::Judge` with `JudgeKind::Classify`. The `perform_judge` function builds the judge input, and `call_judge` calls `Services::judge`. The judge answers with JSON that must match a schema. Then the engine appends `SessionEvent::DecisionMade`, and the fold sets the category. [Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md) owns the judge calls.

### Diagram: from the request to a finished execution

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Browser
  participant Server
  participant Engine
  participant Store
  participant Planner
  participant Services
  participant Executor
  Browser->>Server: POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/sessions
  Server->>Engine: create_session
  Engine->>Store: create_session and append SessionCreated
  Engine->>Planner: next_steps
  Planner-->>Engine: Step Judge Classify
  Engine->>Services: judge
  Services-->>Engine: JSON that matches the schema
  Engine->>Store: append DecisionMade
  Engine->>Planner: next_steps
  Planner-->>Engine: Step Spawn explore
  Engine->>Executor: run ExecutionSpec
  Executor-->>Engine: ExecutionResult with submit
  Engine->>Store: append ExecutionFinished
  Engine-->>Server: EngineNotice on the broadcast channel
  Server-->>Browser: ServerMsg SessionEvent on /ws
```

### Step 4: the engine spawns an agent

For a `Step::Spawn`, `perform_spawn` runs an agent. It does these actions in order:

1. Wait for an execution slot. The limit is `limits.max_parallel_executions`, and the default is 3.
2. Resolve the model route for the agent, from the global config and the workspace settings.
3. Get the `Executor` from `Services::executor`. A route picks `ExecutorKind::Native` or `ExecutorKind::Harness(HarnessKind)`.
4. Render the spawn with the `SpawnFactory`: the system prompt, the first message, the spawn block, and the report file.
5. Append `ExecutionStarted`, and insert the execution row.
6. Call `executor.run` with an `ExecutionSpec`, an `ExecutionHost`, and a `CancellationToken`.
7. Store the `ExecutionResult` and append `ExecutionFinished`.

During the run, the executor sends each tool call to the policy engine before the tool runs. The agent ends the run with its `submit_<agent>` call. The fold reads the submitted data, and the planner uses it to choose the next steps. [The engine runner, recovery, and control](engine-runner.md) owns `perform_spawn`, and [Executors: native loop and harness CLIs](executors.md) owns the run.

### Step 5: gates wait for a person

At some points the planner returns `Step::OpenGate`. A gate is a question that the pipeline cannot answer alone: a spec approval, a plan approval, open questions, a permission ask, or a closing review. The engine appends `GateOpened`, and `Inner::push_for` sends a Web Push notice. The session then waits.

The browser answers with `POST /api/gates/{id}/answer`, which calls `Engine::answer_gate`. The engine validates the answer, appends `GateAnswered`, and wakes the driver.

If the session runs in YOLO mode, the engine answers gates without a person. These rules apply:

- **Most gates.** The planner returns `Step::YoloAnswer` for each open gate, and a judge answers it.
- **Permission asks.** The planner skips `GatePayload::Permission`, because the live execution answers the ask. The policy allows the ask with the rule `permission:yolo`.
- **Gates that stay open.** The function `yolo_leaves_open` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/judge_input.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/judge_input.rs) names them. They are a `budget_reached` gate and an `execution_failed` gate for an execution that the user stopped. A person must answer both.
- **Notices.** `Inner::push_for` sends no notice for a gate, unless the gate is `GatePayload::HarnessFailure`. A harness login failure needs a person, so it still sends a notice.

[Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md) owns the full rule.

### Step 6: the session finishes

When all work is done and nothing runs, the planner calls the `Completion` judge. The judge returns a Markdown report. Then the planner returns `Step::Complete`, and the engine handles it with these actions:

1. Write the report to the completion report path in the session folder.
2. For an init session, check the project files. If a file is broken, append `SessionFailed` and stop.
3. Append `SessionCompleted` with the first line of the report as its summary.

The handler for `Step::Complete` does not remove the session download cache. `Inner::append` calls `ostra_sandbox::remove_session_cache` when any event moves the session to a terminal state. This includes `SessionCompleted`, `SessionFailed`, and a stop. The reason is that an ended session runs no more tools, and a later session must not build from its downloads.

The `drive` loop ends when `is_terminal` is true. A failed judge or a failed step ends the session with `SessionFailed` or records a `Note`.

### How the browser sees each event

`Inner::append` is the one function that changes a session. It runs these actions in order:

1. Store the event with `WorkspaceDb::append_event`.
2. Materialize the gate and decision rows.
3. Apply the event to the `SessionState`.
4. Update the session row, then send the `SessionUpdated` notice.
5. Broadcast the `EngineNotice::Event` notice.
6. Call `Inner::push_for`, then call `live.wake.notify_one()` to wake the driver.

The session state lock covers actions 1 to 4: the store write, the materialize, the apply, the session-row update, and the `SessionUpdated` notice. Actions 5 and 6 run after the engine releases the lock. The lock makes the order of stored events the order of the fold, because it allows one append at a time for each session. The session cache removal for a terminal state also runs under the lock, after action 3.

The server forwards each notice to its hub. The `/ws` handler in [`crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs) calls `route` for each notice and sends it to the browsers that subscribed to the channel. A `SessionEvent` goes to the channel `session:{id}`. A session summary goes to `session:{id}`, `workspace:{id}`, and `home`. The page that shows a session updates from these messages without a reload.

## What happens when

- **The server restarts during a session.** `Engine::recover` runs when the server attaches a workspace. It marks each running execution as interrupted, denies the permission asks of dead executions, and starts the driver again. The planner then runs the interrupted work again with the same spawn block. A harness run that waited for an answer stays waiting.
- **A person pauses the session.** The planner returns no step while `paused` is true, not even a YOLO answer. Running executions are interrupted, and `Resume` continues them.
- **A person stops the session.** The state becomes terminal. The engine refuses `ExecutionStarted`, `ExecutionResumed`, and `CommandStarted` after that, so nothing starts between the stop and the check.
- **The session reaches its budget.** The planner opens a `BudgetReached` gate and starts no new execution until the user raises the budget. Running executions finish. YOLO does not answer this gate. The default `limits.session_budget_usd` is 25.0, and a value of 0 means no limit.
- **A judge call fails.** `Inner::call_judge` tries up to 3 times. After every failed try, it waits 500 ms times (attempt + 1). The waits are 500, 1000, and 1500 ms. The last wait comes after the third failed try and before the error returns. If all 3 tries fail, the session ends with `SessionFailed`. [Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md) owns the full rule. Two judge calls are exceptions:
  - The `Completion` judge: the engine writes a report that lists the state only.
  - `JudgeKind::YoloAnswer`: after 3 failed tries, `Inner::perform_yolo` appends a `Note` and leaves the gate open for the user. It does not append `SessionFailed`.
- **An agent run fails.** The run ends with an error status, and the planner decides on a retry or a gate. [Sessions and the pipeline](sessions-and-pipeline.md) owns the retry caps.
- **No project is initialized.** `create_session` returns the error `No project in this workspace is initialized yet`. Start an init session first. [Project init, skills, and lesson memory](project-init-and-memory.md) owns the init flow.
- **A slow browser misses notices.** The `/ws` handler sends the error `lagged` on `RecvError::Lagged`. The web code fetches its REST snapshot again only through `onReconnect` listeners, after a socket reconnect. [Server, REST API, and WebSocket](server-and-api.md) owns the socket rules.

## Limits at a glance

| Name | Value | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `limits.max_parallel_executions` | 3 (default) | Workspace settings |
| `limits.session_budget_usd` | 25.0 (default) | Workspace settings |
| Judge call tries | 3, with waits of 500, 1000, and 1500 ms | `Inner::call_judge` |
| `MAX_DOCS_WRITERS` | 4 | `crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs` |
| `PAUSE_AFTER` (containment signals) | 3 | `crates/ostra-core/src/containment.rs` |
| `MAX_MESSAGE` (one socket message) | 1 MiB | `crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs` |
| `MAX_CHANNELS` (per socket) | 256 | `crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs` |
| Default port | 7878 | `DEFAULT_PORT` in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs` |

The [Configuration reference](configuration.md) owns every setting and its default.

## Build and test commands

Use these commands from the repo root. The toolchain in `rust-toolchain.toml` is Rust 1.98.1 with `rustfmt` and `clippy`.

- Build: `cargo build --workspace`
- Test: `cargo test --workspace`
- Format: `cargo fmt --all`

[Install, run, and the command line](install-and-run.md) owns the scripts, and [Tests and evals](testing.md) owns the test layers.

## Where to read next

- To start Ostra: [Install, run, and the command line](install-and-run.md).
- To learn the pipeline: [Sessions and the pipeline](sessions-and-pipeline.md), then [Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md).
- To learn how an agent runs: [Agents, prompts, and the spawn contract](agents-and-prompts.md), [Executors: native loop and harness CLIs](executors.md), and [Native tools](tools.md).
- To learn how Ostra contains an agent: [Policy engine](policy.md) and [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md).
- To learn how Ostra keeps data: [Storage](storage.md).
- To change a setting: [Configuration reference](configuration.md).

sections.title: Install, run, and the command line
sections.summary: How to build Ostra, run it from source, install it as a per-user service, or run it in Docker. Lists every `ostra` subcommand and serve flag, the port, bind, and host rules, logging, and the cargo commands.
sections.body:
Ostra is one binary named `ostra` that embeds the web console. Without a build step, the binary has no console to serve. Without a start rule, a user does not know which address the server listens on or how to sign in. This page covers four ways to start Ostra, the `ostra` command line, the rules for port, bind address, and allowed hosts, and the logs.

The page covers:

- The toolchain and the build script `build.sh`.
- The run script `run.sh`, and the service scripts `install.sh` and `install.ps1`.
- The `Dockerfile` and `docker-compose.yml`.
- The subcommands and flags of `ostra`.
- Port, bind address, and allowed hosts.
- Logging with `OSTRA_LOG` and the `server.log` file.
- The cargo commands.

The settings in `config.toml` and the `OSTRA_*` variables are in [Configuration](configuration.md). The sign-in token, cookie, and Host check are in [Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md). The tests are in [Tests and evals](testing.md).

## Toolchain and requirements

The repository pins its tools, so every build uses the same compiler.

| Tool | Version | Where it is set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust | `1.98.1`, with the `rustfmt` and `clippy` components | `rust-toolchain.toml` (`channel = "1.98.1"`) |
| Rust edition | `2024`, with `rust-version = "1.98"` | `[workspace.package]` in `Cargo.toml` |
| Node.js | 24 | `install.ps1` names Node.js 24. The `Dockerfile` installs `setup_24.x`. |
| npm | any version that runs `npm ci` | `package.json` (an npm workspace with `design`, `web`, and `site`) |

`rustup` reads `rust-toolchain.toml` and installs the pinned compiler the first time you run `cargo` in the repository.

`.cargo/config.toml` sets two variables for every cargo command. `TS_RS_EXPORT_DIR` is `web/src/api/gen`, relative to the repository root. `TS_RS_LARGE_INT` is `number`. The `ts-rs` crate uses them to write the TypeScript types that the web console imports. The types are the API shapes of the `#[ts(export)]` Rust types. See [The web console](web-console.md).

The release profile in `Cargo.toml` sets `debug = false` and `strip = true`, so `target/release/ostra` has no debug symbols.

## Build the binary with build.sh

`./build.sh` builds the web console, then the release binary at `target/release/ostra`. The script builds the console first because the binary embeds `web/dist` when it compiles.

The script runs these steps:

1. Change to the folder of the script.
2. If the `node_modules` folder does not exist, run `npm ci --no-audit --no-fund`.
3. If `web/dist/index.html` is missing, or any input file is newer than it, run `npm run -s build` in `web/`. Otherwise print `Web UI is up to date`.
4. Run `cargo build --release -p ostra-server`.

The input files for step 3 are `web/src`, `web/public`, `web/index.html`, `web/package.json`, `design/src`, and `design/package.json`. The `design/` folder is an input because `web/` builds against the shared design package. The `site/` folder is also a workspace in `package.json`, but `build.sh` does not read it.

The script stops at the first failure, because it sets `set -euo pipefail`.

## Run from source with run.sh

`./run.sh [ostra flags...]` builds and then starts the server in the foreground. The script passes every argument to `ostra`, so `./run.sh --bind 0.0.0.0` starts the server on every interface.

| Variable | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `SKIP_BUILD=1` | Start the existing `target/release/ostra` and do not run `build.sh`. |
| `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` | Path of a credentials file. The script applies its `export NAME=value` lines before it starts the server. |

The script applies only the lines that match `export NAME=value`, so other lines in the file do not run. The shell evaluates each matching line with `eval`. A value can therefore contain a command substitution, and the substitution runs. Write only trusted lines in the file.

The script ends with `exec ./target/release/ostra "$@"`, so the server replaces the script process. A Ctrl+C reaches the server directly.

## Install as a per-user service

`install.sh` (macOS and Linux) and `install.ps1` (Windows) build Ostra, copy the binary, and register a per-user service that starts at login. Neither script needs administrator rights. Both scripts print a one-time sign-in URL when the service reports a running server.

Use the same five commands with both scripts:

| Command | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `install` (the default) | Build, install, and start the service. Flags after `install` go to `ostra serve`. A first argument that starts with `-` also means `install`. |
| `restart` | Restart the service with the installed binary. |
| `status` | Show whether the service runs. |
| `url` | Print a fresh sign-in URL. The script runs `ostra url`. |
| `uninstall` | Stop the service and delete the service files and the binary. |

The `uninstall` command keeps the config file and the data folder. Use `./install.sh --port 8080` or `.\install.ps1 --port 8080` to install with a fixed port.

### What install.sh does

The script runs on macOS (`Darwin`) and Linux. On another system it prints `Use ./run.sh instead` and exits with an error.

1. Run `build.sh`, unless `SKIP_BUILD=1`.
2. Copy `target/release/ostra` to `$OSTRA_PREFIX/bin/ostra` (default prefix `~/.local`). The script copies to a temporary name and renames it, because a running server keeps its binary and macOS does not stop a process whose file changed.
3. Write the launcher `$OSTRA_PREFIX/bin/ostra-service`. The service runs this script, not the binary.
4. Write the service definition: a launchd plist at `~/Library/LaunchAgents/dev.ostra.server.plist` on macOS, or a systemd user unit at `~/.config/systemd/user/ostra.service` on Linux.
5. Start the service and wait up to 15 seconds (30 checks, 0.5 seconds apart) for a `server.json` file that is newer than a marker file. Then print the sign-in URL.

The launcher records `PATH`, `OSTRA_CONFIG`, and `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` from the shell that ran the installer, because a service manager starts with a minimal `PATH` and the harness CLIs must resolve by name. At each start the launcher applies the `export` lines of `OSTRA_ENV_FILE`, so a changed key needs only a restart and the secrets stay out of the plist or unit file. Then it runs `ostra serve --no-open`. If no `--bind` flag is present, the launcher adds `--bind 127.0.0.1`.

| Part | macOS (launchd) | Linux (systemd user unit) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Restart rule | `KeepAlive` with `SuccessfulExit` set to false: restart when the exit is not clean. `ThrottleInterval` is 10 seconds. | `Restart=on-failure`, `RestartSec=5` |
| Stop signal | launchd default | `KillSignal=SIGINT`, `TimeoutStopSec=20` |
| Stdout | `/dev/null` | `null` |
| Stderr | `service.err.log` in the data folder | The journal: `journalctl --user -u ostra` |

The unit uses `SIGINT` because the server shuts down gracefully on `SIGINT` only. A `SIGTERM` kills the server in the middle of a write. Stdout goes to `null` because the server already writes the same lines to `server.log`.

After the install, the script can print three notices:

- If the bind address is not `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, or `localhost`, a warning that Ostra listens on every interface over plain HTTP.
- If the `bin` folder is not on `PATH`, an instruction to add it, because `ostra url` and `ostra stop` need it.
- On Linux, if linger is off for your user, the command `loginctl enable-linger $USER`. Without linger, the service stops when you log out.

### What install.ps1 does

The script registers a Task Scheduler task named `dev.ostra.server` and installs `ostra.exe` to `$OSTRA_PREFIX\bin` (default `~\.local`). It needs Node.js 24 and Rust with `rustup` on `PATH`. If one is missing, it stops and names the tool to install.

- **Trigger:** the task starts at logon and repeats every 5 minutes. The task uses `MultipleInstances IgnoreNew`, so a repeat does nothing when a server runs. `conhost` exits with code 0 however the server ends, so Task Scheduler never sees a failure. The repeat is the restart rule.
- **Window:** the action runs `conhost.exe --headless ostra.exe serve --no-open`. The headless console gives the server a console without a window.
- **Rights:** `RunLevel Limited` and an interactive logon. The task has no execution time limit.
- **Replace a running binary:** the script renames `ostra.exe` to `ostra.exe.old`, copies the new file, and removes the old one, because Windows cannot overwrite a running file.
- **Single server:** the script refuses to continue if `server.json` records another server, because two servers must not share one data folder.

The task starts with the saved user environment, not the shell of the installer. Thus the script stops with an error in two cases. First, `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` is set, because the task applies no credentials file. Second, `OSTRA_CONFIG` or `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` is set in the shell but not saved as a user variable. Save the variable with `setx`, open a new terminal, and run the script again.

## Run in Docker

The `Dockerfile` builds the web console, the binary, and a small runtime image in three stages. Run `docker build -t ostra .` from the repository root.

| Stage | Base | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `web` | `ubuntu:26.04` | Installs Node.js 24, runs `npm ci`, and builds `web/dist`. |
| `rust` | `ubuntu:26.04` | Installs `rustup`, installs the toolchain from `rust-toolchain.toml`, and runs `cargo build --release -p ostra-server`. The stage copies the binary out of the build cache, because the cache mount vanishes after the step. |
| `runtime` | `ubuntu:26.04` | Installs `ca-certificates`, `git`, `openssh-client`, `curl`, and `bubblewrap`. Copies the binary. |

The runtime image has these settings:

- A user `ostra` with UID and GID 1000. A bind-mounted host folder that the first non-root Linux user owns is then writable without a `chown`.
- `OSTRA_DATA_DIR=/data` and `OSTRA_CONFIG=/config/config.toml`.
- `EXPOSE 7878` and `STOPSIGNAL SIGINT`. The server shuts down gracefully on `SIGINT` only.
- `ENTRYPOINT ["ostra"]` and `CMD ["--bind", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "7878", "--no-open"]`. The container must listen on every interface, because Docker forwards the published port to the container address, not to its loopback.

The image has no harness CLI. The setup check in the console can install one. The CLI lands in `~/.local/bin` or `~/.grok/bin` of the `ostra` user.

### Start with docker compose

`docker-compose.yml` defines one service, `ostra`, and two named volumes. Prepare the host before the first start:

1. Run `mkdir -p config` next to the compose file.
2. Run `sudo chown 1000:1000 config`. A folder that the Docker daemon creates is owned by root. The server runs as 1000:1000, cannot write `/config/config.toml`, and exits at start.
3. Replace `/srv/ostra/projects` on both sides of the projects mount with one absolute host folder. UID 1000 must be able to write to it.
4. Run `docker compose up -d`.
5. Run `docker compose exec ostra ostra url` to print a sign-in URL.

The two halves of the projects mount must be the same path. Ostra stores workspace and project paths as literal text. Only projects and workspaces under that folder persist across a container re-create.

| Mount | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `ostra-data:/data` | The data folder: databases, `server.log`, `server.json`. |
| `ostra-home:/home/ostra` | Installed harness CLIs and their logins. |
| `./config:/config` | `config.toml`. |
| `/srv/ostra/projects:/srv/ostra/projects` | Your projects and workspaces. |

The compose file publishes the port as `127.0.0.1:7878:7878`. Ostra serves plain HTTP. To reach it from another machine, use an SSH tunnel or a TLS reverse proxy. Do not publish the port on every interface.

> The URL that `ostra url` prints inside the container uses the first address of a container interface, because the server listens on `0.0.0.0`. Use `localhost:7878` as the host in your browser. The server always accepts that host. The token after `#token=` stays the same.

In this checkout the `site/` folder is not present, but the `Dockerfile` runs `COPY site/package.json site/`. The image build fails at that step until the folder exists.

## The ostra command line

Run `ostra` with no subcommand to start the server. A subcommand name selects one action. The clap definitions are in [`crates/ostra-server/src/main.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/main.rs). `ostra --version` prints the version, and `ostra --help` lists the commands.

| Command | What it does | Needs a running server |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ostra` or `ostra serve` | Start the server. | No |
| `ostra config` | Print the path of `config.toml`. If the file does not exist, write the default config first. | No |
| `ostra url` | Print a fresh one-time sign-in URL. | Yes |
| `ostra sessions` | List the browsers that are signed in. | No |
| `ostra sessions revoke <id>` | Revoke one sign-in. | No |
| `ostra sessions revoke --all` | Revoke every sign-in. | No |
| `ostra signout` | Same as `ostra sessions revoke --all`. | No |
| `ostra stop <session>` | Stop a session when the server is off. | Must not run |
| `ostra hook ...` | Hook bridge for harness executions. | Called by a harness |
| `ostra mcp-stdio ...` | MCP stdio shim for harness executions. | Called by a harness |

### Serve flags

The flags work with `ostra` and with `ostra serve`. `ostra --port 8080` and `ostra serve --port 8080` are the same. The `ServeArgs` struct defines them.

| Flag | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `--port <n>` | Port to listen on. Overrides `server.port`. |
| `--bind <address>` | Address to listen on. Overrides `server.bind`. |
| `--allow-host <name>` | Extra host name the browser can use. Repeat the flag for more names. |
| `--no-open` | Do not open a browser. |
| `--dev` | Also accept the Vite dev server hosts `localhost:5173` and `127.0.0.1:5173`. Use it for work on the web console. |

### Commands for the sign-in

`ostra url` reads `server.json` in the data folder for the port, the URL host, and the process ID. Then it opens the registry, stores a new token, and prints `http://<host>/#token=<token>`. The token works once and expires after 15 minutes (`TOKEN_TTL_SECS` in `auth.rs`). If `server.json` is missing, the command fails with `No Ostra server is running. Start one with \`ostra\`.`

`ostra sessions` opens the registry directly, so it works with or without a server. It prints one line for each sign-in: the ID (for example `si_3f2a9c1d7e5b6a40`), the sign-in time, the last-seen time, the IP address, and the browser name. If there is none, it prints `No browser is signed in.`

`ostra sessions revoke <id>` deletes one sign-in. If the ID does not exist, the command fails and tells you to run `ostra sessions`. `ostra sessions revoke --all` and `ostra signout` delete every sign-in and print how many. A running server reads the registry again at most every 5 seconds (`RECHECK` in `auth.rs`), so a revoked browser loses access within 5 seconds. After `signout`, run `ostra url` to sign in again.

### Stop a session when the server is off

`ostra stop <session>` ends a session that no server holds. For example, run `ostra stop s_01a0cdab436570b0b522e10ce263a904`. Use it when you do not want the next start to recover the session and run its executions again.

The command works in this order:

1. If `server.json` names a live process, the command fails. The message says to stop the session from its board, to call `POST /api/sessions/{session}/stop`, or to stop the server first.
2. The command opens the registry and looks for the session in the database of each registered workspace.
3. It appends an `ExecutionFinished` event with the status `Cancelled` for each running execution. The usage of each execution stays.
4. It appends a `SessionFailed` event and sets the session status to `Failed` in the `Done` lane.
5. It prints `Stopped <session>; <n> running executions were cancelled.`

If no workspace has the session, the command fails with `No registered workspace has a session <id>.` If the session already ended, it fails with `This session has already ended.` The rules for stop, cancel, and recovery are in [The engine runner, recovery, and control](engine-runner.md).

### Commands that a harness calls

A harness CLI that Ostra starts calls `ostra hook` and `ostra mcp-stdio`. Do not run them by hand. Both read `OSTRA_URL`, `OSTRA_TOKEN`, and `OSTRA_EXECUTION` from the environment of the execution.

- `ostra hook --execution <id> --harness <name> --event <event>` reads a payload on stdin, asks the server, and prints the answer. Outside an Ostra execution it does nothing. Inside one, it denies a `PreToolUse` event when the server is unreachable.
- `ostra mcp-stdio` is a stdio MCP server that forwards each message to the server. Outside an execution it answers the handshake with no tools.

The design of the bridge is in [Executors](executors.md).

The binary also has a hidden argument, `sandbox-init`. It is the first program inside a Linux sandbox, and `--help` does not list it. The binary checks for it before it reads the environment or starts a runtime. See [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md).

## Choose the port, bind address, and allowed hosts

Three settings decide where the server listens and which names the browser can use. Each has a flag and a config key. The flag wins.

| Setting | Flag | Config key | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Port | `--port` | `server.port` | 7878, with a search for a free port |
| Bind address | `--bind` | `server.bind` | `127.0.0.1` |
| Extra host names | `--allow-host` | `server.allowed_hosts` | none |
| Sign in at the IP address | none | `server.use_ip_host` | `false` |

The server reads the config file once at start for these values. Restart the server to apply a change.

### Port

When you set a port, the server binds exactly that port and fails if it is taken. When you set no port, it tries 7878 through 7897 (20 ports). If all 20 are taken, it asks the operating system for a free port. The server prints the final address at start. The function `bind` in `app.rs` does the search.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Port set by --port or server.port?"] -->|yes| B["Bind that port"]
  B -->|port taken| C["Start fails"]
  A -->|no| D["Try 7878 to 7897"]
  D -->|one is free| E["Bind it"]
  D -->|all 20 taken| F["Bind a port that the OS picks"]
```

The `DEFAULT_PORT` constant (7878) is in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs`. The `Dockerfile` passes `--port 7878` so that the published port stays fixed.

### Bind address

The default address is `127.0.0.1`, so only this machine can reach the server. The `--bind` value can be:

- An IP address, such as `127.0.0.1`, `0.0.0.0`, `::`, or the address of one interface. Square brackets around an IPv6 address are removed.
- `localhost`, which means `127.0.0.1`.
- `all` or `*`, which mean `0.0.0.0`.

Any other value stops the start with the message ``... is not an IP address to listen on``.

> Do not bind to `0.0.0.0` or `::` on a network that you do not trust. Ostra serves plain HTTP, so anyone on the network path can read the sign-in cookie and what you type into harness terminals. Anyone who reaches the port with a sign-in link can run commands as you.

When the address is not loopback, the server prints this warning at start and tells you to use an SSH tunnel or a TLS reverse proxy. If the address is `0.0.0.0` or `::` and the machine has more than one LAN address, the server also lists the other addresses. The sign-in link works once, from any of them. Push notifications need HTTPS or `localhost`.

### Allowed hosts

The server accepts a request only if its `Host` header is in a fixed list. `Access::hosts` in `auth.rs` builds the list from these parts, all in lower case:

- **Always:** `127.0.0.1:<port>`, `localhost:<port>`, and `[::1]:<port>`.
- **Bind `0.0.0.0` or `::`:** every interface address with the port, the machine host name, and the host name with `.local`.
- **Bind to one non-loopback address:** that address with the port.
- **Extra hosts:** each name from `server.allowed_hosts` and `--allow-host`. A name with a port, such as `ostra.example.com:8443`, is used as written. A bare name adds both `name:<port>` and `name`, because a reverse proxy on its default port sends the bare name.
- **With `--dev`:** `localhost:5173` and `127.0.0.1:5173`.

To put Ostra behind a reverse proxy, add the proxy domain with `--allow-host ostra.example.com`. Without it, the server refuses the request. The Origin check and the failed-exchange limit are in [Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md).

When the server listens on loopback and `server.use_ip_host` is `false`, the sign-in URL uses a private name of the form `ostra-<16 hex digits>.localhost`. The registry stores the name, so it stays the same across restarts. Browsers resolve every `*.localhost` name to this machine. A cookie for that name does not reach pages on `127.0.0.1` or other names. Set `server.use_ip_host = true` only for a browser that does not resolve `*.localhost`. The cookie then reaches every other port on the machine, because cookies are not scoped to a port.

## What happens at start and at stop

The `serve` function in `main.rs` starts logging. Then `app::run` does these steps:

1. Read `config.toml`. If the file is missing, write the default. If the file cannot be read or parsed, use the defaults for the bind address and the port only. Step 4 reads the file again and stops the server with `reading <path>`.
2. Resolve the bind address and bind the port.
3. If `server.json` names no live process, stop the processes that sandboxes of an earlier server left running. Then remove the stale egress sockets and decoy files. A live server owns them, so the step skips them in that case.
4. Build the app in `app::build`: read the config, check the sandbox, open the registry and unlock the master key, write the assets, build the providers, and detect the harness CLIs. Then open each registered workspace and recover its sessions.
5. Write `server.json` with the port, the URL host, and the process ID.
6. Print `Ostra is running on <address>` and the sign-in URL. Open the browser unless `--no-open` is set.
7. Serve requests.

The server shuts down gracefully on `SIGINT` (Ctrl+C), through `tokio::signal::ctrl_c`. After the shutdown, it removes the hook bridge socket and `server.json`. A `SIGTERM` does not start the graceful shutdown. Thus the service files and the `Dockerfile` set the stop signal to `SIGINT`.

### What happens when

- **The sandbox cannot start:** if `[sandbox] mode = "auto"` finds no backend, the server starts, logs a warning, and prints a warning banner on stderr. If `mode = "off"`, the server only logs a warning. The rules for each mode are in [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md).
- **The config file is unreadable or invalid at start:** `build()` fails with `reading <path>` for any `config.toml` that it cannot read or parse, so the server does not start. Only `app::run` falls back to defaults, and only for the bind address and the port. A `[sandbox]` section that fails validation also stops the start.
- **The config file breaks after the server starts:** the server logs a warning and uses the last good copy. It reads the file again on each call, so edits apply without a restart. A `[sandbox]` section that fails validation gets the same treatment.
- **A workspace folder is missing:** the server logs `workspace <name> is missing at <path>` and skips it. Other workspaces open.
- **A workspace fails to open:** the server logs the error and continues with the other workspaces.
- **The browser does not open:** the server prints `Could not open a browser; copy the URL above.`
- **Two servers share one data folder:** the second server detects a live process in `server.json` and skips the cleanup of sandbox leftovers. Do not run two servers on one data folder, because they share the databases.
- **The server stops by a crash:** `server.json` stays. `ostra url` then prints a URL for a port that no server holds. `ostra stop` sees that the process ID is not alive and works.

## Logging and the server.log file

The server writes logs with the `tracing` crate. The `OSTRA_LOG` variable sets the filter. It uses the `EnvFilter` syntax of `tracing-subscriber`: a level such as `debug`, or a list of targets and levels. If `OSTRA_LOG` is not set or is not valid, the level is `info`.

```
OSTRA_LOG=debug ostra
OSTRA_LOG=warn,ostra_server=debug ostra
```

The server opens `server.log` in the data folder in append mode, and creates it if needed. It then writes each line to stdout and to the file. The file has no color codes. Neither output prints the target of the log line. If the server cannot open the file, it logs to stdout only. The file is a log for problems that you want to read later, for example when the browser runs on another machine.

The code does not rotate or truncate `server.log`, so the file grows without a limit. If the file gets large, stop the server, then delete or move the file. No agent can read the data folder, because the policy treats the server log as private.

Where to find the logs:

| How you run Ostra | Where the logs are |
| --- | --- |
| Foreground (`ostra`, `./run.sh`) | The terminal and `server.log`. |
| macOS service | `server.log`, and `service.err.log` for panics and start failures. |
| Linux service | `server.log`, and the journal for stderr: `journalctl --user -u ostra`. |
| Windows task | `server.log`, and `.\install.ps1 status` for the last task result. |
| Docker | `docker compose logs ostra`, and `/data/server.log` in the `ostra-data` volume. |

The data folder is `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` if set. Otherwise it is `ostra` under the local data folder of the operating system, for example `~/.local/share/ostra` on Linux and `~/Library/Application Support/ostra` on macOS. The config path is `OSTRA_CONFIG` if set, and otherwise `ostra/config.toml` under the config folder. The folder layout is in [Storage](storage.md) and the variables are in [Configuration](configuration.md).

## Cargo commands for development

Use these commands from the repository root. The workspace has 15 crates under `crates/`.

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Build every crate | `cargo build --workspace` |
| Test every crate | `cargo test --workspace` |
| Format the code | `cargo fmt --all` |
| Build the release binary | `cargo build --release -p ostra-server` |

The release command builds only the server crate, and it needs the `web/dist` folder, because the binary embeds it. Run `./build.sh` to build both. The `tests/windows-probes` program is outside the workspace on purpose, so these commands do not build it.

The web console has its own scripts in `web/package.json`: `npm run dev` for the Vite dev server on port 5173, `npm run dev:mock` for the mock API, `npm run build`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm test`, and `npm run check` for Biome. Start the server with `--dev` when the Vite dev server calls it. The test layers are in [Tests and evals](testing.md).

code_refs.note: The serve flags: --port, --no-open, --dev, --bind, --allow-host.
The revoke action of `ostra sessions`, with an id or --all.
The clap definitions of every subcommand.
Logging setup with OSTRA_LOG and server.log, then the call to app::run.

Reads config.toml and fails with `reading <path>` when it cannot.
The port search: exact port, 7878 to 7897, then an OS port.

The allowed Host list, LAN addresses, and the URL host.
