sections.title: Configuration reference
sections.summary: Where Ostra keeps its settings, what every setting means, its default and unit, when a change takes effect, which environment variables exist, and which validation rules refuse a save.
sections.body:
Ostra must hold three kinds of choice: machine-wide choices, choices for one workspace, and facts about one project. It must also stop a repository from raising its own spend limit or opening its own sandbox. Ostra solves both with three settings layers and one rule: some workspace settings never live in a folder file.

This page covers the layers, the files, the data directory, the `OSTRA_*` environment variables, every setting family, route resolution, the validation rules, and the time at which each change takes effect. Other pages own the behavior behind a setting. Links to those pages follow each table.

## The three layers and the registry

Ostra reads three TOML files and one database record. The code for all of them is in [`crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs).

| Layer | Type | File | Written by | Holds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Global | `GlobalConfig` | `config.toml` (path from `OSTRA_CONFIG`) | The user. Ostra writes the defaults when the file is missing. | Providers, tier tables, harness commands, global permission rules, server, sandbox, tool enforcement |
| Workspace | `WorkspaceSettings` | `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.toml`, plus a record in `registry.db` | The Settings screen of the console | Name, projects, routing, instructions, permission rules, notifications, MCP servers. The registry holds the fields in the next section. |
| Project | `ProjectProfile` | `<project>/.ostra/project.toml` | The initializer agent | Stack, commands, test types, module map, skills, conventions, review rules |

The global layer is the base. The workspace layer replaces or extends some global values. The project layer is separate: it describes one folder and does not override the other two.

### Settings that never live in a folder file (Rule A2)

A workspace folder can arrive from a Git clone, so its `workspace.toml` is not trusted for safety settings. Ostra keeps these fields in the registry (`registry.db`) and removes them from the file when it saves:

- `yolo` (`yolo.default`)
- `limits` (`max_parallel_executions` and `session_budget_usd`)
- `permissions.mode`
- `sandbox_mode`, `tool_enforcement`, `sandbox_network`, `sandbox_allowed_hosts`, `sandbox_decoys`, `sandbox_loopback`, and `sandbox_blocked_ports`

The reason is in the code comment on `overlay` in [`crates/ostra-workspace/src/trust.rs`](crates/ostra-workspace/src/trust.rs). Without the rule, a repository can lift its own budget, turn off its own guards, open its own sandbox, or plant decoys that pause every session.

When Ostra loads settings, `overlay` replaces these fields with the registry values. A value for them in `workspace.toml` has no effect.

#### The reset when a user adds a folder that has a `workspace.toml`

The reset happens in `draft` in [`crates/ostra-workspace/src/create.rs`](crates/ostra-workspace/src/create.rs) (lines 47-185). The Rule A2 block is at lines 90-104. `draft` loads the existing file with `load_toml_required`. Then it sets every field in the list above to its default and marks the draft as `adopted`.

After the reset, only the create request can set `permissions.mode` and `yolo.default`. Limits, `tool_enforcement`, and the sandbox fields stay at their defaults.

The flow after `draft` has two functions:

- `register` in `create.rs` (line 241) calls `draft_for`. It stops with `CreateError::Invalid` when the draft has an issue.
- `register` then calls `create_workspace`. This function is defined in `trust.rs` (line 476), not in `create.rs`. It writes `workspace.toml`, stores the registry fields, and records the approval state. When `adopted` is true, it records no approval, so no command of the folder file runs until the user approves it.

### Settings that wait for approval

A folder file can also name programs. Ostra does not run them until the user approves them. If the file waits for approval, `effective` returns settings with these changes:

- Every MCP server has `enabled = false`.
- Every `code_provider` and every `language_servers` list is removed.
- `permissions.allow` is empty.
- Projects outside the workspace folder are dropped.

`effective` first calls `overlay`, so the registry fields also apply. A `commands.format` entry in `project.toml` waits for approval in the same way. The approval flow is in [Workspaces, projects, and approvals](workspaces-and-trust.md).

## Find the files and the data directory

Two functions in [`crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs) decide where state lives: `global_config_path` and `data_dir`. Every other path derives from them, from a workspace root, or from a project root.

- `global_config_path`: the value of `OSTRA_CONFIG` when it is set. Otherwise `<config folder>/ostra/config.toml`. The config folder comes from the `dirs` crate. On Linux it is `~/.config`.
- `data_dir`: the value of `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` when it is set, used as given. Otherwise `<data folder>/ostra`. On Linux it is `~/.local/share/ostra`. On macOS it is `~/Library/Application Support/ostra`.

If the platform has no such folder, both functions fall back to the current directory (`.`).

`ostra config` prints the config path and writes the default file when none exists. The server does the same at start (`ensure_global_config`). The commands are in [Install, run, and the command line](install-and-run.md).

### Data directory layout

On Unix, `ensure_data_dir` creates the data directory with mode `0700` and tightens an existing one. The reason is that the registry holds saved credentials, and SQLite creates its `-wal` and `-shm` side files world-readable. On Windows a new folder inherits the ACL of its parent.

| Path under the data dir | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `registry.db` (with `-wal`, `-shm`) | The registry: workspaces, saved credentials, approvals, the `access` record of each workspace, sign-ins |
| `master.key` | The master key, only when Ostra uses the file backend and not the OS keychain |
| `server.log` | The log that `ostra serve` appends to, next to standard output |
| `server.json` | The port, the sign-in host, and the process ID of the running server |
| `models-dev.json` | The cached model price catalog |
| `assets/` | The embedded agent assets, written at each start |
| `decoys/`, `egress/` | Decoy credential files and egress proxy sockets for the sandbox |
| `hidden-artifacts/` | Artifacts that the user hid from agents, per workspace ID |
| `tmp/`, `no-hooks/` | Private temporary files for Git commands |

Agents never read the data directory. `secret_paths` lists it, the file named by `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE`, and every entry of `HOME_CREDENTIALS` as paths that the policy refuses and the sandbox hides. See [Policy engine](policy.md) and [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md).

### Workspace and project folders

| Path | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.toml` | The workspace settings file |
| `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.db` (with `-wal`, `-shm`) | The workspace database with the event log |
| `<workspace>/.ostra/sessions/<session id>/` | One session: cross-project artifacts, one folder per project key, `uploads/`, and the engine-owned `.state/` |
| `<workspace>/.ostra/uploads/` | Uploads that wait for a session to claim them |
| `<workspace>/.ostra/artifacts/` | The visible artifacts of the workspace |
| `<project>/.ostra/project.toml` | The project profile |
| `<project>/.ostra/INVENTORY.md` | The project inventory |
| `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3` | The lesson memory store |
| `<project>/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | Project skills. Ostra writes new skills here. |
| `<project>/.ostra/skills/` | Older skill folder. Ostra still reads it and never writes it. |

At the project root, Ostra also reads the instruction files `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `AGENT.md` in any letter case, in that order. Report files that the engine names start with the prefix `ostra-`. The database and folder details are in [Storage](storage.md) and [Project init, skills, and lesson memory](project-init-and-memory.md).

## Environment variables

Ostra reads the variables in the first table to find files and to change behavior. A running process cannot see a changed environment, so restart the server after you change one.

| Variable | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OSTRA_CONFIG` | Platform config folder, `ostra/config.toml` | Path of `config.toml`. The sandbox hides this file from agents. |
| `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` | Platform data folder, `ostra/` | The data directory. |
| `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` | Not set | Path of a file that holds the master key. When set, Ostra uses it in place of the keychain and the `master.key` file. |
| `OSTRA_SANDBOX_CACHE` | `~/.cache/ostra/sandbox` | Base folder of the sandbox tool caches: one set for each session and one for each project. |
| `OSTRA_MODELS_DEV_URL` | The models.dev catalog URL | Catalog URL for model prices. An empty value turns fetching off. |
| `OSTRA_LOG` | `info` | Log filter of the server. The filter syntax is the one of `tracing_subscriber::EnvFilter`. |
| `OSTRA_ENV_FILE` | Not set | Used by `run.sh` and `install.sh`. A credentials file: Ostra applies only its `export NAME=value` lines. |
| `OSTRA_PREFIX` | `~/.local` | Used by `install.sh` and `install.ps1`. The binary goes to `$OSTRA_PREFIX/bin`. |

The installers record `OSTRA_CONFIG` and `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` in the service when you set them. The Docker image sets `OSTRA_DATA_DIR=/data` and `OSTRA_CONFIG=/config/config.toml`. On Windows, `install.ps1` refuses `OSTRA_ENV_FILE`, because the Windows task runs `ostra.exe` directly and applies no credentials file.

### Variables that Ostra sets for child processes

Do not set these variables yourself. Ostra sets them for a child process and removes inherited copies.

| Variable | Set for | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OSTRA_TOKEN`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_URL`, `OSTRA_HARNESS` | Harness and MCP child processes | The execution identity (`BRIDGE_ENV`). Ostra drops inherited copies and sets new values. |
| `OSTRA_CODE_PROTOCOL` | Custom `code_provider` programs | The protocol version of the code navigation request. |
| `OSTRA_GIT_HOST`, `OSTRA_GIT_USERNAME`, `OSTRA_GIT_PASSWORD` | Git commands that use a saved token | Input of a temporary credential helper that answers only for the credential host. |
| `OSTRA_CMD`, `OSTRA_CWD`, `OSTRA_PWD_FILE` | The native Bash tool script | The command, its folder, and a file that records the final folder. |

The test suites read the `OSTRA_EVAL_*` variables and `OSTRA_LIVE_*` variables. [Tests and evals](testing.md) owns them.

### Credential variables that Ostra hides

Ostra does not pass a credential variable to an agent process or an MCP server. `credential_env_names` builds the list from these sources:

- The default provider variables: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `OPENAI_API_KEY`, and `OPENAI_BASE_URL`.
- The `BRIDGE_ENV` variables.
- Each `api_key_env`, `auth_token_env`, and `base_url_env` in `[providers.*]`.
- Each `oauth.client_secret_env` of an MCP server.

At start, the server also adds the installer folders of the harness CLIs to `PATH` (`extend_path`). A harness that you install after the server starts then resolves by name without a restart.

## Load, save, and reload rules

The functions `load_toml`, `load_toml_required`, and `save_toml` in `config.rs` read and write every settings file.

- `load_toml` returns the type default when the file does not exist. A read error or a parse error is an error that names the path.
- `load_toml_required` fails when the file does not exist.
- `save_toml` writes to a temporary file with the extension `.toml.tmp`, then renames it over the target. A reader never sees a half-written file.

### Which structs accept a missing key

Most settings structs have `#[serde(default)]`, so a file that lacks a key gets the default for that key. Four structs have no struct-level default: `McpServerConfig`, `ProjectEntry`, `LanguageServerConfig`, and `CodeProviderConfig`. Each has required fields, and a file that lacks one causes a parse error:

| Struct | Required fields |
| --- | --- |
| `McpServerConfig` | `name` |
| `ProjectEntry` | `key`, `path` |
| `LanguageServerConfig` | `command`, `languages` |
| `CodeProviderConfig` | `command` |

The other fields of these four structs have a field-level default. For example, `enabled` is `true` and `timeout_secs` is `120` for an MCP server and `10` for a language server or a code provider.

### What happens when a file is missing or wrong

- **`config.toml` has a syntax error:** `Shared::global()` logs a warning and returns the last good copy. The same happens when `[sandbox]` holds a value that `ostra_sandbox::validate::global` refuses.
- **`workspace.toml` has a syntax error:** the workspace falls back to the seeded defaults and Ostra logs the error.
- **`workspace.toml` has a `[[projects]]` entry without `key` or `path`:** the parse fails, and the file counts as a file with a syntax error.
- **`project.toml` does not exist:** `load_toml` returns an empty profile.
- **A user saves invalid workspace settings:** `save_settings` refuses and returns every issue. It writes nothing.

## Global config reference

`GlobalConfig` has seven top-level keys. A new `config.toml` holds the defaults below. The server re-reads the file on every call, so most edits apply without a restart. The last section of this page lists the exceptions.

### Tool enforcement

`tool_enforcement` takes `disabled` or `enabled`. The default is `disabled` (Rule G1).

- `enabled` adds the write-scope guard, the report-path guard, self-protection, and the shell and interpreter checks behind them.
- `disabled` lets an agent reach files by any route, for example one script that edits several files. The secret-read, git-metadata, state-ownership, artifact-ownership, and no-tests guards, the workflow gates, the permission rules, and the sandbox still apply.

A workspace can set its own value. `enforces_tool_calls` returns the workspace value when it exists and the global value otherwise. The guards are in [Policy engine](policy.md).

### Providers

`[providers.<name>]` tells Ostra which environment variables hold the credentials of a native provider. The config holds variable names, never keys.

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `api_key_env` | Variable that holds the API key |
| `auth_token_env` | Variable that holds a bearer token. Ostra sends it as `Authorization: Bearer` when no API key is set. |
| `keychain_service` | OS keychain service to read the key from when the variables are unset |
| `base_url` | Fixed API base URL. It wins over every other source. |
| `base_url_env` | Variable that holds the base URL |

The defaults are two providers:

| Provider | `api_key_env` | `auth_token_env` | `base_url_env` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `anthropic` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` | `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` |
| `openai` | `OPENAI_API_KEY` | not set | `OPENAI_BASE_URL` |

A native model name starts with `anthropic:`, `openai:`, or `mock:`. The console saves credentials for `anthropic` and `openai` only.

#### Key and URL lookup order

`lookup_key` in [`crates/ostra-providers/src/lib.rs`](crates/ostra-providers/src/lib.rs) tries these sources in order and stops at the first hit:

1. The variable in `api_key_env`.
2. The variable in `auth_token_env`.
3. The API key saved from the browser.
4. The token saved from the browser.
5. The OS keychain entry (`keychain_service`, user name = provider name).

`resolve_base_url` uses this order: `base_url` in the config, the `base_url_env` variable, the URL saved from the browser, and then the provider default. The reason for the order is that an environment variable is a deliberate act of the operator and wins over a value that someone typed in a browser. The console shows only a cleaned URL: no user, password, query, or fragment.

Ostra builds the providers at start. It rebuilds them in place each time a user saves a provider credential in the console. The registry holds saved credentials encrypted. See [Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md) and [Model providers, tiers, and cost](providers-and-cost.md).

### Tier tables

`[tiers.<table>]` maps the four tiers (`fast`, `balanced`, `advanced`, `frontier`) to a model name. There is one table for each executor: `native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, and `agy`. An executor reads only its own table. The defaults are:

| Table | `fast` | `balanced` | `advanced` | `frontier` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `native` | `anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` | `anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5` | `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5` | `anthropic:claude-fable-5-1` |
| `claude` | `haiku` | `sonnet` | `opus` | `fable` |
| `codex` | `gpt-5.6-luna` | `gpt-5.6-terra` | `gpt-5.6-sol` | `gpt-5.6-sol` |
| `grok` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` |
| `agy` | `flash` | `flash` | `flash` | `flash` |

A native entry is `provider:model`. A harness entry is the model name that the CLI itself accepts. A tier that has no entry in the table of its executor is a validation error at save time. See [Route resolution](#route-resolution).

### Harness commands

`[harness.<name>]` has one entry for each of `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, and `agy`.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `command` | The harness name, for example `codex` | The program to start. An empty value falls back to the name. |
| `args` | Empty list | Arguments that Ostra adds to every launch |

Ostra checks installation with `which` on the command. It also runs `<command> --version` with a timeout of 8 seconds. It caches the result for 60 seconds. The harness executor is in [Executors](executors.md).

### Permission rules

`[permissions]` has three lists: `allow`, `ask`, and `deny`. The default is `deny = ["Bash(rm -rf /*)"]`. Ostra concatenates the lists of the global scope, the workspace, and the session, in that order (`PermissionRules::merged`). The rule syntax and the order of evaluation are in [Policy engine](policy.md).

### Server

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `port` | Not set | A fixed port. When it is not set, Ostra tries 7878 and the next 19 ports, then asks the OS for a free port. |
| `bind` | `127.0.0.1` | The address to listen on. `0.0.0.0` or `::` listens on every interface. The words `localhost`, `all`, and `*` also work. |
| `allowed_hosts` | Empty list | More host names that the browser can use, for example the domain of a reverse proxy |
| `use_ip_host` | `false` | Sign in at `127.0.0.1` in place of a private `ostra-….localhost` name |

The command-line flags `--port`, `--bind`, and `--allow-host` override or extend these keys. `--allow-host` adds to `allowed_hosts`. With a fixed `port`, a busy port is an error and Ostra does not try another one. When `bind` listens on every interface, Ostra allows every local interface address and the host name of the machine automatically.

Set `bind` to `0.0.0.0` only on a trusted network, because Ostra serves plain HTTP. Set `use_ip_host` to `true` only for a browser that does not resolve `*.localhost`. The session cookie then reaches every port on the machine, because cookies are not scoped to a port. The checks are in [Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md).

### Sandbox

`[sandbox]` sets the profile for agent commands: the native Bash tool, harness CLIs, and the programs that Ostra starts for a project.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `mode` | `required` on Linux and macOS. `auto` on Windows. | `auto` sandboxes when the machine can and runs unsandboxed with a warning otherwise. `required` refuses to start an execution that cannot be sandboxed. `off` runs without a sandbox. |
| `network` | `allowlist` | What a sandboxed program can reach. See the next table. |
| `allowed_hosts` | Empty list | More hosts that the egress proxy lets through under `allowlist`: `host`, `*.domain`, or either with `:port` |
| `upstream_proxy` | Not set | An HTTP proxy that the egress proxy connects through, written `http://host:port` |
| `extra_writable` | Empty list | More paths that agent commands can write. Absolute or `~/...`. |
| `extra_hidden` | Empty list | More paths that agent commands cannot see. Absolute or `~/...`. |

The default of `mode` is `auto` on Windows because Windows has no sandbox backend yet. On Windows, `required` refuses every execution, because no execution can be sandboxed.

The `network` values are:

| Value | What the sandbox reaches |
| --- | --- |
| `none` | No network. A harness CLI still reaches its own model API. |
| `allowlist` | Package registries, source hosts, the model API of a harness, and `allowed_hosts` |
| `public` | Any public address. Loopback, private, and link-local addresses stay refused. |
| `host` | The host network, unfiltered |

Every value except `host` gives each sandbox its own network namespace. Traffic leaves only through the egress proxy of Ostra. The server logs a warning at start when `mode` is `off`. The behavior of the sandbox is in [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md).

The struct also has the fields `loopback` and `blocked_ports`. Ostra never reads them from `config.toml` (`#[serde(skip)]`). They come from the workspace.

## Workspace settings reference

`WorkspaceSettings` is the content of one workspace. Ostra seeds a new workspace with `WorkspaceSettings::seeded`. The settings search lists each key in `SETTING_KEYS`, and a test checks that each key names a real field.

| Key | Default | Stored in | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `workspace` until set | File | The workspace name. It must not be empty. |
| `projects` | Empty list | File | The projects, see [Projects](#projects) |
| `routing` | Seeded routes | File | Executor, model, and effort for each agent |
| `instructions` | Empty | File | Text added to agent prompts |
| `permissions.allow`, `ask`, `deny` | Empty lists | File | Workspace permission rules |
| `permissions.mode` | `default` | Registry | The permission mode |
| `notifications.push` | `true` | File | Web Push for gates and finished sessions |
| `mcp_servers` | Empty list | File | External MCP servers |
| `yolo.default` | `false` | Registry | Start new sessions in YOLO mode |
| `limits.max_parallel_executions` | `3` | Registry | Executions that run at once |
| `limits.session_budget_usd` | `25.0` | Registry | Dollars that one session can spend before it pauses |
| `sandbox_mode`, `sandbox_network` | Not set (follow global) | Registry | Replace the global `mode` and `network` |
| `sandbox_allowed_hosts` | Empty list | Registry | Added to the global `allowed_hosts` |
| `sandbox_decoys` | Empty list | Registry | More decoy credential files |
| `sandbox_loopback` | `open` | Registry | Loopback access on macOS |
| `sandbox_blocked_ports` | Empty list | Registry | Loopback ports that are always blocked on macOS |
| `tool_enforcement` | Not set (follow global) | Registry | Replaces the global value |

### Routing

`[routing]` has three tables: `executor`, `model`, and `effort`. Each table has `byAgent` (a map from route key to value) and `byPhaseComplexity` (a map from route key to a map from `low`, `medium`, or `high` to a value). A route key is an agent name or `judge`. The 14 agent names are `explore`, `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `plan`, `implementer`, `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `write-test`, `documentation`, `system-architecture`, `prompt-generation`, `initializer`, `quick-answer`, and `advisor`.

- **`executor`:** `native` or `harness:<claude|codex|grok|agy>`. A missing entry means `native`.
- **`model`:** a tier name, `default`, a concrete model, or a table with one entry for each executor, for example `{ native = "anthropic:x", codex = "gpt-y" }`. `default` means the default tier of the agent.
- **`effort`:** `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, or `max`. A missing entry means the effort in the agent definition. The older flat form (a table from agent to effort) reads as `byAgent`.

Only `implementer` and `write-test` run for each plan phase, so only they use `byPhaseComplexity`. `byPhaseComplexity` wins over `byAgent`. Work with no phase file counts as `low`.

The seeded model routes are:

| Route key | Tier |
| --- | --- |
| `explore`, `generate-spec`, `plan`, `fact-check`, `documentation`, `system-architecture`, `prompt-generation`, `judge`, `advisor` | `advanced` |
| `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `initializer`, `quick-answer` | `balanced` |
| `implementer`, `write-test` (`byPhaseComplexity`) | `low` and `medium`: `fast`. `high`: `balanced`. |

The seeded `executor` and `effort` tables are empty. This example routes the implementer to Codex on low and medium phases:

```toml
[routing.executor.byPhaseComplexity.implementer]
low = "harness:codex"
medium = "harness:codex"
high = "native"

[routing.model.byAgent]
quick-answer = { native = "anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5" }
```

Two routes have fixed rules. Judge calls always run on the native executor, because a judge call is an engine call and not an agent execution. Quick answers run on the native executor only. Validation refuses any other value for these two. See [Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md) and [Model providers, tiers, and cost](providers-and-cost.md).

### Instructions

`instructions.all` is text that every agent receives. `instructions.agents.<agent>` is text for one agent. `instructions_for` returns the `all` text first and then the agent text. It skips an entry that is empty after trimming. A tag in the text that names an artifact must name one that every agent can read (Rule W3).

### Permissions, YOLO, and notifications

`permissions.mode` is one of `default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, or `bypass`.

- `default`: ask for edits and for commands that no rule lists.
- `acceptEdits`: allow edits inside the project.
- `plan`: read-only.
- `bypass`: no asks.

`yolo.default` makes new sessions start in YOLO mode. The user can still choose for each session. `notifications.push` turns Web Push on or off for gates and finished sessions. See [MCP servers and Web Push](mcp-and-notifications.md).

### Limits

`limits` exists because a fan-out stage, such as init scouts, skill generation, or explores, can otherwise start dozens of top-tier executions at once.

- `max_parallel_executions` (count, default `3`, minimum `1`): the number of agent executions that run at once in the workspace. Other spawns wait. The slot rules are in [The engine runner, recovery, and control](engine-runner.md).
- `session_budget_usd` (US dollars, default `25.0`): the amount that one session can spend before it pauses for a decision. The value `0` means no limit. The planner reads it as `None` when it is `0` or less.

### Workspace sandbox overrides

`SandboxConfig::for_workspace` merges the workspace entries into the global `[sandbox]`:

- `sandbox_mode` and `sandbox_network` replace the global value when they are set.
- `sandbox_allowed_hosts` are added to the global list. A duplicate is skipped. A workspace never removes a global or built-in host.
- `sandbox_loopback` and `sandbox_blocked_ports` come from the workspace only.
- `sandbox_decoys` are added to the built-in decoys. A workspace cannot remove a built-in decoy.

`sandbox_loopback` applies to macOS, where all sandboxes share the host loopback. On Linux each sandbox has its own loopback, so the setting changes nothing. `open` allows every port except the blocked ports and the server of Ostra, under `allowlist` and `public`. `listed` allows only the loopback ports in `allowed_hosts`.

### MCP servers

`[[mcp_servers]]` names an external MCP server. Set `command` for a local server that Ostra starts over stdio in the workspace root. Set `url` for a remote server over streamable HTTP. Set one of them, not both.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | Required | Lowercase letters, digits, and dashes. It starts with a letter and has at most 24 characters. It cannot be `ostra`. |
| `enabled` | `true` | Turns the server off without removing it |
| `command` | Empty | Program and arguments of a local server |
| `env` | Empty | Environment of a local server |
| `url` | Not set | An `http://` or `https://` address |
| `headers` | Empty | Headers for a remote server |
| `oauth` | Not set | `client_id`, `client_secret_env`, and `scopes` for a remote server. Without it, Ostra still signs in when the server asks. |
| `disabled_tools` | Empty | Tools that Ostra does not offer to agents |
| `agents` | Empty | Agents that get the tools. An empty list means every agent. |
| `timeout_secs` | `120` | Seconds that one tool call can take. The range is 1 to 600. |

A value in `env` or `headers` can name an environment variable as `${VAR}`, so secrets stay out of the file. Ostra refuses a variable that holds a credential it keeps from MCP servers. When a user types a literal secret in the console, Ostra seals it in the registry and writes `${ostra_secret}` in the file. See [MCP servers and Web Push](mcp-and-notifications.md).

### Projects

`[[projects]]` lists the project folders of the workspace.

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `key` | Required. The project key: `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*`. It is unique in the workspace. |
| `path` | Required. The absolute path of the folder |
| `stack` | Optional free text, at most 64 characters, used to seed skills for an empty folder |
| `code_provider` | Optional. A program that answers code navigation requests: `command` (a list, required) and `timeout_secs` (default `10`). |
| `language_servers` | Optional. A list of language servers: `command` and `languages` (both required), `timeout_secs` (default `10`), and `initialization_options`. |

A language server answers after `code_provider` and before the built-in index. Each language belongs to one server only, because each file asks one server. The provider chain is in [Code navigation](code-navigation.md).

## Route resolution

A route that does not resolve is a settings error at save time, not a failure at spawn time. `resolve_route` runs at save time for every route key and at spawn time for the real execution. The function takes a `RouteQuery`: the key, the default tier of the agent, the phase complexity, and two optional overrides. The tier override forces a tier, for example `advanced` for the initializer step that generates skills. The executor override forces an executor, for example when Ostra re-routes a failed harness run to native.

### How a route resolves

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["resolve_route(key, complexity)"] --> B["executor: override, else byPhaseComplexity, else byAgent, else native"]
  B --> C["tier table: native or the harness name"]
  C --> D{"tier override set?"}
  D -- yes --> T["from_tier: tier table lookup"]
  D -- no --> E["choice: byPhaseComplexity, else byAgent"]
  E --> F{"choice found?"}
  F -- no --> X["RouteError: no model route"]
  F -- yes --> G{"kind of choice"}
  G -- "default" --> T2["from_tier with the default tier"]
  G -- "tier name" --> T
  G -- "concrete model" --> H["check_model"]
  G -- "per-executor table" --> I{"entry for the table name?"}
  I -- no --> X2["RouteError: names the missing entry"]
  I -- yes --> J{"entry parses as a tier name?"}
  J -- yes --> T
  J -- no --> H
  T --> H
  T2 --> H
  H --> R["ResolvedRoute: executor, model, tier"]
```

In the per-executor path, `resolve_route` first parses the entry as a tier name. If it parses, the route goes to `from_tier`, which reads the tier table. If it does not parse, the entry is a concrete model and the route goes to `check_model`. A plain string choice uses the same parse: `default` first, then a tier name, then a concrete model.

`check_model` refuses an empty model. For the native executor it also refuses a model that does not have the form `anthropic:<model>`, `openai:<model>`, or `mock:<model>`.

### What happens when a route does not resolve

- **The tier table has no entry for the tier:** the route fails with a message that names the key, the tier, and the `[tiers.<table>]` table.
- **A route key has no model route:** the route fails and the message tells the user to add the key under `[routing.model.byAgent]`. A new agent that ships after a workspace was saved causes this case.
- **A per-executor table has no entry for the executor:** the route fails. The message names the missing entry, which is the executor table name, for example `codex`. The per-executor model table itself exists.
- **The route key has `byPhaseComplexity` for some complexities only:** `keys_without_route` reports the key, because every complexity must resolve.

The console offers an automatic fix for the first missing-route case. `settings_fixes` proposes `default` for each key without a route, and `apply_fixes` writes the fixes without validating the rest of the settings. The reason is that an unrelated problem must not block a fix.

## Project profile

`ProjectProfile` is the machine-readable summary of one project. The initializer writes `project.toml` next to `INVENTORY.md`, and the output contract is in [`assets/refs/inventory-and-profile.md`](assets/refs/inventory-and-profile.md). The profile is not edited in the Settings screen.

| Key | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | Number | The number `1` |
| `generated_at` | Text | Date of generation |
| `stack` | Text | The stack name, for example `rust` or `python-django` |
| `build_tool`, `test_framework` | Text | Names of the tools |
| `commands` | Table | `build`, `test`, `test_one`, `format`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `run` |
| `test_types` | Map | A name to `command`, `command_one`, `matches` (globs), `note`, `reports` |
| `module_map` | List | Rows of `glob` and `area` |
| `skills` | List | `name`, `kind`, `path`, `component_type`, `source` |
| `conventions` | Table | `immutability_keyword`, `naming`, `notes` |
| `review_rules` | List | `id`, `rule`, `severity`, `auto_fixable` |

The value sets are:

- `skills.kind`: `convention`, `creation`, `test`, or `other`.
- `skills.source`: `generated`, `reused`, `adopted`, or `user`.
- `review_rules.severity`: `H`, `M`, or `L`.

`Commands::entries` returns only the commands that are not empty and are not the placeholder `—`. The placeholders `{MODULE}`, `{TEST}`, and `{PATH}` appear in the command strings of `test_one`. The caller fills them in.

### Review rules that the engine can fix

`auto_fixable_ids` returns the IDs of the rules with `auto_fixable = true`. It never returns an ID that starts with `SEC-BLOCK` or `PHASE-REQ`, even when the rule says `true`. The reason is that security blocks and phase requirements need a human decision. The use of these IDs is in [Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md).

### Older and broken files

Projects that were initialized before stacks became free text have a `[stack]` table with `language`, `frameworks`, and `build_tool`. The reader accepts both forms. It joins the table into one name, for example `java/spring,jpa`, and keeps `build_tool` when the top-level key is missing.

`check_profile` parses a generated file and returns text that tells the initializer how to fix it. It detects these mistakes that models make when they copy JSON into TOML:

- A `null` value. TOML has no null, so the key must be omitted.
- `[[conventions]]`. `conventions` is one table: `[conventions]`.
- `[stack]` or `[[stack]]`. `stack` is a string.
- A `schema_version` in quotes. It is the number `1`.

The fixes come before the parser message, because some harnesses clip a long tool error. The initializer flow is in [Project init, skills, and lesson memory](project-init-and-memory.md).

## Validation rules

`validate_settings` in [`crates/ostra-workspace/src/settings.rs`](crates/ostra-workspace/src/settings.rs) collects every issue before a save. Each issue is a `ValidationIssue` with a dotted `path`, for example `routing.model.byAgent.plan`, and a `message`. Ostra sorts issues by path and message and removes duplicates. A save with one or more issues writes nothing.

| Area | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Workspace | `name` is not empty |
| Project key | Matches `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*` and is unique |
| Project path | Absolute (a path with a root but no drive counts) and an existing folder |
| Project stack | If set: trimmed, not empty, at most 64 characters, no control character |
| `code_provider` | The first item of `command` is not empty. `timeout_secs` is from 1 to 120. |
| `language_servers` | Each has a command. `languages` is not empty and uses ids from the code navigation language list. No language belongs to two servers. `timeout_secs` is from 1 to 120. |
| Routing keys | Each `byAgent` key in `executor` and `model` is an agent or `judge`. Each `byAgent` key in `effort` is an agent. The retired name `module-documentation` is ignored. |
| Effort by phase | Only agents that run for each plan phase can use `byPhaseComplexity` |
| Judge and quick answer | No executor route for `judge`. The `quick-answer` executor is `native`. |
| Route resolution | Every route key resolves on every complexity that it uses |
| Installed harness | A route to a harness requires that the CLI is installed on this machine |
| Provider key | A native route requires a usable key for its provider, except `mock` |
| Limits | `max_parallel_executions` is at least 1. `session_budget_usd` is finite and at least 0. |
| Permission rules | Each rule in `allow`, `ask`, and `deny` passes `validate_rule` |
| Instructions | Artifact tags name artifacts that agents can read |
| MCP servers | See the next list |
| Workspace sandbox | See the next list |

The rules for `mcp_servers` (`ostra_core::mcp::validate`) are:

- The name follows the name rule, is not `ostra`, and is unique.
- Exactly one of `command` and `url` is set. The first item of `command` is not empty.
- `url` starts with `http://` or `https://`.
- `headers` and `oauth` are for remote servers only.
- Each name in `agents` is an agent.
- `timeout_secs` is from 1 to 600.

The rules for the workspace sandbox entries (`ostra_sandbox::validate`) are:

- Each `sandbox_allowed_hosts` entry is a host name, `*.domain`, or an IP address, with an optional `:port`. A URL is refused, because the egress proxy matches hosts and not URLs. A loopback host needs a port, because programs connect to loopback directly and the sandbox forwards only the ports in the list.
- Each `sandbox_decoys` entry is a file path that starts with `~/`, with no `.` or `..` part. A harness sign-in file is refused, because a decoy on that file signs the CLI out in the sandbox. A list has at most 32 entries.
- Each `sandbox_blocked_ports` entry is from 1 to 65535. A list has at most 64 entries, because each port is a rule in every sandbox policy.

The rules for the global `[sandbox]` table are:

- `extra_writable` and `extra_hidden` entries are absolute or start with `~/`, because the folder where an execution starts changes the meaning of a relative path.
- `allowed_hosts` follows the host rule above.
- `upstream_proxy` has the form `http://host:port`, without a path or credentials, because the egress proxy connects with plain HTTP CONNECT.

The permission rule syntax is in [Policy engine](policy.md).

## When a change takes effect

Ostra reads most settings from disk each time it needs them. Only a few values are fixed at start.

| Setting | When Ostra reads it | Effect of a change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `config.toml`: `tool_enforcement`, `tiers`, `harness`, `permissions`, `sandbox` | On every call of `Shared::global()` | Applies to the next call, without a restart. A bad file keeps the last good copy. |
| `config.toml`: `server` | At start | Restart the server. |
| `config.toml`: `providers` | At start, and when a user saves a provider credential in the console | Restart the server, or save a credential. |
| Harness install status | Cached for 60 seconds | The next check after the cache is stale shows the change. |
| `workspace.toml` and registry fields | On every `settings()` call | Applies to the next spawn or plan step. Ostra resolves the route when it spawns an execution. |
| `limits.max_parallel_executions` | Each time a waiting spawn checks for a free slot | Raising it starts waiting spawns. Lowering it cancels nothing. |
| `limits.session_budget_usd` | Each time the engine builds the planning context of a session | Applies to the next planning step. |
| `project.toml` | When the engine builds the planning context and when a stage needs it | Applies to the next step. |
| Environment variables | At start, or when a path function runs | Restart the server. A running process cannot see a changed environment. |

For the slot rules, read [The engine runner, recovery, and control](engine-runner.md). For the price cache, which refreshes every 24 hours and retries after 1 hour on failure, read [Model providers, tiers, and cost](providers-and-cost.md).

## Limits and defaults at a glance

| Value | Number | Where it is set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default server port | 7878, then the next 19 ports | `DEFAULT_PORT`, `bind` in `app.rs` |
| Parallel executions | 3 (minimum 1) | `Limits::default` |
| Session budget | 25.0 US dollars (0 = none) | `Limits::default` |
| MCP tool call timeout | 120 seconds (1 to 600) | `default_mcp_timeout`, `MAX_TIMEOUT_SECS` |
| MCP server name | 24 characters | `MAX_SERVER_NAME` |
| MCP tool bare name | 52 characters | `MAX_BARE_NAME` |
| Code provider and language server timeout | 10 seconds (1 to 120) | `default_provider_timeout`, `MAX_PROVIDER_TIMEOUT` |
| Project stack | 64 characters | `MAX_STACK_LEN` |
| Workspace decoys | 32 entries | `MAX_WORKSPACE_DECOYS` |
| Blocked loopback ports | 64 entries | `MAX_BLOCKED_PORTS` |
| Harness version check | 8 seconds timeout, 60 seconds cache | `env.rs` |

## Project keys and slugs

[`crates/ostra-core/src/slug.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/slug.rs) holds the naming helpers that settings use. `is_project_key` accepts a lowercase letter or a digit first, then lowercase letters, digits, and dashes. `suggest_project_key` turns a folder name into a key: it lowercases, replaces each run of other characters with one dash, trims trailing dashes, and returns `project` when nothing is left. For example, `Shop Backend_v2` becomes `shop-backend-v2`. `topic_slug` does the same for artifact names and cuts the result to a maximum length.

`is_stack_name` accepts free text because the set of real stacks has no end. `Kotlin Ktor` and `c++/qt` are valid. A value with a leading or trailing space, a control character, or more than 64 characters is not valid, and `stack_issue` returns the message that says why.
