sections.title: Typed pipeline documents
sections.summary: How the research document, the spec, and the plan are written as typed JSON through the Document tool, validated by check, merged by id, and rendered to Markdown. Covers the phase fields complexity, test policy, and depends_on.
sections.body:
## The problem that typed documents solve

Three pipeline stages produce a long document that the next stage reads: `explore` writes a research document, `generate-spec` writes a spec, and `plan` writes a plan with phases. A model that writes free Markdown can break a reference, repeat an ID, or skip a section that a later agent needs. The browser also cannot show each part of free Markdown as a native element.

Ostra solves this with typed documents. The agent sends JSON through the `Document` tool. Ostra validates the JSON against a schema, runs code checks, stores the JSON, and renders the Markdown that the next agent reads. The JSON is the source of truth. The Markdown is a product of it.

This page covers:

- The three document kinds and the agent that owns each one.
- The files on disk and their names.
- The `Document` tool: whole write, `update`, and `remove`.
- The merge rule for revisions.
- The checks that block or warn.
- The submit gate that refuses a submit call with an unclean document.
- The Markdown render and the derived tables.
- The phase fields `complexity`, `test_policy`, and `depends_on`.

The step order of the pipeline is in [Sessions and the pipeline](sessions-and-pipeline.md). The submit tools are in [Agents, prompts, and the spawn contract](agents-and-prompts.md).

## The three document kinds

`DocKind` in `crates/ostra-core/src/doc/store.rs` names the three kinds. A fourth variant, `Document::Phase`, is not a kind of its own. It is one phase of a plan, stored as its own file pair.

| Kind | Owner agent | File prefix | Submit field that names the file | Root type |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Research` | `explore` | `ostra-research-` | `research_path` | `ResearchDoc` |
| `Spec` | `generate-spec` | `ostra-spec-` | `spec_path` | `SpecDoc` |
| `Plan` | `plan` | `ostra-plan-` | `master_plan_path` | `PlanDoc` |

`DocKind::for_agent` returns `None` for every other agent. Only the three owner agents have the `Document` tool.

## Files on disk

Each document is a pair of files in the session directory. The JSON file is the source. The Markdown file beside it has the same name with the extension `.md`.

- The agent chooses a path of the form `ostra-research-{run-stamp}-{topic-slug}.md`. The spec and the plan use their own prefix.
- `json_path(md)` returns the sibling `.json` path.
- A plan also writes one pair per phase. `phase_path(master, id)` builds the name `{master-stem}-phase-{id}.md`.
- `doc_kind_for(path)` finds the kind from a file name. It accepts `.md` and `.json` names that start with a kind prefix. A phase file reports `Plan`.

The `write` function in `store.rs` does these steps:

1. Parse the JSON as the kind's document with `DocKind::parse`.
2. Run `check` and keep the issues.
3. Write the pretty JSON, then the rendered Markdown.
4. For a plan, write one JSON and Markdown pair for each phase.
5. For a plan, remove each file named `{master-stem}-phase-*` that no phase uses any more.

Step 5 matters when a revision removes a phase. The files of that phase leave the session directory in the same write. The test `plan_writes_master_and_phase_files` checks this.

## The Document tool

The `Document` tool is the only way to write these files. `crates/ostra-tools/src/doc.rs` implements it. `document_tool_definition` in `crates/ostra-tools/src/defs.rs` builds its definition for one agent, and the input schema embeds the JSON schema of that agent's document type. An agent sees only its own document schema.

### Inputs

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | string, required | Absolute path of the Markdown file, in the session directory. |
| `document` | object | The whole document. It replaces what is stored. |
| `update` | object | Top-level fields to change. Lists of items with an `id` merge by id. |
| `remove` | array of strings | IDs of list items to remove, for example `R4` or a phase number. |

The tool accepts `document` alone, or `update` and `remove` without `document`. If a call sends `document` with `update` or with a non-empty `remove`, the tool returns the error ``Send either `document` (the whole document) or `update` with `remove`, not both.`` (`crates/ostra-tools/src/doc.rs`, line 59).

If a weaker model sends `document` as a string that holds JSON text, Ostra parses the string back into an object before it validates the call. The function `coerce_json_strings` in `crates/ostra-core/src/args.rs` does this for every top-level argument that the schema types as an object or an array.

### Order of checks in one call

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Agent
    participant Policy
    participant Tool as document tool
    participant Merge as apply_update
    participant Store as write
    participant Check as check
    participant Render as render
    Agent->>Policy: Document(path, document or update)
    Policy->>Tool: allowed
    Tool->>Tool: check agent, file name, session dir
    Tool->>Merge: load stored JSON, update, remove
    Merge->>Store: merged JSON value
    Store->>Store: DocKind::parse (schema)
    Store->>Check: check(document)
    Store->>Render: render(document, md)
    Store->>Tool: Written (files, issues)
    Tool->>Agent: counts, file list, issues
```

The policy runs before every tool, including this one. The guard `check_document` in `crates/ostra-policy/src/guards.rs` denies a target that is a protected path or engine state. It denies a file that another agent owns, with the rule `artifact-ownership`. In strict mode it denies a path outside the session directory, with the rule `write-scope`. A run that can only answer questions (`answer_only`) cannot call `Document` at all. See [Policy engine](policy.md).

The tool then checks these items in order. Each failure returns an error and writes nothing:

1. The agent must be `explore`, `generate-spec`, or `plan`.
2. `path` must be present and not blank.
3. The file name must start with the kind prefix and end with `.md`. A plan name must not contain `-phase-`, because phase files belong to the plan.
4. The file must lie directly in the session directory of the run. The tool compares both paths through `ostra_core::paths::fold`, because on Windows the prefix, the case, and the separators of two paths to one folder can differ.
5. `remove` must be a list. The tool reads each entry as a string or as a number.

After the write, the tool calls `mark_read` on every written file and on its JSON file. `mark_read` in `crates/ostra-tools/src/lib.rs` only satisfies the read-before-write check (`has_read`) of the file tools. It does not lift the policy guard. A `Write` or `Edit` call on these files stays denied with the rule `document-tool`, and the agent must use `Document` for each change. See [Direct writes are refused](typed-documents.md#direct-writes-are-refused). The result lists the counts, the file paths, and the issues.

### The result text

The result starts with a line such as `Wrote the spec: 4 criteria, 2 deliverables, 4 requirements, 7 acceptance criteria, 1 evidence rows, 0 open questions.` The counts depend on the kind. Then the tool lists each file. Then it shows one of three texts:

- `Ostra's checks found nothing to fix.` when no issue exists.
- `Warnings to review:` and the issue lines when only warnings exist.
- ``Fix the N errors below with an `update` before you submit, because the submit call is refused while any remain:`` and the issue lines when at least one error exists (`crates/ostra-tools/src/doc.rs`, line 140). `N` is the error count.

An issue line has the form `- error (R3): message` or `- warning: message`. The text in parentheses is the element that the issue is about.

### Direct writes are refused

The agent cannot write these files with `Write`, `Edit`, or the shell. The guard in `check_write` in `crates/ostra-policy/src/guards.rs` denies any write to a file in the session directory whose name `doc_kind_for` recognizes. The rule name is `document-tool`. Ostra renders the Markdown from the typed document, so a direct write is overwritten and the browser does not show it.

Harness executors reach the same tool through the MCP bridge as the tool `document`. See [Executors](executors.md).

## Revise a document with update and remove

A long document is too large to resend after each fix. Ostra lets the agent send only what changed. `apply_update` in `crates/ostra-core/src/doc/merge.rs` merges the update into the stored JSON.

These rules apply:

- Each top-level field in `update` replaces the stored field.
- The exception is a list in which every item has an `id`. Then Ostra merges the list by id. An item with a known id replaces the stored item. An item with a new id joins the list.
- A keyed list ends in natural id order. `R2` comes before `R10`, and `AC1.2` comes before `AC1.10`. A new `R12` lands after `R11` wherever the agent sent it.
- An `id` can be a string or a number. Phases use numbers.
- A list is keyed only if it is not empty and every item has an `id`. A list of plain strings, such as `notes`, is replaced as a whole.
- `remove` drops each keyed item whose id is in the list. The function looks only in the keyed top-level lists of the document. It does not look in a nested list, such as `acceptance` under a requirement.
- If a call has no stored document, `update` builds the document from nothing. A first call with `update` only works if the fields are complete enough to pass the schema.

To change or drop a nested item, send the whole parent item in `update`. For example, to drop the acceptance criterion `AC1.1`, send the requirement `R1` again without it. The parent item replaces the stored item.

The merge runs before schema validation. A merged document that fails the schema is not written.

### What happens when

- **`remove` names an id that no keyed top-level list has.** The tool returns `Nothing to remove for R9: no list item has that id. Check the ids and call again; nothing was written.` The stored files do not change. An id of a nested item, such as `AC1.1`, gets this error too, because `apply_update` does not look in nested lists.
- **`remove` is sent and no document exists.** The tool returns `There is no spec at <path> yet, so there is nothing to remove.`
- **`update` is not an object.** The merge returns the message ``` `update` must be an object of top-level document fields.``` (`crates/ostra-core/src/doc/merge.rs`, line 64).
- **The merged document fails the schema.** The tool returns `The spec does not match its schema, so nothing was written: <field path>: <message>. Fix that field and call Document again.` The message names the failing field, for example `requirements[0].acceptance[0]: missing field then`. Ostra builds the path with `serde_path_to_error`.
- **The document has a field that the schema does not list.** `ResearchDoc`, `SpecDoc`, `PlanDoc`, and most of their nested parts carry `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`. For these types the write fails with `unknown field` and the name. Five types do not carry the attribute: `Question` (`crates/ostra-core/src/pipeline.rs`, line 210), `QuestionOption` (`crates/ostra-core/src/pipeline.rs`, line 265), `PhaseDoc` (`crates/ostra-core/src/doc/mod.rs`, line 723), `Document`, and `DocumentView`. `Question` sits in `open_questions` of the research document and the spec, and in `clarifying_questions` of the plan. `QuestionOption` sits in the options of a question. Ostra does not reject an unknown field inside a question or inside a question option. The agent never sends a `PhaseDoc`, because Ostra derives it from the `phases` of the plan. `Document` and `DocumentView` are the wrappers that the browser receives.
- **A plan removes a phase.** Ostra deletes the `.md` and `.json` files of that phase.

The Document tool description in `defs.rs` also tells the agent that it can write a long document in parts. The first call sends `document` with every required field. Later calls send `update` with more list items.

## The research document

`ResearchDoc` holds what the codebase does for one research task and what external technology documents about itself. The `explore` agent writes it. Field comments in `crates/ostra-core/src/doc/mod.rs` are the schema descriptions that the model sees, so they are written as instructions.

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `title`, `date`, `repo`, `areas` | The topic, the date as `YYYY-MM-DD`, the repo key, and areas from the repo module map. |
| `scope` | The exact `Task:` of the spawn and what it does not cover. Required. |
| `problem` | The problem in two to four sentences. Required. |
| `asks` | What the request demands, one entry per demand, in the user's words. |
| `files` | `FileRef` entries: `path`, `purpose`, and `symbols`. |
| `patterns` | `Pattern` entries: `name`, `description`, `files`, and an optional `snippet` with `language`, `code`, and `source`. |
| `data_flow` | `FlowStep` entries: one hop each, with an optional `location` of the form `path:Symbol`. |
| `dependencies` | `Dependency` entries with `kind` of `internal` or `external`. |
| `external` | `ExternalFinding` entries: `technology`, `fact`, `consequence`, `source`, and `version`. |
| `approaches` | `Approach` entries with `pros`, `cons`, `precedent`, `best_for`, and `recommended`. |
| `recommendation` | The chosen approach. Absent for an investigative task. |
| `open_questions` | `Question` cards numbered `Q1`, `Q2`. |
| `sources` | `Source` entries: `url`, `version`, and `established`. One per page that the run retrieved. |
| `lessons` | `LessonUsed` entries: `area`, `lesson`, and `verified`. |
| `not_covered`, `next_steps` | Lists of strings. |

The fields `title`, `date`, `repo`, `scope`, and `problem` are the only required fields. Every list has a default of empty. A research document with only these five fields passes the schema.

## The spec

`SpecDoc` is the one specification for the request. The `generate-spec` agent writes it. Ostra derives the Delivery Order table, the Traceability table, and every count from the lists, so the agent does not write them.

The parts of the spec build a chain. A criterion is one verifiable demand. A deliverable is a unit of delivery in one repo. A requirement belongs to one deliverable, covers criteria, and has acceptance criteria. An evidence row is an external fact with a binding rule.

| Part | Type | Key fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Criteria | `Criterion` | `id` (`C1`), `statement`, `kind`, `repo`, `grounding`, `depends_on`, `provisional` |
| Deliverables | `Deliverable` | `id` (`D1`), `title`, `repo`, `areas`, `depends_on`, `outcome` |
| Requirements | `Requirement` | `id` (`R1`), `deliverable`, `title`, `pattern`, `statement`, `covers`, `rests_on`, `acceptance` |
| Acceptance | `Acceptance` | `id` (`AC1.1`), `given`, `when`, `then` |
| Contracts | `ProvidedContract`, `ConsumedContract` | `name`, `shape`, `provided_by` and `consumed_by`, or `source` |
| Evidence | `Evidence` | `id` (`E1`), `fact`, `rule`, `source`, `version`, `note` |
| Other | `DataChange`, `Assumption`, `Exclusion`, `ScopeItem` | Data impact, assumptions, out of scope, in scope |

`CriterionKind` has the values `Functional`, `Data`, `Integration`, `Constraint`, and `Quality`.

`EarsPattern` names the sentence form of a requirement statement. The JSON values are in kebab case: `ubiquitous`, `event-driven`, `state-driven`, `unwanted`, `optional`, and `complex`. For example, an event-driven statement has the form `WHEN {trigger} THE SYSTEM SHALL {response}.` A statement must hold exactly one `SHALL`.

A criterion with a `provisional` value names a question, for example `Q2`. The criterion waits for the answer. The render shows its status as `Provisional (Q2)`. Without the field, the status is `Confirmed`.

The spec also has `title`, `date`, `research` (the paths of the research documents, oldest first), `repos`, `objective`, `current_behavior`, `open_questions`, and `notes`.

## The plan and its phases

`PlanDoc` holds the master plan and every phase. The `plan` agent writes it. Ostra writes the master plan file and one phase file for each phase from it. Ostra derives the Deliverable Index, the Phase Index, the Test Policy Rationale, the Requirement Traceability table, and the step counts.

The plan has these top-level fields:

- `title`, `date`, `spec` (the spec file path), and `repos`.
- `stakes` (`Low`, `Medium`, or `High`) and `stakes_rationale`.
- `summary`, `success_criteria`, `clarifying_questions`, and `deliverables` (ID and title only).
- `phases`, `risks`, `verification`, and `pre_checks`.

Each `Phase` is self-contained. The implementer reads only its phase file and never reads the spec. For this reason a phase repeats the text of the requirements and the evidence rules that its steps use.

### Phase fields

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | number | The bare phase number, in one sequence across the plan. |
| `name`, `description` | string | The name, and one sentence for the Phase Index. |
| `deliverable` | string | The deliverable ID, for example `D1`. |
| `repo`, `repo_root` | string | The repo key that the phase changes and its absolute root. |
| `complexity` | `Low`, `Medium`, or `High` | The model-routing tier of the phase. |
| `test_policy` | `Required` or `Skip` | Whether a requested test run covers the phase. |
| `test_rationale` | string | One sentence with the evidence for the policy. Required and not blank. |
| `depends_on` | list of numbers | Phase IDs that must complete first. |
| `areas`, `skills` | list of strings | Module areas, and the skills the implementer loads. |
| `context` | string | What the phase does and which earlier artifacts it needs. |
| `requirements` | list of `QuotedRequirement` | Each requirement a step delivers, with its EARS statement copied from the spec. |
| `constraints` | list of `Evidence` | Each evidence row that a step must obey, copied from the spec. |
| `steps` | list of `PlanStep` | The ordered steps. At least one. |
| `verification` | string | The build command of the repo. |

A `PlanStep` has `id` of the form `{phase}.{n}` (for example `2.3`), `title`, `file`, `change` (`Create`, `Modify`, or `Delete`), `read_first`, `delivers`, `action`, `binding_rules`, `skills`, `verify`, and `size` (`Small`, `Medium`, or `Large`). A binding rule is an evidence ID with the rule sentence copied from the evidence row.

The step `size` is not the phase `complexity`. The first sizes one step. The second routes the whole phase.

### complexity

`complexity` is the model-routing tier of the phase. It uses the type `Level`, so the JSON values are `Low`, `Medium`, and `High`. The plan prompt in `assets/agents/plan/prompt.md` (rule P9) tells the agent to classify a phase from its own difficulty, bounded by the stakes:

- `Low`: a mechanical or isolated change, such as one file, config, or wiring.
- `Medium`: several related files, or moderate business logic in one area.
- `High`: an architectural change, a schema or data migration, a cross-module change, or complex logic.

The engine copies `complexity` from the submit call into the phase info and uses it to choose the model tier for the implementer and the test agents of that phase. A phase with no file counts as `Low`. See [Model providers, tiers, and cost](providers-and-cost.md).

### test_policy

`test_policy` tells the engine which phases a test run covers. The plan does not decide whether tests run. Tests are optional and run only if the user asks for them after every phase is implemented (see [Sessions and the pipeline](sessions-and-pipeline.md)).

- `Required`: the test pipeline covers the phase. The pipeline is `execution-path-analyzer`, then `write-test`, then the test code-review loop.
- `Skip`: the test pipeline leaves the phase uncovered.

Rule P12 in the plan prompt sets the decision. If any step has logic, the policy is `Required`. If every step is boilerplate, the policy is `Skip`. If the agent cannot classify a step with confidence, the policy is `Required`. A `Skip` phase needs a `test_rationale` that names what each step contains. The master plan lists every `Skip` phase and its rationale in the section Test Policy Rationale. If no phase is `Skip`, the section says `None: every phase is Test policy Required.`

The engine function `test_stage` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs` covers a phase when it has no file or when its policy is `Required`.

### depends_on

`depends_on` lists the phase IDs that must complete before the phase starts. The engine schedules phases as a graph with these edges. The Phase Index calls the columns Repo and Depends on "the orchestrator's scheduling graph".

- An empty list means no prerequisite. The render shows `none`.
- `check` gives an error for an ID that names no phase.
- `check` gives a warning for an ID that is the same as or larger than the phase's own ID, because a phase must depend only on earlier phases.
- `check` gives an error for a cycle and prints it, for example `1 -> 2 -> 1`.
- If the engine reads a list that names a missing phase or the phase itself, it treats the phase as dependent on every earlier phase (rule M5 in `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs`).

Phase IDs are one unbroken sequence from 1. `check` names the first phase that breaks the sequence with the text `Number phases 1 to N in order; expected phase K here (P10).`

## What check finds

`check(&Document)` in `crates/ostra-core/src/doc/check.rs` returns a list of `DocIssue`. Each issue has a `level` (`Error` or `Warning`), an optional `element` such as `R3` or `step 2.1`, and a `message`. The list is sorted with errors first.

An error is a broken reference or a rule that code can decide. An error blocks the submit call. A warning is shown to the agent and to the reader and does not block. `check` runs on every write, and `load_view` runs it again when the browser opens a document.

The tags in parentheses in a message, such as `(P10)` or `(S1)`, refer to numbered rules in the agent prompts under `assets/agents`.

### Rules for all kinds: open questions

The function `Issues::questions` checks every question list.

- Error: two questions have the same `id`.
- Error: a question has fewer than 2 or more than 4 options.
- Error: `recommended` is not the index of an option.
- Warning: a `tag` is longer than 12 characters, because the question card clips it.

### Research rules

- Error: an `external` finding cites a `source` that is not in `sources`. Every external fact cites a page that the run retrieved.
- Error: more than one approach has `recommended` set.
- Warning: a source URL does not start with `http://` or `https://`.
- Warning: `approaches` has entries but `recommendation` is absent.

### Spec rules

| Level | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Error | Two criteria, deliverables, requirements, acceptance criteria, or evidence rows have the same ID. |
| Error | A `depends_on` of a criterion or a deliverable names an ID that does not exist. |
| Error | The deliverables form a cycle. The message asks the agent to merge the deliverables in the cycle. |
| Error | A criterion is not in the `covers` list of any requirement (S1). |
| Error | A requirement names an unknown deliverable, has an ID that is not `R{n}`, has an empty `covers`, or covers an unknown criterion. |
| Error | A requirement `rests_on` names an unknown evidence row. |
| Error | A requirement has no acceptance criterion, or an acceptance ID is not `AC{n}.{m}` for its requirement, or its `given`, `when`, or `then` is blank. |
| Error | A deliverable has no requirement. |
| Error | A provided contract names an unknown deliverable in `provided_by`, or a `consumed_by` entry of the form `D{n}` is unknown. |
| Warning | A criterion `provisional` names a question that is not open. |
| Warning | Requirements are not in one flat sequence `R1` to `R{n}`, or are not in deliverable order. |
| Warning | A statement does not hold exactly one `SHALL`. |
| Warning | A deliverable covers more than 6 criteria and no note names its ID (S4). |
| Warning | An evidence row has no requirement that rests on it. |

### Plan and phase rules

| Level | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Error | Two phases have the same ID, or the IDs are not 1 to N in order (P10). |
| Error | A phase `depends_on` names a missing phase, or the phases form a cycle. |
| Error | A phase has a blank `test_rationale` (P12), or has no steps. |
| Error | A step ID is not `{phase}.{n}`, or two steps have the same ID. |
| Error | A step `verify` is blank (P5). |
| Error | A binding rule names an ID that is not in the phase `constraints`, or its text differs from the constraint text, or it is blank (P13). |
| Error | The repo has skills installed and a phase with code steps names none, or a step names a skill that is not installed (P6). |
| Warning | A phase depends on itself or on a later phase. |
| Warning | The plan lists deliverables and a phase names one that is not in the list. |
| Warning | A step has an empty `delivers`, or delivers a requirement that the phase does not quote (P11). |

The skill check is the only check that reads the file system. `installed_skills` lists each directory in the skill folders of the repo root that holds a `SKILL.md`. If the repo has no installed skill, the check does not run. A code step is a step whose `change` is not `Delete`. The reason for the rule is that the implementer loads only the skills that the phase file lists. A plan that names no skills makes the implementer build without the patterns of the project.

A phase also lists every skill that its steps name. `DocKind::parse` adds each step skill to the phase `skills` list when it is missing (rule P7). The agent does not need to repeat them.

## The submit gate

The submit tool of each owner agent carries a path and counts. `check_submit(agent, input)` runs before Ostra records the submit. Both executors call it: the native loop in `crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs` and the harness bridge in `crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/bridge.rs`. A failure returns the message and the text `Nothing was recorded.`

`check_submit` does these steps for `explore`, `generate-spec`, and `plan`:

1. Read the path from `research_path`, `spec_path`, or `master_plan_path`.
2. Load the JSON beside it. If it is missing, return `Write the spec with the Document tool before you submit: <path> has no document behind it.`
3. Parse the JSON and run `check`. If any error exists, return `Fix these in the document with the Document tool, then submit again:` and the error lines.
4. Compare the submit counts with the document.

Step 4 depends on the kind:

- **Spec.** `external_evidence_rows`, `deliverables`, and `requirements` must equal the number of evidence rows, deliverables, and requirements.
- **Plan.** `step_count` must equal the total number of steps. `phases` must list the same number of phases. Each submitted phase must agree with the document on `id`, `deliverable`, `project` (the phase `repo`), `complexity`, `test_policy`, `depends_on`, and `file` (the path that `phase_path` gives).
- **Research.** No count check exists.

The plan comparison matters because the engine does not read the plan JSON to schedule work. `adopt_plan_phases` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs` builds the phase set from the `phases` list of the submit call. If the two disagree, the engine schedules a plan that differs from the files that the implementer reads.

For the `initializer` agent, `check_submit` runs a different check. It confirms that the inventory file exists and that the profile parses. That check is part of [Project init, skills, and lesson memory](project-init-and-memory.md).

## Render to Markdown

`render(doc, md)` in `crates/ostra-core/src/doc/render.rs` turns a document into Markdown. The section names match the templates that the downstream prompts and the fact-check refer to. The model does not write the derived tables, so they cannot disagree with the lists.

| Kind | Title line | Main sections |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Research | `# Research: {title}` | Scope of this document, Problem Statement, What the request asks, Findings (Relevant Files, Existing Patterns, Data Flow, Dependencies, External Technology, Lessons Used), Approaches, Open Questions, Not Covered, Sources, Next Steps |
| Spec | `# Specification: {title}` | Objective, Current Behavior, Scope, Criteria, Delivery Order, Requirements, Contracts Provided, Contracts Consumed, External Evidence, Data Impact, Assumptions, Open Questions, Traceability, Notes |
| Plan | `# Plan: {title}` | Summary, Success Criteria, Clarifying Questions, Deliverable Index, Phase Index, Test Policy Rationale, Requirement Traceability, Risks and Mitigations, Verification Strategy, Step Count Summary, Mechanical Pre-Checks |
| Phase | `# Phase {id}: {name}` | Required Skills, Context, Requirements Delivered, External Constraints, Steps, Phase Verification |

The render computes these values:

- **Spec header.** `Deliverables`, `Requirements`, and `Criteria covered: {met} of {total}`.
- **Delivery Order.** One row for each deliverable with the requirement span (for example `R1–R3`) and the criteria that its requirements cover.
- **Traceability (spec).** One row for each criterion with its deliverables, requirements, and acceptance criteria. A criterion with no requirement shows `none`.
- **Plan header.** `Delivers requirements` as a span of IDs, built from the `delivers` lists of all steps.
- **Phase Index.** One row for each phase with complexity, test policy, `Depends on`, the path of the phase file, and the step count.
- **Requirement Traceability (plan).** One row for each requirement with the phase and step that deliver it, and the matching `AC` IDs from `success_criteria`.

`id_span` shortens a contiguous run of requirement IDs to `R1–R4`. It shows a list when the numbers are not contiguous. `cell` makes each table cell one line and escapes the pipe character. The renderer ends the output with one newline.

A phase file holds what an implementer needs: skills, context, the quoted requirements, the external constraints, and the steps with their binding rules and verify commands.

## The browser view

The artifact route of the server returns a `DocumentView` for a session file when the file has a typed document. `load_view(path)` in `store.rs` reads the sibling JSON and parses it. A phase file parses as a `PhaseDoc`, and every other file parses with `DocKind::parse`. The view holds the `Document` (a tagged union of `research`, `spec`, `plan`, and `phase`) and the issues from `check`. The Artifact screen in `web/src/screens/artifact/doc/DocumentView.tsx` shows each part natively. See [Server, REST API, and WebSocket](server-and-api.md) and [The web console](web-console.md).

`load_view` returns nothing when the file name has no kind prefix, when the JSON is missing, or when the JSON no longer parses. The Markdown still shows in that case.

## What happens when a call or a submit fails

- **The agent is not `explore`, `generate-spec`, or `plan`.** The tool returns `Only explore, generate-spec, and plan write documents. Write your output where your prompt says.`
- **The file name has the wrong prefix or extension.** The tool returns a message that gives the required shape `ostra-spec-{run-stamp}-{topic-slug}.md` and says that later stages find the file by it.
- **The path is outside the session directory.** The tool returns a message that names the session directory. In strict mode the policy denies the call first.
- **The JSON fails the schema.** Nothing is written. The old files stay as they were.
- **The JSON passes the schema but has errors from `check`.** Ostra writes the files and returns the errors. The submit call is refused until the agent fixes them.
- **A warning exists.** The files are written. The submit call is not refused.
- **The agent edits a document file with `Write`, `Edit`, or the shell.** The policy denies the call with the rule `document-tool`.
- **A plan keeps fewer phases than before.** Ostra removes the files of the dropped phases.
- **The plan submit disagrees with the plan document.** The submit call is refused with a message that lists the values to send.
- **A document is written for a spec with a number such as `R10`.** The merge sorts keyed lists in natural order, so `R10` follows `R9`.

## Limits and defaults

| Item | Value | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Options for one question | 2 to 4 | `Issues::questions` in `check.rs` |
| Question tag length | 12 characters, a warning above it | `Issues::questions` |
| `SHALL` words in one requirement statement | exactly 1, a warning otherwise | `spec` in `check.rs` |
| Criteria for one deliverable | 6, a warning above it without a note | `spec` in `check.rs` |
| Recommended approaches in a research document | at most 1 | `research` in `check.rs` |
| Phase IDs | one sequence from 1 | `plan` in `check.rs` |

The documents have no size cap in these files.

## Workspace artifacts are not typed documents

The word artifact names two different things. A typed document is a session file that an agent writes. A workspace artifact is a file that the user keeps for every session of a workspace, such as a custom skill or a guideline. `crates/ostra-core/src/artifacts.rs` handles workspace artifacts. It keeps them in `<workspace>/.ostra/artifacts/` or, for a hidden artifact, in the data directory where no agent can read them. The limits there are `MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES` (25 MB), `MAX_ARTIFACTS` (2000 files), and `MAX_BRIEF_ARTIFACTS` (40 files named in the repo brief). A tag of the form `@_artifacts/<path>` names an artifact in a request. The server routes for artifacts are in [Server, REST API, and WebSocket](server-and-api.md), and the storage layout is in [Storage: databases and data layout](storage.md). The `Document` tool does not read or write workspace artifacts.

sections.title: Agents, prompts, and the spawn contract
sections.summary: The 14 agents and their capabilities, the embedded assets folder, prompt rendering for each executor, the typed spawn block, the submit tools, and the repo brief with its limits.
sections.body:
Ostra runs many different model agents, and each one needs the same four things: a prompt, a set of tools, a typed input, and a typed way to return a result. Without a fixed contract, each executor (the native loop or a harness CLI) receives different tool names, free-form input, and a free-text answer that the engine must scrape. The `ostra-agents` crate and the `ostra-core` types `AgentName` and `submit` define that contract in one place.

This page covers:

- The 14 `AgentName` values, their tiers, timeouts, and capabilities.
- The `assets/` folder and how Ostra embeds and materializes it.
- How `render_prompt` builds a prompt for each executor from `assets/tool-mapping.toml`.
- The spawn contract: `SpawnParams`, one struct for each agent, and `parse_block`.
- The `submit_<agent>` tools and their validation.
- The repo brief that Ostra appends to the first message of every execution.

Other pages own the neighbors of this contract. [Sessions and the pipeline](sessions-and-pipeline.md) says when the planner spawns each agent. [Executors](executors.md) says how the native loop and the harnesses run a spawn. [Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md) owns the judge prompts. [Subagent coordination](subagent-coordination.md) owns `assets/coordination.md`.

## The 14 agents

`AgentName` in `crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs` lists every leaf agent that Ostra runs. The serialized name is kebab-case and matches the folder `assets/agents/<name>/`. `AgentName::ALL` holds all 14 values.

| Agent (`as_str`) | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `explore` | Researches one task and writes one research document. Research is the job of this agent. |
| `generate-spec` | Reads every research document and writes one spec with requirements, deliverables, and an External Evidence table. |
| `fact-check` | Checks a spec or a plan for claims that break the implementer and for external facts that lost their cited page. |
| `plan` | Turns one approved spec into a master plan and one file for each phase. |
| `implementer` | Writes the code for one plan phase or one inline change, then reports what changed. |
| `code-reviewer` | Reviews the unstaged changes of one review loop against the Review Rule Set. It also runs a security scan that can raise a BLOCKER. |
| `execution-path-analyzer` | Plans the verification of an implementer phase. Its report is the EPA report. |
| `write-test` | Writes the tests that the EPA report assigns and runs them. It runs only when the user asked for tests. |
| `documentation` | Writes one project's part of a documentation book. |
| `system-architecture` | Writes the architecture of a book that covers two or more projects. |
| `prompt-generation` | Writes or edits instruction files: system prompts, `SKILL.md` skills, and agent definitions. |
| `initializer` | Bootstraps a project in one of six modes (see below). |
| `quick-answer` | Answers one question in the side panel. It is read-only. |
| `advisor` | Diagnoses a failed or stuck step and tells the engine how to continue. |

### Name parsing and old names

`AgentName::from_str` trims the text and removes a leading `ostra:` or `ultracode:`. It then matches the kebab-case name. It also accepts `module-documentation`, the name of the agent that `documentation` replaced. The serde alias on `Documentation` does the same for logs and execution rows that books pre-date. `RETIRED_AGENTS` holds `module-documentation`, so workspace settings that still carry the name pass validation.

`route_keys()` returns the 14 agent names plus `judge` (`JUDGE_ROUTE`). Every key must have a model route in the workspace settings. See [Configuration](configuration.md) for the routing settings.

### Tier, timeout, and capabilities

Each agent has a file `assets/agents/<name>/agent.toml`. `load_defs` parses all 14 files into `AgentDef` the first time any code asks for a definition. A missing or malformed file panics with `embedded agent definitions are invalid`, because the crate tests check the embedded files and so the fault is a build defect, not a run-time condition.

The fields are `description`, `default_tier`, `timeout_seconds`, `capabilities`, and an `[effort]` table with one key for each executor table (`native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, `agy`).

| Agent | Default tier | Timeout (seconds) | Capabilities |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `explore` | advanced | 1800 | read, shell, search_text, glob, web_search, web_fetch, memory_recall, memory, document, code, coordinate, docs_search |
| `generate-spec` | advanced | 1800 | read, shell, search_text, glob, web_search, web_fetch, document, code, coordinate, docs_search |
| `fact-check` | advanced | 1800 | read, write, shell, search_text, glob, web_search, web_fetch, code, coordinate, docs_search |
| `plan` | advanced | 1800 | read, shell, search_text, glob, document, code, coordinate, docs_search |
| `implementer` | balanced | 2400 | read, edit, write, shell, search_text, glob, skill, memory_recall, memory, report, code, manage_projects, coordinate, docs_search |
| `code-reviewer` | balanced | 1200 | read, shell, search_text, glob, code, coordinate, docs_search |
| `execution-path-analyzer` | balanced | 1200 | read, shell, write, search_text, glob, report, code, docs_search |
| `write-test` | balanced | 2400 | read, edit, write, shell, search_text, glob, skill, memory_recall, memory, report, code, coordinate, docs_search |
| `documentation` | advanced | 2400 | read, shell, search_text, glob, code, docs_search |
| `system-architecture` | advanced | 1800 | read, shell, search_text, glob, code, docs_search |
| `prompt-generation` | advanced | 1800 | read, edit, write, shell, search_text, glob, skill, report, code |
| `initializer` | balanced | 2400 | read, write, edit, shell, search_text, glob, code |
| `quick-answer` | balanced | 300 | read, search_text, glob, web_search, web_fetch, memory_recall, code, docs_search |
| `advisor` | advanced | 900 | read, shell, search_text, glob, web_search, web_fetch, memory_recall, docs_search |

The factory passes the tier, the capabilities, and the timeout to the engine as `AgentMeta`. See [Model providers, tiers, and cost](providers-and-cost.md) for the tier names and the routing.

### What a capability means

`Capability` has 17 values. `Capability::native_tool` gives the native tool name of each one.

| Capability | Native tool | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read`, `write`, `edit` | `Read`, `Write`, `Edit` | `writes()` is true for `write` and `edit`. Ostra uses it to derive read-only runs and sandbox modes. |
| `shell` | `Bash` | On Windows it also grants `PowerShell` and `Cmd`. |
| `search_text`, `glob` | `Grep`, `Glob` | |
| `skill` | `Skill` | |
| `web_search`, `web_fetch` | `WebSearch`, `WebFetch` | |
| `report` | `Report` | |
| `document` | `Document` | The typed-document tool. See [Typed pipeline documents](typed-documents.md). |
| `memory`, `memory_recall` | `Memory`, `MemoryRecall` | |
| `docs_search` | `DocsSearch` | Searches the documentation books. |
| `code` | `CodeOutline` and 7 more | The 8 tools of `CODE_TOOLS`: outline, find, callers, callees, implementations, neighbors, impact, map. |
| `manage_projects` | `ProjectList`, `ProjectCreate` | `PROJECT_TOOLS` in `ostra-core`. |
| `coordinate` | `SubagentList`, `SubagentAsk`, `SubagentReply` | `COORD_TOOLS` in `ostra-core`. See [Subagent coordination](subagent-coordination.md). |

The `submit` tool is not a capability. Every agent gets its own `submit_<agent>` tool.

### Agent classes

The code treats some agents as a class. Each class has one rule that the rest of Ostra reads.

- **Session-only** (`is_session_only`): `explore`, `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `plan`, `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `advisor`, `documentation`, and `system-architecture`. The write-scope guard confines these agents to the session folder and the OS temp folder. The policy page owns the guard. See [Policy engine](policy.md).
- **Not session-only:** `implementer`, `write-test`, `prompt-generation`, `initializer`, and `quick-answer`. The first four can change project files. `quick-answer` has no write or shell capability.
- **Creates projects** (`manages_projects`): only `implementer`. Only the phase of an approved plan starts a new project, so only this agent has the `manage_projects` capability.
- **Routes by complexity** (`routes_by_complexity`): `implementer` and `write-test`. The `**Complexity:**` line of the phase picks their model tier.
- **Writes documents through the `Document` tool:** `explore`, `generate-spec`, and `plan`. They have the `document` capability and no write capability. A crate test checks this.
- **Read-only checkers:** `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, and `fact-check` have no `edit` capability. A crate test checks this. The last two can write, because they save a report or a finding file in the session folder.

### The initializer modes

`initializer` is one agent with six modes. `InitializerMode` names them: `detect`, `scout`, `propose`, `generate-skill`, `generate-inventory`, and `adopt`. The `Mode:` line of the spawn block selects the mode, and each mode has its own required lines (see the spawn contract). [Project init, skills, and lesson memory](project-init-and-memory.md) describes what each mode does.

### Effort

`effort_for(agent, executor)` returns the reasoning effort. It reads the `[effort]` table of the agent for the executor table, falls back to the `native` value, and falls back to `High` if both are missing. Nearly every value is `high`. These values differ:

- `quick-answer` uses `medium` on every executor.
- `initializer` uses `xhigh` on `codex` and `grok`, and `max` on `agy`. On `native` and `claude` it uses `high`.

The native value of the initializer is `high` and not `max` because a self-initialization once cost about 240 USD on a top-tier model at `max` effort. A crate test records the change. A workspace setting can override the effort: the factory calls `resolve_effort` first and uses `effort_for` only when the setting gives no value.

## The assets folder

The folder `assets/` at the repo root holds every text that Ostra shows to a model. The `ostra-agents` crate embeds it with `rust-embed` (`#[folder = "../../assets"]`). In a release build, the embed happens at compile time, so the release binary needs no asset files at run time. A debug build reads the folder from disk at run time, because the `debug-embed` feature of `rust-embed` is off. The web build in `web/dist` follows the same `rust-embed` rule. See [Server, REST API, and WebSocket](server-and-api.md) for that embed.

| Path | Content | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `assets/agents/<name>/agent.toml` | The definition of one agent: description, tier, timeout, capabilities, effort. | `agent_def`, `load_defs` |
| `assets/agents/<name>/prompt.md` | The prompt of one agent, as a minijinja template. | `render_prompt` |
| `assets/judges/*.md` | The system prompts of the judges: `classify`, `completion`, `feedback`, `rescue`, `resolve-review`, `route-answer`, `stakes`, `sufficiency`, `track`, `yolo-answer`. | `judge_prompt` |
| `assets/refs/*.md` | Stack references and output contracts: `_generic`, `go`, `java-spring`, `python`, `typescript-node`, `inventory-and-profile`, `skill-archetypes`. | `reference`, `stack_names`, the initializer |
| `assets/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | Skills that ship with Ostra. Today only `meta-author`. | `embedded_skill`, the skill resolver |
| `assets/tool-mapping.toml` | Capability to tool name for each executor, and the harness strategy texts. | `mapping.rs` |
| `assets/output-rules.md` | The output rule that opens every prompt. | `render_prompt` |
| `assets/code-tools.md` | The guide to the code navigation tools. | `render_prompt` for agents with `code` |
| `assets/coordination.md` | The guide to the subagent tools. | `render_prompt` for agents with `coordinate` |

There are 14 agent folders, one for each `AgentName`. `agent.toml` and `prompt.md` must exist for each of them.

### Judges

`judge_prompt(name)` returns the text of `assets/judges/<name>.md`, or `None` for an unknown name. It builds a cache of all judge files the first time it runs. The 10 files are listed above. The doc comment of the function names only 8 of them and omits `track` and `feedback`, but the tests check all 10. Each judge prompt must name the `decide` tool. [Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md) explains each judge.

The factory also accepts the special name `__agent:<agent>`. `judge_prompt("__agent:quick-answer")` returns the native prompt of that agent. The engine uses it for the side-panel quick answer, which runs like a judge call.

### References and skills

`stack_names()` lists the stacks that have a seed reference. A reference counts when its text starts with `# Stack Reference:` and its name does not start with `_`. The result today is `go`, `java-spring`, `python`, and `typescript-node`. `_generic` is the fallback when no stack matches. `inventory-and-profile` defines the exact structure of `INVENTORY.md` and `project.toml` that the initializer writes. `skill-archetypes` holds the three skill templates.

`reference(name)` and `embedded_skill(name)` return the text with `{{assets_dir}}` replaced by the real folder. `reference_path(name)` returns the absolute path of a materialized reference. The spawn block of the initializer `scout` mode carries this path in its `Stack reference:` line.

### Materialize the assets on disk

Agents read references and skills with their file tools, so the files must exist on disk. At server start, `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs` runs these two calls:

```rust
ostra_agents::set_assets_dir(assets.clone()); // <data_dir>/assets
ostra_agents::materialize_assets(&assets)
```

`materialize_assets` writes these files under `<data_dir>/assets`:

- `refs/<name>.md` for each reference.
- `skills/<name>/...` for each embedded skill.
- `agents/<name>.md` for each of the 14 agents, rendered for the native executor.

The agent files exist because the advisor reads the instructions of a failed agent to see what the step can do and what it must return. The function rewrites only a file whose content changed, and returns the list of files that it wrote. Judge prompts are not written to disk. They stay in memory.

Call `set_assets_dir` once, before any prompt renders. It returns `false` if the folder was already set. If nothing sets it, `assets_dir()` uses `<data_dir>/assets`. See [Storage](storage.md) for the data folder layout.

## Render a prompt for one executor

`render_prompt(agent, executor)` returns the system prompt. The prompts name tools with tokens such as `{{tool_read}}`, because the same prompt must work with the native tools and with the different tool names of each harness.

### The tool mapping

`assets/tool-mapping.toml` has one table for each capability, with one value for each executor table. The native names follow the names of Claude Code, because the prompts were tuned on them.

| Capability | native | claude | codex | grok | agy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `read` | `Read` | `Read` | `exec_command` | `read_file` | `view_file` |
| `edit` | `Edit` | `Edit` | `apply_patch` | `search_replace` | `replace_file_content` |
| `write` | `Write` | `Write` | `apply_patch` | `search_replace` | `write_to_file` |
| `shell` | `Bash` | `Bash` | `exec_command` | `run_terminal_command` | `run_command` |
| `search_text` | `Grep` | `Grep` | `exec_command` | `grep` | `grep_search` |
| `glob` | `Glob` | `Glob` | `exec_command` | `list_dir` | `find_by_name` |
| `web_search` | `WebSearch` | `WebSearch` | `web_search` | `web_search` | `search_web` |
| `web_fetch` | `WebFetch` | `WebFetch` | `web_search` | `web_fetch` | `read_url_content` |
| `report` | `Report` | `mcp__ostra__report` | `report` | `report` | `report` |
| `code` (outline) | `CodeOutline` | `mcp__ostra__code_outline` | `code_outline` | `code_outline` | `code_outline` |
| `submit` | `submit_<agent>` | `mcp__ostra__submit_<agent>` | `submit_<agent>` | `submit_<agent>` | `submit_<agent>` |

The tools that Ostra itself provides (`report`, `document`, `memory`, `memory_recall`, `docs_search`, `code_*`, `project_*`, `subagent_*`, and `submit_*`) have the same pattern. On `native` they have a plain name. On `claude` they have the prefix `mcp__ostra__`. On `codex`, `grok`, and `agy` they have a plain lowercase name. On a harness they come from the `ostra` MCP server.

Three rules apply to the values:

- `{agent}` in a value becomes the snake_case agent name, for example `code_reviewer`.
- `{op}` and `{Op}` become the operation in lowercase or with a capital letter. The key `code:callers` gives `CodeCallers` on `native` and `code_callers` on `codex`.
- A value that is not a bare tool name is prose. The `skill` capability uses it, for example `Read on the skill's SKILL.md`. Ostra writes the prose into the prompt as it is.

### The template tokens

`mapping.rs` holds the constant `TOKENS`: 28 pairs of a token name and a mapping key, for example `tool_read` to `read` and `tool_code_callers` to `code:callers`. `Mapping::context` builds a map with all 28 tokens for one agent and one executor, plus `assets_dir`. A token whose key has no value for the executor falls back to the key itself.

`render_str` uses minijinja with `UndefinedBehavior::Strict`. A token that is not in the context is an error, so a prompt with a misspelled token fails the render and the crate test `every_prompt_renders_for_every_executor_with_no_unresolved_token` fails with it. The same test checks that each prompt names its own submit tool for every executor.

### The order of the parts

The flowchart shows the checks of `render_prompt`. The function prepends each part, so the last part that it prepends is the first part of the text.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["prompt.md of the agent"] --> B{"capability code?"}
  B -->|yes| C["prepend code-tools.md"]
  B -->|no| D{"capability coordinate?"}
  C --> D
  D -->|yes| E["prepend coordination.md"]
  D -->|no| F["prepend output-rules.md"]
  E --> F
  F --> G{"executor"}
  G -->|native| H["return the prompt"]
  G -->|harness| I["prepend the tool vocabulary"]
  I --> H
```

The final order of the text is:

1. The tool vocabulary (harness executors only).
2. `output-rules.md`.
3. `coordination.md` (agents with `coordinate`).
4. `code-tools.md` (agents with `code`).
5. The `prompt.md` of the agent.

### The output rule

`assets/output-rules.md` is the first text of every prompt. It tells the agent to write no text outside tool calls. Every report goes in `{{tool_report}}` or `{{tool_document}}`, every memory in `{{tool_memory}}`, and the result in the submit tool, because Ostra reads only those calls. The rule holds over any instruction in the task, the brief, a skill, or a file. A crate test checks that every prompt for every executor contains the sentence `Write no text outside tool calls`.

### The tool vocabulary of a harness

A harness has its own tool names, and its model cannot see the native names. For a harness executor, `Mapping::vocabulary` builds a section `## Tool vocabulary` that opens the prompt. It holds:

- A sentence that names the harness, for example `Claude Code`, `Codex`, `Grok Build`, or `Antigravity`.
- A table of each capability of the agent with the tool that serves it. Capabilities with several operations (`code`, `manage_projects`, `coordinate`) list all tools. The `submit` row is always present.
- The strategy texts of the harness from the `[strategies.*]` tables.
- The rule not to start the harness subagents. The only way to reach another agent is the Ostra subagent tools when the table lists them.
- An instruction to reply with only `Done!` after the submit call, because Ostra reads the result from the submit call and other text costs output tokens.

The strategies are:

| Strategy | Included when | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `skill` | The agent has `skill` or `read`. | How to load a skill by reading its `SKILL.md` completely before it acts. Per-project skills live in `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, and in `.ostra/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` for older projects. Skills that ship with Ostra live in `<assets_dir>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`. |
| `write` | The agent has `write` or `edit`. | Only `codex` has a text: use `apply_patch` with an `*** Add File:` hunk or an `*** Update File:` hunk. |
| `ostra_tools` | Always. | How to reach the `ostra` MCP server tools. `claude` loads a deferred tool with `ToolSearch`. `grok` finds one with `search_tool` and calls it with `use_tool`. |

### What happens when

- **A prompt asset is missing:** `asset_text` returns `AgentsError::Missing(path)`. For an agent definition this panics, because the crate tests treat it as a build defect.
- **A template has an undefined token:** the render fails with `AgentsError::Template { path, source }`.
- **A capability has no value for an executor:** the token falls back to the mapping key, and the vocabulary table omits the row.
- **The assets folder content changed:** the next server start rewrites only the changed files.
- **You want to see a rendered prompt:** run `cargo run -p ostra-agents --example render -- implementer harness:codex`. The first argument is an agent name and the second is `native` or `harness:<claude|codex|grok|agy>`.

## The spawn contract

The first message of an execution is a block of `Label: value` lines. The prompts of the agents name these lines in their "Required invocation parameters" paragraph, for example `Task:`, `Repo root:`, and `Report file:`. The module `crates/ostra-agents/src/spawn.rs` defines the block as typed Rust code.

### One struct for each agent

The trait `SpawnParams` has these methods:

- `agent()` returns the `AgentName`.
- `mode()` returns `Some(InitializerMode)` for initializer structs and `None` for all others.
- `common()` returns the `Common` value.
- `render()` returns the `Label: value` block.
- `to_json()` returns the same data as JSON for the execution record.
- `report_file()` returns the report path for agents that write one.

Required parameters are non-`Option` fields. A struct without them does not compile, so the engine cannot build a spawn that lacks a required line. Optional lines are `Option` fields or lists. An absent optional field renders nothing.

`Common` has the four lines that every spawn carries: `Workspace root`, `Repo root`, `Session dir`, and `Repo key`. `Workspace root:` replaces the line `Primary repo root:` of the earlier plugin that Ostra replaces.

`Extras` holds the optional lines that the engine adds under the required ones: `Research docs`, `Repos in scope`, `User answers`, `Findings`, `Required skills`, `Review ledger`, `Rescue context`, `Resume instructions`, `Prior phase reports`, `Context files`, `User notes`, `New project`, and a free-form note that renders below the block.

### The lines of each struct

The table lists the lines in render order. A question mark marks an optional line.

| Struct | Agent | Lines |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ExploreParams` | `explore` | `Task`, common, extras |
| `GenerateSpecParams` | `generate-spec` | `Task`, common, `Spec file`?, `New research docs`, `Requirement changes`, extras |
| `FactCheckParams` | `fact-check` | `Target`, `Target type`, `Prior findings`, `Spec file`, `Source check`, common, `Research docs` |
| `PlanParams` | `plan` | `Spec file`, common, `Repos in scope`, `Findings`?, `Master plan`? |
| `ImplementerParams` | `implementer` | `Report file`, `Phase file` or `No plan`, common, extras |
| `CodeReviewerParams` | `code-reviewer` | `Phase`, `Changed files`, `Change rationale`, `Phase file` or `No plan`, common, `Review scope`?, `Review context`?, `EPA report`? |
| `EpaParams` | `execution-path-analyzer` | `Implementer report`, `Report file`, common, `Phase file`?, extras |

The initializer has one struct for each mode. Each renders `Mode:` first, then its own lines, then `Advisor guidance:` when an earlier run failed, then the common lines.

When no scout ran because existing skills already covered the project, `Scout findings:` still renders and its value is `none`. The label is required.

### Rules in the field types

The types carry the pipeline rules that the prompts depend on:

- **`WorkSource`** (hard rule 13): an agent that is bound to a phase declares either `PhaseFile(path)` or `NoPlan(reason)`. It never declares neither. The factory picks `NoPlan` text from the request: a revision, a verify request, a direct test request, a direct documentation request, a prompt change, a quick change, the light track, or a low-stakes spec that skipped the plan tier.
- **`TargetType`:** `spec` or `plan`.
- **`SourceCheck`** (rule D3b): `citations`, or `refetch`. Use `refetch` only on the first pass of a spec target whose External Evidence table has rows.
- **`FactCheckParams.prior_findings`** (rule D3a): `none` on the first pass. Later passes carry the earlier findings verbatim. If the previous pass had no findings, the line holds the text `no findings on the previous pass`. `NO_PRIOR_FINDINGS` (`crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs`) is only the Rust constant name of that text.
- **`FactCheckParams.research_docs`:** only for a spec target. Rule D5 withholds research documents from a plan target.
- **`PlanParams`** (rule D4, hard rule 16): the plan agent gets the spec and nothing else. The only other inputs are the fact-check findings of a re-pass and the master plan under revision.
- **`CodeReviewerParams.phase`:** `N`, `N-tests`, or `none`. It names the loop, not the pass.

### How the block renders

The private type `Block` renders every line, with these rules:

- A single-line value renders as `Label: value`.
- A value with a line break renders as `Label:` and then each line indented by two spaces.
- An empty list renders nothing. An empty optional value renders nothing.
- A list renders as `Label:` with one indented line for each item.
- `Repos in scope` lists each project as `key -> /absolute/path`.

This block is the first message that an `explore` run receives:

```text
Task: Find out how sessions are stored
Workspace root: /home/me/ws
Repo root: /home/me/ws/api
Session dir: /home/me/ws/.ostra/sessions/s_1/api
Repo key: api
```

### Build the block in the engine

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Runner as Engine runner
  participant Factory as AgentsFactory
  participant Params as SpawnParams struct
  participant Brief as brief::augment
  participant Assets as render_prompt
  participant Exec as Executor
  Runner->>Factory: build(SpawnRequest, SpawnEnv)
  Factory->>Params: construct the struct from SpawnInputs
  Factory->>Params: render()
  Params-->>Factory: Label: value block
  Factory->>Brief: augment(block, BriefInput)
  Brief-->>Factory: block, rule, repo brief
  Factory->>Assets: render_prompt(agent, executor)
  Assets-->>Factory: system prompt
  Factory-->>Runner: BuiltSpawn
  Runner->>Exec: system prompt, first message, submit schema
```

`AgentsFactory::build` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/factory.rs` implements the `SpawnFactory` trait. It picks the struct from `req.agent`, fills it from `SpawnInputs`, and renders it. It returns a `BuiltSpawn` with these fields: `system_prompt`, `first_message`, `spawn_block`, `params` (the JSON of the struct), `report_file`, and `effort`.

A missing input returns an error string such as `missing task`, `missing report file`, or `initializer without a mode`. The engine does not spawn the agent in that case.

### Check a block with parse_block

`parse_block(agent, text)` validates a `Label: value` block and returns the values by parameter id. The static table `PARAMS` holds each id, its accepted labels, and its type. The function `contract(agent, mode)` returns the required ids and the one-of ids for each agent. The rules are:

1. Read each line. Stop at a line that is exactly `---` or that starts with `## `. This is where the repo brief starts, so brief text cannot inject a parameter.
2. Append an indented line to the label above it.
3. Look up the text before the first `:` in the label index. Ignore unknown labels. If a label repeats, the first value wins.
4. Check the four common parameters and the required parameters of the agent. The error is `missing required parameter `Label:`` or a type error.
5. For an agent that is bound to a phase (`implementer`, `write-test`, `code-reviewer`), check that exactly one of `Phase file:` and `No plan:` is present.
6. For the initializer, read `Mode:` first and check the lines of that mode. A missing mode gives `missing required parameter `Mode:``. An unknown mode gives `` `Mode: x` is not an initializer mode``.

The parameter types are:

| Type | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `AbsoluteDir`, `AbsolutePath` | The value must be absolute or have a root. A rooted path without a Windows drive, such as `/ws`, passes, so prompts stay portable. |
| `RepoKey` | The value must be a lowercase slug (`is_project_key`). |
| `Phase` | `none`, or digits with an optional `-tests` suffix. |
| `Enum` | `Target type` is `spec` or `plan`. `Source check` is `citations` or `refetch`. `Mode` is one of the six initializer modes. |
| `Path`, `Text` | Any non-empty value. |

Every value must be non-empty after trimming.

In the code that this page covers, only the unit tests call `parse_block`. The tests check that each struct renders a block that its own contract accepts. The engine does not parse the block again. The check at run time is the instruction in each prompt: return `ERROR: missing required parameter {label}` for an absent line, before the first tool call.

## The submit tools

Each agent ends its run with a call to its own submit tool, `submit_<agent>`. `AgentName::submit_tool_name` builds the name from the snake_case agent name, for example `submit_code_reviewer`. The engine reads structured data, not the final message (hard rule 4).

The description of the tool is the same for every agent: return the result, call the tool exactly once as the last action, after every file that the task asked for exists, and know that the engine reads only this call.

### The payloads

`submit_schema(agent)` returns the JSON schema of the payload. It comes from the type with `schemars`.

| Agent | Payload type | Main fields |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `explore` | `ExploreSubmit` | `research_path`, `scope_covered`, `findings_summary`, `sources_retrieved`, `open_questions`, `not_covered` |
| `generate-spec` | `GenerateSpecSubmit` | `spec_path`, `open_questions`, `external_evidence_rows`, `deliverables`, `requirements`, `summary` |
| `fact-check` | `FactCheckSubmit` | `verdict` (`PASS`, `FAIL`, `ERROR`), `target`, `findings` |
| `plan` | `PlanSubmit` | `spec_path`, `master_plan_path`, `phases`, `stakes`, `summary`, `step_count`, `requirement_coverage`, `clarifying_questions`, `new_projects` |
| `implementer` | `ImplementerSubmit` | `status`, `report_path`, `changed_files`, `summary`, `stuck`, `handoff` |
| `code-reviewer` | `CodeReviewerSubmit` | `findings`, `security_block`, `ledger_path`, `summary` |
| `execution-path-analyzer`, `write-test`, `prompt-generation` | `ReportSubmit` | `status`, `report_path`, `changed_files`, `summary`, `stuck` |
| `documentation` | `DocumentationSubmit` | See [Documentation books](documentation-books.md). |
| `system-architecture` | `ArchitectureSubmit` | See [Documentation books](documentation-books.md). |
| `initializer` | `InitializerSubmit` | `status`, `summary`, `files`, `result` (an object that depends on the mode), `stuck` |
| `quick-answer` | `QuickAnswerSubmit` | `answer` (Markdown), `sources` |
| `advisor` | `AdvisorSubmit` | `action` (`retry` or `escalate`), `guidance`, `reason` |

`SubmitStatus` has three values: `ok`, `stuck`, and `handoff`. `stuck` means that the agent hit its retry ceiling on the same failure. It carries `StuckInfo` with `diagnostic` (the exact failing output) and `need` (the fact or decision that the agent needs). `handoff` means that the agent needs a specialist. It carries `HandoffInfo` with `specialist` (always `prompt-generation` today), `request`, `target_files`, and `resume_instructions`.

A `ReviewFinding` has `severity` (`BLOCKER`, `HIGH`, `MEDIUM`, or `LOW`), `file`, `rule`, `description`, `fix`, and `guidance`. The `guidance` field is for a BLOCKER only: the risk, the failure scenario, and what to research, never a ready-made fix. `ReviewFinding::line` formats a finding as one line for the ledger and the fix prompts.

### Validation rules

`validate_submit(agent, input)` deserializes the payload into its type and adds these rules:

- **`code-reviewer`:** `security_block` must be true exactly when a `BLOCKER` finding is present.
- **`advisor`:** an action of `retry` needs a non-empty `guidance`.
- **`documentation` and `system-architecture`:** the book checks `check_documentation` and `check_architecture` must return no issues.

After that, `ostra_core::doc::check_submit` runs. For `explore`, `generate-spec`, and `plan` it reads the typed document at `research_path`, `spec_path`, or `master_plan_path` and rejects the submit when the document has a blocking fault. For a spec it also compares the counts in the payload with the document. For the initializer it checks the inventory submit. See [Typed pipeline documents](typed-documents.md).

### What happens when

The two executors run the checks in the same order but answer differently.

- **Native executor** (`Run::submit` in `crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs`): The loop first coerces JSON strings in the payload (see below). It then runs the policy check on the call and denies it on a rule. It then runs `validate_submit` and `check_submit`. On a fault the tool result is an error such as `The submit_x input is invalid: ... Fix it and call submit_x again.` or `... Nothing was recorded.` The agent can call the tool again.
- **Report file check:** if the status is `ok`, the spawn declares a `Report file:`, and that file does not exist, the call fails with `Write your report to <path> before you call <tool>, because the engine reads the report at that path.` The code reviewer is exempt, because its ledger is in the payload.
- **Harness executor** (`HarnessBridge::call_tool` in `crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/bridge.rs`): The bridge exposes the submit tool and the other Ostra tools over MCP. A run that was woken with a question must reply first. Then the bridge coerces the arguments, runs `validate_submit` and `check_submit`, and records the result once. A second call returns `A result was already recorded for this run. End your turn now.`
- **Wrong submit name on a harness:** a call to any other `submit_*` tool returns `Call <the right name> instead: that is this agent's submit tool.`
- **The status field:** on the native executor, `status` values `stuck` and `handoff` set the execution status. Any other value, or no value, means `ok`.

`coerce_json_strings` fixes a common model fault. If the schema allows an array or an object but the model sent a JSON string, the function parses the string. Both executors call it on submit payloads.

The session pipeline reads the stored result. [Sessions and the pipeline](sessions-and-pipeline.md) and [The engine runner](engine-runner.md) explain the next steps: review loops, fact-check loops, rescue, and the advisor.

## The repo brief

A model that starts with only a task spends its first tool calls on facts such as the build command and the skill paths. The repo brief gives those facts in the first message. The module `crates/ostra-agents/src/brief.rs` builds it from the project profile and the inventory.

The function `augment(first_message, input)` returns the first message, then a line `---`, then the brief. If the message already contains one of the five brief headings, `augment` returns it unchanged, so a re-render never stacks two briefs. If there is nothing to add, it returns the message unchanged.

The brief has these parts, in this order. A part appears only when it has content.

| Part | Heading | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repo brief | `## Repo brief for <agent>` | The project profile (`project.toml`) and the inventory. Only when the agent has sections and a profile exists. |
| Project instructions | `## Project instructions` | The files `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `AGENT.md` in the project root. |
| Created projects | `## Projects created in this session` | Projects that agents created in this session (rule O3), from the `ProjectCreate` facts. |
| Artifacts | `## Workspace artifacts` | The visible files in the workspace artifacts folder (rule W1). |
| Books | `## Workspace documentation` | The documentation books of the workspace (rule B5). |
| Instructions | `## Workspace instructions` | The custom instructions of the user: `instructions.all`, then the entry of the agent. |

The brief of a documentation run, like the one that this book was written from, has the sections Stack, Commands, and Module map.

### The sections for each agent

`sections(agent)` decides which profile sections an agent receives. The sections always render in this fixed order: Stack, Commands, Test types, Skills, Conventions, Review Rule Set, Module map.

| Agent | Sections |
| --- | --- |
| `implementer` | Commands, Skills, Conventions, Module map |
| `write-test` | Commands, Test types, Skills, Conventions, Module map |
| `code-reviewer` | Commands, Review Rule Set, Conventions, Skills |
| `execution-path-analyzer` | Commands, Test types, Module map |
| `explore` | Stack, Skills, Module map |
| `plan` | Stack, Commands, Skills, Module map |
| `generate-spec` | Stack, Module map |
| `documentation` | Stack, Commands, Module map |
| `system-architecture` | Stack, Module map |
| `fact-check` | Stack, Module map |
| `prompt-generation` | Skills |
| `quick-answer` | Stack, Commands, Skills, Module map |
| `advisor` | Stack, Commands, Skills, Module map |
| `initializer` | none |

The `initializer` gets no repo brief, because it creates the profile.

### What each section holds

- **Stack:** the stack, the build tool, and the test framework.
- **Commands:** the commands of the profile, with the rule to use these exact strings and to replace the `{MODULE}`, `{TEST}`, and `{PATH}` placeholders.
- **Test types:** for each test type, the command for the whole level and the command for one test. The test stage runs a whole level for regression and single tests while it writes. The section can add the paths that the type covers, a note, and a reports path.
- **Skills:** a list of the skills with name and path. The agent loads a skill by name with the skill tool or reads its file. It never searches for skills or guesses paths.
- **Conventions:** the naming rule, the immutability keyword, and the notes that the inventory tables do not state.
- **Review Rule Set:** the complete rule catalog of the profile, with ID, severity, and an `auto-fixable` mark. The text says that this is the whole set and not a summary.
- **Module map:** the rows of the module map whose path covers a path that the task names.

### Do not state a fact twice

The brief must not repeat what the inventory already says, and it must not hide a fact that only the profile has. `stated_in(haystack, value)` makes the choice. It compares text without regard to white space, so a value that wraps across lines or has padding in a table cell still counts as stated. A value of fewer than 3 characters counts as stated, because it is too short to tell anything. The brief leaves out a convention, a test note, or a skill description that the inventory text already contains.

The Review Rule Set does not use this test. For the reviewer, the catalog is the whole basis of judgment, and a partial catalog narrows the review without notice.

Routing settings never enter the brief, because they mean nothing to an agent and put tier names into its context.

### Select skills and module rows

The skill list keeps a skill only if its path is not empty. A skill of kind `convention` is always kept. `write-test` keeps other skills only when the name or the kind contains `test` or `spec`. `code-reviewer` keeps only conventions. All other agents keep every skill.

The module map is large in a big repo, so the brief omits it when the task names no path. `scope_hints(prompt)` finds the hints with the pattern `[\w.-]+/[\w./-]+` in the spawn block and the task text. It ignores hints of 3 characters or fewer and hints that contain `ostra-`. A module row matches when its path stem (the glob without `*` and the trailing `/`) has at least 3 characters and the stem and a hint contain each other.

### Limits of the brief

| Limit | Value | Behavior |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_BRIEF_CHARS` | 3600 characters | Cuts the whole repo brief part, which includes its heading and the inventory path sentence, then adds `(brief truncated; see the inventory for the rest)`. |
| `MAX_PROJECT_DOC_CHARS` | 12000 characters for each file | Cuts the file and adds `(truncated; read the file for the rest)`. |
| `MAX_SKILL_ROWS` | 16 | Lists at most 16 skills. |
| `MAX_MODULE_ROWS` | 10 | Lists at most 10 module rows. |
| Scope hints | 40 | Stops after 40 hints. |
| `MAX_BRIEF_BOOKS` | 20 | Lists 20 books and says how many more exist. |
| `MAX_BRIEF_ARTIFACTS` | 40 (in `ostra_core::artifacts`) | Lists 40 artifacts and says how many more exist. |

`build_brief` builds the repo brief part in this order:

1. It joins the heading, a fixed intro sentence, and the section bodies.
2. It appends the sentence that gives the path of the full `INVENTORY.md`. The sentence says that reading the file is a fallback and not the first step.
3. It counts the characters of the whole text. If the count is more than `MAX_BRIEF_CHARS` (3600), it keeps the first 3600 characters and adds the truncation note.

The inventory sentence is the last text before the cut, so the cut removes it first. A brief that Ostra cuts has no inventory path, and the end of its last section can be missing. Reading `INVENTORY.md` is a fallback only when the brief has 3600 characters or fewer, because only then the path is in the brief. The truncation note names the inventory but gives no path. In that case, the agent must find the file at `.ostra/INVENTORY.md` in the repo root.

The cut applies to the repo brief part only. The project instruction files, the artifacts, the books, and the instructions have their own limits in the table.

### Project instruction files

`project_docs(repo_root)` reads the agent instruction files of the project root. It skips a file that is empty, a file that links to a file already read, and a file that has the same text as one already read, because repos often ship `AGENTS.md` as a link to `CLAUDE.md`. The brief tells the agent to follow these files unless they conflict with its own rules, which win.

### Artifacts, books, and instructions

- The artifacts part lists each file with its size in bytes. It tells the agent to read the files that bear on the task and not to write in the folder, because the folder belongs to the user. An artifact named `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` is a skill.
- The books part lists each book with its `index.md`, its projects, its section count, and whether it has a system architecture. If the agent has the `docs_search` capability, the factory sets `search_tool` to the name of that tool for the executor, and the text tells the agent to search the books before it reads code. Otherwise the text tells it to read the sections that bear on the task. The text also warns the agent to check what it finds against the code, because a book describes the code when it was written. See [Documentation books](documentation-books.md).
- The instructions part holds the custom instructions of the user. The factory adds the absolute paths of tagged files and artifacts to the text (rule W3), so that every executor can read them. A tag that names a hidden or missing artifact resolves to nothing.

### What happens when

- **The project has no profile:** the repo brief part is absent. The other parts still appear.
- **The profile section is empty:** the section is absent. If all sections are empty, the repo brief part is absent.
- **The repo brief part is more than 3600 characters:** Ostra keeps the first 3600 characters and adds the truncation note. The inventory path sentence is at the end, so the brief loses it.
- **The repo brief part is 3600 characters or fewer:** the brief ends with the inventory path, and the agent can read `INVENTORY.md` as a fallback.
- **The message already has a brief:** `augment` returns it unchanged.
- **The task names no path:** the module map is absent.
- **A project was created in this session and has no inventory yet:** its facts come from the `ProjectCreate` call, because Ostra initializes the project right after it is created and before other work runs in it.
