## What this page does not guarantee

- The prompt text controls the model. The block, the submit schema, and the checks catch a wrong shape, but not a wrong answer.
- `parse_block` checks the form of a line, not its truth. A path in a `Phase file:` line can point to a file that does not exist.
- The repo brief is a copy of the profile at the time of the spawn. A later change to `project.toml` does not reach a run that already started.
- A cut repo brief can lose its last sections and its inventory path. The agent then reads the other files or the code.

sections.title: Executors: native loop and harness CLIs
sections.summary: How Ostra runs one agent: the `Executor` trait, the native model loop with its limits, and the harness executor that runs Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, or Antigravity in a terminal behind a hook bridge.
sections.body:
## Why two executors exist

An agent run needs a part that talks to a model, runs the tool calls of the model, and returns one structured result. Ostra has two such parts. The native executor calls a model API with an API key and runs the tools itself. The harness executor starts an installed CLI in a terminal and routes each tool call of that CLI through Ostra. Both parts return the same `ExecutionResult`, so the engine does not need to know which one ran.

This page covers these topics:

- The `Executor` trait and the types that the engine and an executor share.
- The native loop: turns, compaction, token continues, and limits.
- The harness executor: launch plans, the PTY, the adapters for `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, and `agy`, the hook bridge, and the MCP stdio shim.
- How a harness run ends, and how launch and sign-in failures show in the result.
- The harness setup check, the install terminal, and the login terminal.

The page stops at two borders. [Policy engine](policy.md) owns the rules that allow or deny a tool call. [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md) owns the kernel boundary under agent commands. The page says where each executor calls them, but not how they decide.

## The Executor contract

The `Executor` trait in [`crates/ostra-core/src/exec.rs`](../crates/ostra-core/src/exec.rs) has one method. The engine calls it once for each agent run.

```rust
#[async_trait::async_trait]
pub trait Executor: Send + Sync {
    async fn run(
        &self,
        spec: ExecutionSpec,
        host: Arc<dyn ExecutionHost>,
        cancel: CancellationToken,
    ) -> ExecutionResult;
}
```

The trait lives in `ostra-core`, so the engine, the two executors, and the server all depend on one small contract. The engine has no dependency on the executor crates. See [Ostra at a glance](overview.md).

### What the engine passes in

`ExecutionSpec` holds everything that one run needs.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | The `ExecutionId` of the run. |
| `agent` | The `AgentName` of the agent. |
| `route` | The `ResolvedRoute`: the executor, the model, and the tier. |
| `effort` | The `Effort` level for the model. |
| `system_prompt` | The agent prompt, rendered for the tool names of this executor. |
| `first_message` | The spawn block, the repo brief, and the custom instructions. |
| `capabilities` | The `Capability` list of the agent. It decides which tools the run gets. |
| `submit_schema` | The input schema of the `submit_<agent>` tool. A null value selects the default schema. |
| `timeout_secs` | The time budget of the run. It comes from `timeout_seconds` in the agent definition. |
| `ctx` | The `ExecContext` that the policy layer needs: roots, session dirs, permission mode, rules, sandbox choices, and the flags `answer_only` and `owes_reply`. |
| `resume` | A `ResumeInfo` when the run continues an earlier run. |
| `harness_session_id` | A session id that Claude Code and Grok Build accept up front. |

See [Agents, prompts, and the spawn contract](agents-and-prompts.md) for how the engine builds the prompt and the first message.

### What the executor calls back

The engine implements `ExecutionHost`. An executor uses it for these callbacks:

- `emit(delta)` streams one `ExecutionDelta` to the Activity view and to storage. The variants are `Text`, `Thinking`, `ToolCall`, `Policy`, `ToolOutput`, `ToolResult`, `Usage`, `Turn`, `Status`, `NativeSessionId`, `Egress`, and `Decoy`.
- `ask_permission(call, reason, rule)` waits for the answer of the browser. Under YOLO it answers at once.
- `record_message(role, content)` stores one transcript message of a native run, so a resume can continue from it.
- `transcript(execution)` returns the stored messages of an earlier run.
- `yolo()` tells whether the session is under YOLO now. The user can toggle it during a run.
- `wait_for_wake()` holds a harness run that asked another subagent. It returns `None` when no message will come.

### What the executor returns

`ExecutionResult` has the fields `status`, `submit`, `final_text`, `usage`, `native_session_id`, and `error`. The `submit` field holds the payload of the `submit_<agent>` call. `ExecutionStatus` has nine values:

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `running` | The run has not ended. It is the only value that is not terminal. |
| `ok` | The run ended and the agent reported success. |
| `stuck` | The agent reported `status: stuck` in its submit call. |
| `handoff` | The agent reported `status: handoff` in its submit call. |
| `waiting` | The run asked another subagent and waits for the answer. |
| `error` | The run failed. `error` holds the text. |
| `denied` | The policy denied the run. |
| `interrupted` | A restart ended the run. |
| `cancelled` | The user or the engine cancelled the run. |

The `Usage` struct counts `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `cache_read_tokens`, `cache_write_tokens`, `cache_write_1h_tokens`, `cost_usd`, `tool_calls`, `build_ms`, and `context_tokens`. `Usage::add` sums all fields except `context_tokens`. That field keeps the latest value, because it is the size of the latest request. See [Model providers, tiers, and cost](providers-and-cost.md) for the cost values.

### Executor kinds and streams

`ExecutorKind` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/executor.rs`](../crates/ostra-core/src/executor.rs) is `Native` or `Harness(HarnessKind)`. `HarnessKind` has four values: `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, and `agy`. The text form is `native` or `harness:<name>`. The parser also accepts `antigravity` as a name for `agy`.

| Harness | Display name |
| --- | --- |
| `claude` | Claude Code |
| `codex` | Codex |
| `grok` | Grok Build |
| `agy` | Antigravity |

`ExecutorKind::tier_table` returns the key of the table in `[tiers.<table>]`: `native` or the harness name. `ExecutorKind::stream` returns `ExecStream::Activity` for the native executor and `ExecStream::Terminal` for every harness. The browser shows an Activity feed for the first and a live terminal for the second.

The server picks the executor in `ServerServices::executor` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs`](../crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs). It returns the shared `NativeExecutor` for `Native`. It returns a wrapped `HarnessExecutor` for `Harness`.

## The native loop

The native executor is `NativeExecutor` in [`crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs`](../crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs). It runs one agent against a provider API in a loop. In this page, a turn is one request to the model and its response. The agent ends the run with its `submit_<agent>` call.

### Build the executor

`NativeExecutor::new` takes the `Providers`, a `SkillResolver`, and an optional `CodeNav`. The builder methods `with_mcp`, `with_manage`, and `with_coord` add the connectors for workspace MCP tools, management tools, and the coordination tools. The server builds one executor at start in `crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs` and shares it.

### Start of a run

The `run` method does these steps:

1. It makes a child of the cancel token and a time budget of `spec.timeout_secs`, at least 1 second.
2. It builds a `Run` and races the run against the cancel token and the time budget.
3. The `Run::execute` method finds the provider for `spec.route.model`. If the provider has no key, the run fails with the text "The `<provider>` provider has no API key. Set its key in the environment or the OS keychain."
4. It opens the MCP connector, which adds the tools of the workspace MCP servers.
5. It builds the `ExecutionPolicy` from the project profile commands: `build`, `test`, `test_one`, `lint`, and `typecheck`. The policy uses them to tell build and test commands from other commands.
6. It builds the `ToolEnv` and calls `sandbox_for` to get the sandbox decision (see below).
7. It builds the tool list and the first messages.
8. It runs the turn loop.

### The sandbox decision of a run

The run reads the sandbox settings fresh from `config.toml`, so a change applies to the next run. The decision has three results:

- **`Sandbox::On`.** The run makes a scratch directory, an egress proxy, and decoy files, and gives them to the `ToolEnv`. The run removes the scratch directory when it ends, even when the run future is dropped.
- **`Sandbox::Off(Some(warning))`.** This result happens in mode `auto` when the machine has no available backend. The run emits a `Status` delta with the text "Bash runs without a sandbox." and the warning. It also logs the warning once for each server process.
- **`Sandbox::Off(None)`.** This result happens in mode `off`. The function `decide` returns `Unsandboxed(None)` in [`crates/ostra-sandbox/src/backend.rs`](../crates/ostra-sandbox/src/backend.rs) (line 140), and the run emits nothing.

If the config requires a sandbox that the machine cannot give, `sandbox_for` returns an error and the run fails before the first turn. See [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md) for the rule that picks the result.

### The tool list

The loop sends these tools to the model:

- The tools that `ostra_tools::definitions` returns for the `capabilities` of the agent. See [Native tools](tools.md).
- The `Document` tool, when the agent has the `Document` capability.
- The tools of the workspace MCP servers.
- The `submit_<agent>` tool. It is the last tool and has `cache: true`. It uses `spec.submit_schema` when that value is not null.

The provider can run web search and web fetch on its own servers. The loop asks for web search only when the provider offers it and the agent wants it. It asks for server web fetch only when the provider offers it and the agent has the `WebFetch` capability. In that case, the loop removes the local `WebFetch` tool.

The system prompt is sent as one cached system block. The request uses `ToolChoice::Auto` and the effort of the spec. The loop sets `max_tokens` to the full output limit of the model from the models.dev catalog. It uses `DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT` when the catalog does not list the model. The code comment gives the reason: the user chose the effort knowing what it costs, so no effort level is cut short by the request.

### What one turn does

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Start of turn"] --> B{"Cancelled?"}
  B -- yes --> Z1["Return cancelled"]
  B -- no --> C{"Context at 95 percent of window?"}
  C -- yes --> D["Compact the conversation"]
  C -- no --> E["Send the chat request"]
  D --> E
  E --> F{"Stop reason"}
  F -- refusal --> Z2["Return error"]
  F -- "max tokens, no tool call" --> G["Add a continue message, 3 times at most"]
  G --> A
  F -- "no tool call" --> H["Remind once, then return ok"]
  H --> A
  F -- "tool calls" --> I["Run the tools through the policy"]
  I --> J{"Submit accepted?"}
  J -- yes --> Z3["Return the result"]
  J -- no --> A
```

Each turn does these steps in order:

1. Return `cancelled` if the cancel token fired.
2. Compact the conversation when it is nearly full (see the next part).
3. Send the request with the full message list. The loop streams text and thinking deltas to the host through a `Coalescer`.
4. Add the usage of the response. The loop emits a `Turn` delta with the usage of this response and its tool call ids. It then emits a `Usage` delta with the running total.
5. Store the assistant message with `record_message`.
6. Look at the stop reason.
7. Run the tool calls, if any, and store the results as one user message.

The `Coalescer` collects streamed text. It sends a delta when the buffer reaches 160 bytes (`FLUSH_AT`), when the text ends with a newline, or when the stream switches between text and thinking. Without it, the Activity log gets one row for each token.

The stop reason decides what happens next:

- `PauseTurn`: the loop starts the next turn at once.
- `Refusal`: the run fails with "The model refused to continue" and the refusal category when there is one.
- `MaxTokens` with no tool call: the loop adds the user message "You reached the output limit. Continue from exactly where you stopped." It does this at most `MAX_TOKEN_CONTINUES` times. The next failure ends the run with "The model kept hitting its output limit without finishing."
- No tool call, first time: the loop adds a reminder to call the submit tool. The text says that the engine reads only that call, so a result in plain text is lost. If the run owes a reply to another subagent, the reminder tells the model to call `SubagentReply` instead.
- No tool call, second time: the loop returns status `ok` with `final_text` and no `submit`. The engine then treats the run as an agent that ended without a result.
- Tool calls: the loop runs them.

### How the loop runs tool calls

The loop reads the calls of one response in order and handles each by its kind.

| Kind | Which calls | What the loop does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concurrent group | `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `WebFetch`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch`, `Skill`, and each code navigation tool | The loop runs a run of adjacent calls of this kind at the same time with `join_all`. Read-only calls cannot conflict. |
| Submit | The `submit_<agent>` call | The loop checks it (see below). If it passes, the run ends. |
| Coordination | `SubagentList`, `SubagentAsk`, `SubagentReply` | The loop runs the call alone. The result can end the run (see below). |
| Sequential | Every other call | The loop runs the call alone, in order. |

A call with the name `submit_<agent>` is checked in these steps. Each failing step returns an error result to the model, and the run goes on:

1. The input must be valid JSON. The loop marks unreadable input with the key `__invalid_json`.
2. The policy must not deny the call.
3. `validate_submit` must accept the input against the submit schema.
4. `doc::check_submit` must accept the typed document in the input. The error text ends with "Nothing was recorded."
5. If the status is `ok` and the agent has a report file, that file must exist. The `CodeReviewer` agent is exempt. The error text tells the agent to write the report first, because the engine reads the report at that path.

After a good submit call, every other call in the same response gets the result "Not run: the run ended with the submit call." The status of the result comes from the `status` field of the payload: `stuck` gives `stuck`, `handoff` gives `handoff`, and any other value gives `ok`.

A coordination call returns a `RunEnd` value. `Continue` keeps the loop going. `Wait` ends the loop with status `waiting`, because a run that asked another subagent waits for the answer. `Finish` ends the loop with status `ok`, because a consult run that answered is done. In both cases, the other calls of the response get "Not run: the run stopped to wait for another subagent." See [Subagent coordination](subagent-coordination.md).

For each other tool call, `tool_end` does these steps:

1. It turns the call into its canonical form, so the policy, the user, and the tool all see the same paths and the same working directory.
2. It emits `ToolCall`, counts the call in `Usage.tool_calls`, and checks the input.
3. It asks the policy, and emits the `Policy` delta. A deny returns an error result with the layer and the rule. An ask waits for `host.ask_permission`. The answer `AllowOnce` lets the call run. The answer `AlwaysInWorkspace` also adds a session allow rule when the policy suggests one. The answer `Deny` returns an error result that tells the model to go on without the call.
4. It runs `ostra_tools::execute` with a live output callback that emits `ToolOutput` deltas.
5. After a `Bash` call, it repairs git directories where a planted `commondir` points out of the repository. Each repair adds a note to the result and a `git-metadata` denial, which counts as a containment signal. It also adds the run time to `Usage.build_ms` when the command is a build or test command.
6. It lets the policy observe the outcome. The policy can add notes. It can also ask for lesson recall: the loop then searches the memory database (5 lessons at most) and adds the lessons to the result.
7. It emits `ToolResult`. The Activity output is cut to `EMIT_LIMIT`. The model gets the full text.

### Compaction

Long runs fill the context window of the model. The loop compacts the conversation before a request that exceeds the window. The loop estimates the size of the next request as the context of the last response plus an estimate for the new messages. The estimate is 4 characters for each token.

Compaction starts when all these conditions are true:

- The estimate is at least `COMPACT_AT` (0.95) of the context window.
- The last message is a user message. A user message last means that no tool call is open, and compaction needs that.
- The last compaction did not fail, or the context grew by at least 2 percent of the window since it failed (`COMPACT_RETRY_GROWTH`). Each try sends the whole conversation, so the loop waits for growth.

The context window comes from the models.dev catalog. The loop uses `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` (200,000 tokens) when the catalog does not list the model.

The loop calls `provider.compact` with `COMPACT_INSTRUCTIONS`. The instructions ask for a summary that keeps the task and each requirement, the files read, the files changed, the decisions, the failed commands, the work that is left, and the next step. The loop adds the usage of the compaction call to the run. Three outcomes are possible:

- The provider returns a window. The loop replaces the messages with it and adds the user message `AFTER_COMPACTION`. That message says that earlier tool results are gone, so the model must read a file again when it needs the content. The loop stores the new window as a `compaction` record through `record_message`.
- The provider returns no summary. The run continues with the full conversation, and the loop remembers the size of this failure.
- The call fails. The loop emits "Compaction failed, so the run continues without it" and remembers the size. A cancel during compaction ends the run as `cancelled`.

### Resume of a native run

When `spec.resume` is set, the loop rebuilds the messages from the stored transcript of the earlier run. `stored_messages` merges adjacent messages of one role. A `compaction` record replaces everything before it. `resume_turn` adds a `tool_result` with the text "Interrupted: this call did not finish." for each tool call that the interruption left open. Then it adds the resume note, or the default text "The previous run was interrupted. Continue from where it stopped." If the stored transcript is empty, the loop starts again from the first message.

Rule P2 decides what the loop stores. If the run resumes in place (`resume.from == spec.id`), the stored transcript already belongs to this run, so the loop stores only the new turn. The replayed prefix then matches the prompt cache. In any other case, the loop stores all messages again.

### Time limit and cancel

The run races its future against the cancel token and the time budget. On either event, the loop cancels its inner token and waits `CLEANUP_GRACE` (3 seconds) for the tools to stop. It then returns the result. A cancel gives `cancelled` and the status text "Cancelled." A timeout gives `error` with the text "timed out after N s" and a status text. The result keeps the usage counted so far.

### Native limits

| Name | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_TURNS` | 400 | Model turns in one run. The run then fails with "The run passed 400 model turns without calling `submit_<agent>`." |
| `MAX_TOKEN_CONTINUES` | 3 | Continue messages after the model hits its output limit with no tool call. |
| `COMPACT_AT` | 0.95 | Share of the context window that starts compaction. |
| `COMPACT_RETRY_GROWTH` | 0.02 | Growth of the context, as a share of the window, before a new try after a failed compaction. |
| `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` | 200,000 tokens | Window for a model that the catalog does not list. |
| `DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT` | 32,000 tokens | Output limit for a model that the catalog does not list. |
| `EMIT_LIMIT` | 8 KiB | Size of tool output in the Activity feed. The model gets the full text. |
| `CLEANUP_GRACE` | 3 seconds | Time that a cancelled or timed-out run gets to stop its tools. |
| `Coalescer::FLUSH_AT` | 160 bytes | Size of buffered text that triggers a delta. |
| `timeout_secs` | From the agent definition | Time budget of the whole run, at least 1 second. |

### What happens when (native)

- **The provider has no key.** The run fails before the first turn with the text that names the provider.
- **The model call fails.** The run fails with "The model call failed" and the provider error. The loop has no retry of its own. See [Model providers, tiers, and cost](providers-and-cost.md) for the retry policy of the clients.
- **The model asks for a tool that the policy denies.** The model gets an error result with the layer and the rule. The run goes on.
- **The user denies an ask.** The model gets an error result and can go on without the call.
- **The model writes text and never calls submit.** The loop reminds it once. After the second text-only turn, the run returns `ok` with no `submit`.
- **The model calls submit with an invalid payload.** The model gets the error and calls again. The turns still count toward `MAX_TURNS`.
- **The conversation is long.** The loop compacts at 95 percent of the window.
- **The user cancels.** The run returns `cancelled` after at most 3 seconds of cleanup.
- **The server restarts.** The engine marks the run as `interrupted`. A later resume rebuilds the messages from the stored transcript. See [The engine runner, recovery, and control](engine-runner.md).

## The harness executor

The harness executor is `HarnessExecutor` in [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/executor.rs`](../crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/executor.rs). It runs one agent in an installed CLI under a PTY (a pseudo terminal). The CLI uses its own model login, its own loop, and its own tools. Ostra cannot see inside that loop. Ostra gets control at two points: each hook event that the CLI sends before and after a tool call, and each tool call that the CLI makes to the Ostra MCP server.

This design has one reason. A harness run must obey the same guards as a native run, and the result must reach the engine in the same shape. The hook bridge enforces the guards. The submit call through the MCP shim gives the result.

### Parts of a harness run

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Exec as HarnessExecutor
  participant PTY as PtySession
  participant CLI as Harness CLI
  participant Hook as ostra hook
  participant Shim as ostra mcp-stdio
  participant Bridge as HarnessBridge
  participant Svc as ServerBridge
  Exec->>PTY: spawn(plan)
  PTY->>CLI: start the program
  CLI->>Hook: PreToolUse payload on stdin
  Hook->>Bridge: POST /internal/policy
  Bridge->>Svc: policy_check(call)
  Svc-->>Bridge: Allow, Deny, or Ask
  Bridge-->>Hook: PolicyResponse
  Hook-->>CLI: decision JSON on stdout
  CLI->>Shim: tools/call submit_agent
  Shim->>Bridge: POST /internal/mcp
  Bridge->>Bridge: record_submit(args)
  Bridge-->>Shim: McpResponse
  Shim-->>CLI: Recorded
  CLI->>Hook: Stop payload
  Hook->>Bridge: POST /internal/policy
  Exec->>PTY: terminate(3 s)
```

The `ostra` binary serves the two subprocesses: `ostra hook` and `ostra mcp-stdio`. See [Install, run, and the command line](install-and-run.md). The server serves the two routes `/internal/policy` and `/internal/mcp`. See [Server, REST API, and WebSocket](server-and-api.md).

### The steps of `HarnessExecutor::run`

1. Check that the route is a harness route. A native route returns an error.
2. Register the run in the `LiveRegistry`. This makes the per-run token.
3. Call `launch` to build the plan, write the files, wrap the command in the sandbox, and spawn the PTY. A failure here gives an error result.
4. Put the PTY in the `PtyRegistry`, so the Terminal tab can attach.
5. Start the usage follower as a task.
6. Call `supervise` until the run ends with an `End` value.
7. Repair git directories one more time, stop the follower, and wait for it. This stops a late usage reading from overwriting the final result.
8. On a cancel, press Esc in the CLI and wait 400 ms, so the CLI saves its session whole and a resume can use it.
9. Read the screen text, then call `pty.terminate` with a 3-second grace period.
10. Remove the PTY from the registry and clean the per-run directory. For Codex, also remove the profile file.
11. Turn the `End` value into an `ExecutionResult` with `outcome::result`.
12. Remove the run from the `LiveRegistry`. The token stops working at this point.

### The server wrapper

The server wraps the executor in `Wrapped` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs`](../crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs). Before the harness starts, `Wrapped::run` opens the MCP connector. The reason is in the code comment: the CLI lists the Ostra MCP tools once at startup. The wrapper then builds a `Running` record with the `ExecutionPolicy`, the `ToolEnv`, and the host, and puts it in a map. The hook bridge reads this map. The wrapper removes the record when the run returns.

`HarnessRuntime::new` in the same file makes the `LiveRegistry`, the `PtyRegistry`, and the `HarnessBridge`. The executor itself is made on first use, in `HarnessRuntime::inner`. That method sets the binary path, the server URL, and the bridge socket in a `HarnessExecutorConfig`. The home directory, `idle_nudge`, `cols`, and `rows` keep the defaults of `HarnessExecutorConfig::new`.

`HarnessExecutor::set_global` ([`executor.rs`](../crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/executor.rs), line 258) replaces only the `global: GlobalConfig` field. The binary path, the server URL, the bridge socket, the home directory, `idle_nudge`, `cols`, and `rows` stay as `inner` set them. `inner` calls `set_global` on each use, so a change of settings applies to the next run.

## Launch plans for each harness

[`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/launch.rs`](../crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/launch.rs) builds a `LaunchPlan` for each harness. The plan holds the program, the arguments, the environment, the working directory, files to write, links to create, and the session id that Ostra chose. The plan makes sure that every hook event reaches `ostra hook` and that the Ostra tools come from `ostra mcp-stdio`. The code comment lists the CLI versions that the flags were checked against: claude 2.1.280, codex 0.153.4, grok 1.0.30, and agy 1.2.6.

### What every plan does

- The working directory is the repo root of the run.
- The environment has `OSTRA_URL`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_TOKEN`, and `OSTRA_HARNESS`. The hook and shim processes read them. The agent environment variables from `ostra_core::git::agent_env` are added too.
- `plan` removes the credential variables of the Ostra environment from the CLI environment. It keeps the variables that the CLI needs to sign in: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, and `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` for Claude Code, `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_BASE_URL` for Codex, and `GEMINI_API_KEY` and `GOOGLE_API_KEY` for Antigravity. Grok Build keeps none. Commands that the agent runs inside the CLI can still read the kept variables.
- The PTY removes the variables in `PARENT_SESSION_ENV`, such as `CLAUDECODE` and `CODEX_THREAD_ID`. If a child kept them, it runs as a nested child of the session that started Ostra. Claude Code does not save such a session, so a resume fails.
- The PTY sets `TERM` to `xterm-256color` and `COLORTERM` to `truecolor`.
- `materialize` writes the plan files with owner-only permission, because the Grok config holds the bridge token. It creates the links only when no file exists at the link path.
- A first message longer than `MAX_ARG_PROMPT` (96 KiB) goes into `first-message.md` in the run directory. The argument then tells the CLI to read that file before its first other tool call.
- On a resume, the prompt is the resume note, or the default text that tells the agent to check what is done and then call its submit tool. In an inspect run, the CLI gets no prompt.
- The hook timeout is `HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECS`, 86,400 seconds, because a permission ask waits for the user and must not time out first.
- The run directory is `harness_execution_dir(session_root, execution_id)`.

### Differences between the harnesses

| Harness | Hooks and MCP | Notable flags | Session id |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `claude` | A settings file `claude-settings.json` with hooks `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `Stop`, and `SessionStart`. An MCP file `claude-mcp.json` with a stdio server. | `--setting-sources user` and `--strict-mcp-config`, so only user settings and the Ostra MCP config load. `--append-system-prompt-file`, `--add-dir` for the session dir, `--disallowed-tools Agent,Task,AskUserQuestion,EnterPlanMode,ExitPlanMode`, `--tools` from the capabilities plus `ToolSearch`, `--permission-mode default`, `--model`, and `--effort` (at most `max`). | Ostra chooses one: `--session-id`, or `--resume` on a resume. |
| `codex` | `-c hooks.*` and `-c mcp_servers.ostra.*` options, with `developer_instructions` for the prompt. | `check_for_update_on_startup=false`, `--disable multi_agent`, `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust`, `-C`, `-m`, and `model_reasoning_effort` (at most `xhigh`). A `-p` profile that marks the repo untrusted. | None up front. The hook payload reports it. A resume uses `resume <id>`. |
| `grok` | A per-run `GROK_HOME` with its own `config.toml` that holds the hooks, the MCP server, and an `env` table. | `--leader-socket`, `--cwd`, `--no-subagents`, `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`, `--rules` (the system prompt), `-m`, and `--reasoning-effort` (at most `high`). The env has `GROK_SUBAGENTS=0`. | Ostra chooses one: `--session-id`, or `--resume`. |
| `agy` | A global plugin and a global MCP registration, installed once (see the setup part). | `--agent ostra-<agent>`, `--add-dir`, `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, `--model`, `--effort` (at most `high`), and the prompt with `-i`. | None up front. A resume uses `--conversation <id>`. |

Three harness details need more words.

**Claude Code.** The hook settings file also sets `disableAllHooks` to `false`. Flag settings win over a user settings file, so the user cannot switch off the Ostra hooks. When the run is in the Ostra sandbox, the file sets `sandbox.enabled` to `false`, because macOS cannot nest Seatbelt sandboxes. The tool list adds `ToolSearch`. The code comment says that interactive Claude Code connects MCP servers after startup and shows their tools only as deferred tools. Without `ToolSearch`, the `mcp__ostra__*` tools never reach the model.

**Codex.** Codex reads folder trust only from config files, not from `-c`. Ostra writes a profile file `ostra-restricted-<execution>.config.toml` in `CODEX_HOME` (default `~/.codex`). The profile marks the repo and each parent folder up to the git root as `untrusted`. Codex then opens the folder restricted: its own `.codex/` config, hooks, and exec policies stay off, and the saved trust of the user does not change. If `[harness.codex].args` has `-p` or `--profile`, Ostra writes no profile. The executor deletes the profile file at the end of the run.

**Grok Build.** The per-run `GROK_HOME` is a folder of symbolic links to the entries of the real `GROK_HOME` (default `~/.grok`). It skips `config.toml`, `trusted_folders.toml`, `leader.sock`, entries that start with `leader-`, and entries that end with `.lock`. The skipped files are those that Ostra rewrites or that must not be shared, so that the session runs its own leader and reads the hooks of this run. The new `config.toml` is the user config without any `[mcp_servers.ostra]` table, plus the Ostra hooks and server. The new `trusted_folders.toml` adds the session dir only. The repo is trusted only if the user trusted it in Grok.

**Antigravity.** Antigravity reads hooks and MCP servers only from global config. Ostra installs one integration that does nothing unless `$OSTRA_EXECUTION` is set. The plan writes only the agent file `ostra-<agent>.md` under the plugin directory. The file has the system prompt as instructions, the `tools:` list, `subagent: false`, `hidden: true`, and `inheritMcp: true`. See the setup part.

The `extra_args` of each plan come from `[harness.<name>].args` in `config.toml`, and the program comes from `[harness.<name>].command`. See [Configuration reference](configuration.md).

## The PTY

`PtySession` in [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/pty.rs`](../crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/pty.rs) runs the CLI in a pseudo terminal and mirrors the screen. A `vt100` parser holds the screen. A browser that attaches in the middle of a run receives the current screen with its scrollback, and then every new output chunk.

### How the PTY works

- Three threads serve one session: a reader, a writer, and a waiter. The reader parses output, copies it to the broadcast channel and the log, and answers terminal queries. The waiter publishes the exit code on a `watch` channel.
- Ostra alone answers the terminal queries that a full screen program sends: cursor position, status, device attributes, text colors, the keyboard protocol, the program version, and mode queries. The browsers mute their own replies. Thus any number of viewers, or none, gives the CLI exactly one answer.
- The `write` method puts bytes in a queue of `WRITE_QUEUE` (256) entries. If the CLI stops reading and the queue is full, `write` returns an error and does not block the caller.
- The `type_line` method pastes the text in bracketed paste mode, waits 150 ms, and presses Enter. Bracketed paste keeps a full screen program from treating a newline in the text as a submit.
- A viewer that falls more than `STREAM_BUFFER` (256) chunks behind is resynced from a fresh snapshot.
- The `terminate` method asks the CLI to exit and kills its process tree when it is still alive after the grace period. It then kills the members of the sandbox, even when the CLI has exited. On Unix, the request is `SIGTERM` to the process group. On Windows, it closes the pseudoconsole.

### PTY limits

These constants are in `pty.rs`:

| Name | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DEFAULT_COLS`, `DEFAULT_ROWS` | 120, 40 | Size of a harness terminal at start. |
| `MIN_COLS`, `MIN_ROWS` | 20, 5 | Smallest size. The `vt100` crate panics below this size. |
| `MAX_COLS`, `MAX_ROWS` | 1000, 500 | Largest size. |
| `SCROLLBACK` | 2000 lines | Scrollback of the screen model. |
| `WRITE_QUEUE` | 256 | Pending input writes. |
| `STREAM_BUFFER` | 256 | Output chunks that a viewer can fall behind. |

`TRANSCRIPT_CAP` (2 MiB) and `TermLog` are not in `pty.rs`. Both are in [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/term_log.rs`](../crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/term_log.rs) (`TRANSCRIPT_CAP` at line 12). `TermLog` writes the raw output to `terminal_transcript(session_root, execution_id)`, so the Terminal tab can replay an ended run. The replay shows at most `TRANSCRIPT_CAP` bytes of output.

The file can grow to twice `TRANSCRIPT_CAP`. Then `TermLog` rewrites it with the last `TRANSCRIPT_CAP` bytes. Writes stay appends and memory stays flat. The file is readable by its owner only, because harness output can hold secrets. A failed write stops the transcript, but the run goes on. A run that resumes under the same execution id adds to the file.

The `PtyRegistry` holds the live PTYs by execution id. The server uses it to forward browser input, resizes, and streams. See [Server, REST API, and WebSocket](server-and-api.md).

## The hook bridge

The hook bridge is the path that every tool call of a CLI takes before it runs. It has three parts: the `ostra hook` subprocess, the `/internal/policy` route, and `HarnessBridge::handle_policy` with its services.

### The hook subprocess

The CLI starts `ostra hook --execution <id> --harness <name> --event <event>` for each hook event. The command reads the payload on stdin, posts it to `/internal/policy` with the bearer token, and prints the answer to stdout. The `--execution` argument falls back to `$OSTRA_EXECUTION`, and `--harness` falls back to `$OSTRA_HARNESS`.

The subprocess fails closed. If the URL or the token is missing, or the server does not answer, or the answer is unreadable, a `PreToolUse` event gets a deny with the text "Stop and end your turn: Ostra could not check this call" and the reason. Other events print nothing. Only the Antigravity hook has no `--execution` argument, because that integration is global. Outside an Ostra run, with no `$OSTRA_EXECUTION`, the command does nothing and exits with 0.

The request has no timeout for `PreToolUse`, because an ask waits for the user. Other events time out after 60 seconds.

### The decision on a PreToolUse event

`handle_policy` does these steps:

1. Check the token against the `LiveRegistry` and ask `BridgeServices::authorize`. If either check fails, a `PreToolUse` event gets a deny that says the execution is not running under Ostra. Other events get `{}`.
2. Check that the harness of the hook is the harness of the execution.
3. Read the metadata with the adapter, and note the session id and the transcript path in the `LiveExecution`.
4. Parse the payload into a canonical `ToolCall`. The parse can refuse the call at once (see the adapter part).
5. Count the call, and run `decide`.

`decide` has these rules:

- A call to `submit_<other agent>` is denied with the name of the right submit tool.
- `policy_check` returns `Allow`, `Deny`, or `Ask`.
- On `Deny`, the model reads the reason first, then "(Ostra layer: rule)".
- On `Ask`, `resolve_ask` waits for the browser card or YOLO. An allowing answer gives `Allow`. A denying answer tells the model that the user denied the call.

The server side of the check is `ServerBridge` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs`](../crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs). It handles these cases:

- An unknown execution gets a deny from the guard `self-protection`.
- Workspace MCP tools and management tools pass the hook unchecked, because they reach the harness only through the Ostra MCP server. That server checks and logs the call when it runs it (Rules M2 and O1). Thus an ask reaches the user once.
- In an inspect run, every call gets a deny from the guard `read-only-session`.
- Otherwise the `ExecutionPolicy` of the run checks the call, with the YOLO state read at that moment.
- The server emits `ToolCall` and `Policy` deltas with a call id of the form `h<N>`. It skips this for tools that the MCP handler logs itself.

See [Policy engine](policy.md) for the guards and the permission rules.

### Other events

- `PostToolUse` and `PostToolUseFailure`: the bridge parses the outcome and calls `policy_observe`. The policy can return notes, and lesson recall adds lessons (5 at most). The adapter puts the notes in its response, so the model sees them. The server also reports each successful write to the file watcher, so the Files view updates live.
- `Stop`: the bridge calls `live.on_stop`, which can turn the stop back (see the next part).
- `SessionStart`, `PreInvocation`, and `PostInvocation`: the bridge marks activity and answers `{}`.

### The Stop rule

A CLI can end its turn with no submit call. `LiveExecution::on_stop` decides what to do:

| State at the Stop event | Verdict |
| --- | --- |
| An inspect run, or a run that waits for a wake message | Allow. |
| A submit is recorded | Allow, and set `stopped_after_submit`. |
| Fewer than `MAX_STOP_NUDGES` (2) stops without a submit | Block with the instruction `missing_submit_instruction`, or with the reply instruction when the run owes a reply. |
| Two nudges were already used | Allow, and set `gave_up`. |

The instruction tells the agent to call its submit tool before it stops, because a run that ends without it is recorded as failed. The CLI continues its turn when the hook blocks the stop. A third stop without a submit gives the end `GaveUp`.

### Tokens and the bridge socket

The `LiveRegistry` makes one token for each run: two random UUIDs in simple form, joined. The token dies when the registry removes the run. The comparison runs in constant time. The server adds a second check: the run must have a `Running` record. See [Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md).

On Unix, `serve_bridge_socket` serves the two internal routes on a Unix socket in the egress directory. It answers nothing else of the server. A sandbox with its own network reaches the bridge through this socket, so the sandbox cannot reach `/api`. The `bridge_socket` field of `HarnessExecutorConfig` holds its path. See [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md).

## The adapters

Each harness has its own hook payload and its own response format. An adapter in [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/adapters/`](../crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/adapters/mod.rs) turns the payload into a canonical `ToolCall` that uses the Claude Code tool names and input shapes. It also formats the decision in the exact shape that the CLI accepts. The `Adapter` trait has the methods `kind`, `meta`, `parse_pre`, `parse_post`, `pre_response`, `post_response`, and `stop_response`. The method `kind` returns the `HarnessKind` of the adapter. `for_harness` returns the adapter of a `HarnessKind`.

### Rules for all adapters

- A call to a spawn tool (`Task`, `Agent`, `spawn_agent`, and similar names) is refused with `LEAF_REFUSAL`. Every Ostra agent is a leaf. A delegated task runs outside the guards, and its result never reaches the engine.
- A call to an ask tool (`AskUserQuestion`, `request_user_input`, and similar names) is refused with `ASK_REFUSAL`. Nobody watches the terminal for questions. Ostra asks the user from the gate of the pipeline.
- `ostra_mcp_tool` and `canonical_ostra_tool` map the name of an Ostra MCP tool, in each spelling of the harnesses (`mcp__ostra__report`, `ostra__report`, and others), to the native name: `report` to `Report`, `memory_recall` to `MemoryRecall`, `code_callers` to `CodeCallers`, and so on. `submit_*` keeps its name. A tool of a workspace MCP server becomes `mcp__<server>__<tool>`.
- The adapter clips the tool output to `MAX_OUTCOME_CHARS` (64 KiB) before it goes to the policy. It reads an exit code from the text with `exit_code_from`, because each harness reports the code in its own words. A Bash call with no code gets 1 when the harness flagged an error, else 0.

### Differences between the adapters

| Harness | Payload | Special rules | Response shape |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `claude` | snake_case, with the Claude names already | `MultiEdit` and `NotebookEdit` become `Edit`. `LS` becomes `Glob`. `PowerShell` stays an opaque shell. | `hookSpecificOutput` with `permissionDecision`. A top-level `overwrite` field fails the hook schema, so the adapter never sends one. |
| `codex` | `exec_command`, `shell`, and `local_shell` carry a command string or array | The array is quoted word by word, so the policy sees the words that Codex runs. `apply_patch` becomes `ApplyPatch`. On Windows, a command that does not start `bash` or `sh` becomes `PowerShell`. | The schema rejects `allow` without `updatedInput` and rejects `ask`, so an allowed call answers `{}`. Codex gives hooks the raw output without an exit status, so a missing code stays unknown. |
| `grok` | camelCase with snake_case aliases | `use_tool` unwraps to the inner tool. A payload with `toolInputTruncated` is refused, because Grok cuts input over 128 KiB and the input cannot be judged. | Claude shape. Grok clips a reason to 256 characters (`GROK_REASON_MAX`), so `fit_reason` keeps the head and the final sentence. |
| `agy` | The call is nested in `toolCall.{name,args}` with PascalCase arguments. `call_mcp_tool` carries the server name. | The `PostToolUse` payload has no tool result, so the outcome has `result_known: false`. | The hook output is validated against a proto. An unknown field discards the whole response, so `PreToolUse` answers only `decision` and `reason`, and `PostToolUse` answers `{}`. |

## The MCP stdio shim

The CLI gets the Ostra tools from an MCP server named `ostra`. The server is the `ostra mcp-stdio` subprocess. It reads JSON-RPC messages from stdin, line by line. A line can hold one message or an array. The shim forwards each message to `/internal/mcp` with the bearer token and writes the reply to stdout. It handles each message in its own task, so a slow tool call does not block the others.

The server side is `HarnessBridge::handle_mcp`. It answers these methods:

| Method | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| `initialize` | The protocol version, `tools` capability, and server info. |
| `server/discover` | The supported versions. |
| `ping` | `{}`. |
| `tools/list` | The submit tool of the agent, then the tools that `BridgeServices::mcp_tools` returns. |
| `tools/call` | The result of the tool. |
| `resources/list` and `prompts/list` | An empty list. |
| Any other method | Error `-32601`. |

A message with no `id` is a notification and gets no answer. A token that does not match gets error `-32001`. A parse error in the shim gets `-32700`. A server failure gets `-32603`.

The shim speaks `MCP_VERSIONS`: `2024-11-05`, `2025-03-26`, `2025-06-18`, and `2025-11-25`. It leaves out `2026-07-28` on purpose. That version needs the fields `resultType`, `ttlMs`, and `cacheScope` in results. Claude Code rejects a `tools/list` without them, so the run gets no Ostra tools. A client that asks for an unknown version gets `2025-11-25`.

### Tools the shim serves

- `submit_<agent>`: the result of the run. See the next part.
- `report`, `document`, `memory`, `memory_recall`, and `docs_search`.
- `code_<operation>`: the code navigation tools.
- The management tools and the coordination tools. The server lists them only when the run has the handle for them.
- The tools of the workspace MCP servers, in a bare name that the adapter maps back to `mcp__<server>__<tool>`.

`HarnessBridge::tool_list` in [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/bridge.rs`](../crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/bridge.rs) always lists the submit tool first, so `tools/list` always returns that tool. In an inspect run, `ServerBridge::mcp_tools` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs`](../crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs) returns an empty list, so the submit tool is the only entry. Claude Code gets no MCP config in an inspect run, because the plan leaves out `--mcp-config`. Thus Claude Code never lists tools in an inspect run.

When the shim has no execution, URL, or token, it works offline. It answers the handshake with no tools and answers `tools/call` with the error "Ostra tools work only inside an Ostra execution." Thus the global registration of Antigravity is inert outside Ostra.

### The submit call of a harness run

`call_tool` handles a call to the submit tool in these steps:

1. If the run owes a reply (Rule H3), the call returns an error that tells the agent to reply first.
2. The bridge coerces strings that hold JSON to the types of the schema.
3. `validate_submit` checks the payload. On an error, the text says "Fix the arguments and call ... again" and "Nothing was recorded."
4. `doc::check_submit` checks the typed document.
5. `record_submit` stores the payload. The first call wins. A later call gets the error "A result was already recorded for this run. End your turn now."
6. A good call gets the text "Recorded. Your run is complete: end your turn now, without further tool calls."

A call to the submit tool of another agent gets a pointer to the right tool. Any other tool goes through `decide` and then `mcp_call`, which runs the tool on the server with `ostra_tools::execute`. The `RunEnd` value of a coordination tool works as in the native loop. `Wait` sets the waiting flag. `Finish` records a submit from the message.

## How a harness run ends

`supervise` is the loop that watches one run. It wakes on a cancel, on a change of the live state (at least every 500 ms), or on the exit of the CLI. Each pass does these checks in order:

1. If the cancel token fired, end with `Cancelled`.
2. If the CLI exited, end with `Submitted` when a submit exists, else with `Exited`.
3. Every 2 seconds (`GIT_CHECK_EVERY`), repair planted git `commondir` files in the repos of the run. The CLI commands never pass a hook that Ostra could check, so a clock does it. This keeps short the time that a planted `commondir` could reach the git of the user.
4. If the session id changed, emit a `NativeSessionId` delta.
5. If a submit exists, wait for the end of the turn (see below).
6. If the run waits for a wake message (Rule H2), hold the loop (see below).
7. If `gave_up` is set, end with `GaveUp`.
8. If the deadline passed, end with `Timeout`.
9. In the first 120 seconds and before the first tool call, answer startup screens (see below).
10. If the run was quiet for `idle_nudge`, type a reminder.

In an inspect run, steps 5, 6, 7, and 10 do not apply. The user drives the run, and it ends when the CLI exits or the time budget ends. The result is then `ok` with the text "The read-only session ended."

### The end of the turn after a submit

A recorded submit does not end the run at once. The CLI must finish its turn first. `supervise` returns `Submitted` when one of these is true:

- A Stop event arrived after the submit (`stopped_after_submit`).
- The harness is `agy` and the terminal was quiet for `AGY_QUIET_AFTER_SUBMIT` (4 seconds). Antigravity has no Stop hook.
- `AFTER_SUBMIT_GRACE` (20 seconds) passed after the submit.

### Idle nudges

A run is idle when both the hook activity and the terminal output were quiet for `idle_nudge` (default `DEFAULT_IDLE_NUDGE`, 240 seconds). The loop then types the missing-submit instruction into the terminal with `type_line` and emits a status text. After `MAX_IDLE_NUDGES` (2) nudges, the next idle period ends the run with `Idle`.

### Waiting for another subagent

When the run asks another subagent (Rule H2), the CLI stays alive. `supervise` waits in `host.wait_for_wake()`. The deadline moves forward by the time of the wait, so the wait does not count against the time budget. When the wake message arrives, the loop clears the waiting flag, sets `owes_reply` from the message, and types the note into the terminal. If no message will come, the run ends with `Fatal`. See [Subagent coordination](subagent-coordination.md).

### Startup screens

In the first 120 seconds and before the first tool call, `supervise` reads the screen text and answers prompts that block the run:

- **Folder trust prompts.** `TRUST_MARKERS` find them. The loop answers at most 6 times. `trust_answer` decides by harness:
  - Claude Code: yes. It loads only user settings and the Ostra MCP config, so trust adds nothing from the repo.
  - Codex: only "Open restricted", which the restricted profile offers. The option "Trust and continue" saves trust and loads the `.codex/` config and hooks of the repo. Thus the run fails with a message that tells the user to remove `-p` or `--profile` from `[harness.codex].args`.
  - Grok Build: never. The run fails with a message that tells the user to trust the folder in Grok. Grok runs the hooks and MCP servers of a trusted folder outside the guards of Ostra.
  - Antigravity: like Claude Code.
  - The key is Enter when the highlighted option is right, else Down. Prompt defaults differ between versions.
- **New-model offers.** The marker `use existing model` finds the offer that Codex shows. The loop keeps the routed model, because accepting the offer switches the model of the run and the default model of the user.
- **Sign-in screens.** `AUTH_MARKERS` find them, for example "please log in", "not logged in", "run /login", "invalid api key", "finish signing in", and "select login method". The run ends with `Auth`.
- **Fatal screens.** `FATAL_MARKERS` ("failed to construct executor", "unknown component:", "unknown model", and "model not found") end the run with `Fatal`.
- **A session id on screen.** The loop reads the id from the Antigravity resume line `--conversation=<id>` (32 characters at least).

## Results, launch failures, and sign-in failures

`outcome::result` in [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/outcome.rs`](../crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/outcome.rs) turns an `End` value into an `ExecutionResult`. It first reads the usage and the last message from the session file of the CLI, and takes the larger of the tool call counts of the file and the bridge.

| `End` value | Status | Error text |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Submitted` | `ok`, `stuck`, or `handoff` from the payload | None. The result has the `submit` payload. |
| `Cancelled` | `cancelled` | None. |
| `Auth` | `error` | `harness-auth:` and "<name> is not logged in. Log in from its terminal, then retry." |
| `Auth`, Antigravity on macOS with Seatbelt | `error` | `harness-auth:` and the advice to set `GEMINI_API_KEY` or `GOOGLE_API_KEY` in the environment of Ostra, because Antigravity keeps its login in the keychain, which the sandbox closes. |
| `Exited` in less than 20 seconds with no tool call | `error` | `harness-launch:` and the exit code and the last 12 screen lines. The prefix is `harness-auth:` when the screen has an `AUTH_MARKERS` text. |
| `Exited` later | `error` | The CLI exited before the agent called its submit tool. |
| `GaveUp` | `error` | The agent ended its turn three times without calling its submit tool. |
| `Idle` | `error` | The session went quiet, and two reminders did not help. |
| `Fatal` | `error` | `harness-launch:` and the reason and the last 12 screen lines. |
| `Timeout` | `error` | The execution passed its budget and was stopped. |

The constant `LAUNCH_WINDOW` is 20 seconds. A CLI that dies faster is a launch failure, not a run failure, because a CLI that already did work is not a launch problem.

The `launch` step has its own failures. Each has the prefix `harness-launch:`:

- The command is not on `PATH`: "`<command>` (<display name>) is not installed".
- The Antigravity integration cannot be installed.
- The run directory or the config files cannot be written.
- The sandbox wrap fails, for example when the config requires a sandbox that the machine cannot give.
- The PTY cannot start.

The prefix is the first word of the error text. It tells the cause before the reader reads the rest.

## Usage watch and session files

A CLI keeps its own session file with token counts. Ostra reads it for the usage of the run. Two modules do this.

`transcript.rs` reads the files with best effort. It finds the last assistant message and the token usage. `TranscriptReader` reads only the bytes that were added since the last read, and a partial last line waits for the next read.

| Harness | Session file |
| --- | --- |
| `claude` | `~/.claude/projects/<dir>/<session>.jsonl` |
| `codex` | `~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-*-<session>.jsonl` |
| `grok` | `~/.grok/sessions/<cwd>/<session>/updates.jsonl` |
| `agy` | `brain/<conversation>/.system_generated/logs/transcript_full.jsonl` |

`usage_watch::follow` runs as a task during the run, so harness spend shows while the run is live, as native spend does. It does these steps:

1. It looks for the session file every `LOCATE_EVERY` (2 seconds) until the file exists. The path depends on a session id that the CLI can report late.
2. It watches the directory of the file, not the file, so a replaced file is still seen. If the platform watcher cannot start, it polls every `POLL_EVERY` (5 seconds).
3. After each change, it waits `SETTLE` (500 ms), because a turn writes many lines in a burst.
4. It emits a `Usage` delta when the sum changed. The tool call count comes from the bridge.

The follower does not run for Antigravity, and the usage of an Antigravity run comes from the file at the end of the run. The executor stops the follower and waits for it before it builds the final result.

## Harness setup: check, install, and login

The setup code lets a user see which CLIs are ready and fix a missing one from the console. It has two parts: `crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/setup.rs` for the checks and the commands, and [`crates/ostra-server/src/harness_setup.rs`](../crates/ostra-server/src/harness_setup.rs) for the terminals.

### The status check

`harness_status` returns a `HarnessStatus` with the command, `installed`, `version`, and `logged_in`. It uses `which` to find the command. Each command it runs has a 15-second timeout and no stdin. If the command is not installed, it does not run anything.

| Harness | How `logged_in` is found |
| --- | --- |
| `claude` | `<command> auth status` prints JSON. The check reads `loggedIn`. |
| `codex` | `<command> login status` exits with 0 and prints "Logged in". |
| `grok` | The file `auth.json` exists in the Grok home. |
| `agy` | The file `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/antigravity-oauth-token` or `~/.gemini/oauth_creds.json` exists. |

The version is the first non-empty line of `<command> --version`. `all_harness_status` checks all four harnesses in order. The server runs the check at start and after each setup terminal exits.

### Install and login commands

| Harness | Login command | Install command on Unix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `claude` | `claude auth login` | `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh \| bash` |
| `codex` | `codex login` | `curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh \| sh` |
| `grok` | `grok login` | `curl -fsSL https://x.ai/cli/install.sh \| bash` |
| `agy` | `agy` (no arguments) | `curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh \| bash` |

The program name comes from `[harness.<name>].command`. On Windows, Claude Code uses `irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 \| iex` and Codex uses `npm install -g @openai/codex`. Grok Build and Antigravity have no Windows installer command in Ostra. Their terminal prints a message that says where to look and exits with 1.

`installer_tool` names the tool that the installer needs: `curl` on Unix, and `npm` for Codex on Windows. The setup terminal checks for it first. If the tool is missing, the terminal prints "Install <tool> on the machine that runs Ostra, then try again" and exits with 127.

`install_dirs` lists the folders where the official installers put their binaries: `~/.local/bin` and `~/.grok/bin`, and on Windows also the npm folder under `AppData\Roaming`. The server adds them to its `PATH` at start. Without this, Ostra cannot find by name a CLI that the user installs when Ostra already runs.

### The setup terminals

A setup terminal is a PTY on the machine of the server. The browser streams and types into it like a harness terminal. `start` in `harness_setup.rs` does these steps:

1. Build the command: `sh -c <script>` on Unix, or PowerShell with `-NoProfile -Command` on Windows.
2. Make the terminal id `setup_<harness>_<action>`, where the action is `install` or `login`. The id is fixed for each harness and action. If that terminal still runs, `start` returns it, so a second click reattaches.
3. For a login, check that the command is on `PATH`. If not, return "Install <display name> first, because `<program>` is not on this machine's PATH."
4. Spawn the PTY in the home directory with a size of 100 columns and 30 rows. Setup terminals have no output log.
5. When the PTY exits, detect the environment status again and push `ServerMsg::HarnessStatus` on the `home` channel.

### The Antigravity integration

`ensure_agy_integration` installs the global parts that Antigravity needs. It is idempotent, and the executor calls it before each Antigravity run. It does these steps:

1. Write `plugin.json` and `hooks.json` in `~/.gemini/config/plugins/ostra/`. The hooks cover `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` with the matcher `.*`, and `PreInvocation` and `PostInvocation`. Each hook command is `<ostra> hook --harness agy --event <event>`, with no `--execution`, so it is inert unless `$OSTRA_EXECUTION` is set.
2. Set `plugins.ostra.enabled` to `true` in `~/.gemini/config/config.json`.
3. Run `agy mcp list`. If no line has the name `ostra` and the path of the binary, run `agy mcp add ostra <ostra> mcp-stdio`. This is the one registration that Antigravity honors.

The agent file of each run lists only the native tools that Ostra verified: `view_file`, `write_to_file`, `replace_file_content`, `run_command`, `grep_search`, `find_by_name`, `search_web`, and `read_url_content`. The code comment gives the reason. An agent file with no `tools:` list gets no native tools, and one unknown name makes the whole session fail to start.

## What happens when (harness)

- **The CLI is not installed.** The run fails before the PTY starts, with a `harness-launch:` text. The Environment status in the console shows the same fact.
- **The CLI shows a sign-in screen.** The run ends with `harness-auth:` in the first 120 seconds. The user logs in from a setup terminal and runs again.
- **The CLI asks to trust the folder.** Claude Code and Antigravity get a yes. Codex opens restricted. A Codex or Grok prompt that Ostra cannot accept ends the run with the reason.
- **The CLI tries to spawn a subagent or ask the user.** The hook refuses the call, with a reason that tells the model what to do.
- **The server is down when a hook runs.** `ostra hook` denies the `PreToolUse` call. The CLI cannot run tools without Ostra.
- **The CLI stops without a submit.** The bridge turns the Stop back two times. The third Stop ends the run with `GaveUp`.
- **The CLI goes quiet.** After 240 seconds of quiet, Ostra types a reminder, two times. Then the run ends with `Idle`.
- **The submit call arrives but the turn does not end.** The run ends after 20 seconds, or after 4 seconds of quiet for Antigravity.
- **The user cancels.** Ostra presses Esc, waits 400 ms, and terminates the CLI with a 3-second grace. The result is `cancelled`.
- **The time budget ends.** The run ends with `Timeout`. The budget is `timeout_secs`, at least 30 seconds, plus the time spent waiting for other subagents.
- **The server restarts.** The run becomes `interrupted`. A resume uses the saved session id with `--resume`, `resume`, or `--conversation`. A harness run that waited for an answer stays waiting. See [The engine runner, recovery, and control](engine-runner.md).
- **A CLI writes to a repo `.git` file.** The git repair runs every 2 seconds and again at the end. Each repair counts as a containment signal.

## Harness limits

| Name | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DEFAULT_IDLE_NUDGE` | 240 seconds | Quiet time before a reminder. |
| `MAX_IDLE_NUDGES` | 2 | Reminders before `Idle`. |
| `MAX_STOP_NUDGES` | 2 | Stops without a submit that the bridge turns back. |
| `AFTER_SUBMIT_GRACE` | 20 seconds | Time to wait for the end of the turn after a submit. |
| `AGY_QUIET_AFTER_SUBMIT` | 4 seconds | Terminal quiet that ends an Antigravity turn after a submit. |
| `LAUNCH_WINDOW` | 20 seconds | An exit sooner than this, with no tool call, is a launch failure. |
| `GIT_CHECK_EVERY` | 2 seconds | Interval of the git `commondir` repair. |
| `HOOK_TIMEOUT_SECS` | 86,400 | Hook and MCP tool timeout given to the CLI. |
| `MAX_ARG_PROMPT` | 96 KiB | Largest first message on the command line. |
| `TRANSCRIPT_CAP` | 2 MiB | Bytes of terminal output that a replay shows. Defined in `term_log.rs`. |
| Supervise budget | `timeout_secs`, at least 30 seconds | Time budget of a run. Waits for other subagents do not count. |
| Startup screen window | 120 seconds, 6 trust answers | When Ostra answers trust prompts and checks sign-in screens. |
| Terminate grace | 3 seconds | Time between the exit request and the kill. |
| `MAX_OUTCOME_CHARS` | 64 KiB | Largest tool output that goes to the policy. |
| Status command timeout | 15 seconds | Time for `--version` and the login check. |

## Change the executors with care

Keep these rules when you change this code:

- Keep the bridge fail closed. A `PreToolUse` event that Ostra cannot read or check must deny the call.
- Check each new harness flag against the installed CLI. The launch plans depend on exact flags and config keys, and a wrong name can stop the whole session.
- Add a new harness in four places: `HarnessKind`, a plan in `launch.rs`, an `Adapter`, and the transcript reader.
- Do not give the harness more of the Ostra environment than it needs to sign in. Credential variables stay out of the CLI environment by default.

The page does not claim that a harness run is as strictly bounded as a native run. The CLI runs its own loop. Ostra checks each tool call that passes a hook and each call to its own MCP tools. It cannot check what the CLI does between hooks, which is why the sandbox and the git repair exist. See [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md).
