sections.title: Model providers, tiers, and cost
sections.summary: How Ostra calls model APIs, retries failures, maps tiers and effort to models, prices each response from models.dev, and reports spend in the Cost screen.
sections.body:
The native executor and the judge calls send requests to model APIs from two vendors. Without one neutral interface, the agent loop needs vendor code. Without a retry rule, one overload response ends a run. Without a price table, every cost shows as 0. Without tiers, every agent route holds a raw model name.

This page covers these parts:

- The `Provider` trait and the neutral request and response types.
- The registry that finds keys and builds the Anthropic and OpenAI clients.
- The retry policy and the error classes.
- The scripted provider for tests.
- Tier routing, complexity, and effort.
- Prices from models.dev, the cost of one response, and the cost report.

The page stops at the native loop (turns, compaction trigger), which [Executors](executors.md) owns. It also stops at the setting tables of `config.toml` and `workspace.toml`, which [Configuration reference](configuration.md) owns.

## The Provider trait and the neutral types

`Provider` in [`crates/ostra-providers/src/lib.rs`](crates/ostra-providers/src/lib.rs) is the one interface that the agent loop and the judge calls use. Each vendor client converts the neutral types to its own wire format and back.

```rust
#[async_trait::async_trait]
pub trait Provider: Send + Sync {
    fn name(&self) -> &str;
    fn server_tools(&self, _model: &str) -> ServerTools { ServerTools::default() }
    async fn chat(&self, req: ChatRequest, on_event: EventSink<'_>,
                  cancel: CancellationToken) -> Result<ChatResponse, ProviderError>;
    async fn compact(&self, req: ChatRequest, instructions: &str,
                     cancel: CancellationToken) -> Result<Compacted, ProviderError> { ... }
}
```

`chat` streams. It calls `on_event` with each `StreamEvent` (`TextDelta`, `ThinkingDelta`, `ToolUseStarted`, `ToolInputDelta`, `ServerToolUsed`) and returns the whole `ChatResponse` at the end. `server_tools` tells the agent loop which provider-side tools exist for a model. The loop supplies a local tool for each one that is missing, for example web fetch on OpenAI.

### The request

`ChatRequest::new(model)` sets these defaults:

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `model` | the argument | The model id without the provider prefix. |
| `max_tokens` | `32_000` | The output limit that the caller asks for. |
| `effort` | `Effort::High` | The reasoning effort. |
| `tool_choice` | `ToolChoice::Auto` | `Auto`, `Any`, `None`, or `Tool(name)`. |
| `refusal_fallback` | `true` | Lets the provider re-run a declined request on its fallback model, on models that offer it. |

A `SystemBlock` has a `cache` flag that marks the end of a stable prefix for prompt caching. `ToolChoice::Any` and `ToolChoice::Tool` become `Auto` on models that reject forced tool calls.

### The content blocks

A `Message` has a `Role` (`User` or `Assistant`) and a list of `Block` values:

- `Text`, `Thinking` (with its signature), and `RedactedThinking`.
- `ToolUse` and `ToolResult`.
- `Opaque`: a provider-specific block, such as a server tool call or an OpenAI reasoning item.
- `Compaction`: earlier turns that one summary block replaces.

The client sends an `Opaque` block back verbatim to the provider that made it and drops it for any other provider. A `Compaction` block carries the signed or encrypted form for its own provider. Any other provider gets the `summary` as text.

### The response

`ChatResponse` holds `content`, a `StopReason`, a `Usage`, the `model` that answered, and an optional `refusal_category`. The `model` can differ from the request after a server-side fallback. `StopReason` is `EndTurn`, `ToolUse`, `MaxTokens`, `PauseTurn`, `Refusal`, or `Other(String)`. `PauseTurn` means that a server-side tool loop paused, and the caller sends the assistant turn back unchanged to resume.

## The provider registry

`Providers` holds the usable providers by name. It also keeps a `ProviderStatus` for each configured name, which the console shows. `Providers::from_config` builds one client for each `[providers.<name>]` entry that has a key.

Only two names have a client: `anthropic` and `openai`. `rebuild` in `lib.rs` gives every configured name a `ProviderStatus` entry. If a name has a key but no client, `rebuild` logs a warning that the provider in the config is unknown and ignored. Then it skips the name. If an unknown name has no key, `rebuild` skips it without a warning, but the name keeps its `ProviderStatus` entry. `register` adds a provider by hand, for example the scripted provider under the name `mock`. The status of such a provider has the source `registered`.

### Key lookup

`lookup_key` tries these sources in order and stops at the first hit:

1. The environment variable in `api_key_env`.
2. The environment variable in `auth_token_env`. Ostra sends this value as `Authorization: Bearer`.
3. The API key that a user saved in the browser.
4. The token that a user saved in the browser.
5. The OS keychain entry (`keychain_service`, with the provider name as the user).

The `source` field of the status shows the hit: `env:NAME`, `saved`, `keychain`, or `none`. An environment variable wins over a saved value because the operator set it on purpose. [Configuration reference](configuration.md) lists the variable names. [Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md) explains how Ostra seals saved credentials.

`resolve_base_url` uses this order: `base_url` in the config, the `base_url_env` variable, the saved URL, and then the default. The defaults are `https://api.anthropic.com` and `https://api.openai.com`. `display_url` removes the user, password, query, and fragment from a URL before the console shows it, because any of them can carry a credential. `ApiKey` prints `ApiKey(***)` and `***` in `Debug` and `Display`, so a log line never holds a key.

### Reload and model lookup

`reload` rebuilds the registry in place after the config or the saved credentials change. Executors hold the registry, so the next model call uses the new keys. Providers that `register` added stay in place.

`for_model("provider:model")` splits at the first `:` and returns the provider and the bare model id. Three errors can occur:

- `BadModel`: the string has no `provider:model` form.
- `NoKey`: the name is `anthropic` or `openai` and no client exists, because no key was found.
- `UnknownProvider`: any other name that is not registered.

### What happens when a key or a provider is missing

- **A native run has no key:** `execute` in `impl Run` ([`crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs), around line 390) fails the run with the message "The `<provider>` provider has no API key. Set its key in the environment or the OS keychain." The message does not come from a method on `NativeExecutor`.
- **A user saves a key in the console:** the registry reloads, and the next model call uses the key. No restart is needed.
- **A route names an unknown provider:** the run fails with "Cannot run model ..." and the error text.
- **A configured name is not `anthropic` or `openai`:** the name has a `ProviderStatus` entry. It gets a client never. Only `register` can add a provider for it.

## The Anthropic client

`Anthropic` in [`crates/ostra-providers/src/anthropic.rs`](crates/ostra-providers/src/anthropic.rs) calls the Messages API at `<base_url>/v1/messages` with `stream: true`. It sends the headers `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01`, `content-type: application/json`, and `accept: text/event-stream`. A key from `ApiKey::new` goes in `x-api-key`. A bearer token goes in `Authorization: Bearer`.

The HTTP client has a connect timeout of 20 seconds and sets no total timeout, because a response streams for a long time. It follows no redirect, because a redirect to another host carries the key header to that host.

### Request body

`request_body` builds the JSON body in these steps:

1. It sets `max_tokens` to the smaller of the request value and the model output limit from models.dev. A model that models.dev does not list gets the request value.
2. It writes the system blocks. It marks up to two flagged blocks with a cache breakpoint. If no block is flagged, it marks the last one.
3. It adds the server tools (`web_search_20250305`, `web_fetch_20250910`) and then the client tools with `eager_input_streaming`. It marks the last client tool with a cache breakpoint.
4. It sets `tool_choice`. A forced choice becomes `auto` if the model rejects forced calls.
5. It sets the thinking mode and `output_config.effort`.
6. It sets `fallbacks: "default"` when `refusal_fallback` is true and the model supports fallbacks.
7. It collects the beta names for the `anthropic-beta` header.

Every cache breakpoint uses the 1-hour TTL (`cache_mark`). The turns of one execution can be more than 5 minutes apart, for example after a long build or a permission question. A request that mixes TTLs must put the longer entries first, so one TTL for all breakpoints keeps the order simple. The most recent user turn also gets a breakpoint on its last `text` or `tool_result` block. So a request has at most 2 system, 1 tool, and 1 message breakpoint.

### Model capabilities

`caps(model)` returns the features of a model. A dated snapshot, such as `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`, counts as its base id. The suffix is a hyphen and 8 digits.

| Models | Thinking | Effort values | Forced tool choice | Server fallbacks | Compaction |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `claude-fable-5-1`, `claude-mythos-5-1`, `claude-opus-5-5` | Adaptive | All five | No | Yes | Yes |
| `claude-opus-5` | Adaptive | All five | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `claude-sonnet-5-5` | Adaptive | All five | No | No | Yes |
| `claude-fable-5`, `claude-mythos-5`, `claude-opus-4-8`, `claude-opus-4-7`, `claude-sonnet-5` | Adaptive | All five | Yes | No | Yes |
| `claude-opus-4-6`, `claude-sonnet-4-6` | Adaptive | `xhigh` becomes `high` | Yes | No | Yes |
| `claude-opus-4-5` | Budget | `low`, `medium`, `high` | Yes | No | No |
| `claude-haiku-4-5`, `claude-sonnet-4-5`, `claude-opus-4-1`, `claude-opus-4`, `claude-sonnet-4`, `claude-3*` | Budget | None sent | Yes | No | No |
| Any other model | Adaptive | All five | No | No | Yes |

The last row treats an unknown model as a newer model, with the features that every current model accepts.

### Thinking and effort

An adaptive model gets `thinking: {"type": "adaptive", "display": "summarized"}` and `output_config.effort`. A forced tool call runs without an explicit thinking config.

A budget model gets `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens}`. `budget_tokens` is a share of the model output limit:

| Effort | Budget |
| --- | --- |
| `low` | No thinking |
| `medium` | Output limit / 8 |
| `high` | Output limit / 4 |
| `xhigh` | Output limit / 2 |
| `max` | Output limit minus `ANSWER_RESERVE` (16,000) |

The budget must stay below `max_tokens` by `ANSWER_RESERVE`, because an answer can be a whole file that a tool call writes. The exception is a model with interleaved thinking that has client tools. Its budget spans the whole turn and can pass `max_tokens`. A budget below `MIN_BUDGET` (1,024 tokens) turns thinking off.

### Beta headers

- `compact-2026-09-04`: the request holds a signed compaction block, or it is a compaction request.
- `server-side-fallback-2026-07-01`: the request sets `fallbacks`.
- `interleaved-thinking-2025-05-14`: a budget model thinks between tool calls (`claude-opus-4-5`, `claude-sonnet-4-5`, `claude-opus-4-1`, `claude-opus-4`, `claude-sonnet-4`).
- `model-context-window-exceeded-2025-08-26`: models before Claude 4.5. With it, input plus `max_tokens` past the window stops generation at the window and does not fail validation.

### Stream accumulation

`Accumulator` applies each SSE event in order. `content_block_start` sets the `started` flag, which the retry rule reads. Text, thinking, and tool-input deltas go to `on_event` as they arrive. At `content_block_stop`, the accumulator turns each part into a `Block`.

The accumulator reads token counts from `message_start` and `message_delta`: `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens`, `cache_creation_input_tokens`, and the 1-hour part of the cache writes. A compaction request reports zero at the top level and bills its summary call in `usage.iterations`. The accumulator adds those iterations to the usage.

`finish` maps the stop reason: `end_turn` and `stop_sequence` to `EndTurn`, `tool_use` to `ToolUse`, `max_tokens` and `model_context_window_exceeded` to `MaxTokens`, `pause_turn` to `PauseTurn`, `refusal` to `Refusal`, and any other value to `Other`. It then sets `usage.cost_usd` with `pricing::cost`.

### What happens when the Anthropic stream misbehaves

- **Tool input is not valid JSON:** the block gets the input `{"__invalid_json": <text>}` (`INVALID_INPUT_KEY`). The agent loop answers it with an error result and does not run the tool.
- **A server-side fallback happens in the middle of the output:** `strip_before_fallback` drops thinking, tool use, and unpaired server tool use before the last `fallback` marker. The declined partial output is not run and not sent back.
- **The stream ends before `message_stop`:** the client raises a `Network` error. The retry rule then applies.
- **An SSE `error` event arrives:** `overloaded_error` becomes `Overloaded`, `rate_limit_error` becomes `RateLimited`, `api_error` becomes `Server` with status 500, and any other type becomes `InvalidRequest`.

## The OpenAI client

`OpenAi` in [`crates/ostra-providers/src/openai.rs`](crates/ostra-providers/src/openai.rs) calls the Responses API at `<base_url>/v1/responses`. It always sends `Authorization: Bearer`. It runs stateless (`store: false`), so each request carries the whole conversation. The HTTP client has the same 20-second connect timeout and the same no-redirect rule as the Anthropic client.

`request_body` builds the body in these steps:

1. It joins the non-empty system blocks with a blank line into `instructions`.
2. It converts each block to an input item: `message`, `function_call`, `function_call_output`, `reasoning`, or a compaction item.
3. For a reasoning model, it sets `reasoning: {effort, summary: "auto"}` and `include: ["reasoning.encrypted_content"]`. A model counts as a reasoning model when its id starts with `gpt-5`, `gpt-6`, or `o`. The effort string goes through as written. A non-reasoning model gets no `reasoning` field.
4. It adds the client tools as `function` tools and a `web_search` tool when the request allows it. OpenAI has no server-side web fetch.
5. It sets `parallel_tool_calls: true` and maps the tool choice: `Auto` to `auto`, `Any` to `required`, `None` to `none`, and `Tool(name)` to a named function.

An error result that does not start with "Error" gets the prefix "Error: ". The client round-trips reasoning items in `Opaque` blocks, with their encrypted content, to the same provider only.

The usage mapping differs from Anthropic. OpenAI reports `input_tokens` with the cached part included. `read_usage` subtracts the cached tokens and the written tokens, so `input_tokens` in `Usage` never holds cache tokens. OpenAI has one cache write TTL, so `cache_write_1h_tokens` stays 0.

`StopReason` comes from the final event. `response.incomplete` with `max_output_tokens` gives `MaxTokens`. A `content_filter` reason or a `refusal` content part gives `Refusal`. A response with a function call gives `ToolUse`. Any other completed response gives `EndTurn`.

### What happens when the OpenAI stream misbehaves

- **`response.failed` arrives:** the client raises `Server` with status 500, which the retry rule can retry.
- **An `error` event arrives:** `rate_limit_exceeded` becomes `RateLimited`. `server_error`, `server_is_overloaded`, and `slow_down` become `Server`. Any other code becomes `InvalidRequest`.
- **The stream ends before `response.completed`:** the client raises a `Network` error.
- **Compaction:** `compact` posts to `/v1/responses/compact` and keeps the encrypted compaction item. If the endpoint answers `InvalidRequest`, for example on a compatible gateway, the client compacts on the client side.

## Retry policy

`RetryPolicy` in [`crates/ostra-providers/src/retry.rs`](crates/ostra-providers/src/retry.rs) wraps each request in both clients. It uses exponential backoff with jitter. It never retries after output started, because a retry sends the same text and tool calls a second time.

| Field | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `max_retries` | `4` | Retries after the first attempt, so 5 attempts at most. |
| `base_delay` | 1000 ms | The delay base for the first retry. |
| `max_delay` | 60 s | The cap before jitter. |

The delay before retry number `n` (from 0) is `min(base_delay * 2^n, max_delay)` multiplied by a jitter factor from 0.5 up to 1.0. With the defaults, the four waits are 0.5 to 1 s, 1 to 2 s, 2 to 4 s, and 4 to 8 s. If the error has a `Retry-After` value in seconds, the wait is the longer of the jittered delay and that value. `Retry-After` is not capped by `max_delay`.

### Retry decision

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Send the request"] --> B{"Result"}
  B -- "success" --> Z["Return the response"]
  B -- "error" --> C{"Retryable error?"}
  C -- "no" --> E["Return the error"]
  C -- "yes" --> D{"Output started?"}
  D -- "yes" --> S["Return ProviderError::Stream"]
  D -- "no" --> F{"Retries used below max_retries?"}
  F -- "no" --> E
  F -- "yes" --> G["Wait: backoff or Retry-After"]
  G --> A
```

The `started` flag becomes true at the first content block (Anthropic) or the first output item or text delta (OpenAI). The OpenAI compaction call never sets it, so every retryable error there can be retried. A cancel stops the request and the wait at once and returns `Cancelled`.

### Error classes

`status_error` maps an HTTP status and body to a `ProviderError`. The message is `error.message` from the body, or the first 300 characters of the body. `network_error` removes the URL from the message. `is_retryable` is true for the four classes marked in the table.

`status_error` tests the status in this order: 401 and 403 (`Auth`), 429 (`RateLimited`), 529 (`Overloaded`), then the error type `overloaded_error` (`Overloaded`), then 408, 409, and 500 to 599 (`Server`). Any other status gives `InvalidRequest`.

| Error | Source | Retried |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Auth` | HTTP 401 or 403 | No |
| `InvalidRequest` | Any status that no other row takes, and unknown stream error types | No |
| `RateLimited` | HTTP 429, or a rate limit stream error | Yes |
| `Overloaded` | HTTP 529, or the error type `overloaded_error` on a status other than 401, 403, and 429 | Yes |
| `Server` | HTTP 408, 409, and 500 to 599 that the `Overloaded` row does not take | Yes |
| `Network` | Connect or transport failure, or a stream that ends early | Yes |
| `Stream` | A retryable error after output started | No |
| `Decode` | A bad SSE payload, or a structured call that fails | No |
| `Cancelled` | The cancel token fired | No |
| `NoKey`, `UnknownProvider`, `BadModel` | The registry | No |

## Structured output and compaction

`structured` and `structured_cancellable` make one structured decision for the judge calls. The call forces a tool named `decide` (`DECIDE_TOOL`) whose input schema is the decision schema. It uses `max_tokens` 16,000, a cached system block, and the effort that the caller passes. It returns the tool input and the usage of every attempt.

The call allows 2 attempts. Models that reject forced tool calls get `auto`, so the first answer can be plain text. In that case the second attempt adds the answer and the reminder "Call the `decide` tool now with your decision. Do not answer in text." A `Refusal` stop reason fails the call at once with a `Decode` error. [Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md) explains what the engine does with the result.

The engine runs a judge on route key `judge`, with effort `low`. `Inner::call_judge` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs) makes 3 attempts. It sleeps 500 ms times (attempt + 1) after each failed attempt, including the third. A call that fails the schema check counts as a failed attempt. [Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md) owns this rule.

`compact` asks the provider to summarize `req.messages`. The messages must end on a user turn with no open tool call. The default form, `compact_on_client`, sends the same request plus the instructions as a last user turn, so the cached prefix stays valid. It sets `ToolChoice::None`. It keeps the answer as a `Compaction` block only if the stop reason is `EndTurn` and the text is not empty. A cut-off summary is not used.

Anthropic uses its own on-demand compaction (`compaction: {type: "summarize"}`) on models with the compaction feature. If that call answers `InvalidRequest`, it falls back to `compact_on_client`. [Executors](executors.md) explains when the native loop starts a compaction.

## The scripted provider

`ScriptedProvider` in [`crates/ostra-providers/src/mock.rs`](crates/ostra-providers/src/mock.rs) is a provider for tests. It makes no network call. Its default name is `mock`, and `check_model` accepts `mock:<model>` for the native executor.

- `push(response)`, `push_text`, `push_tool_use`, and `push_tool_uses` queue responses in order. `push_error` queues an error.
- `with_responder(f)` sets a function that answers each request after the queue is empty. Use it when executions run in parallel and the order is not fixed.
- `requests()` returns every request that the provider received. `remaining()` returns the queue length.
- `chat` returns `Cancelled` if the token already fired. Otherwise it records the request, takes the next queued item or calls the responder, and replays text, thinking, and tool-use blocks as `StreamEvent` values.
- If the queue and the responder are both empty, `chat` returns a `Decode` error: "the scripted provider has no response left".

The responses carry zero usage and the model name `mock`, so the cost is 0.

## Tier routing

A tier is a name for a class of model: `fast`, `balanced`, `advanced`, or `frontier`. `Tier` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/model.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/model.rs) orders them from `fast` (lowest) to `frontier`. The tier tables in `config.toml` map each tier to a concrete model for each executor, so a workspace route can say `advanced` and work on every executor.

### The tier tables

`[tiers.<table>]` has one table for each executor: `native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, and `agy`. A native entry is `provider:model`. A harness entry is the name that the CLI accepts. These are the defaults:

| Table | `fast` | `balanced` | `advanced` | `frontier` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `native` | `anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` | `anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5` | `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5` | `anthropic:claude-fable-5-1` |
| `claude` | `haiku` | `sonnet` | `opus` | `fable` |
| `codex` | `gpt-5.6-luna` | `gpt-5.6-terra` | `gpt-5.6-sol` | `gpt-5.6-sol` |
| `grok` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` | `grok-4.5` |
| `agy` | `flash` | `flash` | `flash` | `flash` |

To run a native agent on OpenAI, set an `openai:<model>` entry in the `native` table, or give the route a concrete model.

### Route resolution

`resolve_route` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs) returns a `ResolvedRoute` with the executor, the model, and the tier (`None` when the route names a concrete model). The runner calls it with a `RouteQuery`: the route key (an agent name or `judge`), the default tier of the agent from `agent.toml`, the phase complexity, and two optional overrides.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Pick the executor: override, routing.executor, or native"] --> B["Pick the table: native, claude, codex, grok, or agy"]
  B --> C{"tier_override set?"}
  C -- "yes" --> T["Look up the tier in the table"]
  C -- "no" --> D["Find the choice: byPhaseComplexity, then byAgent"]
  D --> E{"Choice found?"}
  E -- "no" --> X["RouteError: no model route"]
  E -- "yes" --> F{"What is the value?"}
  F -- "default" --> G["Use the agent default tier"]
  F -- "a tier name" --> T
  F -- "a model" --> H["check_model"]
  G --> T
  T --> I{"Entry in the table?"}
  I -- "no" --> Y["RouteError: no entry"]
  I -- "yes" --> H
  H --> Z["ResolvedRoute"]
```

The rules in the diagram work like this:

- **Executor:** `executor_override` wins. Otherwise `routing.executor.byPhaseComplexity` wins over `byAgent`. With no entry, the executor is native. The `judge` key always runs native, because a judge call is an engine call and not an agent execution.
- **Model choice:** `routing.model.byPhaseComplexity[key][complexity]` wins over `routing.model.byAgent[key]`. The value is `default`, a tier name, a concrete model, or a per-executor table such as `{ native = "anthropic:x", codex = "gpt-y" }`.
- **`default`:** the route uses the `default_tier` of the agent definition.
- **`check_model`:** an empty model is an error. A native model must be `anthropic:<model>`, `openai:<model>`, or `mock:<model>`.

### Defaults of the agent tier

Each agent has a `default_tier` in its `assets/agents/<name>/agent.toml`:

- **`advanced`:** `explore`, `generate-spec`, `plan`, `fact-check`, `documentation`, `system-architecture`, `prompt-generation`, `advisor`.
- **`balanced`:** `implementer`, `write-test`, `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `initializer`, `quick-answer`.

The judge route has the default tier `advanced`. A new workspace seeds a route for every agent. Most routes name the same tier. The `implementer` and `write-test` routes depend on the complexity, which the next part explains. [Configuration reference](configuration.md) lists the seeded routes.

### What happens when a route fails or an executor changes

- **The tier has no entry in the table of the executor:** `resolve_route` returns a `RouteError` that names the table and the tier. Validation reports this error when a user saves the settings.
- **A route key has no model route:** the error says to add the key under `[routing.model.byAgent]`. This happens when a new agent ships and a workspace saved before it has no entry. The fix `default` solves it.
- **`resolve_route` fails when the runner starts a spawn:** the runner records the execution as denied with the reason `route: <message>`. No model call happens.
- **A harness execution fails with an error that starts with `harness-`:** `exec_failed_gate` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/plan.rs) opens a `HarnessFailure` gate. The gate text says that the harness failed to start or is not logged in. If the user answers the gate with the choice `native`, the state adds the agent to `native_fallback` (`crates/ostra-engine/src/state.rs`, around line 3830). Then `forced_executor` returns native for that agent, and the retry runs on the native executor. [Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md) explains the gate and its other choices.
- **Any other harness execution fails:** `exec_failed_gate` opens the generic `ExecutionFailed` gate. This gate has no `native` choice. The executor does not change by itself.
- **The category is a quick change, or the agent is `quick-answer`:** the executor is native. A quick change skips the harness start-up cost. The side-panel quick answer always uses native, with the tier from its route and the fixed effort `medium`.
- **The initializer runs the `GenerateSkill` mode:** the tier is `advanced` (`tier_override`), whatever the model route says.
- **A run resumes, or a new run continues a conversation:** the run keeps the executor and model of the earlier run. This also keeps the prompt cache.

## Complexity and effort

Complexity says how hard a plan phase is. Effort says how much a model reasons on one call. Both change the cost of a run.

### Complexity

`Complexity` is `low`, `medium`, or `high`, and the default is `low`. It comes from the `**Complexity:**` line of a plan phase. [Typed pipeline documents](typed-documents.md) explains the phase fields. `SpawnRequest::complexity()` returns `None` outside a phase. For a phase without a phase file, it returns `low`.

Only `implementer` and `write-test` route by complexity (`AgentName::routes_by_complexity`). A new workspace sends both on `low` and `medium` phases to `fast`, and on `high` phases to `balanced`. Validation requires a model route for each of the three complexities of these two agents.

### Effort

`Effort` is `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, or `max`, in rising order. The runner picks the effort of one spawn in this order:

1. `routing.effort.byPhaseComplexity[agent][complexity]`. Without a complexity, the lookup uses `low`.
2. `routing.effort.byAgent[agent]`.
3. The `[effort]` table of the agent in `agent.toml`, for the executor table (`native`, `claude`, `codex`, `grok`, or `agy`). A missing executor entry uses the `native` value. A missing native value uses `high`.

The seeded `routing.effort` tables are empty. Most agent defaults are `high` on every executor, with two exceptions:

- **`quick-answer`:** `medium` on every executor.
- **`initializer`:** the `[effort]` table in `assets/agents/initializer/agent.toml` sets `native` to `high`, `claude` to `high`, `codex` to `xhigh`, `grok` to `xhigh`, and `agy` to `max`.

A judge call always uses `low`. The older flat form of `routing.effort`, a table from agent to effort, reads as `byAgent`.

Each executor applies the effort in its own way:

- **Anthropic, adaptive models:** the value goes to `output_config.effort`. `xhigh` becomes `high` on the 4.6 models. `claude-opus-4-5` accepts `low`, `medium`, and `high`, and every higher value becomes `high`.
- **Anthropic, budget models:** the effort sets the thinking budget (see the table in the Anthropic part).
- **OpenAI reasoning models:** the value goes to `reasoning.effort`.
- **Harness CLIs:** the launch code lowers the effort to the highest value that the CLI supports: `max` for Claude Code, `xhigh` for Codex, and `high` for Grok Build and Antigravity. The `initializer` values `xhigh` on Grok and `max` on Antigravity fall under this cap.

## Pricing from models.dev

Ostra prices every response from the models.dev catalog (`https://models.dev/api.json`). Until a catalog is installed, every cost is 0. [`crates/ostra-core/src/pricing.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/pricing.rs) parses the catalog and computes costs. [`crates/ostra-server/src/prices.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/prices.rs) fetches and caches it.

### The catalog

`Catalog::from_models_dev` reads the JSON by provider and model. For each model it keeps three things:

- **Prices** (`Pricing`): `input`, `output`, `cache_read`, and `cache_write`, in USD per 1 million tokens. A model without both `input` and `output` prices has no `Pricing`.
- **Context tiers:** price entries whose tier type is `context`. A request with a prompt longer than the tier `size` uses the rates of that tier. The prompt is the input, the cache reads, and the cache writes together. The tier with the largest size below the prompt wins.
- **Limits:** the context window and the maximum output tokens. A value of 0 is dropped.

The parser fills the gaps in the rates:

- A missing `cache_read` price is the `input` price.
- A missing `cache_write` price is `input * 1.25`.
- `cache_write_1h` is `input * 2` for Anthropic and equal to `cache_write` for every other provider. models.dev lists only the 5-minute write.

### The lookup

`Catalog::price`, `context_window`, and `max_output` take a model id with or without a `provider:` prefix. The lookup uses this order:

1. An exact id in the hinted provider, then in the first-party providers: `anthropic`, `openai`, `xai`, `google`, `mistral`, `deepseek`.
2. The longest first-party id that is a prefix of the model id and is followed by a hyphen.
3. An exact id in any provider, in alphabetical order.

A first-party listing wins over a reseller, because resellers list the same id at other prices. The prefix rule prices a dated snapshot, such as `claude-sonnet-5-5-20260901`, as its base model. The longest prefix wins, so `claude-opus-5-5-x` does not get the price of `claude-opus-5`. An id such as `claude-opus-50` matches no prefix, because the next character is not a hyphen. A model that no step finds costs 0.

### Fetch and cache

`prices::start(data_dir)` runs when the server starts. It does these steps:

1. It reads `<data_dir>/models-dev.json`. If the file parses, it installs the catalog at once. A restart without network still prices every execution.
2. If `OSTRA_MODELS_DEV_URL` is set to an empty value, it stops. This turns fetching off for tests and air-gapped machines. A non-empty value replaces the catalog URL.
3. Otherwise it starts a background loop. If the cache file is less than 24 hours old, the loop waits for the rest of the 24 hours. If the file is older or missing, it fetches the catalog.

The fetch has a 60-second timeout and fails on a non-success status. It parses the body and requires at least one priced model. It writes `models-dev.json.tmp` and renames it over the cache file. A failed parse or an empty catalog leaves the old file in place. After a success, the loop waits 24 hours (`REFRESH_EVERY`). After a failure, it logs a warning, keeps the cached prices, and retries after 1 hour (`RETRY_AFTER`).

## Cost of one response

`pricing::cost(model, usage, web_searches)` returns USD for one response. Both provider clients call it in `finish`, and the harness transcript reader calls it for harness runs. The `input_tokens` field of `Usage` excludes cache reads and writes. Every provider and harness reading is normalized to this form before the call.

```rust
pub fn cost(model: &str, usage: &Usage, web_searches: u64) -> f64 {
    let Some(p) = price(model) else { return 0.0 };
    let r = p.rates(usage.input_tokens + usage.cache_read_tokens + usage.cache_write_tokens);
    let m = 1_000_000.0;
    let write_1h = usage.cache_write_1h_tokens.min(usage.cache_write_tokens);
    usage.input_tokens as f64 * r.input / m
        + usage.output_tokens as f64 * r.output / m
        + usage.cache_read_tokens as f64 * r.cache_read / m
        + (usage.cache_write_tokens - write_1h) as f64 * r.cache_write / m
        + write_1h as f64 * r.cache_write_1h / m
        + web_searches as f64 * WEB_SEARCH_USD
}
```

Each server-side web search costs 0.01 USD (`WEB_SEARCH_USD`) on both providers. With the test sample prices, 1 million input tokens, 1 million output tokens, 1 million cache reads, and 1 search on `claude-sonnet-5-5` cost 2.0 + 10.0 + 0.2 + 0.01 USD.

### What the cost does not guarantee

- The cost is an estimate from catalog prices. If a model is missing from the catalog, its cost is 0 and no error appears.
- The native clients read token counts from the API response. The harness executor reads them from CLI session files on a best-effort basis. [Executors](executors.md) explains this.
- A price change at the provider shows in Ostra only after the next catalog refresh. The `Usage` of earlier executions keeps the cost that Ostra computed at that time.

## The cost report

`GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/cost` returns a `CostReport`. The optional `since` query value must be an RFC 3339 time, for example `2026-09-24T00:00:00Z`. Any other value gives a 400 error. Without `since`, the report covers all time.

`WorkspaceDb::cost_report` in [`crates/ostra-store/src/workspace.rs`](crates/ostra-store/src/workspace.rs) reads the `executions` table. It counts the executions that started at or after `since`. It sums the stored `Usage` of each execution into four groupings and a total:

| Field | Group key | Missing key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `by_session` | The session id | `side-panel` (quick answers) |
| `by_stage` | The stage | `none` |
| `by_agent` | The agent name | Not applicable |
| `by_executor` | The executor | Not applicable |
| `total` | The fixed key `total` | Not applicable |

Each `CostRow` has the key, the execution count, the summed `Usage`, and `cache_reads_per_tool_call`. The helper `cost_row` builds the row. That value is the cache read tokens divided by the tool calls, or 0 if there are no tool calls. Rows sort by cost, highest first, and then by key.

The usage of a running execution is written to its row while it runs, so the report includes spend that is in progress. Judge calls have no execution row. They do not appear in the report. The session list adds the judge cost to the session total. [Storage](storage.md) describes the `executions` table.

## The Cost screen

`CostScreen` in [`web/src/screens/CostScreen.tsx`](web/src/screens/CostScreen.tsx) shows the report for the resource `ws:cost`. A segmented control selects the range:

- **This week:** the default. The screen passes `week_since` from `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/activity` as `since`. The week is today plus the six days before it, from local midnight on the server. The totals match the status bar. The screen waits for the activity data before it asks for the report.
- **All time:** no `since` value.

The summary strip shows the total for the range, the spend since local midnight (`spend_today_usd`), and, in the all-time view, the week spend. It also shows runs, cache reads, tool calls, cache reads per tool call, and build time.

Four tables follow: By session, By stage, By agent, and By executor. Each table has these columns: Runs, Input, Output, Cache reads, Cache writes 5m, Cache writes 1h, Cache / tool call, Build time, Cost, and Share. The 5-minute column is `cache_write_tokens` minus `cache_write_1h_tokens`. Share is the row cost divided by the total cost, rounded to a whole percent. A click on a session row opens that session. The side-panel row does not open.

Two figures show waste. Cache reads per tool call rise when an agent loops, because each step reads the context again. Build time rises when an agent runs many builds and tests that fail in a row.

The screen reloads the report when the `workspace:<ws>` channel sends an `activity` or `session_updated` message. A throttle limits the reload to once in 2,000 ms. If the report has no executions, the screen shows one of two texts:

- **This week:** "No spend this week. Switch to All time for earlier runs."
- **All time:** "No spend yet. Costs appear here after a session runs its first execution." A New task button follows the text.

## Session budget

The workspace setting `limits.session_budget_usd` (default `25.0`, in USD) limits what one session spends. A value of `0` means no limit. The planner reads it in `plan_ctx`.

Before the planner emits a `Spawn` step, it compares the spend of the session with the budget plus any raised amount. The spend is the summed `cost_usd` of the finished executions. If the spend reaches the limit, no new execution starts. The planner opens one `BudgetReached` gate. Executions that already run finish. The user raises the budget or stops the session. [Sessions and the pipeline](sessions-and-pipeline.md) explains the planner, and [Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md) explains the gate.

## Limits and defaults

| Name | Value | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RetryPolicy::max_retries` | 4 | `retry.rs` |
| `RetryPolicy::base_delay` | 1000 ms | `retry.rs` |
| `RetryPolicy::max_delay` | 60 s | `retry.rs` |
| Connect timeout of both clients | 20 s | `anthropic.rs`, `openai.rs` |
| `ChatRequest` default `max_tokens` | 32,000 | `lib.rs` |
| `structured` `max_tokens` and attempts | 16,000 and 2 | `lib.rs` |
| Judge call attempts | 3 attempts. `call_judge` sleeps 500 ms times (attempt + 1) after each failed attempt, including the third. | `Inner::call_judge` in `runner.rs` |
| `ANSWER_RESERVE` | 16,000 tokens | `anthropic.rs` |
| `MIN_BUDGET` | 1,024 tokens | `anthropic.rs` |
| Error body clip | 300 characters | `retry.rs` |
| `WEB_SEARCH_USD` | 0.01 USD per search | `pricing.rs` |
| `REFRESH_EVERY` | 24 hours | `prices.rs` |
| `RETRY_AFTER` of the price fetch | 1 hour | `prices.rs` |
| Price fetch timeout | 60 s | `prices.rs` |
| `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_WINDOW` for an unlisted model | 200,000 tokens | `ostra-exec-native` |
| `DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT` for an unlisted model | 32,000 tokens | `ostra-exec-native` |
| `limits.session_budget_usd` | 25.0 USD | `config.rs` |
| Cost screen reload throttle | 2,000 ms | `CostScreen.tsx` |
