sections.title: Native tools
sections.summary: The tool set in `ostra-tools`: what each tool accepts, what it returns, the output limits, and why the policy check always runs before `execute`. Includes the Windows shell and the `ProjectList` and `ProjectCreate` management tools.
sections.body:
A model cannot change a file, run a command, or fetch a page by itself. The `ostra-tools` crate gives the native loop and the MCP bridge a fixed set of tools that do these actions. Each tool has a name and an input shape that follow the tools of Claude Code, because the agent prompts are tuned to those names. The crate checks no permission. The policy engine runs first, and `execute` runs only a call that the policy allowed.

This page covers:

- the list of tools and the capability that grants each one
- the rule that policy runs before `execute`, and the state that `ToolEnv` keeps
- the file tools, the search tools, and Bash
- the Windows shell tools
- WebFetch and WebSearch
- the Skill, Report, memory, and documentation tools
- the code navigation tools, the MCP tools, and the coordination tools
- the management tools `ProjectList` and `ProjectCreate`
- every output limit

The rules of the policy have their own page: [Policy engine](policy.md). The kernel boundary under Bash has its own page: [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md).

## The tools and the capabilities that grant them

An agent definition lists capabilities (`Capability` in `crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs`). The function `definitions` in `crates/ostra-tools/src/defs.rs` maps each capability to its tool definitions, in declaration order. It ignores a capability that appears twice. Each `ToolDefinition` has a `name`, a `description`, and a JSON `input_schema`.

| Capability | Tools | Required input | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Read` | `Read` | `file_path` | Optional `offset` and `limit` |
| `Write` | `Write` | `file_path`, `content` | Replaces the file |
| `Edit` | `Edit` | `file_path`, `old_string`, `new_string` | Optional `replace_all` |
| `Shell` | `Bash` | `command` | Optional `timeout` and `description`. On Windows, also `PowerShell` and `Cmd` |
| `SearchText` | `Grep` | `pattern` | Eleven optional fields: `path`, `glob`, `type`, `output_mode`, `-i`, `-n`, `-A`, `-B`, `-C`, `head_limit`, and `multiline` |
| `Glob` | `Glob` | `pattern` | Optional `path` |
| `Skill` | `Skill` | none | `name` or `path` |
| `WebFetch` | `WebFetch` | `url` | Optional `prompt` |
| `WebSearch` | none locally | none | Runs on the model provider side |
| `Report` | `Report` | `content` | Optional `reason` |
| `Document` | `Document` | `path` | Built for each agent by `document_tool_definition` |
| `Memory` | `Memory` | `area`, `lesson` | Optional `source` |
| `MemoryRecall` | `MemoryRecall` | `query` | Optional `area` and `limit` |
| `DocsSearch` | `DocsSearch` | `query` | Optional `project` and `limit` |
| `Code` | `CodeOutline`, `CodeFind`, `CodeCallers`, `CodeCallees`, `CodeImplementations`, `CodeNeighbors`, `CodeImpact`, `CodeMap` | varies | See the code navigation part |
| `ManageProjects` | `ProjectList`, `ProjectCreate` | see below | Only the `implementer` agent has it |
| `Coordinate` | `SubagentList`, `SubagentAsk`, `SubagentReply` | `message` for ask and reply | See [Subagent coordination](subagent-coordination.md) |

The `Document` capability returns no definition from `definitions`. The document tool depends on the agent, because its schema is the schema of the research document, the spec, or the plan. Only the `explore`, `generate-spec`, and `plan` agents have it. The page [Typed pipeline documents](typed-documents.md) owns the document format.

Harness executors (Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build, Antigravity) use their own Read, Write, Edit, and Bash tools. In that case, only the MCP tools of Ostra reach `ostra_tools::execute`: `report`, `document`, `memory`, `memory_recall`, `docs_search`, the `code_*` tools, the `project_*` tools, the subagent tools, and the tools of external MCP servers. The table `MCP_TOOLS` in `crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs` holds the names. [Executors](executors.md) explains the two executor kinds.

## Policy runs before execute

The module comment of `crates/ostra-tools/src/lib.rs` states the rule: the policy layer runs before `execute`, and nothing in the crate checks permissions or guards. The reason is the division of work. The policy engine knows the permission mode, the allow, ask, and deny rules, and the guards. The tools only do the work. A caller that runs `execute` without a policy check bypasses every guard.

Two callers run tools, and both follow the same order:

- The native loop calls `tool_end` in `crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs`.
- The MCP bridge calls `mcp_call` in `crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs` for a harness executor.

### One tool call from model to output

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Exec as Executor
    participant Env as ToolEnv
    participant Pol as Policy
    participant User
    participant Run as execute
    Exec->>Env: canonical_call(call)
    Env-->>Exec: call with absolute paths
    Exec->>Pol: check(call)
    Pol-->>Exec: Allow, Ask, or Deny
    Exec->>User: ask_permission (only on Ask)
    User-->>Exec: AllowOnce, AlwaysInWorkspace, or Deny
    Exec->>Run: execute(env, id, call, live, cancel)
    Run-->>Exec: ToolOutput with duration_ms
    Exec->>Pol: observe(call, outcome)
```

### Steps of the native loop

1. `ToolEnv::canonical_call` makes the call canonical. Relative paths become absolute against the shell working directory. For Bash, PowerShell, and Cmd, it sets `cwd` to that directory. For WebFetch, it replaces `url` with the parsed form. The policy checks this call, the user approves this call, and the tool runs this call. All three see the same target.
2. The loop emits a `ToolCall` event.
3. If the input holds `__invalid_json`, the loop returns an error and does not run the tool.
4. The loop sets the YOLO flag and calls `policy.check`.
5. On `Deny`, the loop returns `Denied by <layer> `<rule>`: <reason>` as an error result.
6. On `Ask`, the loop asks the user. The answer `AllowOnce` lets the call run. The answer `AlwaysInWorkspace` also adds an allow rule to the session. The answer `Deny` returns an error that says that the user denied the call.
7. The loop calls `ostra_tools::execute` with a live-output callback.
8. After a Bash call, the loop repairs git metadata folders. If the command is a build command, the loop adds the call time to the build time.
9. `policy.observe` can append notes to the result, for example the build streak note or recalled lessons.
10. The loop emits a `ToolResult` event. The Activity view gets at most `EMIT_LIMIT` (8 KB). The model gets the full output.

The bridge follows the same order. It differs in two details. It passes no live-output callback, so the Activity view shows no stream. It passes a new `CancellationToken` that no other code holds, so a stop request cannot cancel the tool through the token.

### Why the canonical call exists

The test `canonical_webfetch_url_is_the_parsed_form` shows the reason. A URL such as `https://evil.example\@docs.rs/x` can show one host to a text rule and another host to the HTTP client. `canonical_call` parses the URL first. Thus the policy rule and the client use the same host. The test `canonical_call_uses_the_shell_cwd` shows the same idea for paths: a relative `file_path` resolves against the shell directory, not against the repo root.

### What happens when

- **The policy denies the call:** `execute` does not run. The model gets the denial text and can continue with other tools.
- **The user denies the call:** `execute` does not run. The model gets the text `The user denied this call` and the reason.
- **The call names an unknown tool:** `execute` returns the error ``Unknown tool `<name>`.``.
- **A required field is missing:** the tool returns ``Missing required parameter `<key>`.``.
- **The model sends a string where the schema needs an object or array:** `execute` first calls `coerce_json_strings` with the tool schema. It parses each top-level argument that holds JSON text for a non-string property.
- **The run is cancelled during a tool that is not a shell:** `execute` returns `Cancelled.` and drops the work.
- **The run is cancelled during Bash, PowerShell, or Cmd:** the shell tool handles the cancel itself. See the Bash part.

## ToolEnv: the state of one execution

`ToolEnv` holds the state that tools share inside one execution. `ToolEnvConfig` supplies its inputs.

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `agent`, `repo_root`, `workspace_root`, `session_dir` | Who runs, and the folders of the run |
| `report_file` | The fixed path that `Report` writes. `None` when the prompt declared none |
| `memory_db`, `memory_source` | The lesson store, and the default `source` of a lesson |
| `skill_resolver` | A function that resolves an embedded skill name to its path and content |
| `code` | A `CodeNav` handle, or `None` where no index is wired in |
| `mcp` | An `McpTools` handle for the MCP server tools of this execution |
| `manage` | A `Manage` handle, or `None` for an agent without the capability |
| `coord` | A `Coordinate` handle, or `None` for an agent without the capability |

The private state of `ToolEnv` has six parts:

- **The shell working directory.** It starts at `repo_root`. Bash, PowerShell, and Cmd update it after each call. The file tools resolve relative paths against it.
- **The set of files read.** `Read` adds a path to the set. `Write` and `Edit` need a path in the set. The set stores the folded form of the path (`ostra_core::paths::fold`), so a verbatim Windows path and a resolved path match.
- **The HTTP client** of WebFetch.
- **The private hosts** (`private_hosts`). These are the exact hosts from `WebFetch(domain:...)` rules. WebFetch can reach them even when they resolve to private addresses. See the WebFetch part.
- **The scrub list.** These are the variable names that Bash removes from the child process. See the Bash part.
- **The sandbox.** `with_sandbox` sets a backend and a profile. Without it, Bash runs without a sandbox.

`ToolEnv::resolve` turns a model path into a host path. It expands a leading `~/` to the home folder and resolves the path against the shell directory. Under bubblewrap, the sandboxed shell sees the scratch folder as `/tmp`. `resolve` maps that path back to the host path, so the file tools and Bash name the same file.

## File tools: Read, Write, and Edit

`crates/ostra-tools/src/fs.rs` holds the three file tools.

### Read

`Read` takes `file_path`, and optionally `offset` (1-based line, minimum 1) and `limit` (line count, minimum 1). It returns numbered lines in the format of `cat -n`: the line number right-aligned to 6 characters, a tab, then the line. The line number and the tab are not part of the file. The model must leave them out of an `Edit` `old_string`.

These rules apply:

- The default is `DEFAULT_LINES`, 2000 lines from the start.
- A line longer than `MAX_LINE_CHARS`, 2000 bytes, is cut and ends with `... [line truncated]`.
- A file larger than `MAX_READ_BYTES`, 50 MB, gives an error that tells the model to use `head`, `tail`, or `sed -n`.
- A directory gives an error that names `Glob` and `ls`.
- A file is binary when its first 8192 bytes hold a zero byte or invalid UTF-8. `Read` then returns a normal result with the size and no content. It still marks the file as read.
- An empty file returns a note that the file exists and is empty.
- An `offset` past the last line returns a note with the line count.
- When the result does not start at line 1 or does not reach the last line, `Read` appends `Showing lines X to Y of N`.
- A missing file gives the error `File does not exist: <path>`.

A successful `Read` marks the file as read in `ToolEnv`. Skill files and the report file get the same mark.

### Write

`Write` takes `file_path` and `content`. It replaces the whole file, and it creates missing parent folders. It never appends.

If the file exists and the run did not read it, `Write` returns an error. The text says that the model must read the file first, so that it does not overwrite content that it has not seen. A new file needs no read. A directory gives an error. After a write, the file counts as read, so the model can write it again. The result carries a unified diff for the Activity view.

### Edit

`Edit` replaces exact text. It takes `file_path`, `old_string`, `new_string`, and optionally `replace_all` (default `false`). The checks run in this order:

1. If `old_string` equals `new_string`, the call fails.
2. If the file does not exist and `old_string` is empty, `Edit` creates the file with `new_string` as content.
3. If the file does not exist and `old_string` is not empty, the call fails.
4. If the run did not read the file, the call fails.
5. If the file exists and `old_string` is empty, the call fails.
6. If `old_string` has no match, the call fails. The text tells the model to read the file again.
7. If `old_string` has more than one match and `replace_all` is `false`, the call fails. The text gives the match count.

A successful single edit returns the 4 lines before and after the change, numbered. A successful `replace_all` over many matches returns `All N matches were replaced`. Both results carry a diff.

The diff of `Write` and `Edit` is capped at 50,000 bytes by `unified_diff` in `crates/ostra-tools/src/text.rs`.

## Search tools: Grep and Glob

`crates/ostra-tools/src/search.rs` holds both tools. They use the `ignore`, `grep-regex`, `grep-searcher`, and `globset` crates, and run in a blocking task.

### What both tools walk

Both tools share one file walker. The walker follows these rules:

- It includes hidden files, so `.ostra/` is searched.
- It respects `.gitignore`, the git exclude file, the global git ignore, and the ignore files of parent folders. A folder without a `.git` folder still uses them.
- It skips every `.git` folder.
- It skips credential stores and the Ostra data folder, except the `assets` folder of the data folder. `SecretFilter` applies this rule. The reason is in its comment: a search that starts in a parent folder must not walk into those paths.

### Grep

`Grep` takes `pattern` (a Rust regex) and these optional fields: `path` (file or folder, default the shell directory), `glob`, `type`, `output_mode`, `-i`, `-n`, `-A`, `-B`, `-C`, `head_limit`, and `multiline`.

- `glob` can hold many globs. Commas or spaces outside braces separate them. A `{a,b}` group stays one glob.
- `type` accepts the ripgrep type names. `type_alias` maps `rs`, `python`, `golang`, `javascript`, `typescript`, `kt`, `rb`, `md`, `yml`, `c++`, `sh`, and similar names to the ripgrep names.
- `multiline` lets `.` match a newline and lets a pattern span lines.
- `-C` sets both context sizes. `-A` and `-B` override it. Context applies only in `content` mode.
- The searcher uses `BinaryDetection::quit(0)`. In a file that holds a zero byte, the search stops at the first zero byte. Matches before that byte can still appear in the result. Matches after it do not.

The `output_mode` field selects the result:

| Mode | Result | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `files_with_matches` (default) | `Found N file(s)` and the paths, newest first by modification time | `head_limit` cuts the list |
| `content` | Lines as `path:line:text`. Context lines use `-` in place of `:`. `--` separates non-adjacent groups | `head_limit` counts output lines, including context. A line over 500 bytes ends with `...` |
| `count` | One `path:count` row for each file and a total line | `head_limit` cuts the rows |

In every mode, the whole output is cut at `MAX_GREP_OUTPUT`, 30,000 bytes, with a note of how much was cut. With no match, the tool returns `No files found` or `No matches found`. These are normal results, not errors.

These cases return an error: a `path` that does not exist, an invalid regex, an unknown `output_mode`, an invalid glob, and an unknown file type.

### Glob

`Glob` takes `pattern` and optionally `path`, which must be a folder. `*` does not cross a folder separator, and `**` does. The pattern matches the path relative to `path`. On Windows, the match uses forward slashes, so `**/*.rs` works. The result lists paths newest first. The tool returns at most `MAX_GLOB_RESULTS`, 100, and appends a note with the total when it cuts the list.

## Bash

`crates/ostra-tools/src/bash.rs` runs shell commands. The tool takes `command` and optionally `timeout` in milliseconds. The default is `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS`, 120,000 (2 minutes). The code clamps the value to the range 1 to `MAX_TIMEOUT_MS`, 600,000 (10 minutes). The schema also has a `description` field. The tool does not use it. The Activity view can show it.

### How a command runs

The tool starts `bash -c` with a fixed script. The command text goes to the script through the environment variable `OSTRA_CMD`, so no quoting problem can occur. The script does these steps:

1. It merges stderr into stdout (`exec 2>&1`).
2. It changes to the saved working directory.
3. It removes `OSTRA_CMD`, `OSTRA_PWD_FILE`, and `OSTRA_CWD` from the environment of the command.
4. It sets an `EXIT` trap that writes the final directory to a temporary file.
5. It runs the command with `eval`.

The comment in the code gives the reason for `eval`: the command runs in the same shell, so a `cd` reaches the `EXIT` trap. After the call, the tool reads the file and updates the working directory of `ToolEnv`. The next call, and the file tools, start there. On Windows, Git Bash prints the path with `pwd -W`, so the saved path is a Windows path. If the saved directory no longer exists, the tool goes back to `repo_root`.

The child process gets this environment:

- Stdin is closed.
- `GIT_PAGER` and `PAGER` are `cat`.
- `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF` is removed, and `ostra_core::git::agent_env()` adds the git variables for agents. The test `repo_git_config_cannot_run_fsmonitor` shows the goal: a `core.fsmonitor` setting in the repo must not run a hook.
- The scrub list is removed (see below).

### Which variables the child never sees

`scrubbed_vars` builds the list of variables to remove. It holds:

- the credential variables that `config.toml` names, plus the default provider variables and the bridge variables (`configured_secret_vars`)
- the secrets of the workspace MCP servers (`with_scrub_env`)
- every inherited variable whose name starts with `OSTRA_`

The test `child_does_not_see_scrubbed_vars` checks this. The page [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md) describes the other protections.

### Sandbox or no sandbox

If `ToolEnv` has a sandbox, the tool starts bash through `profile.command(backend, ...)`. It first creates the temporary file for the directory and adds it to the profile as a writable file, because the `EXIT` trap writes there from inside the sandbox. If the sandbox cannot start, the tool returns `Cannot prepare the sandbox: <error>` and does not run the command without it. If `ToolEnv` has no sandbox, the tool starts the bash that `ostra_core::shells::bash()` finds.

### How a call ends

The tool waits for four events at the same time. The first event decides the end.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Start bash with the script"] --> B{"First event"}
    B -->|"Process exits"| C["Exited"]
    B -->|"Deadline passes"| D["TimedOut"]
    B -->|"Cancel token fires"| E["Cancelled"]
    B -->|"wait fails"| F["WaitFailed"]
    D --> G["Kill the process tree"]
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H["Wait up to 5 seconds for the exit"]
    C --> I["Drain output for 300 ms"]
    H --> I
    I --> J["Kill the tree if a pipe stays open"]
    J --> K["Read the saved directory"]
    K --> L["Build the ToolOutput"]
```

The shell tools are the only tools that `execute` does not wrap in the cancel select. They drain their own output and handle the cancel themselves. `execute` cancels another tool by dropping its future, and a dropped future loses the output that the tool already captured.

The tests give the reasons for the kill rules:

- `timeout_kills_process_group` starts a background child with a `sleep` and a `touch`. After the timeout, the marker file must not appear. A child must not outlive the call.
- `background_process_does_not_hang_the_call` runs `sleep 30 & echo started`. The call must return in less than 5 seconds. A background process that holds the pipe open does not block the call, because the tool drains for only 300 ms (`DRAIN_GRACE`) and then kills the tree.
- The wait after a kill is limited to `KILL_WAIT`, 5 seconds. On Windows, a process that is killed during its own creation can fail to exit.

The `ToolOutput` depends on the end:

| End | `is_error` | Text | `exit_code` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Exit 0 | no | The output, or `(no output)` | `Some(0)` |
| Exit N | yes | The output, then `Exit code: N` | `Some(N)` |
| Killed by a signal | yes | The output, then `The command was terminated by a signal.` | none |
| Timeout | yes | `The command timed out after <ms> ms and was stopped. Output so far:` and the output | none |
| Cancel | yes | `The command was cancelled. Output so far:` and the output | none |
| Wait failure | yes | `Waiting for the command failed: <error>` and the output | none |

### Output capture and limits

`Capture` keeps the output in bounded memory. It keeps the first `CAPTURE_HALF` bytes (128 KB) and the last 128 KB. If the output is longer, the middle is lost and the text `... [N bytes dropped] ...` marks the place. Then `truncate_middle` cuts the joined text to `MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS`, 30,000 bytes: the first 15,000 and the last 15,000, with `... [N characters truncated] ...` between them. The test `streams_live_output_and_truncates` prints 20,000 lines and checks that the result starts with `line1`, ends with `line20000`, and stays under 31,000 bytes.

The live callback (`LiveOutput`) gets each chunk when it arrives, so the Activity view shows progress. `Utf8Stream` holds back an incomplete UTF-8 sequence until the next chunk completes it.

## Windows shell tools

On Windows, the `Shell` capability grants three tools: `Bash`, `PowerShell`, and `Cmd`. The module `crates/ostra-tools/src/winshell.rs` exists only on Windows (`#[cfg(windows)]`). The input shape is the same as for Bash: `command`, `timeout`, and `description`. The timeout rules, the capture, and the texts for exit, timeout, and cancel are the same as for Bash, because the module reuses `Capture`, `Utf8Stream`, `spawn_reader`, and `KILL_WAIT` from `bash.rs`.

Two texts differ from Bash or have no separate form:

- **Signal:** when the process has no exit code, the Windows tools return `The command was terminated.` Bash returns `The command was terminated by a signal.`
- **Wait failure:** the Windows tools have no separate wait-failure text. A failed wait returns the same `Waiting for the command failed: <error>` text as Bash, with the output after it.

### Why the policy treats these tools differently

The command parser of Ostra reads bash (tree-sitter-bash). It cannot read PowerShell or cmd text. The write-scope and secret-read guards need a parsed command, so they cannot check these commands. The policy therefore handles the two tools like an unparsed shell command:

- The permission layer never allows them automatically. They always depend on the permission mode.
- The guard `check_opaque_shell` refuses a command outright when its raw text names a state path of Ostra or a credential path.

The tool descriptions tell the model to prefer Bash. The rules of the guards are in [Policy engine](policy.md).

### How each shell runs

- **PowerShell** starts with `-NoProfile -NonInteractive -Command`. The script runs `Set-Location` to the saved directory, runs the command in a `try` block, and writes `(Get-Location).Path` to the temporary file in the `finally` block. Single quotes in the paths are doubled.
- **Cmd** gets one raw argument, which `raw_cmd_line` builds: `/d /s /c "cd /d "{cwd}" && {command} & cd > "{pwd_file}""`. The code passes it raw because the standard library quotes an inner `"` as `\"`, and cmd does not understand that form. The `/s` switch strips the outer quotes. The trailing `cd` records the final directory and keeps `ERRORLEVEL`. The code does not group the command in parentheses, because a `)` in the command ends the group.

Both shells remove the scrub list from the child process, run with the git variables of `agent_env`, use a closed stdin, and kill the whole process tree when the call ends.

> Caution: the code of `winshell.rs` starts the shell program directly. It does not read the sandbox of `ToolEnv`, and it does not remove `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF`. Do not assume that the Bash sandbox rules apply to PowerShell or Cmd. The permission mode and the opaque-shell guard are the controls for these tools.

## WebFetch and WebSearch

### WebFetch

`WebFetch` takes `url` (a full http or https URL) and optionally `prompt`. It returns the page as Markdown. `crates/ostra-tools/src/web.rs` holds the code.

The tool does these steps:

1. It parses the URL. An invalid URL, or a scheme other than `http` and `https`, gives an error.
2. It refuses a URL whose host is a private IP literal, unless an allow rule names the host.
3. It sends a GET request with an `accept` header that prefers HTML, Markdown, plain text, and JSON.
4. If the response is a redirect to another host, it returns a normal result that tells the model to fetch the new URL with a new call.
5. It reads the body up to `MAX_BODY_BYTES`, 5 MiB.
6. It converts the body to text. HTML becomes Markdown with `htmd`. The tool also treats a body with an empty content type as HTML when its first 512 characters hold `<html` or `<!doctype html`. Types that start with `text/`, and types that contain `json`, `xml`, `javascript`, `yaml`, or `markdown`, pass through as they are. Other types, and bodies with a zero byte in the first 8192 bytes, give an error.
7. It cuts the text to `MAX_TEXT_CHARS`, 100,000 bytes.
8. It builds the result: the `Prompt:` line when `prompt` is set, a `Redirected to:` line when the final URL differs, then `Content of <url> (HTTP <status>):` and the text.

A response with a status outside 200 to 299 gives the same text, but `is_error` is `true`. Thus the model sees the body of a 404 page together with the error flag.

### The limits of the client

The client has these properties:

- A total timeout of 20 seconds.
- The user agent `ostra/<version>`.
- A redirect limit of `MAX_REDIRECTS`, 10.
- It follows a redirect only inside one host and port. The comment gives the reason: the policy checked only the first URL. A redirect to another host comes back to the model as a new URL, and the policy checks it.
- It ignores proxy settings (`no_proxy`). A proxy resolves the name itself, so the address check below does not run.
- It uses `PublicResolver`. The resolver removes private and loopback addresses from the DNS answer. If no public address remains, the call fails. The check runs at the connect, so a name cannot change its DNS answer between the check and the connect.

The tool refuses a private or loopback target with this text: add the allow rule `WebFetch(domain:<host>)`. The function `webfetch_hosts` takes the exact hosts from rules of that form. `ToolEnv::with_private_hosts` stores them in lower case and builds the client again. Only an exact host name works. The test `refuses_private_addresses_unless_a_rule_names_the_host` covers `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, `169.254.169.254`, `::ffff:127.0.0.1`, and `localhost`. The function `is_private` comes from `ostra_sandbox::egress`, so the sandbox proxy and WebFetch use one definition of a private address.

### WebSearch

WebSearch has no local code. `definitions` returns nothing for the `WebSearch` capability. The function `wants_web_search` returns `true` when the capability is present, and the native loop then enables the search tool of the model provider. If a call named `WebSearch` reaches `execute`, it returns this error: WebSearch runs on the model provider's side and has no local implementation. [Model providers, tiers, and cost](providers-and-cost.md) describes the providers.

## Skill, Report, memory, and documentation tools

`crates/ostra-tools/src/misc.rs` holds these small tools.

### Skill

`Skill` loads a `SKILL.md` file. It takes `name` or `path`. The tool accepts `skill` as an older name for the `name` field.

- With `path`, the tool resolves the path and reads the file.
- With `name`, the tool removes a leading `ostra:`. It refuses a name that holds `/` or `..`. It then looks in this order: the project skill (`.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, then the older `.ostra/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`), a custom skill kept as a workspace artifact, and an embedded skill from `skill_resolver`.
- If nothing matches, the error lists the paths that the tool tried and tells the model not to guess.

The result starts with `Skill loaded from <path>.` and holds the content. A loaded file counts as read.

### Report

`Report` takes `content` and writes it to `report_file` of `ToolEnv`. The model cannot choose the path, because later stages must find the report. If the run declared no report file, the tool returns an error. The `reason` field is for the lesson gate. When the gate refuses a report, the model records a lesson with `Memory`, or passes `reason` to say why no lesson applies. The gate is part of the policy, not of this tool. See [Policy engine](policy.md).

### Memory and MemoryRecall

`Memory` records a lesson. It needs a non-empty `area` and a non-empty `lesson`. `source` defaults to `memory_source` of `ToolEnv`. If the model records the same area and lesson again, the store updates the lesson. The result says how many lessons the store now holds.

`MemoryRecall` takes `query`, and optionally `area` and `limit`. The default limit is `DEFAULT_RECALL_LIMIT`, 8. The tool clamps the limit to 1 to `MAX_RECALL_LIMIT`, 50. It returns a numbered list with area, lesson, source, and date, most relevant first. [Project init, skills, and lesson memory](project-init-and-memory.md) owns the store.

### DocsSearch

`DocsSearch` searches the documentation books of the workspace. It takes `query`, and optionally `project` and `limit`. The default limit is 5 and the maximum is 15 (`book_search::DEFAULT_LIMIT` and `MAX_LIMIT`). It builds the search index on each call. If the run has no workspace, the tool says that no books exist. If the workspace has no books, or no section matches, it returns a normal result that tells the model to read the code. [Documentation books](documentation-books.md) describes the search.

### Document

`Document` writes the research document, the spec, or the plan. `crates/ostra-tools/src/doc.rs` checks the file name and the folder, then applies `document` or `update` and `remove`. [Typed pipeline documents](typed-documents.md) owns these rules.

## Code navigation tools

The `Code` capability grants eight tools. The constant `CODE_TOOLS` in `crates/ostra-core/src/agent.rs` lists them. The MCP name is `code_<operation>`.

| Tool | MCP name | Required input | Optional input |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `CodeOutline` | `code_outline` | `path` | `limit` |
| `CodeFind` | `code_find` | `query` | `limit` |
| `CodeCallers` | `code_callers` | `symbol` | `path`, `limit` |
| `CodeCallees` | `code_callees` | `path`, `symbol` | `line`, `limit` |
| `CodeImplementations` | `code_implementations` | `symbol` | `path`, `line`, `limit` |
| `CodeNeighbors` | `code_neighbors` | `path` | `limit` |
| `CodeImpact` | `code_impact` | none | `symbol`, `path`, `paths`, `direction`, `depth`, `limit` |
| `CodeMap` | `code_map` | none | `prefix` |

The tools share these rules:

- A path is relative to the project root. An absolute path inside the project also works.
- `limit` is an integer from 1 to 300. The default is 40. For `CodeImpact`, the default is 100.
- `CodeImpact` takes `direction` (`dependents`, the default, or `dependencies`) and `depth` (1 to 10, default 3). With `symbol`, it follows the uses of that name. With `paths`, it works on whole files.

`ostra-tools` does not contain the index. The trait `CodeNav` has one method, `call(repo_root, tool, input)`, and the server supplies the implementation through `ToolEnvConfig.code`. The tool returns its text as a normal result, or its `Err` as an error. If no `CodeNav` is wired in, the tool returns an error that tells the model to use Grep, Glob, and Read. The index, the graph, and the language support are in [Code navigation](code-navigation.md).

## MCP tools

A tool of an external MCP server has a canonical name `mcp__<server>__<tool>`. `is_gateway_tool` recognizes it: the name starts with `mcp__` and the rest holds `__`. A harness sees the same tool as `mcp__ostra__<server>__<tool>`.

The trait `McpTools` serves one execution. Its list is fixed when the execution starts.

- `definitions()` returns the tool definitions under canonical names.
- `read_only()` returns the names of tools that their server marks with `readOnlyHint`.
- `call(tool, input, cancel)` runs a tool.

The trait `McpConnector` opens the tools of an execution. It returns `McpOpened`, with the tools and one note for each server that it could not reach. The Activity view shows the notes. If `ToolEnvConfig.mcp` is `None`, a call returns ``Unknown tool `<name>`.``. The cancel token reaches the MCP call, so a stop request can end it. [MCP servers and Web Push](mcp-and-notifications.md) owns the client, the transports, and the sign-in.

## Management tools: ProjectList and ProjectCreate

A management tool is a call that an agent makes to Ostra itself. The problem that `ProjectCreate` solves: a request can need a codebase that no project in the workspace holds. Without the tool, the agent has nowhere to put the code. The two tools are `ProjectList` and `ProjectCreate`. `crates/ostra-core/src/manage.rs` holds the input rules and `crates/ostra-server/src/manage.rs` holds the server side.

### Who has the tools

The capability `ManageProjects` belongs to the `implementer` agent only (`AgentName::manages_projects`, Rule O2). The reason is in the comment: only a phase of an approved plan starts a project. The server type `Management` implements `ManageConnector`. Its `open` returns `None` when the agent lacks the capability or the run has no session. In that case, a call returns an error that says that the agent does not manage projects. The MCP names are `project_list` and `project_create`.

### ProjectList

`ProjectList` takes no input. It returns:

- the workspace root, with a note that a new project folder is relative to it
- one line for each project: key, path, stack (or `not set`), the init state, and `, in this session's scope` when the session scope holds the key
- the text `No projects yet.` when the list is empty

The init state is `initialized`, `not initialized`, `initializing`, or `folder missing`. The description tells the model to call `ProjectList` before `ProjectCreate`, so the key and folder are free.

### ProjectCreate input

| Field | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `key` | Lowercase letters, digits, and dashes. It starts with a letter or a digit |
| `stack` | The language and main framework in a few words, for example `rust`. It must pass the stack-name check |
| `purpose` | 1 to `MAX_PURPOSE_CHARS` (800) characters |
| `requirements` | 1 to `MAX_REQUIREMENTS` (20) entries. Each entry has at most `MAX_REQUIREMENT_CHARS` (400) characters. One fact for each entry |
| `folder` | Optional. Relative to the workspace root, with no `..`, no absolute path, and no `./`. The default is the key |
| `git_init` | Optional. The default is `true` |

`ProjectCreateInput::parse` trims all text, drops empty requirements, removes trailing `/` and `\` from `folder`, and then checks the rules. These checks need no workspace state. Each error message names the fix. The code comment gives the reason: Ostra can refuse a malformed call before it asks the user.

### Approval comes first

`changes_ostra` returns `true` only for `ProjectCreate`. The permission layer then follows Rule O1:

- The user answers every call, in every permission mode, whatever the allow rules say.
- YOLO mode answers the call in place of the user.
- A deny rule still refuses the call.
- In plan mode, the mode default applies.

The permission card shows `ask_reason`: ``Create project `<key>` (<stack>) in `<folder>/` of the workspace: <purpose>``. The function clips the text to 250 characters, because some harnesses clip ask reasons. The server code runs only after the policy allowed the call and the user approved it. [Gates, judges, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md) describes YOLO.

### What the server does

The method `ExecManage::create` runs these steps:

1. It parses the input again.
2. It asks the session state, `project_creation_refusal`, for a refusal.
3. It validates the target folder with `create_target`. The folder must be new or empty, and outside every other project.
4. It claims the folder with `git::claim`, so no other git operation uses it.
5. It creates the folder.
6. If `git_init` is `true`, it runs `git init --quiet` in the folder.
7. It imports the folder as a project with `import_project`, with the key and the stack.
8. It notifies the workspace views, then adds a `CreatedProject` to the session with `add_created_project`.
9. It returns a text that tells the agent to tag the deliverables with the new key and to write the first deliverable as the project skeleton. Ostra initializes the empty project from the stack and requirements when the build starts, before any phase runs in it.

### What happens when a project creation fails

The session state refuses a call with a reason, and the tool returns it as an error:

- The session is not a pipeline session: `Create projects only from a pipeline session.`
- The session has ended.
- The run that asked for the project has ended.
- The key is already in the session scope.
- The approved plan does not name the key as a new project.
- The phase of the run does not belong to that project.

Other failure cases:

- **The workspace is not open, or the server stops:** the call returns an error that names the cause.
- **`git init` fails:** the server removes what it created (`clear_failed`) and returns `git init failed, so nothing was created`.
- **The import fails:** the server removes what it created and returns the validation messages.
- **The project exists but cannot join the session:** the error says that the project was created at the path but could not join the session.
- **The user denies the call:** the tool description tells the agent to put the work in a project already in scope and to say so in its document.

The `CreatedProject` record holds `key`, `path`, `stack`, `purpose`, `requirements`, `execution`, and `agent`. The comment gives the reason for the fields: the session fold cannot read workspace settings, so the event carries every fact that the fold and later spawns need. [Sessions and the pipeline](sessions-and-pipeline.md) describes the fold.

## Output limits

| Tool | Limit | Name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Read` | 2000 lines for each call | `DEFAULT_LINES` |
| `Read` | 2000 bytes for each line | `MAX_LINE_CHARS` |
| `Read` | 50 MB for each file | `MAX_READ_BYTES` |
| `Write`, `Edit` | 50,000 bytes of diff | `unified_diff` |
| `Edit` | 4 lines of context on each side of the change | `snippet` |
| `Bash`, `PowerShell`, `Cmd` | Timeout 120,000 ms by default, 600,000 ms at most | `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS`, `MAX_TIMEOUT_MS` |
| `Bash`, `PowerShell`, `Cmd` | 30,000 bytes of output, first half and last half | `MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS` |
| `Bash`, `PowerShell`, `Cmd` | 128 KB head and 128 KB tail in memory | `CAPTURE_HALF` |
| `Bash`, `PowerShell`, `Cmd` | 5 seconds to wait for a killed process, 300 ms to drain output | `KILL_WAIT`, `DRAIN_GRACE` |
| `Grep` | 30,000 bytes of output | `MAX_GREP_OUTPUT` |
| `Grep` | 500 bytes for each content line | in `ContentSink::push` |
| `Glob` | 100 paths | `MAX_GLOB_RESULTS` |
| `WebFetch` | 5 MiB of body, 100,000 bytes of text, 10 redirects, 20 seconds | `MAX_BODY_BYTES`, `MAX_TEXT_CHARS`, `MAX_REDIRECTS` |
| `MemoryRecall` | 8 lessons by default, 50 at most | `DEFAULT_RECALL_LIMIT`, `MAX_RECALL_LIMIT` |
| `DocsSearch` | 5 sections by default, 15 at most | `DEFAULT_LIMIT`, `MAX_LIMIT` |
| Code tools | 40 entries by default, 300 at most (`CodeImpact`: 100 by default) | schema `limit` |
| `ProjectCreate` | 800, 20, 400 characters and entries | `MAX_PURPOSE_CHARS`, `MAX_REQUIREMENTS`, `MAX_REQUIREMENT_CHARS` |
| Activity view of the native loop | 8 KB for each tool result | `EMIT_LIMIT` |

The code counts the limits that the constants call characters in bytes. It cuts only at a character boundary (`floor_boundary`), so a cut never splits a multibyte character.

The `ToolOutput` of a call has these fields: `text`, `is_error`, `exit_code`, `duration_ms`, `diff`, and `end`. `execute` sets `duration_ms` for every call. The field `end` is for coordination calls that make the run wait or end.

## What the tools do not guarantee

- The tools check no permission. A caller that skips the policy check gets no protection.
- Read-before-write is a safety rule for the model, not a lock. The tool does not check whether the file changed after the read.
- The file tools and Grep and Glob run in the host process. The sandbox covers Bash only. The policy guards and `SecretFilter` protect the file tools.
- PowerShell and Cmd run without the sandbox of `ToolEnv` and without a parsed command.
- WebFetch refuses private addresses, but a rule `WebFetch(domain:<host>)` removes that refusal for the exact host.
- A truncated output loses the middle of the text. The model must narrow the command or use `Read` with `offset` and `limit` to see the rest.
