sections.title: Policy engine: guards and permissions
sections.summary: How Ostra decides each tool call in two layers: guards that nothing overrides, then permission modes with allow, ask, and deny rules. Covers the Bash parser, rule syntax, rule suggestions, and the limits of the policy.
sections.body:
## The problem and the two layers

An agent calls tools that write files and run shell commands. A prompt that says "do not touch this file" does not stop a wrong call, or a call that a prompt injection causes. The policy engine in the `ostra-policy` crate decides each tool call before the tool runs. Its decision does not depend on what the model intends.

Every tool call of every executor passes two layers in order:

- **Layer 1, the guards** (`crates/ostra-policy/src/guards.rs`). A guard refuses a call that breaks an invariant of the pipeline. No permission rule, user answer, or YOLO setting overrides a guard.
- **Layer 2, the permissions** (`crates/ostra-policy/src/perms.rs` and `policy.rs`). Layer 2 follows the model of Claude Code: a permission mode plus `allow`, `ask`, and `deny` rules. Layer 2 can allow a call, ask the user, or deny the call.

The page covers these topics:

- the order of the checks and the shape of a decision
- each guard of layer 1
- the Bash parser that both layers use
- the permission modes and the rule syntax
- rule validation and rule suggestions
- the build streak and the lesson gate
- what the policy does not guarantee

The sandbox is a separate boundary at kernel level. See [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md). The guards come from the hook libraries of Ultracode, and the code comment of each guard names its source.

## Where the policy runs and what it decides

The policy is one `ExecutionPolicy` object for each execution. The engine builds an `ExecContext` for the execution, and the executor builds the policy from it. See [Executors](executors.md) for the two call paths:

- The native loop calls `ExecutionPolicy::check` for each tool call.
- A harness CLI (Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Antigravity) runs `ostra hook` before each tool call. The hook posts the call to `/internal/policy`, and the server calls `policy_check`.

The harness adapters translate each payload into a canonical `ToolCall` (`crates/ostra-core/src/policy.rs`). A `ToolCall` has a `tool` name and a JSON `input` in the shapes of Claude Code. The canonical names are `Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `Bash`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `Skill`, `WebSearch`, `WebFetch`, `Report`, `Memory`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch`, `ProjectList`, `ProjectCreate`, and `submit_<agent>`. A Codex patch is `ApplyPatch`. A harness tool with no canonical equivalent is `Other:<name>`.

The result is a `PolicyDecision`:

| Decision | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `Allow` | The tool runs. The optional `rule` names the rule that allowed it. |
| `Ask` | The tool waits for a user answer. `reason` says what the user approves. |
| `Deny` | The tool does not run. `reason` tells the model what to do instead. |

Each decision carries a `RuleRef` with a `layer` and a `rule`. The `layer` is `guard` or `permission`. The `rule` is a guard id such as `write-scope`, the text of a permission rule such as `Bash(git push *)`, or a mode label such as `mode:plan`. The Activity view shows the `RuleRef` with every decision.

The text of a denial starts with the correction, for example "Leave test files to write-test: ...". The reason is in the code comment: Grok clips a reason to 256 characters, so the useful part must come first.

## The order of the checks

`ExecutionPolicy::check` runs the same steps for every call. The sequence is short because layer 1 returns early on a denial.

### Flow of one tool call through the policy

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Tool call"] --> B{"Is it Bash?"}
  B -->|"yes"| C["bash::parse splits the command"]
  B -->|"no"| D["Layer 1: guards"]
  C --> D
  D -->|"a guard refuses"| E["Deny with the guard id"]
  D -->|"no guard refuses"| F["Layer 2: mode and rules"]
  F --> G{"Decision"}
  G -->|"Deny"| H["Deny with the rule or mode"]
  G -->|"Allow"| I["Allow"]
  G -->|"Ask"| J{"Is YOLO on?"}
  J -->|"yes"| K["Allow with rule yolo"]
  J -->|"no"| L["Ask the user"]
```

The excerpt below is the end of `check` in `crates/ostra-policy/src/policy.rs`. The `...` stands for the parse and the layer 1 call. The excerpt also puts each `Allow` value on fewer lines than the source does.

```rust
/// Layer 1 then layer 2. Under YOLO every ask becomes an allow; denials stand.
pub fn check(&self, call: &ToolCall) -> PolicyDecision {
    ...
    let decision = self.layer2(call, parsed.as_ref());
    if !self.yolo() {
        return decision;
    }
    match decision {
        PolicyDecision::Ask { .. } => PolicyDecision::Allow { rule: Some(RuleRef::permission("yolo")) },
        PolicyDecision::Allow { rule: Some(r) } if r.rule == "mode:bypass" => {
            PolicyDecision::Allow { rule: Some(RuleRef::permission("yolo")) }
        }
        d => d,
    }
}
```

Under YOLO, an `Ask` becomes `Allow` with the rule `yolo`. An `Allow` from `mode:bypass` also gets the rule `yolo`. A `Deny` from layer 1 or layer 2 stays a `Deny`. The executor sets the YOLO state again before each call, so a change in the browser applies to the next call. [Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md) owns the YOLO answer path.

## Layer 1 order of checks for one call

`layer1` tests the call in this order. The first guard that refuses ends the check.

1. **`answer-only`.** A consult run must change nothing. The guard refuses a file write, `Report`, `Document`, `Memory`, a management tool, and a shell command with a write target.
2. **`Report` tool.** The only check is the lesson gate. See [The build streak and the lesson gate](#the-build-streak-and-the-lesson-gate).
3. **`Document` tool.** `check_document` judges the target path, and `layer1` returns its result at once. A `Document` call never reaches the later steps, so steps 7 to 10 do not judge it.
4. **Management tools.** `check_manage` judges `ProjectCreate`.
5. **`reply-first`.** A run that owes an answer cannot call a `submit_*` tool.
6. **`submit_*` tools.** The lesson gate refuses status `ok` when a lesson is pending. Other statuses pass.
7. **`PowerShell` and `Cmd`.** `check_opaque_shell` scans the raw text.
8. **Write paths.** `check_write` judges each path of `Write`, `Edit`, `MultiEdit`, `NotebookEdit`, and `ApplyPatch`.
9. **Read path.** The Windows path check and `secret-read` judge the path of `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `Skill`, and the write tools. They do not judge `Document`, because step 3 already returned for it.
10. **Bash.** `check_shell`, `check_shell_reads`, and `check_write` for each write target. Then the `build-streak` gate.

`check_write` has its own order, because the guards overlap:

1. `manage-tools` (a run that must create its project first)
2. `windows-path`
3. `self-protection`, with tool enforcement on
4. `workspace-artifacts`
5. `workspace-docs`
6. `git-metadata`
7. `state-ownership`
8. `artifact-ownership` and `document-tool`
9. `no-tests-from-implementer`, then `write-scope`, with tool enforcement on for `write-scope`
10. `report-path` and the lesson gate for the declared report

## The guard ids

The constants of the guard ids are at the top of `guards.rs`. The table lists each id, what it refuses, and whether it needs tool enforcement. [The tool enforcement switch](#the-tool-enforcement-switch) explains the last column.

| Guard id | Refuses | Needs tool enforcement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `write-scope` | A write outside the scope of the agent | Yes |
| `no-tests-from-implementer` | A write to a test file by the `implementer` | No |
| `report-path` | A write to an `ostra-*` file in the session root that is not the declared report | Yes |
| `document-tool` | A direct write to the Markdown of a typed document | No |
| `state-ownership` | A write to engine state or to a file that another role owns | No |
| `artifact-ownership` | A write to a spec, plan, or research file by the wrong agent | No |
| `workspace-artifacts` | A write to the visible artifacts of the workspace | No |
| `workspace-docs` | A write to the documentation books | No |
| `self-protection` | A write to Ostra itself, a run of the Ostra binary, or interpreter code that writes or spawns | Yes, except for engine state in a shell word |
| `git-metadata` | A direct write under `.git` | No |
| `secret-read` | A read of credentials, session records, or process memory | No |
| `manage-tools` | A misuse of `ProjectCreate`, or a write before the project exists | No |
| `answer-only` | A change by a consult run | No |
| `reply-first` | A `submit_*` call by a run that owes an answer | No |
| `lesson-gate` | A report or a submit call when a lesson is pending | No |
| `build-streak` | A build or test command after 5 consecutive failures | No |
| `windows-path` | A Windows path spelling that the guards cannot compare | No (Windows only) |
| `read-only-session` | Every call of an inspect run. The server bridge makes this denial, not `ExecutionPolicy`. | No |

## Write scope and the test-file guard

`write-scope` limits where each agent can write. The guard needs tool enforcement. It compares the resolved target path with these roots:

- The **session dir** and the **session root** of the execution are always allowed.
- **OS temp scratch** is the OS temp dir and `/tmp`. A project that lives under temp is project source, not scratch.
- The **repo root** is the project folder.

The class of the agent decides the scope:

- **Session-only agents** (`AgentName::is_session_only`): `explore`, `generate-spec`, `fact-check`, `plan`, `code-reviewer`, `execution-path-analyzer`, `advisor`, `documentation`, and `system-architecture`. They write in the session dir and in OS temp. A write to project source gets the reason "never modifies project source".
- **`quick-answer`.** It is read-only. Every write is refused, and the agent puts its answer in its submit call.
- **`initializer`.** It writes in the project runtime folder (`.ostra/`), in `.agents/skills/`, and in its session dir. The older skills folder is refused, because Ostra reads it but writes new skills only to `.agents/skills/`. The guard resolves symbolic links, so a skills folder that links to another folder in the project still works.
- **All other agents**, such as `implementer` and `write-test`. They write in the repo root and in the session dir. A write outside both is refused, and OS temp is outside both. A phase path list is a hint and not an allow list, so any path in the repo is writable.

A project that does not exist yet has a stricter rule (Rule O2). The run writes nothing outside its session dir and OS temp until it calls `ProjectCreate`. No project root exists to hold the work.

`no-tests-from-implementer` refuses an `implementer` write to a test path in the repo. A test path is a folder named `__tests__`, `__mocks__`, `test`, or `tests`, or a file such as `*.test.ts`, `*.spec.js`, `test_*.py`, `*_test.go`, `*_spec.rb`, or `*Test.java`. The reason is in the denial: the implementer never writes or fixes tests, and tests run only after the user asks for them at the closing gate. The guard works without tool enforcement.

The `Document` tool has its own scope rule in `check_document`. The function follows these steps:

1. If the target is protected or engine state, it calls `check_write` and returns the result.
2. It checks artifact ownership, for example a `plan` file that another agent targets.
3. With tool enforcement on, it requires the target inside the session dir of the execution.

## Ownership guards

Ownership guards protect records that the pipeline writes. A hand-written value forges a decision and records nothing.

### Engine state

`state-ownership` refuses a write to engine state. Engine state is the `.state` folder of this session, the `.state` folder of any session, and the memory database of the project with its `-wal`, `-shm`, and `-journal` files. `Roots::is_engine_state` tests these paths. The reason in the denial: engine state is a record of something that already happened, and the engine writes it.

The guard also refuses by file name, in any folder:

- `knowledge.sqlite3` is the lesson store. Only the `Memory` tool writes it, because later sessions recall it as fact.
- `workspace.db` and `registry.db` are the databases of Ostra. They record every event, gate, and decision.

Some files belong to one role. Only the owners can write them:

| File name | Owners | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ostra-review-ledger[-name].md` | `code-reviewer`, `implementer`, `write-test` | The engine counts its iterations to cap the review loop. |
| `ostra-security-block.json` | `code-reviewer` | It records BLOCKER findings that nobody can waive. |
| `ostra-implementer-progress[-name].md` | `implementer` | A re-run reads it to learn which steps already succeeded. |

### Artifacts, documents, and books

`artifact-ownership` keeps each pipeline document with one agent:

- `ostra-spec-*.md` and `ostra-spec-*.json` belong to `generate-spec`.
- `ostra-plan-*.md` and `ostra-plan-*.json` belong to `plan`.
- `ostra-research-*.md` and `ostra-research-*.json` belong to `explore`.

A folder named `factcheck-snapshot-*` is exempt, because the copies that `fact-check` makes there are not the artifact.

`document-tool` refuses a direct write to a Markdown file that Ostra renders from a typed document. The agent must call the `Document` tool with `update`. The engine overwrites a direct write, and the browser does not show it. See [Typed pipeline documents](typed-documents.md).

Two more guards protect folders of the workspace:

- `workspace-artifacts` (Rule W1). Agents read the visible artifacts and never write, move, or delete them. Only the user changes them.
- `workspace-docs` (Rule B5). The engine writes the documentation books from the submit calls of the docs stage. A documentation agent returns its book in the submit call.

## Containment guards

Three guards protect the secrets and the control files of Ostra. Their denials are containment signals: the third signal of one execution pauses the session. See [The engine runner, recovery, and control](engine-runner.md). Other guards refuse ordinary mistakes and are not signals.

### The secret-read guard

`secret-read` refuses to read a secret, for the tools that it judges, in every mode, with or without YOLO. A path is secret when it is in one of these places:

- The Ostra data dir, except its `assets` folder, which agents read.
- The file named by `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE`.
- A home credential path from the list `HOME_CREDENTIALS` (for example `~/.ssh` and `~/.aws`). See [Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md).
- A workspace database, with its `-wal`, `-shm`, and `-journal` files, because it holds every tool output of every session.
- `/proc/self`, `/proc/thread-self`, and `/proc/<pid>`, because `environ` and `fd` expose the server environment and open files.
- The `harness` folder under any `.state` folder, because it holds the bridge token of an execution.

The guard judges the path of `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, and `Skill`. It also judges the path of a write tool, after the write guards. It does not judge `Document`, because `layer1` returns the result of `check_document` before the read-path step, and `check_document` never calls `check_read`. For `Bash`, `check_shell_reads` judges each word that looks like a path and each redirect target of every command. A command named `echo` or `printf` is skipped, because printing a path does not open it. A word such as `--file=/path` is split at the `=`. The text `/proc/<pid>/environ`, `mem`, or `fd` is matched in the source text, because a variable can build the pid.

The denial tells the agent to ask for a credential in its report, because agents never see credentials.

### Self-protection

`self-protection` guards the files that enforce the pipeline. `ExecContext::protected_paths` holds six paths: the Ostra executable, the global config file, the data dir, the assets dir, `workspace.toml`, and the workspace database. Two functions build this list:

- `Shared::protected_paths` (`crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs`) returns the first four paths: the executable, the global config file, the data dir, and the assets dir.
- `Services::protected_paths` (`crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs`) starts from that list. It adds `workspace.toml` and the workspace database of the workspace.

Agents never write, move, or delete these paths. `secret-read` also refuses a read of the data dir, so agents cannot read it. The assets dir is inside the data dir, and `secret-read` leaves it open, so agents can read the assets. `Roots::is_protected` also matches the workspace database with its `-wal`, `-shm`, and `-journal` files.

Engine state folders are not in `ExecContext::protected_paths`. `Roots::is_engine_state` and the `state-ownership` guard cover them separately.

With tool enforcement on, the guard also refuses these actions:

- A run of the Ostra binary from a tool call. The check is the command name `ostra`, or a path that points to a protected file. A caller can grant itself what the guards withhold.
- A command that touches a protected path with anything except a plain reader. `PLAIN_READERS` lists the readers, for example `cat`, `grep`, `head`, `ls`, `diff`, `jq`, and `sed` without `-i`.
- Inline interpreter code that writes to the file system or spawns a process. The interpreters are `node`, `bun`, `deno`, `python`, `perl`, `ruby`, `php`, and others. The guard reads the code from `-e`, `-c`, `--eval`, a heredoc, or piped stdin, and looks for write and spawn function names. The denial gives the reason: the write guards read the paths that a call names, and such code names none.

The guard also refuses inline code that names a protected state file, with or without tool enforcement. In that case the guard id is `state-ownership`.

### Git metadata

`git-metadata` refuses a direct write to any path with a `.git` component. This holds for every tool, every mode, and YOLO. The reason is in the denial: files under `.git` decide which programs git runs later (hooks, `fsmonitor`, or a gitfile that points to another git dir). Git commands can change them, and tools cannot. A file such as `.gitignore` is not under `.git`, and the guard allows it.

## Workspace and platform guards

Several guards enforce the rules of the pipeline and not the rules of the file system.

- **`manage-tools`** (Rule O1 and Rule O2). Only the `implementer` of a phase that the approved plan puts in a new project can call `ProjectCreate`. The call must parse, and its `key` must equal the project key of the run. Ostra never creates a project for a call that cannot run.
- **`answer-only`** (Rule H3). A consult run answers a question from its conversation and changes nothing. It answers with `SubagentReply`.
- **`reply-first`** (Rule H3). A run that another subagent asked a question must call `SubagentReply` before it submits. See [Subagent coordination](subagent-coordination.md).
- **`lesson-gate` and `build-streak`.** These two guards come from the post-tool observer. See [The build streak and the lesson gate](#the-build-streak-and-the-lesson-gate).
- **`windows-path`.** On Windows, the guard refuses a path spelling that the other guards cannot compare. `paths::windows_path_problem` (`crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs`, line 503) finds these forms: an NT object path (`\\??\\`), a network or share path such as `\\\\host\\share`, a device path that starts with `\\\\.\\`, a `\\\\?\\` path that does not name a drive, a drive-relative path (`C:foo`), and an alternate data stream (`file:stream`). The function lets a verbatim drive path such as `\\\\?\\C:\\x\\y` through, and a later step normalizes it. `paths::is_reserved_device` finds a reserved device name such as `CON` or `COM1`. The guard also refuses a shell write target with `..` right after a junction or symbolic link, because Git Bash and Windows programs resolve that `..` in different ways. Git Bash paths such as `/c/Users/me` are translated before the guards compare them. On Unix the check always passes.
- **`read-only-session`.** An inspect run is a read-only look back at a finished run. The server bridge denies every tool call of such a run with this guard.

### The NUL device name

The denial text of `windows-path` for a device name says "such as CON, NUL, or COM1". The code does not refuse `NUL`. `paths::is_reserved_device` in `crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs` is true for a device name other than `NUL`. The Windows test `reserved_device_names_are_caught_except_nul` asserts that `CON`, `com1.txt`, and `LPT9` are refused and that `NUL` is not. Do not rely on `windows-path` to refuse a write to `NUL`.

## The tool enforcement switch

Tool enforcement (Rule G1) turns on the guards that check where a call writes. The setting is `tool_enforcement` in `config.toml`, and a workspace can override it. The values are `disabled` and `enabled`. The default is `disabled`. The registry stores the workspace value and not the folder file (Rule A2), because a repository can otherwise turn off its own guards. See [Configuration reference](configuration.md). The engine reads the value when it builds the `ExecContext` of an execution, so a change applies to executions that start after it.

| Check | `disabled` | `enabled` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `write-scope` | Off | On |
| `report-path` mismatch | Off. Any `ostra-*` name is allowed. | On |
| `self-protection` for writes, the Ostra binary, and interpreter code | Off | On |
| `state-ownership`, `artifact-ownership`, `workspace-*`, `git-metadata`, `secret-read`, `no-tests-from-implementer` | On | On |
| Permission rules, workflow gates, and the sandbox | On | On |

The reason for the switch is in the code comment of `ToolEnforcement`. With `disabled`, an agent can reach files by any route, for example one script that edits several files. The sandbox still bounds that script.

## The Bash parser

Both layers need to know what a shell command does. `crates/ostra-policy/src/bash.rs` parses a command with `tree-sitter-bash`. It replaces the regex heuristics of the Ultracode file `shell-paths.js` and keeps its rules: a heredoc body that goes to a data sink is content, a body that goes to a shell runs, `<ID>` placeholders are not redirects, dot-only tokens are prose, and dynamic tokens are skipped.

`bash::parse` returns a `Parsed` value:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `commands` | The simple commands in execution order. |
| `complete` | `false` when the parser found a syntax error or reached the depth limit. The split can be wrong. |
| `modelled` | `false` when the source has a statement that the command list does not model. |

A `SimpleCommand` holds the assignments, the `words`, the `redirects`, the heredoc body, the source text, a `piped_input` flag, and the text of the whole pipeline. A `Word` has a `raw` text and a `value`. The `value` is the unquoted text when the word is static. A word with a variable or a substitution has no value and is dynamic. A word with an unquoted glob character or a brace expansion has the `glob` flag.

### What the parser flattens

The parser puts every command that runs into the `commands` list:

- commands of lists, pipelines, subshells, `if` and `while` statements
- commands inside command substitutions (`$(...)` and backticks) and process substitutions
- the string of `bash -c` and the arguments of `eval`, parsed again as shell
- a heredoc body that goes to a shell, parsed again as shell

A nested parse stops at depth 4 (`MAX_DEPTH`). A deeper level sets `complete` to `false`.

The parser finds the command that actually runs. It skips `VAR=value` words and these wrappers with their options: `sudo`, `doas`, `env`, `nohup`, `nice`, `ionice`, `stdbuf`, `time`, `timeout`, `command`, `exec`, `xargs`, `strace`, `watch`, and `builtin`. For example, `FOO=1 sudo -u me timeout 5 rm -rf a` is the command `rm`. `effective_name` removes any directory part, so `/bin/rm` is `rm`.

### What the parser does not model

`modelled` is `false` for a standalone assignment, `export`, `declare`, `unset`, a `[[ ]]` test with an expansion, a `for` loop header, and a function definition. These statements can change what a later command runs (`PATH`, `GIT_CONFIG_*`) or run code when the shell evaluates them. A test such as `[ -f x ]` over plain words is modelled. An `if` or `while` statement is modelled because it only groups commands.

### Write targets

`write_targets` lists every path that a command creates, overwrites, moves, or deletes:

| Source | Target |
| --- | --- |
| Redirects `>`, `>>`, `>|`, `&>`, `&>>`, `<>`, and `>&` to a file | The redirect target |
| `tee`, `rm`, `rmdir`, `shred`, `truncate`, `touch`, `mkdir`, `unlink` | Each word that is not a flag |
| `cp`, `install`, `ln`, `mv` | The destination. A directory destination gives `dest/name` for each source. All spellings of `--target-directory` and `-t` count, with their unique abbreviations. `mv` also lists each source. |
| `sed -i` and `perl -i` | The files. In `sed`, the first word that is not a flag is the script unless `-e` or `-f` gives it. |
| `dd` | The path in `of=` |
| `git` with `checkout`, `switch`, `restore`, `reset`, `apply`, `am`, `stash`, `clean`, `rm`, `mv`, `merge`, `rebase`, `pull`, `cherry-pick`, `revert`, `commit`, or `add` | The working tree: the `-C` folder or the current folder |

The parser skips `/dev/null`, `/dev/stdout`, `/dev/stderr`, `/dev/tty`, `-`, `&1`, `&2`, and dot-only words. A target with a variable, a substitution, a glob, or `~user` is **unresolved**: only the shell can name the real path. `unresolved_writes` lists the commands with such a target. A relative write after a `cd` with a dynamic target is also unresolved.

The parser follows `cd` and `pushd` with `command_cwds`. A relative target resolves against the new folder. A dynamic `cd` target, or `popd`, makes the folder unknown (`cwd_unknown`). Subshell scope is not modelled.

### Inline interpreter code

`inline_code` finds code that a command hands to an interpreter. The channels are the flags `-e`, `-E`, `--eval`, `-c`, `--command`, `-p`, `--print`, `-r`, and `--exec`, the `deno eval` form, a heredoc, and piped stdin when the command has no script argument. Layer 1 scans this code for the names of protected state files and, with tool enforcement on, for write and spawn calls.

## Layer 2: permission modes

Layer 2 decides what is left after the guards. The permission mode is the default answer. The rules change the answer for single calls.

| Mode | Value | Default answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Default | `default` | Ask for edits and for commands that are not known to be safe. |
| Accept edits | `acceptEdits` | Allow edits inside the project. Ask for the rest. |
| Plan | `plan` | Read-only. Deny what can change something. |
| Bypass | `bypass` | Allow everything that no guard or rule refuses. |

The enum is `PermissionMode` in `crates/ostra-core/src/config.rs`, and the default is `default`. The workspace setting is `permissions.mode`. The registry stores it and not the folder file (Rule A2). The engine copies it into the `ExecContext` of each new execution, so a change does not affect an execution that already runs. YOLO acts like `bypass`: `ExecutionPolicy::mode` returns `Bypass` when YOLO is on, for any mode that the workspace sets.

This table shows the answer of each mode for each kind of call when no rule matches. A matching `deny` or `ask` rule wins over the mode. A matching `allow` rule can change the answer for a shell write. See [Files that run code later](#files-that-run-code-later).

| Call | `default` | `acceptEdits` | `plan` | `bypass` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| File write in the session dir or OS temp | Allow, rule `session-dir` | Allow | Allow | Allow |
| File write in the repo | Ask | Allow, rule `mode:acceptEdits` | Deny | Allow |
| File write outside the repo, session dir, and temp | Ask | Ask | Deny | Allow |
| File-tool write to a file that runs code later (any `allow` rule is ignored) | Ask | Ask | Deny | Allow |
| Shell write to a file that runs code later, with no `allow` rule that matches the command | Ask | Ask | Deny | Allow |
| Shell write to a file that runs code later, with an `allow` rule that matches the command | Allow, rule is the `allow` rule | Allow, same rule | Allow, same rule | Allow |
| Read-only `Bash` command | Allow, rule `read-only` | Allow | Allow | Allow |
| `mkdir`, `touch`, `cp`, `mv` with targets in the repo, session dir, or temp | Ask | Allow | Deny | Allow |
| Other `Bash` command | Ask | Ask | Deny | Allow |
| `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `Skill` | Allow | Allow | Allow | Allow |
| `WebFetch` | Ask | Ask | Ask | Allow |
| Known Ostra tools and `submit_*` | Allow | Allow | Allow | Allow |
| Workspace MCP tool (`mcp__server__tool`) | Allow | Allow | Deny, unless the server marks it read-only | Allow |
| Any other tool, including `Other:<name>`, `PowerShell`, and `Cmd` | Ask | Ask | Deny | Allow, rule `mode:bypass` |
| `ProjectCreate` | Ask | Ask | Deny | Ask |

The known Ostra tools are `WebSearch`, `Skill`, `Report`, `Document`, `Memory`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch`, the code navigation tools, `ProjectList`, the coordination tools, and the harness bookkeeping tools (`ToolSearch`, `TodoWrite`, `update_plan`, and similar). A rule still applies to them, so `deny = ["WebSearch"]` refuses `WebSearch`. The workspace MCP server tools are allowed unless a rule says otherwise (Rule M1). A tool that a harness serves through its own MCP server arrives as `Other:mcp__...` and counts as an unknown tool.

`ProjectCreate` follows Rule O1. The user answers every call that changes Ostra, in every mode that allows writes and whatever the allow rules say. An allow rule never answers for the user. A `deny` rule still refuses the call, plan mode refuses it, and only YOLO answers it.

## Layer 2: the order of the rules

A permission rule has the form `Tool` or `Tool(pattern)`. The rules come from three places:

- The global `[permissions]` table in `config.toml`. The default is `deny = ["Bash(rm -rf /*)"]`.
- The workspace `[permissions]` table, with `allow`, `ask`, and `deny` lists.
- The session allow rules. These rules live in memory for one execution, and the answer "Always in this workspace" adds them. See [Rule suggestions](#rule-suggestions-and-always-in-this-workspace).

`PermissionRules::merged` joins the global and workspace lists, in that order. The engine does this when it spawns an execution, and `ExecutionPolicy::new` parses the lists once. A change to the rules applies to executions that start after the change.

The order is the same for every kind of call: **deny, then ask, then allow**. The first rule that matches in a list wins. A matching `deny` rule refuses the call, whatever else matches. A matching `ask` rule asks the user, even in `bypass`. An `allow` rule allows the call when no `deny` or `ask` rule matches. If no rule matches, the mode decides.

The rules for a file-tool write have two more steps. In `layer2` (`Family::Edit`), a write to a file that runs code later gets the mode answer and not the `allow` answer, even when an `allow` rule matches. The next section lists these files. A write in the session dir or OS temp is allowed when no `deny` or `ask` rule matches. A `Bash` call does not follow this extra step.

### Files that run code later

`runs_code_later` marks files that make a tool run a program the next time someone opens the project. A write to one of them outlives the session and runs outside the policy. The result depends on the kind of call.

- **File-tool write** (`Write`, `Edit`, `MultiEdit`, `NotebookEdit`, `ApplyPatch`). In `layer2` (`Family::Edit`), the `runs_code_later` test comes before any `allow` rule. Outside YOLO and `bypass`, such a write always asks, and plan mode denies it. A matching `deny` or `ask` rule is tested first and wins.
- **Shell write** (`Bash`). The rule "always asks" does not hold. Without an `allow` rule, the write asks in the same way, because `targets_known` is `false` for such a target, so the command is not read-only and `acceptEdits` does not cover it. Plan mode denies it. With an `allow` rule that matches the simple command, `bash_permission` in `crates/ostra-policy/src/policy.rs` does `continue` before the `targets_known`, `writes_ok`, and mode steps. The local variable `allowed_by_rule` (lines 832-840) holds the matching rule. The allow match does `continue` (line 843) before any `runs_code_later` effect. The function `runs_code_later` is used earlier, at line 814, only to make `targets_known` false.

The list of files:

- By file name: `.mcp.json`, `.envrc`, `.pre-commit-config.yaml`, `.lefthook.yml`, `lefthook.yml`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, `.npmrc`, `.yarnrc.yml`, `.pnpmfile.cjs`.
- By path ending: `/.claude/settings.json`, `/.claude/settings.local.json`, `/.codex/config.toml`, `/.gemini/settings.json`, `/.vscode/tasks.json`, `/.vscode/settings.json`, `/.vscode/launch.json`, `/.cargo/config.toml`, `/.cargo/config`.
- By folder: `/.github/workflows/`, `/.github/actions/`, `/.devcontainer/`, `/.husky/`, `/.claude/hooks/`, `/.grok/`.

### A Bash allow rule skips the code-later check

With `allow = ["Bash(echo *)"]`, the command `echo x > .mcp.json` is allowed with no question. The `allow` rule matches the simple command `echo x`, and the loop of `bash_permission` moves to the next command. The redirect target `.mcp.json` is never tested against `runs_code_later`. The same happens in plan mode, because the allow step comes before the mode step.

Review each `Bash` allow rule that can write `.mcp.json`, `.envrc`, or `.github/workflows/`. Such a rule allows the write with no question, and the file runs code after the session ends. A prefix rule such as `Bash(npm run *)` or `Bash(echo *)` can write to any of these files when the script or the redirect names one.

These limits still apply to the shell write:

- A matching `Bash` `deny` or `ask` rule is tested before the `allow` rule and wins.
- The layer 1 guards judge the write targets first. `git-metadata`, `state-ownership`, `self-protection`, and the other guards still refuse their targets.
- The sandbox write scope still applies to a Bash write. See [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md).

The test `files_that_run_code_later_always_ask` (`crates/ostra-policy/tests/policy.rs`, line 1458) builds the policy with empty `allow`, `ask`, and `deny` lists. For `acceptEdits`, it asserts an ask for a file-tool write and for `echo x > <rel>`, for each of 8 paths. For plan mode, it asserts only that a file-tool `write` to `.mcp.json` is denied. It does not cover a `Bash` `allow` rule, so no test shows that an allow rule cannot authorize the shell write.

## Layer 2: how a Bash command is judged

Layer 2 judges each simple command of a `Bash` call. The steps happen in this order:

### Decision steps for one Bash call

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Parsed command"] --> B{"A simple command matches a deny rule?"}
  B -->|"yes"| C["Deny"]
  B -->|"no"| D{"A simple command matches an ask rule?"}
  D -->|"yes"| E["Ask"]
  D -->|"no"| F{"Not modelled or not complete?"}
  F -->|"yes"| G["bypass allows, plan denies, other modes ask"]
  F -->|"no"| H{"Allow rule matches this command?"}
  H -->|"yes: no target check"| N["Next command"]
  H -->|"no"| I{"Read-only, and writes stay in session or temp?"}
  I -->|"yes"| N
  I -->|"no"| J{"acceptEdits, and the command is in scope?"}
  J -->|"yes"| N
  J -->|"no"| K["bypass allows, plan denies, other modes ask"]
  N --> L["Allow when every command passed"]
```

These rules explain the diagram:

- **Deny beats ask beats allow across all commands.** In `npm test && git push` with a `deny` rule for `git push`, the whole call is denied. Each simple command must match a rule on its own, so `Bash(npm test *)` does not allow `npm test && curl evil`.
- **A command that is not modelled asks.** The parser sets `modelled` to `false` for an assignment, `export`, a loop, and similar statements. The ask has the rule `unmodelled`. This check happens before the `allow` rules, so an `allow` rule does not cover such a script.
- **A command that is not complete asks.** A syntax error sets `complete` to `false`. The ask has the rule `unparsed`. An example is `if [ x`.
- **An `allow` rule skips the target checks.** After the two checks above, a matching `allow` rule makes `bash_permission` continue to the next command. The steps for `targets_known`, `writes_ok`, read-only, `acceptEdits`, and the mode do not run for that command. See [A Bash allow rule skips the code-later check](#a-bash-allow-rule-skips-the-code-later-check).
- **A dynamic command name never matches an allow rule.** A command such as `$CMD args` is unknown until the shell runs.
- **A command with an unresolved write target is never read-only.** Ostra did not check the target, so nothing about it is known to be in scope.
- **`git` runs unasked only inside the project.** Git reads the config of its repository, and that config can name programs. The cwd must be known and inside the repo. `git -C src log -1` passes. `git -C "$R" status` and `cd /tmp && git status` ask.
- **`acceptEdits` has a narrow extra allowance.** `mkdir`, `touch`, `cp`, and `mv` pass when every target is known and is in the repo, the session dir, or temp. A command with an assignment prefix, a wrapper, or a path in the command word does not pass.

In plan mode, a command that is not read-only gets this denial: "Stay read-only: this session is in plan mode, so Ostra refuses ...". The agent must put what it found in its report.

### Which commands are read-only

A read-only command runs in every mode without a question. The list is `READ_ONLY` in `policy.rs`: `ls`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `grep`, `rg`, `find`, `git`, `pwd`, `echo`, `printf`, `sort`, `uniq`, `diff`, `stat`, `file`, `which`, `tree`, `cd`, `true`, `test`, `[`, `basename`, `dirname`, `realpath`, and `readlink`.

Only a command that Ostra fully understands qualifies (a hardening rule). The command must meet all these conditions:

- It has no assignment prefix, no wrapper, and no `/` in the command word. An assignment such as `LD_PRELOAD` or `GIT_CONFIG_*` changes what runs. A path-named command can be a script that the agent wrote.
- The command name is static.
- For `git`, `rg`, `sort`, `find`, `tree`, `file`, and `uniq`, every argument is static and has no glob. A dynamic word can expand to an option that starts a program.
- Its flags do not start a program or write a file. The flag rules follow.

These flag rules apply:

- `find` has none of `-exec`, `-execdir`, `-delete`, `-fprint`, `-fprint0`, `-fprintf`, `-fls`, `-ok`, `-okdir`.
- `git` runs only `status`, `diff`, `log`, `show`, `rev-parse`, `ls-files`, or `blame`. The listing forms of `branch`, `tag`, `remote`, `describe`, and `config --get` also pass. The only leading options are `-C <dir>`, `--no-pager`, `-P`, `--no-optional-locks`, `--literal-pathspecs`, and `--no-replace-objects`. The options `--output`, `--ext-diff`, `--textconv`, and `--open-files-in-pager` fail, with their unique abbreviations.
- `rg` has no `--pre`, `--pre-glob`, or `--hostname-bin`.
- `sort` has no `--output`, `--compress-program`, or `-o`.
- `uniq` has at most one argument that is not a flag, because the second one is an output file.
- `tree` has no `-o` and no `-R`. `file` has no `--compile` and no `-C`.
- `printf` has no `-v`, because it assigns a variable. `test` and `[` have no `[`, `$`, or backtick in their arguments, because a subscript runs a command.

A read-only command that redirects its output must write only in the session dir or OS temp. This rule lets an agent write a report with `cat > report.md <<'EOF'` in every mode, including plan mode.

## Rule syntax

`parse_rule` in `perms.rs` reads a rule as `Tool` or `Tool(spec)`. The tool name must start with an ASCII letter. It can hold letters, digits, `_`, `:`, `-`, and `.`. A rule without `(spec)` matches every use of the tool.

This example shows the five common kinds:

```toml
[permissions]
allow = ["Bash(npm run test *)", "Edit(/src/**)", "WebFetch(domain:docs.rs)"]
ask   = ["Bash(npm publish *)"]
deny  = ["Bash(git push *)", "Read(~/.ssh/**)"]
```

### Bash rules

`Bash(spec)` is a glob over the text of one simple command. These rules apply:

- `*` matches any text, including spaces and `/`.
- The match covers the whole text. `Bash(npm test)` does not match `npm test --watch`.
- A trailing ` *` also matches the bare command, so `Bash(npm run test *)` matches `npm run test`.
- The old form `Bash(npm test:*)` is a prefix match. It matches `npm test` and `npm test -- foo`, and does not match `npm tests`.
- `Bash` without a spec matches every command.

The policy tries three texts of each simple command (`bash_forms`): all words, the words without leading assignments, and the words from the effective command on. Thus `Bash(./mvnw *)` matches `FOO=1 ./mvnw -q compile`, and `Bash(rm -rf /*)` matches `sudo rm -rf /var`.

The text of a simple command has the words only. Redirects are not part of it. Thus `Bash(echo *)` matches `echo x > .mcp.json`, and the rule cannot tell which file the command writes.

### Path rules

`Edit(spec)`, `Write(spec)`, and `Read(spec)` use paths in the style of gitignore. The anchor of the pattern depends on its start:

| Pattern starts with | Anchor | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `//` | The file system root | `Edit(//etc/**)` |
| `~/` | The home folder | `Read(~/.ssh/**)` |
| `./`, `/`, or has a `/` inside | The repo root | `Edit(/src)`, `Edit(src/**)` |
| A bare name | Any depth under the repo root | `Edit(*.env)` |

A pattern that ends with `/` means `/**`. In a pattern, `*` does not cross a `/`, and `**` does. Thus `Edit(src/*.ts)` does not match `src/a/b.ts`. A pattern `dir/**` also matches `dir` itself. A rule matches a path when it matches the path or one of its parent folders.

The tool name decides which calls the rule covers:

- An `Edit` rule covers `Edit`, `Write`, `MultiEdit`, `NotebookEdit`, and `ApplyPatch`. A `Write` rule covers the same tools.
- A `Read` rule covers `Read`, `Grep`, and `Glob`, and a `Skill` that loads a file by path. A `Grep(...)` or `Glob(...)` rule covers only that tool.
- An `Edit` or `Write` rule does not cover a `Bash` write. Only a `Bash(...)` rule judges a shell command.

On Windows, the matcher lowercases paths and patterns, changes `\` to `/`, and drops the `\\?\` prefix.

### WebFetch and other tools

`WebFetch(domain:docs.rs)` matches the host `docs.rs` and any subdomain such as `doc.docs.rs`. It does not match `evil-docs.rs` or `docs.rs.evil.com`. The policy takes the host with the same URL parser as the request. Thus `https://evil.example\@docs.rs/` is the host `evil.example`, and the rule does not match it.

Other rules use the bare name of a tool. These forms exist:

- `mcp__github` covers every tool of the MCP server `github`. It does not cover the server `githubx`.
- `mcp__github__create_issue` covers one tool.
- `Other:<harness tool>` covers a harness tool that has no canonical name.
- `submit_<agent>` covers a submit tool.

A rule such as `Memory(text)` is valid, but a spec never matches a tool of this kind. Write `Memory` without a spec.

### The tool names that a rule can use

`KNOWN_TOOLS` lists 29 names: `Bash`, `PowerShell`, `Cmd`, `Read`, `Write`, `Edit`, `MultiEdit`, `NotebookEdit`, `ApplyPatch`, `Grep`, `Glob`, `Skill`, `WebSearch`, `WebFetch`, `Report`, `Document`, `Memory`, `MemoryRecall`, `DocsSearch`, `CodeOutline`, `CodeFind`, `CodeCallers`, `CodeCallees`, `CodeImplementations`, `CodeNeighbors`, `CodeImpact`, `CodeMap`, `ProjectList`, and `ProjectCreate`. A name that starts with `mcp__`, `Other:`, or `submit_` is also valid.

`PowerShell` and `Cmd` have no parser. In `layer2` they are in the family `Other` and are not known tools. A rule with a spec cannot match them, and only a bare `PowerShell` or `Cmd` rule can. Without a rule, the mode decides:

- In `default` and `acceptEdits`, the call asks.
- In `plan`, the call is denied.
- In `bypass` and under YOLO, the call is allowed with the rule `mode:bypass`. Under YOLO the rule shows as `yolo`.

Only the three modes `default`, `acceptEdits`, and `plan` never allow these tools without a rule.

## Rule validation

`validate_rule` checks one rule string. The workspace settings check calls it for each entry of `permissions.allow`, `permissions.ask`, and `permissions.deny`. An error shows as an issue at the path `permissions.<list>[<index>]`. See [Workspaces, projects, and approvals](workspaces-and-trust.md) for the validation flow.

| Fault | Message |
| --- | --- |
| Empty rule | "Write a rule as `Tool` or `Tool(pattern)`: this one is empty." |
| No closing parenthesis | "Close the parenthesis in `...`: a rule is `Tool(pattern)`." |
| Empty parentheses | "Put a pattern inside the parentheses of `...`, or drop them to match every use." |
| Bad tool name | "`name` is not a tool name." |
| Unknown tool | "`name` is not a tool Ostra knows. Use one of ..., or `Other:<harness tool>`." |
| Bad path pattern | "Fix the path pattern in `...`: ..." |
| `WebFetch` without `domain:` | "Write WebFetch rules as `WebFetch(domain:example.com)`, not `...`." |

The check of a path pattern builds the glob, so `Edit(src/[)` fails. The check does not look at the spec of a `Bash` rule.

An invalid rule that reaches the runtime does not stop the run. `parse_rules` skips it and writes the warning `ignoring invalid permission rule` to the log. Fix every issue that the settings check reports. A `deny` rule that is skipped refuses nothing.

## Rule suggestions and "Always in this workspace"

When layer 2 asks, the engine opens a permission gate. The browser shows the call, the reason, and the rule that asked. The card has three buttons: **Allow once**, **Always in this workspace** with the suggested rule, and **Deny**. The execution waits until the user answers. [Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md) owns the gate model. The button for the suggestion is off when the call has no suggestion.

The answer `AlwaysInWorkspace` makes two rules. Three functions take part:

| Function | What it does | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `suggest_rule` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs` | Builds the text of a rule from a call and a root path. The engine calls it two times, with two different roots. | The gate card shows one result. The answer path saves the other. |
| `add_allow_rule` in the `Services` trait | Adds the rule to `permissions.allow` of the workspace and saves the settings. | The rule stays for all later executions. |
| `ExecutionPolicy::allow_rule_suggestion` and `add_session_allow` | Builds a rule and adds it to the memory of the running execution. | The rule applies until that execution ends. |

`suggest_rule` and `allow_rule_suggestion` make rules in these forms:

| Call | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `Bash` | `Bash(<first word> *)`, or `Bash(<first word> <second word> *)` when the second word is not a flag, has no `/`, and is not a glob. `npm run build --prod` gives `Bash(npm run *)`. `./mvnw -q compile` gives `Bash(./mvnw *)`. |
| `Write`, `Edit` | `Edit(/src/**)` from the policy, using the first folder of the path. The engine uses the folder of the file, for example `Edit(src/a/**)`. A file in the repo root gives `Edit(/README.md)` from the policy and `Edit(*)` from the engine. |
| `Read` | `Read(/<first folder>/**)` from the policy. |
| `WebFetch` | `WebFetch(domain:<host>)` |
| Other tools | The bare tool name |
| `ProjectCreate` | No rule. Rule O1 says that no allow rule stands in for the user's answer. |

The gate card and the saved rule come from two calls of `suggest_rule`:

- When layer 2 asks, `ask_permission` builds the suggestion for the card with `suggest_rule(call, &repo)`. The value `repo` is the project path of the execution.
- When the user answers `AlwaysInWorkspace`, the engine builds the saved rule with `suggest_rule(call, &self.inner.workspace_root)` (`crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs`, lines 521-523).

The rule on the card and the saved rule can differ when the project is in a subfolder of the workspace. For example, the workspace root is `/ws` and the project is `/ws/proj`. An `Edit` call on `/ws/proj/src/a.rs` shows `Edit(src/**)` on the card. The saved rule is `Edit(proj/src/**)`. Rules match from the project root, so the saved path can fail to match any file.

The policy function and `suggest_rule` can also give different rules for the same call. For a compound command, the policy picks the first simple command that is not read-only and not yet allowed. The engine reads the first two words of the whole text. For `cd src && npm run build`, the policy suggests `Bash(npm run *)` and the engine suggests `Bash(cd src *)`.

Check the saved rule in the settings after an answer "Always in this workspace". A prefix rule such as `Bash(npm run *)` allows every later command that starts with `npm run`, in every session of the workspace. Such a `Bash` rule also skips the code-later check. See [A Bash allow rule skips the code-later check](#a-bash-allow-rule-skips-the-code-later-check).

The engine calls `add_allow_rule` through the `Services` trait (`crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs`, lines 521-523). The server implements it in `crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs` (line 122). If the server cannot save the settings, `add_allow_rule` writes the warning `could not save the allow rule` (line 130). The running execution keeps its session rule.

## The build streak and the lesson gate

The policy has a post-tool observer. `ExecutionPolicy::observe` runs after each tool call and returns a list of `Observation` values. The code is in `crates/ostra-policy/src/build.rs`. It ports three Ultracode hooks: `build-signal.js`, `build-streak.js`, and `build-streak-gate.js`. The observer has two jobs: it stops a failing build loop, and it makes the agent record what fixed a hard failure.

### Which commands count

The executor passes the build and test commands of the project as `PolicyInputs`. They come from the `build`, `test`, `test_one`, `lint`, and `typecheck` entries of `project.toml`. `is_build_command` tests a `Bash` command:

- A configured command is a matcher. A `{PLACEHOLDER}` token is a wildcard, and spaces are flexible. Thus `./mvnw test -pl {MODULE}` matches a real call.
- The first two words of a configured command also match, because agents change the flags around one build tool.
- If the project has no configured commands, a fallback pattern matches `cargo`, `mvn`, `gradle`, `tsc`, `make`, `pytest`, `go build`, `npm test`, `npm run ...`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, and similar tools.

### How a failure is judged

`failed_from` decides if a command failed. The first fact that applies wins:

1. The exit code of the outcome. A value other than `0` is a failure.
2. An exit code in the text, such as `Exit code 1`, `exited with code 2`, or `exit status 3`.
3. An error result that says `timed out`, `interrupted`, or `canceled`. This gives no evidence either way, and the streak does not change.
4. Any other error result. This is a failure.
5. An empty output from a harness that never reports results (Antigravity). This gives no evidence.
6. Failure markers in the output, such as `BUILD FAILURE`, `error TS1234`, `npm ERR!`, `FAIL`, a Rust `error[E...]` line, or a Python traceback.

After a failure, `diagnostic_signature` makes a short fingerprint of the cause from the first output line that looks like a compiler or test error. It removes paths, line numbers, and versions, and keeps at most 160 characters.

### The thresholds

| Constant | Value | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RECALL_THRESHOLD` | 2 | At the second consecutive failure, the observer asks for lesson recall with the fingerprint. The server searches the memory store and adds at most 5 lessons to the tool result. |
| `WARN_THRESHOLD` | 3 | From the third failure, a note tells the agent to state the root cause and what will change before the next try. The note names how many failures remain. |
| `DENY_THRESHOLD` | 5 | At the fifth failure, the `build-streak` guard refuses every build and test command. |
| `MAX_HISTORY` | 12 | The number of fingerprints and pending recoveries that the streak keeps. |

When `build-streak` refuses a command, the denial tells the agent to call its submit tool with status `stuck` (the STUCK hand-back). The agent must give what it tried to make work, the failing command, the diagnostic, the hypotheses it ruled out, and what it needs. The denial also tells the agent not to retry with another spelling of the command. A pass resets the counter to 0.

### The lesson gate

A pass after 3 or more failures with a known fingerprint is a verified recovery. The observer then adds a pending recovery and a note that tells the agent to call the `Memory` tool. When a recovery is pending, `lesson-gate` refuses these calls:

- the `Report` tool without a non-empty `reason`
- a `submit_*` call with status `ok`
- a write to the declared report file

A successful `Memory` call clears the pending recoveries. A `Report` call with a non-empty `reason` also clears them, because the agent states that the fix teaches nothing reusable. The reason for the gate is in the denial text: the same diagnostic recurs across sessions, and a recorded lesson stops the next run from re-deriving the fix. See [Project init, skills, and lesson memory](project-init-and-memory.md) for the store.

## What happens when

- **A guard and a rule both apply.** The guard wins. Layer 2 does not run, and no rule or YOLO setting changes the denial.
- **The user answers Deny.** The native loop returns the error "The user denied this call (...). Continue without it, or explain in your report why it is needed." The run goes on.
- **A side-panel run asks.** The run has no session. `ask_permission` returns `Deny` at once, because these runs are read-only and never ask.
- **YOLO is on.** Every ask becomes an allow with the rule `yolo`. The engine also records the gate events with the source `Yolo`. Denials from guards and `deny` rules stand.
- **The user turns YOLO on during a run.** The next call sees it, because the executor sets the state before each check.
- **The user changes the mode or the rules.** Executions that already run keep their old values. New executions use the new values.
- **A command has a syntax error.** Layer 1 still checks the commands that the parser found. Layer 2 asks with the rule `unparsed`. Plan mode denies, and `bypass` allows.
- **A `bash -c` string nests deeper than 4 levels.** The parser stops and sets `complete` to `false`. The result is the same as for a syntax error.
- **A command writes to a path that a variable builds.** Layer 1 cannot name the target, so no guard can refuse it. Layer 2 does not allow it automatically, unless a mode or an `allow` rule allows it.
- **A shell command writes to a file that runs code later.** Without a matching `allow` rule, the command asks in `default` and `acceptEdits`, and plan mode denies it. With a matching `Bash` `allow` rule, the command runs with no question.
- **A rule is invalid at run time.** The policy skips it and writes a warning to the log.
- **The agent uses an unknown tool.** Layer 2 asks in `default` and `acceptEdits`, denies in `plan`, and allows in `bypass`.
- **The server does not know the execution.** The bridge denies the call with the guard `self-protection`, because the execution is not running in Ostra.
- **An MCP tool call comes through a harness.** The hook passes a workspace MCP tool and a management tool, because Ostra's own MCP server checks the call again when it runs the call. The ask reaches the user once.

## What the policy does not guarantee

The policy is one layer. It reduces mistakes and blocks known routes to protected files. It does not make an agent safe. These limits apply:

- **Tool enforcement is off by default.** With `disabled`, `write-scope`, the report path, and the interpreter checks do not apply. Set `tool_enforcement = "enabled"` to turn them on.
- **The guards read text and not behavior.** They judge the paths that a call names and the words of a command. A program that the agent starts can write other files. Examples are a build tool, a test runner, and `python script.py`, where the script is a file. Only the sandbox bounds these programs. See [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md).
- **A Bash allow rule can authorize a write to a file that runs code later.** The "always asks" rule holds for file-tool writes only. With `allow = ["Bash(echo *)"]`, `echo x > .mcp.json` runs with no question. Review each `Bash` allow rule that can write `.mcp.json`, `.envrc`, or `.github/workflows/`. The sandbox write scope still applies.
- **The code scan for interpreters uses name lists.** `WRITE_API` and `SPAWN_API` list function names. A spelling that is not on the list passes.
- **Layer 1 cannot judge a path that is built at run time.** A variable, a substitution, or a glob in a write position has no known target. In `bypass` or YOLO, such a command runs without a question.
- **Reads are open.** `Read`, `Grep`, and `Glob` are allowed in every mode, except for the secret paths. Add `deny` rules such as `Read(~/.ssh/**)` to narrow them.
- **`secret-read` does not judge `Document`.** A `Document` call goes through `check_document`, which checks protected paths, artifact ownership, and with tool enforcement the session dir. It never tests for a secret path.
- **Rules match command text.** `Bash(git push *)` does not match `git -C sub push`. A rule `Bash(curl *)` does not match `/usr/bin/curl x`, because the policy keeps the path in the command word. Do not rely on a `deny` rule alone to block a program.
- **An approval covers more than one command.** A rule such as `Bash(npm run *)` allows every command with that prefix, in later sessions too.
- **Windows shells are opaque.** For `PowerShell` and `Cmd`, the policy scans the raw text for protected names and paths. It does not know what the command does. In `default`, `acceptEdits`, and `plan`, no mode allows these tools. In `bypass` and under YOLO, the mode allows them without a question.
- **The `windows-path` guard does not refuse `NUL`.** The denial text names it, but `paths::is_reserved_device` is false for `NUL`.
- **A harness can hide results.** Antigravity does not report tool results. The build streak cannot count failures for it. See [Executors](executors.md).
- **Only three guards raise containment signals.** `secret-read`, `self-protection`, and `git-metadata` count toward the pause after 3 signals. A refusal by another guard does not.

## Limits and constants

| Name | Value | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_DEPTH` | 4 nested parses of `bash -c`, `eval`, and shell heredocs | `bash.rs` |
| `RECALL_THRESHOLD` | 2 consecutive failures | `build.rs` |
| `WARN_THRESHOLD` | 3 consecutive failures | `build.rs` |
| `DENY_THRESHOLD` | 5 consecutive failures | `build.rs` |
| `MAX_HISTORY` | 12 entries | `build.rs` |
| Lessons that a recall adds | 5 | `bridge.rs` and `ostra-exec-native` |
| Fingerprint length | 160 characters | `normalize_diagnostic` |
| Diagnostic line length for a fingerprint | 12 to 400 characters | `diagnostic_signature` |
| Command text in an `unmodelled` or `unparsed` ask | 200 characters | `truncate` in `policy.rs` |
| `PAUSE_AFTER` | 3 containment signals for one execution | `crates/ostra-core/src/containment.rs` |
| Global default `deny` rule | `Bash(rm -rf /*)` | `GlobalConfig` defaults |
| Default permission mode | `default` | `PermissionMode` |
| Default tool enforcement | `disabled` | `ToolEnforcement` |

## Tests

`crates/ostra-policy/tests/policy.rs` holds the cases that define these rules. Many cases come from the Ultracode test file `test_definitions.test.js`. The tests cover the write scope of each agent, the Bash scope, the declared report path, the lesson gate, the build streak, self-protection, state and artifact ownership, each permission mode, YOLO, rule suggestions, the read-only command list, unresolved write targets, git metadata, files that run code later with empty rule lists, secret reads through `Read`, `Grep`, `Skill`, and Bash, MCP tools, Windows path forms, and the effect of tool enforcement. No test covers a `Bash` `allow` rule together with a file that runs code later. Run the tests with `cargo test --workspace`. See [Tests and evals](testing.md).
