sections.title: Sandbox and egress proxy
sections.summary: How the kernel boundary under agent commands works: Profile, the bubblewrap and Seatbelt backends, seccomp, the egress proxy and its allowlist, loopback ports, decoys, git repair, env scrubbing, modes, and the limits of the sandbox.
sections.body:
The policy engine judges a tool call by the paths that the call names. A shell can hide a path in a variable, in a script, or in a child process. The sandbox is the second layer. The kernel enforces it under every command, whatever the command names. The crate [`ostra-sandbox`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/lib.rs) implements it. [Policy engine](policy.md) describes the first layer.

## Why the sandbox exists

Without the sandbox, an agent command has the full rights of the user. It can read `~/.ssh`, append to `~/.bashrc`, connect to the cloud metadata address, or plant a `.git/config` that starts a program in a later shell of the user.

The sandbox gives each execution this boundary:

- The host file system is read-only.
- Only the roots of the execution are writable.
- The data directory of Ostra, the credentials of the user, and the session bus are not reachable.
- The network leaves only through the egress proxy of Ostra.

An *execution* is one run of one agent, on the native loop or in a harness CLI. [Executors](executors.md) describes both.

### Which programs run in the sandbox

| Program | Entry point | Profile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The Bash tool of the native loop | `sandbox_for` in [`crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs) | `Profile::for_execution` |
| A harness CLI and every process that it starts | `wrap` in [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/sandbox.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/sandbox.rs) | `Profile::for_execution` |
| A program that Ostra starts for a project: the format command, an LSP server, a code provider, a stdio MCP server | `host_command` in [`crates/ostra-sandbox/src/host.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/host.rs) | `Profile::for_program` |

The other native tools do not take the sandbox. The policy engine guards them. See [Native tools](tools.md).

## The three layers of the crate

The crate has three layers, so that a difference between operating systems lives in one place.

1. `Profile` ([`profile.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/profile.rs)) describes the boundary of one execution without a backend name. It holds the mounts, the environment, the egress policy, the forwarded ports, and the decoys.
2. `Backend` ([`backend.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/backend.rs)) is an enum with two values: `Bubblewrap` and `Seatbelt`. Each value implements the trait `Enforcer`, which turns a `Profile` into a command. The code of both backends is plain Rust that compiles on every OS. Thus the tests render both on any machine.
3. `sys` ([`sys/mod.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/sys/mod.rs)) is the only code that calls the kernel. It has one implementation of the trait `Os` for each OS, and `sys/mod.rs` picks it at compile time.

Code outside a backend never matches on the backend to choose a behavior. It calls `Backend::enforcer()` and asks. Thus the quirks of a backend stay in the file of that backend.

### How the layers connect

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  cfg["SandboxConfig: mode, network, hosts"] -->|"decide()"| be["Backend"]
  ctx["ExecContext"] -->|"for_execution()"| prof["Profile"]
  prof -->|"command()"| enf["Enforcer::wrap"]
  be --> enf
  enf -->|"bubblewrap"| bw["bwrap.rs: bwrap arguments"]
  enf -->|"seatbelt"| sb["seatbelt.rs: SBPL policy"]
  bw --> os["sys: trait Os"]
  sb --> os
  os --> lin["Linux"]
  os --> mac["MacOs"]
  os --> oth["Other"]
```

### The probe

`backend()` probes the machine one time for each process and keeps the result in a `OnceLock`. `unavailable_reason()` returns the cause when no backend works. `unavailable_message()` adds the fix for the OS.

- **Linux:** `probe_bwrap` finds `bwrap` on `PATH` and finds the `ostra` helper binary. Then it runs a test sandbox with `--unshare-pid --unshare-net` and the helper. The test also checks that the new network namespace brings up its loopback.
- **macOS:** `probe_seatbelt` checks that `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` is owned by root and that no group or other user can write it. Then it applies the policy `(version 1)(allow default)` to `/usr/bin/true`.
- **Other OS:** `probe` always fails. The message says that the Windows sandbox is not built yet, or that the sandbox needs Linux or macOS.

The path of `sandbox-exec` is absolute because the Homebrew prefix on `PATH` is writable by the user.

## Sandbox modes

`SandboxMode` has three values. `decide(cfg)` in `backend.rs` turns the mode and the probe into one result.

| Mode | A backend works | No backend works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `off` | Runs unsandboxed. `decide` returns `Unsandboxed(None)`. | Runs unsandboxed. `decide` returns `Unsandboxed(None)`. |
| `auto` | Runs in the sandbox | Runs unsandboxed. `decide` returns `Unsandboxed(Some(message))`. |
| `required` | Runs in the sandbox | `decide` returns `Err`, and the execution does not start |

The default is `required` on Linux and macOS. The default is `auto` on Windows, because Windows has no backend and `required` there refuses every execution.

The `[sandbox]` table in `config.toml` sets the mode and the network choice for the machine. A workspace can replace both, and the workspace stores them in the registry, not in `workspace.toml`. `SandboxConfig::for_workspace` merges the two. The workspace hosts are added to the global hosts. A workspace never removes a global host or a built-in host. [Configuration](configuration.md) lists every key with its default.

Ostra reads `config.toml` again for each execution. Thus a change of `[sandbox]` applies to the next execution, without a restart.

### What the user sees

This part owns the rule for the stderr banner. Other pages link here.

**The banner rule:** The server prints `WARNING: agent commands run WITHOUT a sandbox` on stderr only when `sandbox.message` is `Some` in `build` ([`crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs)). `status` sets `message` when `decide` returns `Unsandboxed(Some(..))` or `Err`. That happens in mode `auto` with no backend, and in mode `required` with no backend, that is a probe failure. Mode `off` gives `None`. In that case `build` writes only a tracing warning, and it prints no banner on stderr.

The banner goes to stderr because under `auto` Ostra still starts, and a log line is easy to miss.

These are the other signs of the sandbox state:

- At server start, `validate::global` checks the `[sandbox]` table. The server refuses to start when the first issue exists, and the error names the key and the file.
- When a backend works and `message` is `None`, the log says `agent commands run in the <backend> sandbox`. When the backend has a known gap, the log also holds a warning.
- Under mode `off`, the log says that the sandbox is off and that agent commands run with the full rights of the user.
- `status(cfg)` builds `SandboxStatus` for the setup check and the console: `mode`, `default_mode`, `available`, `backend`, `active`, `message`, `gaps`, `decoys`, `builtin_decoys`, and `builtin_hosts`.
- When an execution starts unsandboxed with a message, `first_warning()` is true only for the first call. Thus the warning for a missing sandbox reaches the log one time. The native loop also emits a status line `Bash runs without a sandbox.` for each such execution.

Set `mode` to `off` only when another layer contains Ostra, for example a container. Under `off`, every agent command runs with the full rights of the user.

## What a profile mounts

`Profile::for_execution(ctx, cfg, home)` builds the profile of an agent execution from an `ExecContext`. Each rule is one of three classes: writable, read-only, or hidden.

### Writable

- `workspace_root`, `repo_root`, `session_root`, and `session_dir` of the context. Empty roots are skipped.
- The `.git` directory of each repository. Ostra binds it onto itself so that nobody can rename it.
- The tool caches of the sandbox (see the next part).
- The paths in `[sandbox] extra_writable`.
- The scratch directory that the sandbox shows as `/tmp`.
- For a harness CLI: its state directories and the per-execution config directory. See [Harness CLIs under the sandbox](#harness-clis-under-the-sandbox).

### Read-only, even inside a writable root

- The state files of the session: `session_state_dir(session_root)`.
- `workspace.toml` and the workspace database with its `-wal`, `-shm`, and `-journal` files.
- The directories of workspace artifacts and books. Agents read them and never write them.
- The memory database files.
- Each path in `ctx.protected_paths`.
- In each git directory: `config`, `config.worktree`, `hooks/`, and `info/`. A `.git` file is read-only too.
- The files in the home folder that run code later. The list is `PERSISTENCE_IN_HOME`: shell start files (`.bashrc`, `.zshrc`, `.profile`, and others), `.gitconfig`, `.npmrc`, `.local/bin/`, `.cargo/bin/`, `.cargo/config.toml`, `~/.config/systemd/`, `~/.config/autostart/`, `Library/LaunchAgents/`, and the PowerShell profile folders. They stay read-only even when their folder is writable. Thus an agent cannot leave a program for the user to run later.

### Hidden

- The data directory of Ostra, and the config directory. When `OSTRA_CONFIG` places `config.toml` in a shared directory, only that file is hidden.
- `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, or `/run/user/<uid>` when the variable is not set. The session bus is there.
- The file that `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` names, and the file that `XAUTHORITY` names.
- Every entry of `HOME_CREDENTIALS`, except the sign-in file of the harness that runs. [Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md) lists the entries.
- The paths in `[sandbox] extra_hidden`.
- The sockets of container engines: `/run/docker.sock`, `/var/run/docker.sock`, `/run/podman/podman.sock`, and the sockets of OrbStack, Colima, Rancher Desktop, and Podman machine under the home folder. A read-only file does not stop `connect`, and a container can mount the host. Thus these sockets are hidden.
- The directory of all sessions of the workspace, and the `harness` directory of the session. The harness directories of other executions hold their bridge tokens. A session that the profile made writable is bound again below the hidden directory.

One path stays visible inside the hidden data directory: the `assets` folder is read-only, because agents read skills and references from it.

A hidden directory looks empty under bubblewrap, because the sandbox mounts an empty `tmpfs` there. A hidden file is the device `/dev/null`. Under Seatbelt, a hidden path returns `EPERM`.

### Which rule wins

`Profile::ordered` sorts the rules by path depth, then by path, then by rank. The deepest rule for a path wins. At one path, only the most restrictive rule stays. The order from the least to the most restrictive is: home `tmpfs`, home entry, writable, read-only, hidden, link. Seatbelt applies the last matching rule, so the same order gives the same result in both backends.

### Tool caches

The sandbox sets its own tool caches through variables. `CACHE_ENV` lists them: `CARGO_HOME`, `npm_config_cache`, `npm_config_store_dir`, `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, `GOMODCACHE`, `GOCACHE`, `PIP_CACHE_DIR`, `YARN_CACHE_FOLDER`, `UV_CACHE_DIR`, and `CLANG_MODULE_CACHE_PATH`.

- The base folder is `~/.cache/ostra/sandbox`. `OSTRA_SANDBOX_CACHE` replaces it.
- Each session has one cache set: `session-<session id>`. One session download must not feed a later session build.
- An execution outside a session uses a set that is keyed by the workspace. A program that Ostra starts uses a set that is keyed by its first root.
- The user caches `~/.cargo`, `~/.npm`, and `~/.cache` stay read-only. Builds on the host run what those caches hold, such as extracted crate sources and Go build output. On macOS, tools ignore `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, so they get their own variables.
- `~/.cargo/config.toml` and `~/.cargo/config` are linked into the cache `CARGO_HOME`, so builds keep the linker and registry settings. Credentials are not linked.
- A cache name uses 16 hex digits of SHA-256, not `DefaultHasher`, because the algorithm of `DefaultHasher` can change between Rust releases.
- `remove_session_cache` deletes a session cache on its own thread, because a cache can hold gigabytes.

### The `/tmp` directory

The profile sets `TMPDIR=/tmp`. Under bubblewrap, `/tmp` is a private scratch directory, or an empty `tmpfs` when no scratch directory is set. A native execution gets `ostra-scratch-<uuid>` under the host temp directory, created for the owner only. A harness execution gets `tmp` inside its config directory.

Seatbelt cannot remap `/tmp`. It denies `/private/tmp`, `/private/var/tmp`, and the per-user temp directory under `/private/var/folders`. Then `TMPDIR` names the scratch directory, or the `tmp` folder of the cache. `TMPPREFIX` names `zsh` under it, because `zsh` writes heredocs there.

### Programs that Ostra starts

`Profile::for_program(roots, cfg, home)` applies the same hidden and read-only rules. Only the given `roots` are writable. It has no session rules, and it protects the git directories under the roots. `host_command` also removes the credential variables and every `OSTRA_*` variable from the environment, and adds the git settings in [Environment scrubbing](#environment-scrubbing).

## Linux: bubblewrap

`Bubblewrap` holds the path of the `bwrap` binary. `wrap` builds this command line: the bwrap arguments, `--`, the helper `ostra sandbox-init` with its options, `--`, and the program.

These arguments build the boundary:

- `--ro-bind / /`, `--dev /dev`, and `--proc /proc` give a read-only host with a new `/dev` and `/proc`.
- `--unshare-pid` and `--unshare-ipc` give a pid namespace and an IPC namespace. Thus the command cannot see the processes of Ostra.
- `--unshare-net` gives a network namespace, unless the network choice is `host`. Only the sockets that the profile binds lead out.
- `--die-with-parent` ends every process of the sandbox when Ostra ends. `--new-session` calls `setsid`, which blocks `TIOCSTI` input into the terminal of Ostra. A PTY program turns it off, because it needs its PTY as the controlling terminal.
- `--unsetenv` removes the variables in `UNSET_VARS`, and `--setenv` sets the variables of the profile.

### Placeholders and pinned directories

`Profile::plan` rewrites the mounts before the render.

- A read-only bind below a hidden mount shows the path again, so `plan` drops it. The `assets` folder is the exception.
- A protected path that does not exist, inside a writable host directory, gets an empty placeholder. A directory gets an empty directory. A file gets an empty file, or `{}` when its name ends in `.json`. The agent then cannot create the file. The placeholder exists on the host, because Ostra creates it there.
- A mount point cannot be renamed, but the directories above it can. Without a pin, the command `mv repo r && git init repo` moves the directory that holds the protected `.git`, and the new `.git` has no protection. Thus `plan` binds each directory between a writable bind and a mount inside it onto itself.

### The helper `sandbox-init`

The `ostra` binary starts first inside each bubblewrap sandbox. [`main.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/main.rs) checks for the argument `sandbox-init` before the runtime or the logging starts. The helper does these steps:

1. It binds the fixed forward ports on `127.0.0.1`, and on `::1` when the namespace has IPv6. Fixed ports come first, so the free port of the proxy cannot take one of them.
2. It binds a free port on `127.0.0.1` for the egress proxy and sets the proxy variables of the command to that port.
3. It loads the seccomp filter when it has only one thread.
4. It starts one thread for each listener. The thread splices each accepted connection to the Unix socket that Ostra bound into the sandbox.
5. It starts the command, ignores the terminal signals, and waits.

The helper exits with the status of the command. When a signal ended the command, the helper raises the same signal and returns `128 + signal`. When the helper cannot start the command, it returns `125`. Each listener accepts at most 256 open connections.

The helper uses only standard threads. It has no async runtime.

## Seccomp filter on Linux

The filter in [`sys/linux/seccomp.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/sys/linux/seccomp.rs) is a list of calls that the kernel refuses. The helper loads it with `PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS` and `PR_SET_SECCOMP`. The command and everything that it starts inherit it. A refusal returns an error, so programs that probe for a feature fall back and do not die.

| Call | Result | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Another architecture | The kernel kills the process | The call numbers differ, so no call of another architecture can pass. |
| x32 call numbers (x86_64) | `ENOSYS` | They reach the same calls under other numbers. |
| `bpf`, `userfaultfd`, `perf_event_open`, `keyctl`, `add_key`, `request_key`, `kexec_load`, `kexec_file_load`, `init_module`, `finit_module`, `delete_module`, `open_by_handle_at` | `EPERM` | Builds and tests do not need them, and they widen the kernel surface. |
| `clone3`, `io_uring_setup`, `io_uring_enter`, `io_uring_register` | `ENOSYS` | `clone3` passes its flags in memory that a filter cannot read. Thus glibc falls back to `clone`, whose flags the filter can read. |
| `unshare` or `clone` with `CLONE_NEWUSER` | `EPERM` | A new user namespace gives the command capabilities over fresh namespaces and mounts. |
| `ioctl` with `TIOCSTI` or `TIOCLINUX` | `EPERM` | They type into the terminal and send console requests. |

The filter compares only the low 32 bits of the `ioctl` request, because the kernel treats the request as an `unsigned int`. Other `unshare` and `clone` calls pass, so threads and `fork` work.

The filter builds only for `x86_64` and `aarch64`. On another architecture, `known_gaps` returns this text: run Ostra on `x86_64` or `aarch64` where agent commands must not create user namespaces. The server logs it at start.

## macOS: Seatbelt

The Seatbelt backend renders the profile as a policy in SBPL, the language of Seatbelt. It runs the program with `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec -p <policy>`. Seatbelt has no mount namespace, so these behaviors differ from Linux:

- A hidden path returns `EPERM` and does not look empty.
- `/tmp` is denied, and `TMPDIR` names the scratch directory.
- A harness gets no disposable home folder. A write at the top of the home folder fails.
- Every sandbox shares the loopback of the host. The policy names the ports that it can reach.
- Seatbelt has no pid namespace and no `--die-with-parent`. See [Processes left behind](#processes-left-behind).

### What the base policy allows

`SEATBELT_BASE` starts with `(deny default)`. Then it allows `process-exec`, `process-fork`, signals to the same sandbox, a measured list of `sysctl` names, reads of the file system, and a short list of mach services. The developers measured the list with git, cargo, npm, go, pip, clang, and the four harness CLIs.

The policy leaves these denied, because each one reaches something outside the sandbox: the keychain, the pasteboard, LaunchServices, Apple Events, the window server, and TCC. It also denies all terminal devices, so nothing reads or injects keystrokes in another terminal of the user.

The policy closes a read of another process. A program can read the arguments and the startup environment of another process with `KERN_PROCARGS2`. Two routes allow it: a `sysctl-read` of `kern.procargs2`, and `process-info-pidinfo`. The policy lists the `sysctl` names, and it denies `process-info*` before the allow for the same sandbox.

### How the profile becomes rules

`Profile::seatbelt` emits one rule for each mount, in the order of `ordered()`.

- Writable: allow `file-read*`, `file-write*`, `network-bind`, and `network-outbound` below the path.
- Read-only: deny `file-write*` and `network-bind`. A `literal` rule covers a path that does not exist, in any letter case, so no placeholder is needed.
- Hidden: deny reads, writes, `network-bind`, and `network-outbound` below the path.
- `file-read-metadata` for each directory above an allowed path, because `stat` needs it even inside a denied directory.
- `(deny file-write-unlink ...)` for each writable directory above a protected path. This replaces the self-bind of bubblewrap. Thus `mv .git .g` cannot carry `.git/config` out from under its rule.

Every path goes through `sbpl_str`. It refuses a path that is not UTF-8 or that holds a control character, because such a path could end its string early and rewrite the policy. In that case `command` returns `Err`, and the execution does not start.

## The `sys` layer for each OS

The trait `Os` is the whole list of what the sandbox asks of the operating system. `Platform` is the implementation that the build selects.

| Method of `Os` | Linux (`sys/linux`) | macOS (`sys/macos`) | Other (`sys/other.rs`) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `probe` | `bwrap` and helper test | root-owned `sandbox-exec` test | Always fails |
| `run_helper` | Runs `sandbox-init` ([`helper.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/sys/linux/helper.rs)) | Error: the helper runs on Linux only | Error: the helper runs on Linux only |
| `scrub_startup_env` | Nothing to do | Moves the environment off the stack and zeroes the original strings | Nothing |
| `marked` | None, because the pid namespace ends all processes | Finds processes with `sandbox_check` | None |
| `watch_opens` | `inotify` with `IN_OPEN` | Returns `Err(ErrorKind::Unsupported)` | Returns `Err(ErrorKind::Unsupported)` |
| `watch_refusals` | Returns `Err(ErrorKind::Unsupported)` | Reads `log stream` | Returns `Err(ErrorKind::Unsupported)` |
| Unix sockets | Tokio Unix sockets | Tokio Unix sockets | Not available. The bind and connect calls return `Unsupported`. |

On Other, `watch_opens` and `watch_refusals` return an error, not an empty result ([`sys/other.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/sys/other.rs)). `refusals_readable` returns `false` there, so no decoy exists.

Linux and macOS share [`sys/unix.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/sys/unix.rs): user id, symlinks, `SIGKILL`, a socket directory with mode `0700`, and the Unix socket calls.

The `UNAVAILABLE` text of each OS tells the user how to fix the problem and how to turn the sandbox off on purpose:

- **Linux:** Install bubblewrap, or allow unprivileged user namespaces.
- **macOS:** Run Ostra outside any other sandbox, because macOS cannot nest sandboxes.
- **Windows:** Run Ostra inside WSL 2 or in Docker.
- **Any other OS:** Run Ostra on Linux or macOS.

## Harness CLIs under the sandbox

`wrap` in [`crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/sandbox.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-harness/src/sandbox.rs) puts a harness CLI under a profile. The Bash tool of the CLI and every process that it starts inherit the sandbox. [Executors](executors.md) describes the rest of the launch.

1. `decide` chooses the backend. For `off` or for `auto` without a backend, the plan runs unchanged and `Wrapped.warning` carries the reason. Under `off` the reason is `None`.
2. `for_execution` builds the profile. `allow_hosts` adds the model hosts of the CLI and the hosts of its base URLs. `start_egress` starts the proxy. `watch_decoys` plants the decoys.
3. The hook bridge of Ostra is forwarded into the sandbox. The server bridge socket answers only `/internal/*`, so the sandbox cannot reach `/api`.
4. The profile sets `new_session(false)`, so the CLI keeps its PTY. `tty` lets the program use the PTY. Under Seatbelt, the launcher passes the PTY path as `-D TTY=<path>`.
5. Under bubblewrap, `home_overlay` replaces the home folder with a `tmpfs` that holds read-only binds of its entries. The CLI can write its state directories. New files at the top of the home folder vanish with the execution.

Settings, instructions, and hooks inside a state directory stay read-only. A hook or an instruction that an agent wrote there runs in later sessions of the user in that CLI.

| CLI | Writable state | Read-only inside it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` or `~/.claude`, and `~/.local/state/claude` | `settings.json`, `settings.local.json`, `CLAUDE.md`, `commands/`, `agents/`, `skills/`, `plugins/`, `hooks/`, `output-styles/` |
| Codex | `CODEX_HOME` or `~/.codex` | `config.toml`, `AGENTS.md`, `hooks.json`, `rules/` |
| Grok Build | The real Grok home folder | `config.toml`, `trusted_folders.toml`, `hooks/` |
| Antigravity | `~/.gemini` | `settings.json`, `GEMINI.md`, `config/plugins/` |

Two special cases exist:

- Claude Code rewrites `~/.claude.json` through a temporary file and a rename. A read-only home refuses that. Under bubblewrap, Ostra copies the file into the config directory of the execution (`claude.json`) and links it into the overlaid home. `cleanup` deletes the copy, the token-bearing config of Grok, and the scratch `/tmp` when the execution ends.
- Seatbelt has no home overlay. A write of the CLI at the top of the home folder fails, and the CLIs survive that. Ostra sets `CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR`, and it sets `SSL_CERT_FILE` to `/etc/ssl/cert.pem` when that file exists and the variable is not set. Codex then does not read the trusted roots from the denied keychain.

## The egress proxy

A sandbox in a private network namespace has no route out. The egress proxy is the only way out. It sees the destination host and port of every connection, passes only what the policy allows, and connects to the address that it checked, with no second lookup. The code is in [`egress.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/egress.rs).

### The four network choices

| `network` | Namespace | Proxy | What passes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `none` | Own | Only when a harness adds its hosts | The model API of the harness and the hosts of its base URLs |
| `allowlist` (default) | Own | Yes | The 26 built-in hosts in `DEFAULT_ALLOWED_HOSTS`, the 18 model hosts of the four harnesses, and `allowed_hosts` |
| `public` | Own | Yes | Every public address, and `allowed_hosts` |
| `host` | The host network | No | Everything, with no filter |

The built-in hosts cover package registries and source hosts: crates.io and its mirrors, npm and Yarn, PyPI, the Go proxy, GitHub, Maven and Gradle, `dl.google.com` and `maven.google.com`, RubyGems, and NuGet. Under `allowlist`, every command can reach the model hosts of all four harnesses, so a build or a test can call a model API.

### How one connection passes

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Command
  participant H as Helper sandbox-init
  participant P as Egress proxy
  participant L as Policy
  participant D as Destination
  C->>H: CONNECT host:443 to 127.0.0.1
  H->>P: splice to the Unix socket
  P->>L: route(host, port)
  L->>L: resolve once and check addresses
  L-->>P: Route::Direct(checked addresses)
  P->>D: connect, 10 second timeout
  P-->>C: 200 Connection established
  C->>P: TLS ClientHello
  P->>P: compare server name with host
  P->>D: forward the bytes
```

On Linux, each execution has its own Unix socket in `egress/` inside the data directory. Ostra binds that socket only into the sandbox of that execution. The helper listens on the loopback of the sandbox and splices to it. On macOS, the proxy listens on its own port of `127.0.0.1`. The Seatbelt policy of the execution names that port. The proxy URL is `http://ostra:<credential>@127.0.0.1:<port>`, and every request must carry the credential, because a sandbox with open loopback can reach the proxy ports of other executions. A request without it gets `407 Proxy Authentication Required`.

One proxy serves all commands of a profile. `Profile::start_egress` starts it. A command that is wrapped without a started proxy starts its own, and that proxy reports its decisions to the log only.

### The policy for one destination

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Request host:port"] --> B{"Matches a trusted rule?"}
  B -->|yes| C["AnyAddress"]
  B -->|no| D{"network is public, or a builtin rule matches?"}
  D -->|no| E["Refused: 403"]
  D -->|yes| F["PublicOnly"]
  F --> G{"Local-only name?"}
  G -->|yes| E
  G -->|no| H["Resolve once"]
  C --> H
  H --> I{"PublicOnly and every address private?"}
  I -->|yes| E
  I -->|no| J["Connect to the checked addresses"]
```

`Policy::access` sorts each destination into one of three classes:

- **`AnyAddress`:** the destination matches a *trusted* rule. Trusted rules are the hosts that the user chose: `allowed_hosts`, and the hosts of the base URLs that a harness launch passes. These can resolve to any address, because an internal mirror or a gateway on the LAN is a normal choice.
- **`PublicOnly`:** the destination matches a *built-in* rule, or the network is `public`. The addresses must be public. The built-in rules are `DEFAULT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` and `model_hosts` of the harness. A built-in host that resolves to a private address is refused. DNS tricks then cannot turn a known host into a local one.
- **`Refused`:** nothing matches.

`is_private` defines a private address: loopback, private ranges, link-local (the cloud metadata address `169.254.169.254` is here), carrier-grade NAT `100.64.0.0/10`, unique-local, multicast, unspecified, broadcast, `198.18.0.0/15`, and reserved ranges from `240.0.0.0`. It also unwraps IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible, and NAT64 addresses, and it refuses local-use NAT64 `64:ff9b:1::/48`.

These names are local-only, and the proxy refuses them under `PublicOnly` without a lookup: `localhost`, names that end in `.localhost`, `.local`, `.internal`, `.lan`, or `.home.arpa`, and single labels. A lookup of such a name goes out on the LAN, and on macOS a `.local` lookup waits for seconds before it fails.

### Syntax of a host rule

`HostRule::parse` reads each `allowed_hosts` entry. [`validate.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/validate.rs) reports a bad entry when the user saves settings, not at spawn time.

| Entry | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `registry.example.com` | The name, on ports 443 and 80 |
| `*.example.com` | Every name below `example.com`, but not `example.com` itself |
| `203.0.113.5` | An IPv4 address |
| `[2001:db8::1]` | An IPv6 address, in brackets |
| Any of these with `:8443` | That port only |
| `127.0.0.1:8317`, `localhost:8317` | A loopback service. It needs a port. See [Loopback, forwards, and blocked ports](#loopback-forwards-and-blocked-ports). |

The parser lowercases a name and removes a trailing dot. It refuses whitespace, `/`, `@`, `?`, `#`, port `0`, and a name with a bad label. The reason is that the proxy matches hosts, not URLs. An IPv4-mapped IPv6 entry becomes the IPv4 address.

### What the proxy accepts

`parse_request` reads the head of the first request:

- It accepts only HTTP/1.x.
- `CONNECT host:port` opens a tunnel. Use it for HTTPS.
- Plain HTTP needs an absolute `http://` URL. The proxy rewrites the request to origin form, removes `Proxy-*`, `Host`, `Connection`, and `Keep-Alive` headers, adds the right `Host`, and adds `Connection: close`.
- A folded header line is refused.

### The server name check

After `200 Connection established`, the proxy reads the first bytes of a tunnel to a named host. It parses the TLS `ClientHello`, reassembled across records, and compares the server name with the host of the `CONNECT` line. If they differ, the proxy closes the tunnel and reports a refusal. Without this check, a CDN that routes by server name carries a tunnel to any site that it serves. Thus an allowed name must also be the name in the handshake.

The check has these cases:

- A handshake that Ostra cannot parse, or that is larger than 32 KiB (`MAX_HELLO`), is refused.
- A client that sends no TLS handshake passes. A server that speaks first (an SSH banner) also passes.
- A destination that is an IP address has no check.

### Upstream proxy

Set `[sandbox] upstream_proxy` to `http://host:port` for a machine that reaches the internet only through a proxy. Do not add a path or credentials, because `validate::global` refuses them.

- A trusted host that resolves to a private address connects directly. An internal mirror is rarely behind the corporate proxy.
- Every other allowed destination goes through the upstream proxy. The proxy uses `CONNECT` for a tunnel and the absolute form for plain HTTP.
- A name that does not resolve here goes to the upstream proxy, because that proxy can resolve it. The exception is a local-only name that the user did not list. The proxy refuses it, because the name otherwise reaches the network of the upstream proxy without a check.
- A refusal stays a refusal.

### What the command sees

`proxy_env` sets `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, and `ALL_PROXY`, each in upper and lower case. It sets `NO_PROXY` and `no_proxy` to `localhost,127.0.0.1,::1`, and `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`. Clients skip the proxy for loopback. Thus a loopback entry in `allowed_hosts` works only as a forwarded port.

The reply to a refused request is `403 Forbidden`. Its text starts with the fix, for example: add `host` to `[sandbox] allowed_hosts` in `config.toml`, or set `[sandbox] network = "public"`. Under `none`, the text says to set `network` to `allowlist` first.

### Reports of decisions

The proxy reports the first allowed connection and the first refusal for each `(host, port)`. A retry loop then reports one time. The callback `OnDecision` runs on the runtime of the proxy, so it must not block. `report::egress` sends each decision over a channel to its own thread, and that thread calls `ExecutionHost::emit` with `ExecutionDelta::Egress`.

A refused destination that is loopback, private, or link-local has `local: true`. That one is a containment signal. A refused public host is not, because builds call telemetry hosts. It shows only in the Activity view. See [Containment signals](#containment-signals).

## Loopback, forwards, and blocked ports

A sandbox can need a service on the loopback of the host: a hook bridge of Ostra, a local model gateway, or a test server. The two backends solve this in different ways.

### Linux

A network namespace has a loopback of its own. The loopback of the host, abstract Unix sockets, the LAN, and host services are out of reach. A test checks that a direct connect to a host port fails and that an abstract socket fails.

For each loopback entry with a port in the trusted rules, such as `127.0.0.1:8317`, the profile starts a splice listener (`egress::splice`). The helper binds the same port on the loopback of the sandbox, and it connects each accepted connection to the Unix socket of the splice. `loopback_ports` lists these ports, and it leaves out the blocked ports.

The hook bridge of a harness uses `forward_socket`. The listener is the socket that the server serves. `served_elsewhere` makes sure that the sandbox does not remove it.

Under `network = host`, there is no namespace. The sandbox reaches the loopback of the host and its abstract sockets, and Ostra forwards nothing.

### macOS

Every sandbox shares the loopback of the host. The policy of each sandbox decides which ports it reaches:

- Each sandbox can listen on `localhost`.
- With `loopback = open` (the default), the policy allows a connect to every port, so tests reach the servers that they start. This applies under `allowlist` and `public` only, because `none` reaches nothing.
- With `loopback = listed`, the policy allows only the loopback ports in `allowed_hosts`.
- The policy denies each blocked port, and it denies the TCP port of the Ostra server (`set_server_port`), because that port serves the console API.
- The policy allows the proxy port and the forward ports of the execution last, so they win.

Under `network = host`, the policy allows all outbound IP, a listener on loopback, and the socket of the DNS resolver. Other Unix sockets stay denied: the SSH agent, Docker, password managers, and IDEs. Under the other network choices there is no DNS resolver, because the proxy resolves names and a lookup carries data out in the name. `localhost` still resolves from `/etc/hosts`.

### Blocked ports

`sandbox_blocked_ports` is a workspace setting. It lists loopback ports that no command connects to, even when `allowed_hosts` lists them. Each entry is a rule in every sandbox policy, so the list holds at most 64 ports (`MAX_BLOCKED_PORTS`), and port `0` is invalid. On Linux the list only removes ports from the forwards. On macOS it adds a deny rule.

## Decoy credential files

A decoy is a fake credential file at a path that an agent has no reason to read. When a process opens it, Ostra records a containment signal. The kernel reports the open, so a `cat` in Bash is seen as well as a tool call. The code is in [`decoy.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/decoy.rs).

### Which files are decoys

`HOME_DECOYS` lists four built-in decoys: `~/.ssh/id_rsa`, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, `~/.git-credentials`, and `~/.vault-token`. The content looks real and authenticates nowhere: an OpenSSH private key, a Git URL with a token, or a Vault token.

- A workspace adds decoys with `sandbox_decoys`. A workspace cannot remove a built-in decoy.
- An entry must be a file path that starts with `~/` and has no `.`, `..`, or empty part. The list holds at most 32 entries (`MAX_WORKSPACE_DECOYS`), because each is a watch and a mount.
- An entry cannot name the sign-in file of a harness CLI. A decoy there signs that CLI out in the sandbox.
- A decoy of `~/.ssh/id_*` that does not end in `.pub` has the kind `SshKey`. Other entries are `Generic`.
- Ostra skips the SSH key decoys when a command can reach port 22, because `ssh` reads its keys when it authenticates. `Policy::reaches_port` decides that.
- `~/.netrc` is not a built-in decoy. Python `requests` and Go module downloads read it on every fetch.

### Decoys on Linux

`Decoys::plant` writes each fake file into a private directory `decoys/<16 hex digits>` in the data directory. The sandbox binds the file read-only at the decoy path. An `inotify` watch with `IN_OPEN` on the host file reports the first open. Listing the path or reading its metadata is not an open.

A decoy goes where the host stays unchanged: over an existing file, or into a hidden directory where the `tmpfs` holds a new file. Ostra skips other paths. Each decoy reports one time. After the first open, Ostra removes the watch.

### Decoys on macOS

Seatbelt cannot bind a file in, and it reports no refusal for a path that does not exist. Thus a decoy is an existing file. The policy denies `file-read-data` on it with a message `dev.ostra.decoy.<16 hex digits>`. The kernel writes the message to the system log. A reader runs `log stream` with a predicate that accepts only messages of the kernel Sandbox extension, because any process can log text.

macOS shows the system log to admin accounts only. `log::admin` checks for the group with id 80. `watch_reports` starts the reader at server start and waits up to 10 seconds for `log stream` to attach. When the user cannot read the log, no decoy exists, and `SandboxStatus.decoys` is `false`. The execution runs on without decoys.

### Decoy cleanup

When `Decoys` drops, it ends the watch and deletes the directory of the fake files. At server start, `decoy::remove_stale` deletes directories that an earlier server left behind.

## Git metadata repair

A `.git/config` is written by whoever controls the folder, and that includes an agent. A config can name `core.fsmonitor`, `credential.helper`, or a hook, and git then runs that program. The page [Policy engine](policy.md) describes the `git-metadata` guard for tool calls. This part describes what the sandbox does for a Bash command. The code is in [`git.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/git.rs).

### What the profile protects

`protect_git` calls `git_repos(roots)`. It walks the roots and returns each directory that holds a `.git` directory or a `.git` file. The walk skips symlinks, `node_modules`, and each directory that holds `CACHEDIR.TAG` (Cargo tags `target/` that way). It stops after 20,000 directories (`GIT_WALK_DIRS`) or 128 repositories (`GIT_WALK_REPOS`), and it logs a warning. Repositories below that point keep a writable `.git/config`.

For each repository, the profile makes `config`, `config.worktree`, `hooks/`, and `info/` read-only. The list is `GIT_PROTECTED`. It does the same in each submodule git directory under `modules/` (at most 256 git directories), and it protects `config.worktree` of each linked worktree. A `.git` file is read-only, so it cannot name a planted git directory. A missing `config.worktree` gets an empty placeholder. That is harmless because git reads it only with `extensions.worktreeConfig`, which `config` sets.

### Why a repair is also needed

The file `commondir` cannot have a placeholder, because git refuses to open a repository whose `commondir` is empty. An agent can create a `commondir` that points at another repository. Git then loads the config of that repository. Thus `repair_git_dirs` undoes the change after the fact:

- It deletes a `commondir` in the own git directory of a repository, because git never writes one there.
- It restores the `commondir` of a linked worktree to `../..` when it holds another value.
- It returns the paths that it changed.

`git_repair_note` gives the agent this correction for each path: leave the path to git, because a `commondir` makes git load the config of another repository.

### Where the repair runs

| Caller | When |
| --- | --- |
| Native loop | After each Bash call |
| Harness executor | Every 2 seconds when the CLI runs (`GIT_CHECK_EVERY`), because the commands of the CLI pass no hook that Ostra can check |
| Engine runner | Before `git add` for the stage step of a review |
| Server `run_git` | Before each git command that the server runs for the user |

In the first two cases, each repair becomes a denial of the `git-metadata` guard. The denial counts as a containment signal, and the note goes to the agent in the output of the Bash call.

## Environment scrubbing

Ostra removes variables that carry credentials or point at the desktop session. Four places do this.

| Where | What it removes or sets |
| --- | --- |
| Sandbox command | `UNSET_VARS`: `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`, `DISPLAY`, `WAYLAND_DISPLAY`, `XAUTHORITY`, `DOCKER_HOST`, `GPG_AGENT_INFO`. Bubblewrap uses `--unsetenv`. Seatbelt uses `env_remove`. |
| Bash tool and `host_command` | The names from `credential_env_names`: the provider variables, the bridge variables (`OSTRA_TOKEN`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_URL`, `OSTRA_HARNESS`), and the `oauth.client_secret_env` of each MCP server. It also removes every variable that starts with `OSTRA_`. |
| Harness launch | The credential variables, except those that the own CLI reads to sign in |
| Git settings | `host_command` and the harness add `core.fsmonitor=false`, `safe.bareRepository=explicit`, and `protocol.ext.allow=never` through `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT`. Ostra appends to a count that the parent environment already holds. Hooks stay, because agent commits run the hooks of the repository. |

The sandbox sets the cache variables, `TMPDIR`, and the proxy variables.

### Startup environment on macOS

Any unsandboxed program of the same user can read the startup environment of another process with `sysctl(KERN_PROCARGS2)`. That includes agent commands under `mode = off`. The Seatbelt policy also refuses the read for sandboxed commands. On Linux nothing is needed, because each sandbox has its own pid namespace.

The order in `main` ([`crates/ostra-server/src/main.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/main.rs)) is this:

1. `main` checks whether the first argument is `sandbox-init`. If it is, `main` exits through `ostra_sandbox::init::main`, and the later steps do not run.
2. `main` calls `scrub_startup_env`. This call comes after the `sandbox-init` check and before the runtime and before every other thread.
3. On macOS, `scrub_startup_env` copies the environment to the heap and zeroes the original strings on the stack. On Linux and Other, the call does nothing.

## Containment signals

Three kinds of event are containment signals ([`containment.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/containment.rs)):

- `Guard`: a layer 1 guard refused a tool call. Only the guards `secret-read`, `self-protection`, and `git-metadata` count. A refusal by `write-scope` does not, because it is an ordinary mistake.
- `Egress`: the proxy refused a loopback, private, or link-local destination.
- `Decoy`: a process opened a decoy file.

The runner records at most `PAUSE_AFTER` signals for one execution. `PAUSE_AFTER` is `3`. The third signal pauses the session. [Engine runner](engine-runner.md) describes the pause and how to resume.

## Processes left behind

Under bubblewrap, the pid namespace and `--die-with-parent` end every process of the sandbox with the sandbox. Seatbelt has neither. A child that calls `setsid` or forks twice outlives its shell. The type `Members` solves this.

The policy of each invocation allows a lookup of two mach service names that no daemon registers: a name of its own, and a group name for all sandboxes of the data directory. The kernel answers `sandbox_check` for any process, and a policy is inherited and cannot be dropped. Thus the name finds every descendant. Some system sandboxes allow every name, so a member must also be refused a canary name (`dev.ostra.sandbox.canary`).

When `Members` drops, it kills every process of the invocation. `kill_marked` repeats up to 20 times with a pause of 10 ms, until no process is left. Hold `Members` until the program ends.

At server start, when no other server of the data directory runs, Ostra cleans up what an earlier server left behind:

1. `kill_leftovers` kills processes that carry the group marker.
2. `egress::remove_stale_sockets` deletes `*.sock` files in `egress/`.
3. `decoy::remove_stale` deletes old decoy directories.

## What happens when

### The banner rule

The rule of [What the user sees](#what-the-user-sees) applies. This page owns it. The server prints `WARNING: agent commands run WITHOUT a sandbox` on stderr only when `sandbox.message` is `Some` in `build`. Mode `off` gives `None`, so `build` writes only a tracing warning and prints no banner.

### Cases

- **No backend works and `mode` is `auto`:** The execution runs without a sandbox. `sandbox.message` is `Some`, so the server writes a log warning and prints the stderr banner at start.
- **No backend works and `mode` is `required`:** `decide` returns `Err`, and the execution does not start. The text names the fix for the OS. `status` stores that text in `sandbox.message`, so the server still prints the stderr banner at start.
- **`mode` is `off`:** The execution runs without a sandbox. `sandbox.message` is `None`. The server writes one tracing warning at start and prints no banner.
- **`bwrap` exists but cannot create namespaces:** The probe fails. In a container, the default seccomp or AppArmor profile often blocks user namespaces. On a host, set `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0`, or allow unprivileged user namespaces another way.
- **Ostra runs inside another sandbox on macOS:** The probe fails with the message that macOS cannot start a sandbox inside one. Start Ostra from a terminal that is not sandboxed.
- **The helper binary is missing on Linux:** `wrap` returns the error ``The sandbox helper (the `ostra` binary) is missing.`` ([`crates/ostra-sandbox/src/bwrap.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/bwrap.rs)).
- **A destination is not allowed:** The proxy replies `403 Forbidden` with the fix. It reports a refusal one time for each host and port.
- **A name does not resolve:** The proxy replies `403`, unless an upstream proxy can resolve it.
- **No address accepts a connection:** The proxy tries each checked address with a 10 second timeout. Then it replies `502 Bad Gateway` with the last error.
- **The client sends no request head in 30 seconds:** The proxy closes the connection without a reply.
- **The head is larger than 8 KiB, or is not HTTP/1.x:** The proxy replies `400 Bad Request`.
- **A listener has 256 open connections:** The proxy accepts a new connection and closes it at once.
- **A macOS request has no proxy credential:** The proxy replies `407`.
- **The server name of a tunnel differs from the host:** The proxy closes the tunnel and reports a refusal.
- **The execution ends:** The `Listener` drop cancels the listener, ends the open connections, and deletes the socket file. A socket that the server serves (`served_elsewhere`) stays.
- **The server stops without cleanup:** The next start deletes the old sockets, decoy directories, and leftover processes.
- **A protected path has no placeholder and Ostra cannot create one:** Bubblewrap does not mount that path.
- **A path is not UTF-8 or holds a control character on macOS:** `command` returns `Err`, and the execution does not start.
- **The socket path is too long:** A Unix socket path holds at most 107 bytes. The error tells the user to keep the data directory path short.
- **A user changes `[sandbox]` in `config.toml`:** The next execution uses the change. An execution that runs keeps its profile.

## Numbers

| Name | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_HEAD` | 8 KiB | Largest request head that the proxy reads |
| `HEAD_TIMEOUT` | 30 seconds | Wait for the head, and wait for the TLS handshake |
| `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` | 10 seconds | Connect time for each address, and for the upstream proxy |
| `MAX_CONNECTIONS` | 256 | Open connections for each proxy or splice listener |
| `MAX_HELLO` | 32 KiB | Largest TLS `ClientHello` that the proxy parses |
| Egress runtime | 2 worker threads, named `ostra-egress` | One runtime for all proxies |
| `MAX_OPEN` in the helper | 256 | Open connections for each forwarded port inside the sandbox |
| `MAX_WORKSPACE_DECOYS` | 32 | Decoys that a workspace adds |
| `MAX_BLOCKED_PORTS` | 64 | Blocked ports for a workspace |
| `GIT_WALK_DIRS`, `GIT_WALK_REPOS` | 20,000 and 128 | Limits of the repository walk |
| `GIT_CHECK_EVERY` | 2 seconds | Repair interval for a harness |
| `PAUSE_AFTER` | 3 | Signals that pause a session |
| Log reader attach | 10 seconds | Wait of `watch_reports` on macOS |
| Helper failure code | 125 | Exit status when the helper cannot start the command |

## Limits of the sandbox

The sandbox reduces what a command can do. It does not make a command safe. These limits apply.

### Where no boundary exists

- Windows and every OS other than Linux and macOS have no backend. Under `auto` the commands run with the full rights of the user.
- Under `mode = off`, no boundary exists.
- The sandbox wraps commands only. The other native tools run in the Ostra process, and only the policy engine guards them.
- The sandbox sets no limit for CPU, memory, disk, or process count.

### What the agent can still read and write

- The host is read-only but readable. A file that Ostra does not hide stays readable, for example `/etc` and a secret in a path that `HOME_CREDENTIALS` and `extra_hidden` do not list. Add such a path to `[sandbox] extra_hidden`.
- On Linux, a Unix socket at a path that is not hidden stays reachable, because a read-only file does not stop `connect`. Only the listed container sockets and the runtime directory are hidden.
- The roots of the execution are writable. An agent can change or delete any file of the repository, and it can rewrite git history in `.git`. Only the git metadata that chooses programs is read-only.
- A planted `commondir` exists until the next repair. The repair runs after a Bash call, and every 2 seconds for a harness. It is not a block.

### What the proxy cannot see

- The proxy checks the destination, not the content. An agent can send data to any allowed host, such as `github.com`.
- A tunnel to an allowed name and port can carry any protocol when the client sends no TLS handshake. The server name check covers TLS to named hosts only. An IP address has no check.
- A trusted host can resolve to a private address. The user chose it, so the proxy allows it.
- Under `network = host`, no filter exists, and on Linux the sandbox shares the abstract Unix sockets of the host.

### Backend gaps

- Seatbelt returns `EPERM` for a hidden path, denies `/tmp` instead of making it private, and has no disposable home folder. Its sandboxes share the loopback of the host.
- Under `loopback = open`, a macOS sandbox can connect to every local port that is not blocked. Block the ports of sensitive local services with `sandbox_blocked_ports`.
- Decoys on macOS need an existing file and an admin account. Otherwise no decoy exists.
- The seccomp filter exists only for `x86_64` and `aarch64`. It is a short deny list, not a full allow list.
- A decoy reports a read after it happens. It detects, and it does not prevent.
- Process cleanup on macOS is best effort. It finds processes by a policy name.

### How the signals limit the damage

A containment signal does not stop an execution. The session pauses at the third signal for one execution. Until then, the execution continues.

## Settings that change the sandbox

[Configuration](configuration.md) owns the full tables. This list is only a map.

| Setting | Where | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `[sandbox] mode`, `network` | `config.toml`, and the workspace registry | The mode and the network choice |
| `[sandbox] allowed_hosts` | `config.toml`, plus `sandbox_allowed_hosts` of the workspace | Trusted hosts |
| `[sandbox] upstream_proxy` | `config.toml` | Proxy for outbound traffic |
| `[sandbox] extra_writable`, `extra_hidden` | `config.toml` | More writable or hidden paths. Each is absolute or starts with `~/`. |
| `sandbox_loopback`, `sandbox_blocked_ports` | Workspace registry | The macOS loopback choice and the blocked ports |
| `sandbox_decoys` | Workspace registry | More decoy files |
| `OSTRA_SANDBOX_CACHE` | Environment | The base folder of the tool caches |

The tests of the crate are in [`crates/ostra-sandbox/src/tests.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/src/tests.rs) and [`crates/ostra-sandbox/tests/env_scrub.rs`](crates/ostra-sandbox/tests/env_scrub.rs). A test skips itself when no backend works. [Tests and evals](testing.md) tells how to run them.
