sections.title: Sign-in, host checks, and secrets
sections.summary: How a browser signs in with a one-time token and a cookie, how Ostra refuses foreign hosts and origins, how it seals saved credentials with a master key, and how it keeps home credentials and bridge tokens from agents.
sections.body:
Ostra runs on the machine of the user. It can run commands, write files, and hold API keys. Without access control, any web page that the user opens can call the local API. Any local program can read the saved keys, and an agent can read `~/.ssh`. This page describes the parts that stop these cases:

- The sign-in with a one-time token and a session cookie.
- The Host and Origin checks that block foreign pages and DNS rebinding.
- The limit on failed token exchanges.
- The revoke of sign-ins from the browser and the command line.
- The master key and the sealed credentials in the registry.
- The home credential paths that no agent can read.
- The per-execution bearer tokens of the harness bridge.

The page ends with the limits of these defenses. Other pages own the neighbor topics. [Install and run](install-and-run.md) owns the `ostra url`, `ostra sessions`, and `ostra signout` commands and the port and bind flags. [Configuration](configuration.md) owns `config.toml`. [Policy](policy.md) owns the secret-read guard. [Sandbox](sandbox.md) owns the kernel boundary and the decoy files. [Storage](storage.md) owns the registry database.

## Sign in with a one-time token

A browser signs in in two steps. First, it gets a one-time token in a URL. Second, it exchanges the token for a session cookie. The token is useless after the exchange. A copy of the URL in a history file or a chat cannot sign in a second browser.

### Mint the token

The `Auth::sign_in_url` function and the `request_url` function (the `ostra url` command) call `mint_token`. `mint_token` makes 32 random bytes and writes them as 64 hex characters. It stores only the SHA-256 hash of the token. The registry key is `auth:token:<sha256 of the token>`. The value is the expiry time in Unix seconds. A token lives `TOKEN_TTL_SECS`, which is 900 seconds (15 minutes).

The URL has the form `http://<host>/#token=<token>`. The token is in the fragment because a browser does not send the fragment to the server. The fragment is also not part of the `Referer` header.

`ostra url` works for a running server because both processes use the same registry file. The server writes `server.json` in the data dir. The file holds the port, the host for printed URLs (`url_host`), and the process ID of the server. `request_url` reads this file. `server_running` checks that the process ID is alive. If `server.json` is missing, `ostra url` fails with `No Ostra server is running. Start one with ostra.`

### Exchange the token for a cookie

The web app reads the token in `exchangeTokenFromUrl` ([`web/src/auth.ts`](web/src/auth.ts)). The function runs these steps:

1. Read `#token=` from `location.hash`.
2. Wait for the `prerenderingchange` event if the browser loads the page in the background. A background load must not spend the token that the real visit needs.
3. Skip the token if this page already exchanged it. The page keeps the tokens that it sent in the `exchanged` `Set`.
4. Remove the fragment from the address bar with `history.replaceState`.
5. Send `POST /api/auth/exchange` with the body `{"token": "..."}`.

If the user pastes a new link into an open tab, only the hash changes. The `watchForTokens` function adds a `hashchange` listener that reloads the page. Then the boot code sees the new token. The sign-in screen also accepts a pasted link or a bare token of 16 or more hex characters.

#### The exchange flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant CLI as ostra url
    participant Browser
    participant Guard as guard middleware
    participant Route as exchange route handler
    participant Auth
    participant Reg as RegistryDb
    CLI->>Reg: kv_set auth:token:HASH with expiry
    CLI-->>Browser: URL with #token=TOKEN
    Browser->>Browser: history.replaceState removes the fragment
    Browser->>Guard: POST /api/auth/exchange
    Guard->>Auth: allowed_host and allowed_origin
    Guard->>Route: request passes the checks
    Route->>Auth: exchange_wait(ip)
    Route->>Auth: exchange(token, meta)
    Auth->>Reg: kv_replace token to used:TIME
    Auth->>Reg: kv_set auth:cookie:HASH with Record
    Route->>Auth: note_exchange(ip, ok)
    Route-->>Browser: 204 and Set-Cookie ostra_session
```

The `guard` middleware checks only the host and the origin of this route. The route handler `exchange` ([`crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs), line 616) calls `exchange_wait`, `exchange`, and `note_exchange`.

The `Auth::exchange` function runs these checks in order:

1. Hash the trimmed token and read `auth:token:<hash>`. A missing row gives `ExchangeError::Unknown`.
2. If the value starts with `used:`, return `ExchangeError::Used` with the seconds since the use. Ostra keeps a used token as a row. A second try then says "already used" and does not look like an unknown token.
3. Claim the token with `kv_replace`. It changes the value to `used:<time>` only when the row still holds the old value. If two requests race, only one wins. The other gets `Used` with `seconds_ago: 0`.
4. If the stored expiry is in the past, return `ExchangeError::Expired`. The token is already marked used at this point. An expired token cannot be tried again.
5. Make the cookie value: 32 random bytes as 64 hex characters. Store a `Record` under `auth:cookie:<sha256 of the cookie>`. Return the cookie value.

The server never stores the cookie value or the token. It stores only their hashes. A read of the registry file does not give an attacker a working cookie.

### The cookie

The server sets the cookie with `Auth::cookie_header`. The name is `ostra_session` (the `COOKIE` constant). These attributes apply:

| Attribute | Value | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `HttpOnly` | always | A script in the page cannot read the cookie. |
| `SameSite=Strict` | always | The browser does not send the cookie on a request that another site starts. |
| `Path=/` | always | The cookie covers the app and the API. |
| `Max-Age` | `COOKIE_TTL_SECS`, 2592000 seconds (30 days) | A sign-in expires 30 days after its creation. Use of the app does not extend it. |
| `Secure` | only when the `Origin` header starts with `https://` | A TLS reverse proxy in front of Ostra makes the browser use HTTPS. |

The server does not read `X-Forwarded-Proto` to decide on `Secure`, because any client can send that header. It uses `Origin`, which a browser sets by itself.

### The sign-in record

Each cookie has a `Record` in the registry key-value table. The record holds these fields:

- `id`: `si_` and 16 hex characters.
- `created` and `last_seen`.
- `user_agent`: cut to 300 characters.
- `ip`: the address of the browser.

The `id` is random and is not derived from the cookie. The settings screen and `ostra sessions` can show it without a risk.

A sign-in survives a server restart because the record is in the registry. Older servers stored only the creation time as a number. `parse_record` reads both forms, and `load_records` rewrites an old row with an `id`. `load_records` also deletes a row that it cannot read or that is past its expiry.

### Check a cookie on each request

`Auth::check_cookie` decides if a cookie is valid. It keeps a memory cache of the cookie hash, the expiry, and the time when the registry last confirmed the sign-in. The cache has these rules:

- If the registry confirmed the sign-in less than `RECHECK` ago (5 seconds), the function answers from the cache.
- Otherwise, it reads the registry row. The cookie is valid if the row exists and its expiry is in the future.
- If the row is expired, the function deletes it and removes the cache entry.
- If `last_seen` is 60 seconds old or more (`SEEN_EVERY_SECS`), the function updates it with `kv_replace` over the row that it just read. An active tab does not write on each request. A revoke that lands at the same time is not undone.

The 5-second cache bounds how late a revoke from another process takes effect. See [Revoke a sign-in](#revoke-a-sign-in).

## Check Host and Origin on every request

The `guard` middleware in [`crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs) runs before every route. It blocks DNS rebinding and requests from pages on other origins. In a DNS rebinding attack, a name of the attacker points at `127.0.0.1`. The browser then treats the local server as the origin of the attacker. The attack fails because the `Host` header still holds the name of the attacker. The server does not know that name.

### The order of the checks

The guard runs these checks in order. The first check that fails ends the request.

1. **Host.** The `Host` header must match a name in the allowlist (`Auth::allowed_host`, compared without case). If not, the answer is `421 Misdirected Request` with `This host is not allowed.` This check applies to every path, including `/`, assets, `/ws`, and `/internal/*`.
2. **Private name redirect.** Some servers use a private name (see below). On such a server, a request to `127.0.0.1`, `localhost`, or `[::1]` gets a `307` redirect to the private name for a page load. The redirect keeps the path and the query. An API request gets `421`. Paths under `/internal/` skip this step.
3. **Bridge peer.** A request to `/internal/` must come from a local address (`is_local_address`: loopback or an address of an interface of this machine). Other peers get `403` with `This endpoint accepts local connections only.` Harnesses always run on this machine. This rule holds when the server listens on every interface.
4. **Bridge and browsers.** A request to `/internal/` that has an `Origin` header or a `Sec-Fetch-Site` header gets `403` with `This endpoint is for Ostra's harness bridge, not for web pages.` A browser always sends one of the two headers. The hook and the MCP shim send neither.
5. **Origin and fetch metadata.** For `/api/*` and `/ws`, the request gets `403` with `This origin is not allowed.` if any of these is true: the `Origin` header is present and not in the allowlist, `Sec-Fetch-Site` is `cross-site` or `same-site`, or `Sec-Fetch-Dest` is not `empty`, `websocket`, or `document`.
6. **Cookie.** For `/api/*` and `/ws`, except `/api/auth/exchange`, the request needs a valid `ostra_session` cookie. If not, the answer is `401` with `Sign in with the URL the ostra command printed.` Ostra logs the reason at info level: the cookie is missing, or it is sent but not recognized.

The code of the checks is in the `guard` and `refusal` functions (`api.rs`, lines 135-268).

The `Sec-Fetch-Site` rule covers a case that `Origin` does not. A page on another localhost port is same-site with the app. The `SameSite=Strict` cookie goes with its requests. A simple `GET` from that page can have no `Origin` header. The `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site` value shows the case, and the guard refuses it. The `Sec-Fetch-Dest` rule stops page content from reaching the API with the cookie. A Markdown image that an agent wrote is an example. The app itself uses `empty` (fetch), `websocket`, and `document` (download links).

### Security headers

`secure_headers` adds these headers to every response, including the refusals:

- `Content-Security-Policy` with `default-src 'self'`, `script-src 'self'`, `img-src 'self' data:`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`, and `connect-src 'self'`. The `connect-src` value also holds the `ws://` and `wss://` form of the host.
- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.
- `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`.
- `X-Frame-Options: DENY`.
- `Cache-Control: no-store` for the API.

Ostra names a host in the policy only after the host passes the allowlist.

### Which Host values are allowed

`Access::hosts` builds the allowlist when the server starts. The `Access` struct comes from the port, the bind address, `server.allowed_hosts` in `config.toml`, the `--allow-host` flag (repeatable), the `--dev` flag, and `server.use_ip_host` (see [Configuration](configuration.md)).

| Source | Names that it adds |
| --- | --- |
| Always | `127.0.0.1:<port>`, `localhost:<port>`, `[::1]:<port>` |
| Bind to all interfaces | `<address>:<port>` for every interface address, including container and VM bridges, and `<hostname>:<port>` and `<hostname>.local:<port>` |
| Bind to one non-loopback address | That address with the port |
| `server.allowed_hosts` and `--allow-host` | Each name. A name with no port is added with and without the port, because a reverse proxy on its default port sends the bare name. |
| `--dev` | `localhost:5173` and `127.0.0.1:5173` (the Vite dev server) |

The list is lowercased, sorted, and made unique. `Access::hosts` does not add the private name. `Auth::new` (`auth.rs`, lines 408-418) adds `ostra-<16 hex>.localhost:<port>` after `hosts()` returns. It adds the name only when `private_host` is set and the bind is loopback (`!access.is_remote()`).

The URL that Ostra prints uses `Access::url_host`. It is `127.0.0.1:<port>` for a local server. It is the first LAN address for a server that listens on a non-loopback address. `lan_addresses` skips loopback and IPv6 link-local addresses. It also skips interfaces whose name starts with `docker`, `br-`, `veth`, `cni`, `flannel`, `virbr`, `vnet`, `tailscale`, or `lo`.

### Which Origin values are allowed

`Auth::allowed_origin` accepts a request with no `Origin` header, because a non-browser client and a same-origin `GET` do not send one. If the header is present, it must start with `http://` or `https://`. The rest must equal an allowed `Host` value exactly. The `https` form is accepted for a TLS reverse proxy. The header value `null` and any foreign site are refused.

### The private name

A cookie is not scoped to a port. A cookie that the server sets for `127.0.0.1` goes to every other local server on the machine. To prevent this, `Auth::new` calls `private_name` when two conditions hold. The server is bound to loopback, and `server.use_ip_host` is `false` (the default). The function makes a random name, `ostra-<16 hex>.localhost`, and stores it under the registry key `server:private_host`. The name is stable across restarts.

A browser resolves each `*.localhost` name to this machine. The cookie for that name does not go to pages on `127.0.0.1` or other names. `Auth::new` sets `url_host` to the private name, so the printed sign-in URL uses it. It also keeps the three loopback names in `ip_hosts`. `private_redirect` uses that list for the `307` redirect.

Set `server.use_ip_host` to `true` for a browser that does not resolve `*.localhost`. The cookie then goes to every local port.

### What happens when

- **The Host is unknown:** the answer is `421`, with the security headers. No route runs.
- **A page on another localhost port sends a request with the cookie:** the answer is `403`, because the `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` check fails.
- **A page on another site sends a form, a fetch, a script tag, or a frame request:** the answer is `403`, or the browser blocks the request before it leaves. The WebSocket does not open.
- **An `img`, `script`, or stylesheet tag on the app origin names an `/api` URL:** the answer is `403` for the `Sec-Fetch-Dest` value, although the browser sends the cookie.
- **The cookie is missing, expired, or revoked:** the answer is `401`. The page shows the sign-in screen.
- **A page navigates the top-level window to an API URL from another origin:** the answer is `403`.

## Limit failed exchanges

The exchange route refuses a client after repeated failures. A token has 256 bits, so a guess is not a real risk. The limit stops a guessing loop from filling the log and the registry.

The constants are `MAX_FAILURES` (5) and `FAILURE_WINDOW` (60 seconds). The server keeps the times of the failures for each peer IP address in memory. The route handler `exchange` (`api.rs`, lines 616-670) works in this order:

1. Call `exchange_wait(ip)` before it reads the token. If the address has 5 failures in the last 60 seconds, the answer is `429` with `Wait N s before trying another sign-in link...`. `N` is the time until the oldest failure leaves the window, at least 1 second.
2. Read the body with a limit of 64 KB. A body that is not `{"token": ...}` gets a 400-class refusal. The limit does not count it.
3. Run `exchange`, then call `note_exchange(ip, ok)`. A failure adds the current time to the list. A success removes the address from the list.

These cases apply:

- **A loopback peer fails many times:** nothing happens. Loopback peers are not limited, because any local process can otherwise lock the user out of sign-in with bad tokens.
- **The address is in the wait state and the token is valid:** the answer is still `429`, because the check runs before the route reads the token.
- **The server restarts:** the failure lists are gone, because they are in memory only.
- **A second address fails:** it has its own list.

The unit test `failed_exchanges_are_limited_per_address` pins these rules.

A failed exchange returns `401` with one of three messages:

- `Unknown`: this server did not issue the link. The message tells the user to run `ostra url` as the same user.
- `Used`: the message says how many seconds ago the link was used.
- `Expired`: the message says that links last 15 minutes.

Each message tells the user to run `ostra url` for a new link.

## Revoke a sign-in

A sign-in ends when its record leaves the registry. A user can revoke from the browser or from the command line. A revoke from the server process takes effect at once. A revoke from another process takes effect within `RECHECK`, 5 seconds.

| Action | Route or command | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| List sign-ins | `GET /api/auth/sessions`, `ostra sessions` | Lists each sign-in, oldest first, with the id, creation time, last seen time, address, and browser. The browser list marks the caller with `current`. |
| Revoke one | `DELETE /api/auth/sessions/{id}`, `ostra sessions revoke <id>` | Removes one record. The route answers `404` if the id is unknown or expired. |
| Revoke the others | `POST /api/auth/sessions/revoke-others` | Removes every record except the one of the caller. |
| Sign out | `POST /api/auth/signout` | Removes the record of the caller and clears the cookie with `Max-Age=0`. |
| Revoke all | `ostra signout`, `ostra sessions revoke --all` | Removes every record. The user runs `ostra url` to sign in again. |

The route handlers are `list_sign_ins`, `revoke_sign_in`, `revoke_other_sign_ins`, and `sign_out` (`api.rs`, lines 680-729). They call `Auth::drop_sign_in`. It deletes the registry row and removes the cache entry. Then it sends the cookie hash on a broadcast channel (`subscribe_revoked`, capacity 64). The command line functions (`revoke_sign_in` and `revoke_sign_ins`) delete the rows only, because they run in another process. A running server finds the missing row when the 5-second cache ends.

An open WebSocket also ends. [`crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs) runs `check_cookie` every `RECHECK`. It also listens on the revoke channel. When its own cookie hash arrives, it sends a close frame with code `4401` and the reason `Signed out`. If the channel lags, the socket checks the registry. The socket also checks once after the subscription, because a revoke between the upgrade and the subscription went to no listener. `drop_sign_in` deletes the row before it broadcasts, so this check sees the revoke.

After a revoke, the browser keeps its cookie, but the cookie is no longer valid. The API answers `401`, and the app shows the sign-in screen.

## Keep the master key

The registry holds provider API keys, git credentials, MCP secrets, and the push private key. Without encryption, a copy of `registry.db` gives an attacker all of them. Ostra encrypts these values with a 32-byte master key. The key lives outside the registry file, in the OS keychain or in an owner-only file. [`crates/ostra-server/src/master_key.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/master_key.rs) owns this.

`master_key::unlock` runs at server start (`app.rs`) and returns a `RegistryDb` that has a `Sealer`. It runs these steps:

1. `load_key` finds the key.
2. `check_key` checks that the key opens the sealed check value.
3. `with_sealer` gives the key to the registry.
4. `seal_plaintext_secrets` encrypts credentials that older versions stored as plaintext.

### How `load_key` picks the key

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Start unlock] --> B{OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE set?}
    B -->|yes| C[Read or create that file]
    B -->|no| D{Recorded backend is file?}
    D -->|yes| H[Use master.key in the data dir]
    D -->|no| E{Keychain has the key?}
    E -->|yes| F[Use it and record keychain]
    E -->|no entry| G{Keychain stores a new key?}
    G -->|yes| F
    G -->|no| H
    E -->|unreachable| I{Recorded backend is keychain?}
    I -->|yes| J[Stop startup with an error]
    I -->|no| H
```

The `secrets:backend` registry key records the backend that holds the key: `keychain` or `file`. The record has a purpose. Suppose the keychain held the key and is now locked. Ostra must not make a new key and then lose access to the saved credentials. So it stops.

- **`OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` is set:** Ostra uses that file and skips the keychain and the record. Use it for a mounted Docker secret. If the file does not exist, Ostra creates it.
- **Keychain:** the entry has the service `ostra` and the account `master-key <canonical data dir>`. One entry for each data dir keeps separate installs apart. The value is the key as 64 hex characters. Each keychain call runs on its own thread and ends after `KEYCHAIN_TIMEOUT`, 10 seconds. A call can block on an unlock prompt or a dead D-Bus.
- **No keychain entry:** Ostra makes a random key, saves it, reads it back, and compares. If the keychain does not keep the key, Ostra falls back to the file. If the record said `keychain` but the entry is gone, Ostra logs that it makes a new key and that the user must enter saved credentials again.
- **Keychain unreachable and the record says `keychain`:** startup stops with the message `Unlock the system keychain and start Ostra again...`. The message also names `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` as the way to move to a file.
- **Keychain unreachable and no record says `keychain`:** Ostra logs the reason and uses the file.
- **The file:** `<data dir>/master.key` holds 64 hex characters. Ostra creates it with `create_new` and mode `0600` on Unix. If the file exists with group or other permissions, Ostra sets mode `0600`. If it cannot, for example on a read-only secret mount, it logs a warning and goes on. On Windows the file keeps the ACL that it inherits from the data dir. A file that does not hold 64 hex characters stops startup with an error that names the file.

### What happens when the key changes

`check_key` stores the text `ostra` sealed under the row key `secrets:check`. At each start, it opens the value with the current key.

- **It opens:** nothing else happens.
- **It does not open:** the saved credentials were sealed with a different key. Ostra logs a warning and writes a new check value. It reads the old credentials as not set. The user must enter them again in settings. Ostra does not stop in this case.
- **There is no check value:** this is a first start. Ostra writes it.

Caution: do not delete `master.key` or the keychain entry while credentials are saved. The sealed values cannot be decrypted without the key, and the user must enter them again.

## Seal credentials in the registry

[`crates/ostra-store/src/secrets.rs`](crates/ostra-store/src/secrets.rs) holds the `Sealer`. It encrypts each credential value with AES-256-GCM.

### The sealed format

A sealed value is the bytes `enc:v1:` followed by the base64 text of `nonce || ciphertext`. The nonce has `NONCE_LEN` bytes (12) and is random for each seal. The same plaintext gives a different value each time. The associated data of the cipher is the registry key of the row. A sealed value that an attacker copies to another row does not open there.

`Sealer::open` returns `OpenError::Undecryptable` when the value was sealed under another key or was changed. If the value has no `enc:v1:` prefix, `open` returns it as it is. Registries from before encryption hold plaintext until the migration seals them.

### Which rows are credentials

`SECRET_KEYS` lists the registry keys that hold credentials. A name that ends with `:` is a prefix. Other names must match exactly.

| Registry key | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `vapid_private` | The private key for Web Push |
| `provider_credentials:` | Saved base URL, API key, and auth token of a model provider |
| `git_credential:` | Git credentials |
| `mcp_oauth:` | OAuth tokens of MCP servers |
| `mcp_secret:` | Other MCP secrets |

The sign-in rows (`auth:token:` and `auth:cookie:`) are not in this list. They hold hashes, not secrets. See [MCP servers and Web Push](mcp-and-notifications.md) for the users of `vapid_private`, `mcp_oauth:`, and `mcp_secret:`.

### The `RegistryDb` methods

- `secret_set(key, value)` seals and stores the value.
- `secret_get(key)` opens and returns the value. A value that does not open reads as absent, and Ostra logs `the saved credential under <key> cannot be decrypted...`.
- `secret_scan(prefix)` returns every credential under a prefix and skips values that do not open.
- Each of these methods returns `StoreError::Locked` if the registry has no `Sealer`. `RegistryDb::open` makes a registry without a `Sealer`. `open_in_memory` uses `Sealer::ephemeral`, a key that exists for the life of the process.

Add a new credential row to `SECRET_KEYS` before you call `secret_set` for it. Debug builds fail an assertion for a key that the list does not name. `seal_plaintext_secrets` never migrates such a row.

### The migration of plaintext rows

`seal_plaintext_secrets` seals each row that `is_secret_key` names and that has no sealed prefix. It uses `kv_replace`, so a concurrent write is not lost. Then it runs `VACUUM` and `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)`. The plaintext does not stay in free pages or in the write-ahead log.

The vacuum also runs in one more case. An earlier start sealed rows but stopped before it finished the rewrite. The registry marker `secrets_vacuumed` (the constant `SECRETS_VACUUMED` in `crates/ostra-store/src/registry.rs`, line 49) is then missing. The function writes the marker after the vacuum. `RegistryDb::open` sets `secure_delete` to `ON`, which zeroes freed pages.

The server logs `encrypted N saved credentials that were stored as plaintext`. The unit test in `master_key.rs` checks that the plaintext string is gone from `registry.db` and `registry.db-wal`.

### Provider credentials

[`crates/ostra-server/src/credentials.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/credentials.rs) stores the provider credentials that the user types in the browser. They live in the registry under `provider_credentials:<provider>`. They never reach `config.toml` or a response body. `save` calls `secret_set`, or deletes the row if the credentials are empty. `load_all` reads every row and skips a row that is not valid JSON, with a warning. `Shared::reload_providers` rebuilds the providers from the global config and the saved credentials.

`apply` merges an edit over the saved value with these rules for each field (`base_url`, `api_key`, `auth_token`):

- **The edit field is absent:** the saved value stays.
- **The edit field is an empty string:** the saved value is cleared.
- **The edit field has text:** the trimmed text replaces the saved value.

`apply` then checks the result and returns every problem at once:

- The base URL must start with `http://` or `https://` and have a host.
- The base URL must not have a user name, a password, or a query. Settings show the base URL, so the key must go in the API key field.
- The API key and the auth token must not have spaces, line breaks, or control characters, because Ostra sends them in an HTTP header.

## Hide home credential paths from agents

An agent that runs in a repository can try to read `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` or `~/.aws/credentials`. [`crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs) holds one list of such paths, `HOME_CREDENTIALS`. Each entry is a `HomeCredential` with a path relative to `$HOME` and an optional `harness`.

### What the list holds

- **Tool credentials:** `.ssh`, `.gnupg`, `.aws`, `.azure`, `.config/gcloud`, `.kube`, `.docker`, `.netrc`, `.git-credentials`, `.config/gh/hosts.yml`, `.config/hub`, `.cargo/credentials`, `.cargo/credentials.toml`, `.pypirc`, `.vault-token`, `.terraform.d/credentials.tfrc.json`, `.password-store`, `.local/share/keyrings`, and `.Xauthority`.
- **Browser and personal data on Linux:** `.mozilla`, `.config/google-chrome`, `.config/chromium`, and `.config/BraveSoftware`.
- **macOS stores under `Library`:** `Keychains`, `Cookies`, `HTTPStorages`, `Safari`, `Messages`, `Mail`, `Group Containers`, `Containers`, the profile folders of Chrome, Chromium, Brave, Edge, Arc, and Firefox, `com.apple.TCC`, and the VS Code `globalStorage`.
- **Windows stores under the profile folder:** `_netrc`, `AppData/Roaming/gcloud`, `GitHub CLI`, `Microsoft/Protect`, `Microsoft/Credentials`, the browser profile folders, the VS Code `globalStorage`, and the PowerShell `ConsoleHost_history.txt`.
- **Sign-in files of harness CLIs:** `.claude/.credentials.json` (`HarnessKind::Claude`), `.codex/auth.json` (`Codex`), `.grok/auth.json` (`Grok`), and `.gemini/oauth_creds.json` and `.gemini/google_accounts.json` (`Agy`). These entries have a `harness` value.

`secret_paths(home)` returns the list that the policy and the search tools use. It holds the data dir (registry, `master.key`, server log) and the file that `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` names. It also holds every `HOME_CREDENTIALS` path under `home`.

### Who uses the list

| Component | What it does with the paths |
| --- | --- |
| Policy guards (`ostra-policy`, `Roots.secret`) | Refuse a tool call that names a path in `secret_paths`. See [Policy](policy.md). |
| Search tools (`ostra-tools`, `SecretFilter`) | Skip these paths when Grep or Glob starts from a parent folder. They still search the agent assets inside the data dir. |
| Sandbox profile (`Profile::common`) | Hides the data dir, the Ostra config dir, the XDG runtime dir, the file in `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE`, `XAUTHORITY`, and each `HOME_CREDENTIALS` path. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md). |
| Decoy files (`decoy::invalid`) | Refuse a decoy for a path that has a `harness` value. |

The `harness` field exists because a harness CLI must sign in. When a harness execution starts, the sandbox hides every entry except the entry whose `harness` is the CLI of that execution. The CLI keeps its own sign-in file. It cannot see the sign-in files of the other CLIs. Native executions have no `own` harness, so all entries are hidden. A decoy at a sign-in file path signs that CLI out in the sandbox. For this reason `decoy::invalid` refuses it with `Remove ... because it is a harness CLI's sign-in file...`.

The data dir is also protected on disk. `ensure_data_dir` creates it with mode `0700` on Unix. It holds the registry, and SQLite creates the `-wal` and `-shm` files with open permissions. `create_private_dir_all` and `private_file_options` make new dirs with mode `0700` and new files with mode `0600`.

The list is a fixed set of names. It does not find a credential that a user keeps in another folder. A user can add paths to the sandbox with its `extra_hidden` setting (see [Sandbox](sandbox.md)).

## Authorize the harness bridge with bearer tokens

A harness CLI (Claude, Codex, Grok, or Agy) runs its own tools. Ostra checks each tool call through two parts. A hook calls the server on `POST /internal/policy`. An MCP shim calls `POST /internal/mcp`. These two endpoints must accept only the hook and the shim of a live execution. [Executors](executors.md) owns the hook bridge. This section describes the token check.

### The token

`LiveRegistry::register` makes the token when an execution starts. The token is two random UUIDs (version 4) written without hyphens, which gives 64 hex characters. Each execution has its own token. The token ends when `LiveRegistry::remove` runs for that execution. A finished execution cannot call the bridge.

The launch code gives the token to the harness in the environment variable `OSTRA_TOKEN` (`ENV_TOKEN`). The launch plan removes `OSTRA_TOKEN` and other credential variables from the environment of the agent shell. It keeps the sign-in variables of that CLI, for example `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` for Claude. Grok keeps the token in its config file, so Ostra writes the plan files with owner-only permissions. The sandbox hides the `harness` folder of the other executions in the same session, because those folders hold their bridge tokens.

### The check

The hook and the shim send `Authorization: Bearer <token>` and the execution ID in the body. The server routes `policy_route` and `mcp_route` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs) read the header with `bearer`. A request with no bearer value gets `401`. Then `HarnessBridge::authorize` runs two checks:

1. `LiveRegistry::authorize` finds the execution by its ID. It compares the token with a constant-time function (`constant_time_eq`). The time of the compare does not show how many bytes were right.
2. `BridgeServices::authorize` confirms that the server still has the execution registered.

If either check fails, the bridge never fails open. A `PreToolUse` event gets a deny. The deny text says that the execution does not run under Ostra any more and that the tool call must stop. Other events get an empty answer. A hook whose harness does not match the harness of the execution is also denied.

### Why the endpoints stay closed to other callers

The bearer token is the last of four layers. These layers run before the token check:

- The Host allowlist applies to `/internal/*` too. A rebinding name gets `421`.
- The peer must be a local address.
- A request with `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` gets `403` before the server reads the body or the token. A web page on the same machine is a local peer, but it always sends one of these headers.
- The cookie check does not apply, because `/internal/*` is not under `/api/`. The token replaces it.

On Unix, the server also serves only the two internal routes on a Unix socket (`serve_bridge_socket`) in the egress dir. A sandbox with its own network reaches the bridge through this socket. No other route answers there.

## What these defenses do not guarantee

- **A local process of the same user.** The data dir has mode `0700`. A process that runs as the same user can still read `master.key`, ask the keychain for the key, or run `ostra url` to get a sign-in URL. The sign-in protects against browsers and foreign pages, not against the user account.
- **A copy of the cookie.** `HttpOnly` stops page scripts from reading the cookie. A person who has the cookie value can send it from any program that sends an allowed `Host`. Revoke the sign-in to end it.
- **Plain HTTP on a network.** When the server listens on a LAN address with no TLS proxy, the token and the cookie cross the network in clear text. Put a TLS reverse proxy in front and add its name with `--allow-host`.
- **A shared address behind a proxy.** The failed-exchange limit counts the peer address of the TCP connection. A proxy on the same machine connects from loopback, which the limit does not count.
- **Sealed values in memory.** The server holds decrypted provider keys in memory, and it passes some to harness CLIs. The seal protects values at rest in `registry.db`.
- **Keys in other places.** `config.toml` and project files can hold values that a user types there. The list of home credential paths names fixed paths only.
- **A lost key.** Nobody can recover the sealed credentials. The user enters them again.

## How the browser tests check these rules

The Playwright suite in `tests/browser` runs a real Chromium against a scratch server. [Tests and evals](testing.md) owns how to run it. Two specs cover this page.

- **`signin.spec.ts`.** After sign-in, the address bar and `location.hash` have no token. No request URL or header carries the token. The exchange runs once and answers `204`, also when a second tab loads the page in the background and the page reloads. A replay of the token that the browser profile kept gets `401` with `already used`.
- **`cross-origin.spec.ts`.** An attacker page runs on another localhost port (same-site) and on another site. It sends forms, fetches in each mode, a WebSocket, tags, and frames to every `GET` route of `api.rs`. It also sends them to a list of state-changing routes, including `/api/auth/sessions/revoke-others`, `/api/auth/signout`, `/internal/policy`, and `/internal/mcp`. The suite checks these results:
  - The server refuses each request that reaches it.
  - No response is readable.
  - The WebSocket does not open.
  - The app does not render in a frame.
  - The server state does not change.
  - A rebinding host on the port of the app gets `421` on each path.
  - Image, script, and stylesheet requests from the app origin to `/api` get `403` with the cookie set.

The Rust unit tests in `auth.rs`, `master_key.rs`, and `secrets.rs` pin the token, cookie, revoke, limit, key fallback, and seal rules. The end-to-end test in `crates/ostra-server/tests/e2e.rs` pins the `403` and `421` answers and the security headers.
