The bearer header read and the internal routes of the harness bridge.
Per-execution token mint and constant-time authorize.
The browser side of the exchange: read the fragment, strip it, and send the token. Lines 46-56 hold the `exchanged` Set and `watchForTokens`.
Checks that the token leaves the URL and that a replay fails.
Checks that attacker pages and rebinding hosts get refused.

sections.title: Workspaces, projects, and approvals
sections.summary: How Ostra creates, opens, and deletes a workspace, manages projects, validates settings, approves commands that folder files name, claims checkouts for Git, and stores the console layout.
sections.body:
A workspace folder holds `.ostra/workspace.toml`, and each project folder holds `.ostra/project.toml`. Both files travel with a repository, a `git pull`, or an agent edit. They name programs: MCP servers, language servers, code providers, and format commands. They also hold allow rules and project folders. Without a check, a pulled file can start a program on the machine or widen the folders that agents can write.

The `ostra-workspace` crate solves this with two rules. Rule A1 says that a program from a folder file starts only after the user approved exactly that content. Rule A2 says that the permission mode, YOLO, spend limits, tool enforcement, and sandbox choices never come from a folder file. They live in the registry database. The same crate also creates and deletes workspaces, opens a workspace as a `WorkspaceRt`, validates settings, manages projects, and stores the console layout.

This page covers:

- [The parts of the crate](#the-parts-of-the-crate)
- [Create a workspace](#create-a-workspace)
- [Open a workspace with WorkspaceRt](#open-a-workspace-with-workspacert)
- [Validate, fix, and save settings](#validate-fix-and-save-settings)
- [Import, clone, create, and remove a project](#import-clone-create-and-remove-a-project)
- [Delete a workspace](#delete-a-workspace)
- [The work lock and the busy checks](#the-work-lock-and-the-busy-checks)
- [Approval of commands from folder files](#approval-of-commands-from-folder-files)
- [Settings that live in the registry](#settings-that-live-in-the-registry)
- [Sealed MCP values](#sealed-mcp-values)
- [Git dock claims](#git-dock-claims)
- [UI state](#ui-state)
- [Limits and routes](#limits-and-routes)

The layers and fields of the settings files belong to [Configuration reference](configuration.md). The registry tables belong to [Storage](storage.md). The REST layer belongs to [Server, REST API, and WebSocket](server-and-api.md).

## The parts of the crate

The crate has one file for each concern. The server crate supplies the host that the crate needs.

| File | What it owns |
| --- | --- |
| `crates/ostra-workspace/src/create.rs` | `draft`, `validate`, and `register`: the whole-request check and the write of a new workspace. |
| `crates/ostra-workspace/src/runtime.rs` | `WorkspaceRt`, `unregister`, the busy checks, and `retire`. |
| `crates/ostra-workspace/src/projects.rs` | Project key, stack, and folder checks, `import_entry`, `create_target`, and `git_branch`. |
| `crates/ostra-workspace/src/settings.rs` | `validate_settings`, `settings_fixes`, and `agent_infos`. |
| `crates/ostra-workspace/src/trust.rs` | Command hashes, approvals, the registry-held settings, sealed MCP values, and migration. |
| `crates/ostra-workspace/src/ui_state.rs` | The merge and storage of the console layout. |
| `crates/ostra-workspace/src/host.rs` | The `WorkspaceHost` trait. |
| `crates/ostra-server/src/repo.rs` | The Git dock: status, stage, commit, fetch, push, and checkout. |

`WorkspaceHost` is what a workspace needs from the process that opens it. The server `Shared` value implements it. The trait has these methods:

- `registry()` returns the `RegistryDb`. It holds approvals, the permission mode, YOLO, and sealed secrets.
- `global()` returns the `GlobalConfig`. The host reads it again on every call, so an edit applies without a restart.
- `environment()` returns the machine facts that validation needs.
- `providers()` and `harnesses()` return the status lists that `detail()` shows.
- `services(id, root)` returns the engine services for the workspace.

## Create a workspace

One request creates a workspace. The request becomes complete settings, and Ostra validates them as a whole. Ostra writes nothing if any issue remains. `POST /api/workspaces/validate` runs the same check without a write, so the console can show issues before the user submits.

### Create flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser
    participant Api
    participant Create
    participant Trust
    participant Registry
    participant App
    Browser->>Api: POST /api/workspaces
    Api->>Create: setup::create calls register(host, body)
    Create->>Create: draft(body, ctx) builds and validates the settings
    Create->>Trust: create_workspace(registry, root, settings, adopted)
    Trust->>Registry: set_access and record the approval hash
    Create->>Registry: add_workspace(id, name, root)
    Api->>App: attach(id, root) opens WorkspaceRt and runs recover
    Api->>Browser: WorkspaceDetail
```

### What `draft` does

`draft(body, ctx)` reads the file system and writes nothing. It returns a `Draft` with the `root`, the `settings`, the `issues`, and the flag `adopted`. It runs these steps in order:

1. Trim the `name`.
2. Check the `root`. It must be present, absolute, not a file, and not already registered. `DraftCtx.registered` answers the last question.
3. Load the folder's `workspace.toml` when the folder has one. Otherwise start from `WorkspaceSettings::seeded(name)`.
4. Add each project of the request. A project folder that another project already uses is an issue. So is a folder inside the workspace `.ostra` directory.
5. Apply `permissions.mode`, `yolo.default`, `notifications.push`, and `routing_preset`. A mode must be `default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, or `bypass`. A preset must be `native`, `codex`, or `claude`.
6. Run `validate_settings` on the result and sort the issues by path, then by message.

Each `ValidationIssue` has a `path` and a `message`. The path names the field of the request, for example `root`, `name`, `projects[1].key`, or `routing_preset`. `request_path` maps a settings path back to the request. Projects of the request follow the projects that an existing file already had. A problem with an older entry maps to `root`, because the folder owns it.

### What `register` does

`register(host, body)` calls `draft`. If any issue exists, it returns `CreateError::Invalid(issues)` and writes nothing. Otherwise it runs these steps:

1. Create the root folder with `create_dir_all`.
2. Canonicalize the root and check the registry again. This catches a second request for the same folder.
3. Call `trust::create_workspace`. It seals literal MCP values, writes `workspace.toml`, saves the registry-held settings, and records the approval.
4. Make a new `WorkspaceId` and call `registry.add_workspace(id, name, root)`.

The server then calls `App::attach`. It opens the `WorkspaceRt`, runs `engine.recover()`, and starts the task that forwards engine notices. Last, it marks onboarding done. A write failure returns `CreateError::Failed`, which the API maps to status 500. Invalid input maps to a request error with the issue list.

### Adopt an existing folder file

If the folder already holds a `workspace.toml`, the request builds on it. A folder whose registration was lost can register again this way. The flag `adopted` is true, and Rule A2 applies at once. `draft` resets the mode to the default, sets YOLO off, restores default limits, and clears `sandbox_mode`, `tool_enforcement`, `sandbox_network`, `sandbox_allowed_hosts`, `sandbox_decoys`, `sandbox_loopback`, and `sandbox_blocked_ports`. Only the request can set them. The reason is that a repository must not turn on its own YOLO, lift its own budget, or open its own sandbox.

For an adopted file, `create_workspace` records no approval. Nothing in the file runs until the user approves it. If the file cannot be read, the issue is on `root`, and Ostra does not reuse it.

### What happens when

- **The root is empty or relative:** the issue is on `root`, with the text `Choose a folder for the workspace.` or `Choose an absolute folder for the workspace.`
- **The root is a file:** the issue is on `root`.
- **The folder is registered:** the issue is `That folder is already a registered workspace.`
- **A project key repeats:** the issue is on `projects[i].key`, with the text `used twice`.
- **A project path is missing or relative:** the issue is on `projects[i].path`.
- **The routing preset names a harness that is not installed:** the issue is on `routing.executor.byAgent.<agent>`. The harness check belongs to `validate_workspace`.

## Open a workspace with WorkspaceRt

`WorkspaceRt` is one open workspace in a running server. It holds the `id`, the `root`, the `db` (a `WorkspaceDb`), the `engine`, the `host`, the list `cloning`, and the lock `work`.

`WorkspaceRt::open(host, id, root)` runs these steps:

1. `trust::migrate`: approve commands that an older workspace already had, one time.
2. `trust::seal_file_secrets`: move literal MCP values out of the file.
3. Open `workspace.db` and store the workspace ID in it.
4. Ask the host for `services` and build the `Engine`.
5. `sync_projects`: make the `projects` table match the settings.

`sync_projects` deletes a project row whose key is no longer in the settings. Then it upserts one row for each project, with the key, path, stack, and an init status. The status is `Initialized` when the `INVENTORY.md` of the project exists. Otherwise it is `NotInitialized`.

### Three views of the settings

The runtime has three ways to read the settings. Each one has a different purpose.

| Method | What it returns | Who uses it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `settings()` | The file, with the mode, YOLO, limits, and sandbox choices from the registry. | The settings screen, the API, and project checks. |
| `effective_settings()` | `settings()` without the commands that wait for approval. | Programs: language servers and code providers. |
| `detail()` | The `WorkspaceDetail` for the console. | `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}`. |

If the file cannot be read, `file_settings` logs a warning and uses `WorkspaceSettings::seeded("workspace")`. The seeded settings name no program, so a broken file starts nothing.

### What `detail()` returns

`WorkspaceDetail` holds the `id`, the `root`, the project views, the harness and provider status, the validation issues, the available fixes, the `agents`, the stack names, the global permissions, the `pending_commands`, the sandbox status, the global sandbox values, the global tool enforcement, and the settings. The settings go through `browser_view`. It replaces every literal MCP header or env value with the marker `SAVED_SECRET`. A literal can reach the file with a `git pull` or a hand edit, and only the connection can read it.

### Project views

`project_views()` builds one `ProjectView` for each project. The init status follows this order:

1. `Missing`: the project path is not a folder.
2. `Initializing`: a session of kind `Init` for the project is `Running`, `Waiting`, or `Paused`.
3. `Initialized`: the `INVENTORY.md` of the project exists.
4. `NotInitialized`: none of the above.

The view also holds `is_git` (the `.git` entry exists), `git_branch`, and `ultracode_bootstrap` (`.ultracode/INVENTORY.md` and `.ultracode/repo-profile.json` both exist). The stack comes from the project entry, or from the profile in `project.toml` when the entry has none. `git_branch` reads `.git/HEAD` directly, because a git process for each project on each read is too slow. A `.git` file with a `gitdir:` line, as in a worktree, points to the real git folder. A detached HEAD shows the first 7 characters of the commit.

## Validate, fix, and save settings

A save of settings never writes a file that has an issue. `WorkspaceRt::validate(settings)` returns the issues. `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/validate` calls it. `save_settings` calls it before every write.

### What the checks cover

`validate_settings(global, env, settings)` joins four groups of checks:

- The sandbox entries, from `ostra_sandbox::validate::workspace`.
- The routes, harness availability, keys, and projects, from `validate_workspace` in `ostra-core`. [Configuration reference](configuration.md) lists these rules.
- Each permission rule in `permissions.allow`, `permissions.ask`, and `permissions.deny`, from `ostra_policy::validate_rule`. The path of an issue is `permissions.<list>[i]`.
- Each project path that is absolute: it must be a folder. A relative path already has an issue from `validate_workspace`.

`WorkspaceRt::validate` adds Rule W3. A tag in an instruction names an artifact that every agent can read. It checks the texts in `instructions.all` and in `instructions.agents.<agent>` with `ostra_core::artifacts::tag_issues`.

### Save settings

`save_settings` runs these steps:

1. Call `validate`. If it returns issues, return them and write nothing.
2. Call `trust::save_workspace`. A write error returns one issue with an empty path.
3. Call `sync_projects`.

The route is `PATCH /api/workspaces/{ws}`. After a save, the route renames the registry entry if the name changed.

### Apply fixes

Some problems have a fix that Ostra can apply alone. `settings_fixes(settings)` finds each agent route key that has no model route (`keys_without_route`). For each one it returns a `SettingsFix` with the path `routing.model.byAgent.<key>` and the value `default`. The label is ``Route `<key>` to its default tier (<tier>)``. The value `default` resolves to the tier of the agent. The tier of the judge route is `Advanced`. The tier of an agent comes from its definition. Any other key uses `Balanced`.

`apply_fixes()` writes each fix and returns the count. It does not validate the rest of the settings, because an unrelated problem must not block a fix. If no fix exists, it writes nothing. The route is `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/settings/fix`. The list in `detail().fixes` shows what the route will apply.

`agent_infos` builds one `AgentInfo` for each `AgentName`. It holds the label, description, default tier, effort, capabilities, timeout, the `resolved` route, and the `default_route`. A route that does not resolve is `null`.

## Import, clone, create, and remove a project

A project is a folder that the workspace lists in `workspace.toml` with a key. Removing a project from a workspace deletes nothing on disk.

### Import a project

`import_entry` checks the request. It returns `Result<ProjectEntry, Vec<ValidationIssue>>`: the new `ProjectEntry`, or every issue, each on its field: `key`, `path`, or `stack`. `WorkspaceRt::import_project` calls it and returns `Result<(), CreateError>`. It maps the issues to `CreateError::Invalid`. After it writes the entry, it discards the entry. These rules apply:

- The key must match `is_project_key`: lowercase letters, digits, and dashes, and it starts with a letter or a digit. The key must be new in the workspace.
- The stack is free text. It must be one line with no control character, and at most 64 characters (`MAX_STACK_LEN`). Ostra trims it, and an empty stack means none.
- The path must be absolute and must exist. It must be a folder. It must not be a folder that another project already uses. It must not be inside the workspace `.ostra` folder.

If the check passes, `import_project` adds the entry, writes the settings with `trust::save_workspace`, and runs `sync_projects`. The route is `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects`.

### Clone a project

`POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/clone` clones a repository and imports the checkout. `clone_plan` checks the request first. Its issues are on the fields `url`, `key`, `stack`, `path`, `branch`, and `credential`. Then the clone runs:

1. Check the URL with `parse_remote`, the key and stack with `key_and_stack`, and the branch name with `branch_ok`.
2. Choose a saved git credential. An explicit `credential` must exist, and its kind (ssh or https) must match the URL. If the request names none, `credential_for` picks the one that matches the URL.
3. Choose the destination. It is the absolute `path` of the request, or the workspace root joined with the key. `new_folder_issues` checks it.
4. Run the clone in its own task. A closed browser tab then does not kill git halfway and leave a partial checkout.
5. Take a claim on the key and folder (see [Git dock claims](#git-dock-claims)).
6. Run `git clone --progress [--branch <b>] -- <url> <dest>` with a timeout of 30 minutes (`CLONE_TIMEOUT`).
7. Send each progress line to the channel `workspace:<id>` as `ServerMsg::GitProgress`. Ostra sends at most one line each 250 ms (`PROGRESS_EVERY`) and redacts credentials first.
8. Call `import_project` for the new folder, then send `WorkspaceUpdated`.

If git fails, `clear_failed` cleans up. It removes the destination when the clone made it. It empties the destination when the folder existed empty before. An import failure after a good clone returns `GitError::Import`.

`new_folder_issues` applies to every new project folder. The folder must not exist, or it must be an empty folder. It must not be inside the workspace `.ostra` folder. It must not be inside another project and must not contain another project. The message for a full folder is `<path> already exists and is not empty. Choose another folder, or import it with Add project.`

### Create a project folder for a tool call

`create_target` serves the `ProjectCreate` management tool (Rule O3). The folder must be inside the workspace root and must not be the root itself. It resolves the nearest existing parent first, so a symlinked parent cannot lead outside the root. It then applies the same key, stack, and folder checks as the Add project dialog. [Native tools](tools.md) describes the tool.

### Remove a project

`remove_project(key)` runs these steps:

1. Remove the key from a copy of the settings. If the key is not there, return `NotFound` with the text ``No project `<key>`.``
2. Take the `work` lock for writing with `try_write`. If it fails, return `Busy` with the text in `STARTING`.
3. Run `project_busy(key)`. If it returns a reason, return `Busy`.
4. Write the settings and run `sync_projects`.

The route is `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}`. `Busy` maps to status 409, `NotFound` to 404, and `Failed` to 500. The next sections list what makes a project busy.

## Delete a workspace

Deleting a workspace unregisters it and deletes its settings file and database. The project folders, the session artifact folders, and the `.ostra` files inside projects stay on disk. The route is `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}`. It answers status 204. This page owns the full delete flow. [Storage](storage.md) describes the registry tables that the flow changes.

`App::delete_workspace(id)` runs these steps:

1. Read the registry record. If none exists, return `DeleteError::NotFound`.
2. Take the write lock of the open-workspace map. The lock stays held across the check, so no request reaches the engine between the check and the removal.
3. If the workspace is open, call `retire()`. It fails with `Busy` if work is starting or the workspace is busy. After success, remove the workspace from the map.
4. Call `unregister(registry, id, root)`.
5. Forget the navigation state and the MCP connections of the root.
6. Send `WorkspaceUpdated` to the channels `workspace:<id>` and `home`.

`unregister` runs these steps:

1. Call `registry.remove_workspace(id)`. In one transaction, it deletes the push subscriptions that the workspace owns and the `workspaces` row. [Storage](storage.md) describes both tables.
2. Call `trust::forget`. It removes the approvals and the saved MCP values of the root (see [Migration and removal](#migration-and-removal)).
3. Delete `.ostra/workspace.toml`, `.ostra/workspace.db`, and the files `workspace.db-wal` and `workspace.db-shm`. A file that is already missing is not an error. Ostra logs any other delete error as a warning.

### What happens when

- **A session is `Running`, `Waiting`, or `Paused`:** the delete returns 409. The text tells the user to stop session `<id>` or wait for it to finish, then try again. The reason in the text is that the delete loses the state of the workspace.
- **An execution runs:** the text is `Cancel execution <id> or wait for it to finish, then try again, because it is still running.`
- **A clone or pull runs:** the text is ``Wait for the git operation on `<key>` to finish, then try again.``
- **A request is starting work:** `retire` cannot take the lock and returns the `STARTING` text, `Wait a moment and try again, because Ostra is starting work in this workspace.`
- **The delete succeeds:** the flag in `work` becomes `true`. Later requests that start work get status 404 `No workspace <id>.`
- **The same folder registers again:** it starts fresh, because `forget` removed its approvals.

## The work lock and the busy checks

`WorkspaceRt.work` is a `tokio::sync::RwLock<bool>`. It makes the check and the action one step. Without it, a session could start between the busy check and the removal of a project or workspace. The `bool` is `true` after the workspace is deleted.

These groups use the lock:

- **Hold it shared (read):** the requests that start work. They are `init_project`, `create_session`, `inspect_execution`, and `ask`. Each calls `start_work`. It returns 404 `No workspace <id>.` when the flag is `true`.
- **Take it exclusively with `try_write`:** `remove_project`, `retire`, `artifact_move`, `artifact_delete`, and `book_delete`. If a reader holds the lock, the call does not wait. It returns a busy answer, so the user retries.
- **Take it with `try_read`:** a git claim. It fails with the `STARTING` text if a writer holds the lock or the workspace is deleted.

`project_busy(key)` and `busy()` use the same three tests. `project_busy` limits each test to one project:

1. A session that is `Running`, `Waiting`, or `Paused`. For a project, the session must be allowed to use the key. A session with no scope can use every project that it started with. A scoped session can use only the projects in its scope. A session with no log yet counts as using anything. The helper `may_use` holds this rule.
2. A running execution. For a project, its `project` field must equal the key.
3. A clone or pull in the `cloning` list.

The messages follow one pattern: an instruction, then the reason. For a project, the session text is ``Stop session <id> or wait for it to finish, then try again, because it works on `<key>`.``

## Approval of commands from folder files

The approval system compares a hash of the commands in a folder file with the hash that the user approved. If they differ, the programs do not start. Ostra's own saves keep an approval current, so a change made in the console never asks again.

### What is hashed

`workspace_hash(root, settings)` hashes the part of `workspace.toml` that starts a program or loosens a check. It serializes this canonical form to JSON and takes the SHA-256:

- Every MCP server: `name`, `enabled`, `command`, `env`, `url`, `headers`, and `oauth`.
- Every project that has a `code_provider` or `language_servers`: its `key`, `path`, and those two fields.
- The `permissions.allow` rules.
- Every project folder outside the workspace folder: its `key` and `path`. Agents can write in their project. A file that points a project at the home folder therefore widens what they can change. The list is left out when empty, so files without such projects keep the hash that they had before.

If all four parts are empty, `workspace_hash` returns `None`. The file then needs no approval, and `workspace_approved` is `true`. A change elsewhere in the file, such as instructions or routing, does not change the hash. A change to `enabled` does change it.

A second hash covers the project format command. `format_hash(command)` is the SHA-256 of `format\0<command>` for the trimmed command. It is `None` for an empty command. The format command lives in `.ostra/project.toml`. It is the one project command that Ostra runs itself.

### Where approvals live

Approvals live in the registry key-value store, never in a folder. The key holds the canonical path.

| Key | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `trust:workspace:<root>` | The approved hash of the workspace file. |
| `trust:format:<project>` | The approved hash of the format command. |
| `trust:migrated:<root>` and `trust:migrated-paths:<root>` | The marker `1` after a migration ran. |
| `workspace_access:<root>` | The registry-held settings (see [Settings that live in the registry](#settings-that-live-in-the-registry)). |

### Approval decision

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Read workspace.toml"] --> B{"workspace_hash is None?"}
    B -- yes --> OK["Approved: nothing to approve"]
    B -- no --> C{"Stored hash equals the file hash?"}
    C -- yes --> OK2["Approved: programs start"]
    C -- no --> P["Pending: effective removes the commands"]
    P --> D["User sends POST approve with the shown hash"]
    D --> E{"Hash equals the current hash?"}
    E -- yes --> R["record stores the hash"]
    E -- no --> X["409: Review the commands again"]
    R --> OK2
```

### What pending means

When the workspace file waits for approval, `effective(registry, root, settings)` returns settings with these changes:

- Every MCP server has `enabled = false`.
- Every project has no `code_provider` and no `language_servers`.
- `permissions.allow` is empty.
- Every project outside the workspace folder is removed.

The mode, YOLO, limits, and sandbox choices still come from the registry. Ostra does not hide the file from the user. `pending(registry, root, settings)` lists every folder file that waits. Each `PendingCommands` has the `project` (`None` for the workspace file), the `file` path, the `hash`, and the `items`.

Each `PendingCommand` has a `kind` of `McpServer`, `LanguageServer`, `CodeProvider`, `FormatCommand`, `AllowRule`, or `ProjectOutside`. It also has the name and whether it is enabled. Commands show in shell-quoted form. The `env` and `headers` fields list only the names. The `variables` field names the server environment variables that the values read with `${NAME}`, plus the OAuth `client_secret_env`. A value never leaves the server, because it can hold a secret.

The console shows the list from `detail().pending_commands`. The text `PENDING_MESSAGE` explains the state: `Approve the changed commands in settings, because they changed outside Ostra.`

### Where the rule is enforced

Each place that starts a program asks the approval system first:

- **The engine settings:** `ServerServices::workspace()` returns `trust::effective`. Agents and the planner see only approved commands.
- **Language servers and code providers:** the code service reads `WorkspaceRt::effective_settings()`.
- **MCP servers:** the MCP manager calls `approved_workspace_file`. It starts a server only from the approved copy of the file, and the server config must equal an entry in that copy. Otherwise the connection fails with `PENDING_MESSAGE`. The code reads the file once, because a second read could see a file changed after the check.
- **Format step:** the engine calls `Services::command_approved`, which calls `format_approved`. If the command is not approved, the engine skips the format step and reports `FORMAT_NOT_APPROVED`.

[MCP servers and Web Push](mcp-and-notifications.md) describes the MCP connection. [Policy engine](policy.md) describes how allow rules apply.

### Approve a file

`POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/approve` takes an `ApproveCommands` body with `hash` and an optional `project`. `approve` runs these steps:

1. With no `project`, take the current workspace hash. With a project key, find the project and take the hash of its format command. An unknown key returns `ApproveError::NoProject` and status 404.
2. Compare it with the `hash` in the body. If they differ, return `ApproveError::Changed` and status 409. The text is `Review the commands again, because the file changed after they were shown.`
3. Call `record` to store the hash.

Then the route clears the cached MCP state for the root, announces `WorkspaceUpdated`, and returns the new detail. The hash check means that the user approves exactly the content that the browser showed.

### How Ostra saves keep an approval

- **`save_workspace`:** before the write, it checks whether the file was approved. A missing file counts as approved. After the write, it records the new hash only when the file was approved. A file that waits keeps waiting, so a save cannot approve commands that the user did not see.
- **`saved_format`:** `PUT /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/commands` calls it with the format command before and after the save. If the old command was approved, the new one becomes approved. A command is one line, with no control character, and at most 2,000 bytes. The limit is `MAX_COMMAND_LEN`. It lives in `crates/ostra-server/src/commands.rs` (line 11), not in `ostra-workspace`. The function `clean` in that file compares `v.len()` with the limit, so the count is bytes and not characters.
- **`add_allow_rule`:** the "always in this workspace" answer adds a rule through `save_workspace`. The approval stays current.
- **`create_workspace`:** a new workspace records the hash of its settings. An adopted one records nothing.

### Migration and removal

Workspaces that registered before approvals existed keep what they ran. `migrate` runs when the workspace opens, and it runs one time because of the `trust:migrated` marker. It saves the registry-held settings from the file, records the hash of the current workspace file, and records the format hash of each project. A second migration, `migrate_paths`, covers approvals made before project paths counted in the hash. If the stored hash equals the old hash of the current file, it becomes the new hash. Later changes need approval. A new workspace marks both migrations done.

`forget(registry, root)` runs when a workspace is deleted. It deletes the workspace hash, both migration markers, the access record, every saved MCP value for the root, and every MCP OAuth entry for the root.

### What happens when

- **A `git pull` adds an MCP server:** the hash changes. The server starts disabled, and the file shows as pending.
- **A pull adds a project at the home folder:** the project is `ProjectOutside`. Ostra drops it from the effective settings until the user approves it.
- **A pull changes only the instructions:** the hash does not change, and nothing waits.
- **The user edits the workspace in the console:** the save records a new hash if the file was approved.
- **The user approves, and the file changes before the request arrives:** the hash differs, and the answer is 409.
- **A project `format` command changes by a hand edit:** the engine skips the format step and reports `FORMAT_NOT_APPROVED`.
- **A folder file is adopted at create time:** nothing in it runs until the user approves it, and Ostra ignores its mode and YOLO.
- **The registry cannot store a hash:** the code logs the warning `could not record a command approval`, and the file stays pending.

## Settings that live in the registry

The registry holds these settings, never the folder file (Rule A2): the permission mode, YOLO, the spend limits, tool enforcement, and the sandbox mode, network, allowed hosts, decoys, loopback choice, and blocked ports. If a folder file held them, a repository could lift its own budget, turn off its own guards, open its own sandbox, or plant decoys that pause every session.

The private `Access` record stores them under `workspace_access:<root>`. Three functions use it:

- `overlay(registry, root, settings)` copies the record into the settings. `WorkspaceRt::settings()` and `effective` call it.
- `set_access` writes the record from the settings. Every save and `create_workspace` call it.
- `sandbox(registry, root)` returns the workspace sandbox values, for example for an MCP launch.

`write_file` removes these keys from the TOML before it writes: `yolo`, `limits`, `sandbox_mode`, `tool_enforcement`, `sandbox_network`, `sandbox_allowed_hosts`, `sandbox_decoys`, `sandbox_loopback`, `sandbox_blocked_ports`, and `permissions.mode`. If a folder file holds a key like this, Ostra ignores it. A record that predates the limits has no `limits` field, and Ostra uses the defaults. [Configuration reference](configuration.md) describes each setting. [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md) describes what the sandbox values do.

## Sealed MCP values

Literal values in the `headers` or `env` of an MCP server never stay in the workspace file. `seal_mcp_values` moves each literal into the encrypted registry and puts the marker `SAVED_SECRET` in the file. A value of the form `${NAME}` is not a literal, and it stays in the file.

- **The key:** `mcp_secret:<length>:<root>|<server name>|<16 hex characters of a hash of the url and command>|<field>`. The length prefix means that one root can never be a prefix of the keys of another root. The hash means that a value never follows a server to a new URL or command.
- **Cleanup:** after a save, Ostra deletes each saved value that no server names any more.
- **`stash_file_literals`:** before a save from the browser, Ostra stores the literals that the file on disk holds. The browser only saw the marker, so the save must keep them.
- **`seal_file_secrets`:** when the workspace opens, it seals literals that arrived with a repository or an old file. It approves nothing.
- **`mcp_secret`:** the MCP connection reads a value with this function. The browser never reads a value.

[Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md) describes the registry encryption.

## Git dock claims

Clone, pull, and every Git dock command that changes a checkout hold a claim. The Git dock is the console panel for the branch and the changes of a project. Without the claim, an agent and a user can change the same checkout at the same time, or a workspace can be deleted during a clone.

A claim has three parts:

- `session_in(w, key)` finds a session that blocks the command. The session is `Running`, `Waiting`, or `Paused`, and it lists the project in its `projects` or it is the `Init` session of that project. The refusal text is ``Stop session <id> or wait for it to finish, then try again, because it is working in `<key>`.``
- `claim(w, key, dest)` adds the key and folder to `WorkspaceRt.cloning`. It refuses if the key matches, or if the folders contain each other. The text is ``Git is already running in `<key>`. Wait for it to finish, then try again.``
- The `Claim` value removes the entry when it drops. Ostra releases the claim after success, after failure, and after a panic.

### Which commands wait for sessions

The commands differ in the sessions that they wait for:

- **`pull_project` and the Git dock commands:** they wait for the sessions with `session_in`. The handler `pull_project` in `crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs` calls `session_in` before it runs `git::pull`, and `git::pull` then takes the claim. `Op::run` in `crates/ostra-server/src/repo.rs` calls `session_in` before it takes the claim.
- **`git::clone`:** it takes only `claim` (`crates/ostra-server/src/git.rs`, line 785: `let _claim = claim(w, &plan.key, &plan.dest)?;`). It does not call `session_in`, because the project does not exist yet and no session can work in it.

`Op::run` wraps each Git dock command. It checks `session_in`, checks that the folder is in a git repository, runs the command under the claim, announces the change so the Files view reloads, and returns the new status. Each route runs in its own task, so a closed tab does not stop git halfway.

### Git dock commands

- **`status`:** runs `git status --porcelain=v2 --branch -z` and parses it with `parse_status`. It returns the branch, head, upstream, ahead and behind counts, and the lists `staged`, `unstaged`, and `conflicted`. Each list holds at most 2,000 paths (`LIST_CAP`), and `truncated` shows when more exist. A folder outside git answers `is_git: false`.
- **`branches`:** lists local and remote branches, with the current branch first. It returns at most 500 (`BRANCH_CAP`).
- **`stage` and `unstage`:** run `git add -A` and `git restore --staged`. Before the first commit there is no HEAD, so unstage uses `git rm --cached`. Paths must stay inside the project.
- **`commit`:** needs a non-empty message, and at least one staged change. It refuses when files conflict.
- **`fetch`:** runs `git fetch --prune -- <remote>`. `Op::remote` picks the remote (see [Which remote fetch and push use](#which-remote-fetch-and-push-use)).
- **`push`:** needs a branch, not a detached HEAD. It uses the same `Op::remote` rule as `fetch`. If the branch has no upstream, it pushes to a same-named branch and sets it as upstream.
- **`checkout`:** switches to a branch, or creates one with `create`. A remote branch becomes a local branch that tracks it. The name must pass `branch_ok`.

The pull of `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/pull` runs `git pull --ff-only` with a timeout of 10 minutes (`PULL_TIMEOUT`).

Git errors map to HTTP status as follows: `Busy` to 409, `Git` to 502, `Invalid` to 400, and an import failure to 400 with issues or 500.

### Which remote fetch and push use

`Op::remote` in `crates/ostra-server/src/repo.rs` serves both `fetch` and `push`. It checks these cases in order:

1. The branch has a configured remote (`branch.<branch>.remote`). Ostra uses it.
2. The repository has no remote. The command returns an error that tells the user to add a remote first.
3. A remote named `origin` exists. Ostra uses `origin`.
4. The repository has exactly one remote. Ostra uses it.
5. The repository has several remotes, none is named `origin`, and the branch has no remote. The command returns an error that names the remotes and tells the user to set an upstream with git.

## UI state

The server stores the console layout of a workspace, so another browser restores it. `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/ui` returns it. `PATCH /api/workspaces/{ws}/ui` merges a JSON object into it. The state is one JSON text in the `meta` table of `workspace.db`, under the key `ui_state`.

`WorkspaceUiState` has these fields: `tabs`, `active`, `left_tab` (`sessions` or `files`), `files_project`, `sidebar_open`, `dock_open`, and `theme`. The `theme` value is `light` or `dark`. A `null` theme follows the system. A `UiTab` has an `id`, `pinned`, and `preview`.

The merge in `merge(current, patch)` follows these rules:

1. Refuse a patch over 64 KiB (`UI_STATE_MAX_BYTES`) with `TooLarge`.
2. Parse the patch. If it is not a JSON object, return `Invalid`.
3. Replace the top-level fields of the current state with the fields of the patch. A `null` clears only the `Option` fields: `active`, `left_tab`, `files_project`, `sidebar_open`, and `theme`. For `tabs` and `dock_open`, a `null` fails with `UiStateError::Invalid` in step 4, because `#[serde(default)]` applies only to missing keys.
4. Parse the result as a `WorkspaceUiState`. A wrong field type, or a `null` for `tabs` or `dock_open`, returns `Invalid`. An unknown field is dropped.
5. Set `preview` to `false` on each pinned tab, and sort the tabs so that pinned tabs come first. The sort keeps the order inside each group.
6. Refuse a merged state over 64 KiB with `TooLarge`.

If nothing is stored, or the stored text no longer parses, `ui_state()` returns the default state. The API maps `TooLarge` to status 413, `Invalid` to 400, and a store error to 500. The text for the first case is `Keep the UI state under 64 KiB of JSON.`

## Limits and routes

### Limits

| Name | Value | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `UI_STATE_MAX_BYTES` | 64 KiB (65,536 bytes) | UI state patch and merged state. |
| `MAX_STACK_LEN` | 64 characters | A project stack. |
| `MAX_COMMAND_LEN` | 2,000 bytes | A project command in `project.toml`. The constant lives in `crates/ostra-server/src/commands.rs` (line 11), not in `ostra-workspace`. The function `clean` counts bytes with `v.len()`. |
| `CLONE_TIMEOUT` | 30 minutes | `git clone`. |
| `PULL_TIMEOUT` | 10 minutes | `git pull --ff-only`. |
| `REMOTE_TIMEOUT` | 10 minutes | Git dock fetch and push. |
| `COMMIT_TIMEOUT` | 5 minutes | Git dock commit. Commit hooks can run formatters and tests. |
| `LOCAL_TIMEOUT` | 60 seconds | Other local git commands of the Git dock. |
| `PROGRESS_EVERY` | 250 ms | The least time between two clone progress lines. |
| `LIST_CAP` | 2,000 paths | Each change list of the Git dock status. |
| `BRANCH_CAP` | 500 branches | The Git dock branch list. |

### Routes

| Route | Handler | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `POST /api/workspaces/validate` | `validate_new_workspace` | Check a create request without a write. |
| `POST /api/workspaces` | `create_workspace` | Create and open a workspace. |
| `GET`, `PATCH`, `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}` | `get_workspace`, `patch_workspace`, `delete_workspace` | Read, save, and delete. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/validate` | `validate_workspace` | Validate settings. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/settings/fix` | `fix_settings` | Apply the listed fixes. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/approve` | `approve_commands` | Approve one folder file. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects` | `import_project` | Import a folder. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/clone` | `clone_project` | Clone and import. |
| `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}` | `remove_project` | Remove a project from the list. |
| `GET`, `PATCH /api/workspaces/{ws}/ui` | `get_ui_state`, `patch_ui_state` | The console layout. |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/git` | `git_status` | The Git dock status of a project (`crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs`, line 327). |

The other Git dock routes are under `/api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/git`, with the suffixes `branches`, `stage`, `unstage`, `commit`, `fetch`, `push`, and `checkout`. The route `/api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/pull` runs the pull.

## What the approval system does not guarantee

The approval system protects the start of programs that a folder file names. It has limits:

- It does not check what an approved command does. After the user approves it, the program runs with the access of that feature.
- It does not cover a program that an agent starts with its own shell tool. [Policy engine](policy.md) and [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md) cover that path.
- It does not prevent an agent from editing `.ostra/workspace.toml`. A changed file only waits for approval. The server also lists the file among the protected paths of `Services`.
- It does not hide the file content from the user. The pending list shows each command.
