sections.title: Project init, skills, and lesson memory
sections.summary: How Ostra initializes a project (detect, scout, propose, approval, generate), what the inventory, profile, and skills hold, and how the lesson store records, recalls, and guards project facts.
sections.body:
## What init, skills, and memory solve

An agent that starts in a project knows nothing about it. It does not know the build command, the module layout, or the recurring component patterns. It also does not know which build failures the team already solved. Ostra gives each project three durable assets to fix this:

- An inventory (`.ostra/INVENTORY.md`) and a profile (`.ostra/project.toml`). They name the commands, the areas, the skills, and the review rules.
- Skills. A skill is a `SKILL.md` file under `.agents/skills/<name>/` that teaches one recurring task.
- A lesson store. It is a SQLite file at `.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3`. It holds facts that agents and users recorded.

This page covers the init flow, the inventory and the profile, skills and instruction files, skill management in the console, and the lesson store with its recall rules and guards. It stops at the repo brief, which [Agents, prompts, and the spawn contract](agents-and-prompts.md) owns. It also stops at the gate mechanics in [Judges, gates, and YOLO mode](gates-and-judges.md) and at the policy engine in [Policy engine: guards and permissions](policy.md).

## The init flow at a glance

An init session is a session of kind `SessionKind::Init { project }`. The route `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/init` starts it through `Engine::create_init_session`. The route returns 404 when the workspace has no such project. The session copies its YOLO setting from `settings.yolo.default`. The planner in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/init.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/init.rs) decides the next step from an `InitTrack`. The `InitTrack` is a fold of the session events.

Each stage runs the `initializer` agent in one mode. The `Mode:` line of its spawn block names the mode. The `InitializerMode` values are `detect`, `scout`, `propose`, `generate-skill`, `generate-inventory`, and `adopt`.

### Init stages and their order

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  D["detect"] --> Q{"slices found?"}
  Q -- "yes" --> S["scout, one per slice, parallel"]
  Q -- "no, existing skills" --> P["propose"]
  Q -- "no, no skills" --> F["session fails"]
  S --> P
  P --> G["gate: SkillApproval"]
  G -- "generate or regenerate" --> GS["generate-skill, one per skill, parallel"]
  G -- "reuse or drop only" --> GI["generate-inventory"]
  GS --> GI
  GI --> C{"INVENTORY.md exists and project.toml parses?"}
  C -- "yes" --> OK["init_status becomes initialized"]
  C -- "no" --> F2["fails: Run init again"]
```

The planner is a pure function of the track. Each time the planner runs, it finds the first stage that has no result and starts it. When a stage runs, the planner pushes no new step for that stage. When the approval gate is open, the planner pushes nothing.

## Stage 1: detect

Detect runs one time. It reads the repo and writes a scout plan. It changes no project file, because detect, scout, and propose write only into the session dir.

Detect does these steps:

1. Check the existing setup. It records whether a complete Ultracode bootstrap exists (`.ultracode/repo-profile.json` and `.ultracode/INVENTORY.md`). It lists every existing skill under `.agents/skills/` and `.ostra/skills/`. If both dirs hold the same name, it keeps the `.agents/skills/` skill, because Ostra loads that dir first. It also reads the instruction files and any earlier `project.toml`.
2. Survey the repo. It looks for manifest files and counts source files by extension.
3. Name the stack and choose the stack reference. The stack is free text in kebab-case, for example `java-spring` or `rust-axum`. It is never `generic`. The reference is a file in `assets/refs/`: `java-spring.md`, `typescript-node.md`, `python.md`, `go.md`, or `_generic.md`.
4. Plan the slices. A slice is one unit of parallel scouting, usually one module or one top-level source dir.
5. Detect the commands and the test types. A command that an instruction file states wins over a command that detect infers, because the team wrote it for agents.
6. Write `ostra-scout-plan.md` in the session dir and submit the result.

The detect result has these keys: `scout_plan_path`, `stack`, `reference_name`, `slices` (each with `descriptor`, `slug`, `paths`), `existing_skills`, and `ultracode_bootstrap`.

### Rule I1: zero slices

Detect plans zero slices when every candidate component type has an existing skill of the same name and a `convention` skill exists. Scouting is then not necessary, because the skill setup is complete. The planner accepts zero slices only when `existing_skills` has at least one named entry. If detect finds no slices and no existing skills, the planner ends the init with this error: "Detect found no slices to scout and no existing skills, so there is nothing to build skills from."

A `User focus:` line overrides the zero-slice rule when it names areas to scout. A new project with an empty folder still gets one slice that covers the repo root. Propose then recommends skills that are `convention-seeded` from the stack reference.

## Stage 2: scout

The planner starts one scout for each slice, all in the same planning pass. The scouts run in parallel and are read-only. The planner takes at most `MAX_SCOUTS` (6) slices, in the order that detect listed them. The constant is small because each scout is a full execution.

> The initializer prompt tells detect to cap the slice count at 12. The engine keeps only the first 6, so Ostra never scouts slice 7 and later slices.

Each scout gets these spawn inputs: `Slice`, `Slice paths`, the stack reference name, and `Scout plan`. The reference name is the `reference_name` from detect, or `_generic` when it is empty. The spawn factory turns the name into the path of the extracted refs file.

A scout does this work:

1. Read the scout plan and the stack reference.
2. Search its slice only, with the grep and glob patterns of the reference, and count the matches for each component type.
3. For each type that is present, capture one exemplar (a real file), the invariants (base class, annotations, naming, location, registration), and a distilled template with `{placeholders}`. A type that an existing skill already covers gets only a count and an exemplar path.
4. Write `ostra-findings-<slice-slug>.md` and submit `findings_path`.

The planner waits until every slice has a result. Then it starts propose.

## Stage 3: propose and the approval gate

Propose runs one time. It merges the findings, ranks the component types, and writes the proposal. Its inputs are the list of findings paths and the scout plan path.

Propose follows these rules:

- It ranks component types by `slice_spread` (the count of slices that hold the type), then by total count.
- It recommends one creation skill for each type with `slice_spread >= 2` or a total count of 5 or more.
- It recommends exactly one `convention` skill.
- It matches each recommended skill by name against the existing skills. A match gets `status: existing` and an `existing_path`. No match gets `status: new`.
- It adds each existing skill that matches no recommended skill as a bespoke skill: `kind: other`, `status: existing`, `recommend: true`. Ostra registers a bespoke skill for routing and never regenerates it.
- It writes `ostra-proposal.md` for people and `ostra-proposal.json` for the generate modes. Step P7 of `assets/agents/initializer/prompt.md` writes the JSON. The JSON holds `stack`, `reference_path`, `scout_plan_path`, `findings_paths`, `commands`, `test_types`, `module_map`, and `skills`.

The planner reads the submitted `skills` array and builds a `SkillProposal` for each entry. It drops an entry with an empty name. The function `proposals` sets the default disposition:

| Proposal entry | Default `disposition` |
| --- | --- |
| `status` is `existing` | `reuse` |
| `status` is `new` and `recommend` is true, among the first `MAX_DEFAULT_GENERATE` (8) | `generate` |
| `status` is `new` and `recommend` is true, after the 8th | `drop`, with a note that the skill was dropped to limit cost |
| `status` is `new` and `recommend` is false | `drop` |

The proposal order is the ubiquity order, so the 8 most common component types stay on `generate`. The user can still change any row at the gate.

### The approval gate

If the proposal has no skills, the planner ends the init before it opens a gate. This check in `plan_track` runs in every mode, including YOLO mode. The error is "Scouting found no recurring components, so there are no skills to propose."

Otherwise the planner opens a gate with the title "Approve the skills". The payload is `GatePayload::SkillApproval { project, skills }` and the answer is `GateAnswer::Skills { decisions }`. Each decision has a `name` and a `disposition`. A disposition is one of these four values:

| Disposition | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `generate` | Write a new skill. |
| `regenerate` | Overwrite an existing skill with a new one from the current code. |
| `reuse` | Keep the existing skill file unchanged and register it. |
| `drop` | Leave the skill out of the inventory. |

The console shows the gate in [`web/src/features/gates/SkillsGate.tsx`](web/src/features/gates/SkillsGate.tsx). The table has the columns Skill, Kind, What it covers, and Decision. The column "What it covers" shows the `description` of the `SkillProposal`. The function `proposals` builds that text from the proposal description and the rationale, joined with a space. Below it, the column shows the `exemplars` list. The function `proposals` fills `exemplars` only from the `existing_path` of the entry. An existing skill therefore shows the path of its skill file, and a new skill shows no path. The button "Approve the skills" sends the answer. The footer shows how many skills are not on `drop`. The gate states that Ostra writes nothing until the user approves.

Under YOLO mode, the engine answers this gate with the default dispositions of the proposal and makes no judge call (`YoloPlan::Fixed` in `judge_input.rs`).

## Stage 4: generate skills

After the user answers, the planner walks the decisions in the answer order. It starts one `generate-skill` execution for each `generate` or `regenerate` decision, all in the same pass, so they run in parallel. A `reuse` decision starts nothing. The planner notes the skill as reused with its `existing_path`. The planner ignores a `drop` decision and an unknown value.

Each generate execution gets these inputs: `Skill name`, `Skill kind`, `Component type` (or `none`), `Disposition`, `Proposal`, and `Scout findings`. It writes only `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, so parallel executions cannot write the same file. The engine forces the `Advanced` tier on every `generate-skill` execution, whatever the model route says (`tier_override` in the runner). A model must follow a generated skill in one pass, so the engine uses the strongest tier here.

The skill writer follows the rules in [Skill archetypes and the meta-author standard](#skill-archetypes-and-the-meta-author-standard). It must ground every template line in a captured exemplar. It marks an unconfirmed invariant `{TODO: confirm}`. For `regenerate`, the new file replaces the old content. If the old skill lives in `.ostra/skills/`, the writer creates the new skill in `.agents/skills/` and leaves the old file unchanged, because deleting a user file is the decision of the user.

## Stage 5: generate the inventory and finish

When every generate execution has a result, the planner starts `generate-inventory`. Its inputs are `Generated skills` and `Reused skills` (JSON arrays of `{name, kind, componentType, path}`), `Proposal`, and `Scout findings`. It reads the output contract in `assets/refs/inventory-and-profile.md`, the proposal, and the stack reference. It writes `.ostra/INVENTORY.md` and `.ostra/project.toml`. It also writes `ostra-generate-report.md` in the session dir.

Ostra checks the submit call before the agent ends, so the agent can still fix it. `check_inventory_submit` refuses the submit when `inventory_path` is not a file. It also refuses the submit when `check_profile` cannot parse `profile_path`. The refusal lists each line to fix before the parser text. It names the common errors: a `null` value, `[[conventions]]` in place of `[conventions]`, a `[stack]` table, and a string `schema_version`.

The last step depends on the kind of init:

- **A user-started init session.** The planner pushes `Step::Complete` with a report. The report names the two files and counts the skills that the init generated and reused. The runner then calls `init_problem`. The init fails when `.ostra/INVENTORY.md` is missing or `project.toml` does not parse as a `ProjectProfile`. The session error is "Init did not finish: ... Run init again." If the files are valid, the runner sets the project `init_status` to `initialized`.
- **A project that an agent created.** The planner pushes `Step::FinishInit`. The same check runs. A valid result sets `initialized`, sends a `ProjectsChanged` notice, and appends `ProjectInitFinished`. An invalid result appends `InitStepFailed` for the inventory execution.

## Init limits and defaults

| Name | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MAX_SCOUTS` | 6 | Slices that the planner scouts. |
| `MAX_DEFAULT_GENERATE` | 8 | New skills that default to `generate`. |
| `MAX_ADVICE` | 2 | Advisor rounds for one failing step of a created project. |
| `ERROR_RETRIES` | 1 | Automatic reruns of an initializer step after an execution error. |
| `MAX_STEP_RESULT_CHARS` | 8,000 | Characters of a failed step result that the advisor reads. |
| `timeout_seconds` | 2,400 | Timeout of one initializer execution (`agent.toml`). |
| `default_tier` | `balanced` | Tier of the initializer. The mode `generate-skill` uses `advanced`. |
| `[effort]` | native `high`, claude `high`, codex `xhigh`, grok `xhigh`, agy `max` | Effort of the initializer for each executor. |

The initializer has the capabilities `read`, `write`, `edit`, `shell`, `search_text`, `glob`, and `code`. It never starts other agents. Ostra owns the fan-out and the approval gate.

### What happens when an init step fails

- **An execution ends with an error.** The planner runs the step again one time (`ERROR_RETRIES`). A second error marks the step as failed.
- **A run is interrupted.** An interrupted execution, for example after a restart, runs again. It does not count as a retry.
- **The agent submits `stuck`, or submits nothing usable.** Ostra marks the step as failed at once. The failure text comes from the stuck summary or from the missing-submit message.
- **A user-started init has a failed step.** The planner opens an `ExecutionFailed` gate with the title "The initializer failed". The user chooses `retry` or `abandon`.
- **The user stopped the execution.** The gate title is "You stopped the initializer". YOLO mode leaves this gate open, because Ostra leaves a stopped execution to the user.
- **The init result is invalid at the end.** The session fails with "Init did not finish". Run the init again.
- **The planner finds an open approval gate or failure gate.** It pushes no other step until the user answers.
- **A step runs again after advice.** The spawn block gets an `Advisor guidance:` line with the latest guidance, because a repeat of the earlier approach fails in the same way.

## Init of a project that an agent created

An agent can create a project with the `ProjectCreate` management tool. The engine then runs the same init flow inside the session of that agent. The code names these rules O3 to O5.

1. The event `ProjectCreated` adds the project to the session scope and makes an `InitTrack` in `project_inits`.
2. The run that created the project stops with `Interrupt::ProjectCreated`. Its phase starts again in the new project after the init ends.
3. Detect gets a `User focus:` line from `InitTrack::created_focus`. The line holds the project key, the stack, the purpose, and the base requirements. It also says that the folder is empty.
4. The planner uses `Ending::CreatedProject`. A step that leaves nothing to build on does not fail the whole session. It appends `InitStepFailed` through `Step::RecordInitProblem`.
5. A failed step goes to the advisor first (rule O5). The planner spawns the `advisor` agent when the project has not escalated and fewer than `MAX_ADVICE` (2) rounds ran for that step. The user must also not have stopped the step (rule P4).
6. The advisor gets these lines: `Failed step`, `Problem`, `Step inputs`, `Step result` (cut at 8,000 characters), `Step context`, and `Earlier guidance`.
7. If the advisor submits the action `retry`, the engine stores its guidance, clears the result of the failed step, and runs the step again. For any other answer, or when the advisor fails, the engine marks the project `escalated`. It adds the advisor reason to the failure text, and the user gets the failure gate.

If the init of a created project ends without a valid result, the project stays `not_initialized`. The completion report of the session then says: "Initialize it from the project list before its next session."

The `adopt` mode of the initializer migrates a complete Ultracode bootstrap. The spawn factory builds its parameters with the source `.ultracode` and the skills dir `.ultracode/skills`. The planner in `init.rs` does not start `adopt`. The console instead lists skills in `.ultracode/skills` as harness skills that a user can adopt. See [Manage skills in the console and the API](#manage-skills-in-the-console-and-the-api).

## The inventory and the profile

The inventory and the profile are the two files that the init writes under `.ostra/`. The inventory is the routing table. The profile is its machine-readable twin. The contract is in [`assets/refs/inventory-and-profile.md`](assets/refs/inventory-and-profile.md).

The design rule is to route by inventory, not by description. Models do not reliably route from the `description` field of a skill. The explore, execution-path-analyzer, documentation, plan, and generate-spec agents read `INVENTORY.md` first. The implementer, write-test, and code-reviewer agents use the repo brief. They open `INVENTORY.md` only for a table that the brief lacks. See [Agents, prompts, and the spawn contract](agents-and-prompts.md) for the brief. Every skill row has both a name and a path, because a path is the one mechanism that works on every harness. Claude Code resolves names, but the Codex and Grok subagents need the path.

### Sections of INVENTORY.md

| Section | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `Commands` | A table of purpose and exact command: build, test, test-one, format, lint, typecheck, run. `test-one` uses the placeholders `{MODULE}` and `{TEST}`. |
| `Skills Inventory` | One row for each skill: name, kind, path, and the condition for when to load it. |
| `Skill Application Mapping` | A file type and the skills to load for it. |
| `Module / Area Map` | A path glob and an area name. |
| `Review Rule Set` | Stable rule IDs with a severity (`H`, `M`, `L`) and an auto-fixable flag. The rules come from the stack reference. |

Every skill of the repo must appear in `Skills Inventory`, whether the init generated it, reused it, or a person wrote it. A creation or test skill must also appear in at least one mapping row. The `Path` column must match the `path` of the same skill in `project.toml` exactly.

### Keys of project.toml

Ostra parses `project.toml` into `ProjectProfile`. The parser ignores an unknown key, so a misspelled key is lost without an error. The keys are:

| Key | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | number | Always `1`. Ostra refuses a string. |
| `generated_at` | string | A date. |
| `stack`, `build_tool`, `test_framework` | strings | `stack` is one string. The loader still reads an older `[stack]` table and joins it into a string. |
| `[commands]` | strings | `build`, `test`, `test_one`, `format`, `lint`, `typecheck`, `run`. Omit a command that the repo does not have. |
| `[test_types.<name>]` | table | `command`, `command_one`, `matches` (globs), `note`, `reports`. |
| `[[module_map]]` | array | `glob` and `area`. |
| `[[skills]]` | array | `name`, `kind`, `path`, `component_type`, `source`. |
| `[conventions]` | one table | `immutability_keyword`, `naming`, `notes`. |
| `[[review_rules]]` | array | `id`, `rule`, `severity`, `auto_fixable`. |

These rules apply to the file:

- TOML has no null. The agent must omit a key instead of writing `null`, because Ostra cannot parse the file and the init fails.
- The profile has no `models` or `harnesses` table. Executor and model routing are workspace settings. A copy in the profile is ignored and misleads a reader.
- After an init, the `source` of a skill is `generated` or `reused`. The skill API also writes `adopted` and `user`.
- The `kind` of a skill is `convention`, `creation`, `test`, or `other`.
- A rule is auto-fixable only when `auto_fixable` is true and its ID does not start with `SEC-BLOCK` or `PHASE-REQ` (`ProjectProfile::auto_fixable_ids`).
- `Commands::entries` skips an empty command and a command that is only a dash character.

The fields of `ProjectProfile` are also part of the config layers. See [Configuration reference](configuration.md) for the type.

### How the repo brief uses the skills

By default, the brief-only agents (implementer, write-test, code-reviewer) read the repo brief and not the profile. They open `project.toml` and `INVENTORY.md` only when the brief lacks a table or is absent. Ostra builds the repo brief from the profile and the inventory. See [Agents, prompts, and the spawn contract](agents-and-prompts.md). The function `skill_rows` in `crates/ostra-agents/src/brief.rs` builds the skill rows with these rules:

- It skips a skill with an empty `path`.
- It lets every `convention` skill through the filter.
- The `write-test` agent also gets the skills whose name or kind contains `test` or `spec`.
- The `code-reviewer` agent gets only `convention` skills.
- Other agents get every skill with a path.
- It then keeps at most 16 rows (`MAX_SKILL_ROWS`). The cut runs after the filter, so a `convention` skill after row 16 is not listed.
- It prints a `use for` note only when the inventory text does not already state the component type.

## Skill files and instruction files

A project skill is a directory that holds a `SKILL.md`. The file starts with YAML frontmatter that has `name` (the same as the directory) and `description`. Ostra loads project skills from two dirs, in this order:

1. `.agents/skills/` (`SKILLS_DIR`), the cross-harness standard. Ostra writes every new skill here.
2. `.ostra/skills/` (`LEGACY_SKILLS_DIR`), where older projects kept skills. Ostra still reads it and never writes a new skill to it. The write-scope guard refuses an initializer write there.

### How the Skill tool resolves a skill

The `Skill` tool takes a `path` or a `name`. It does these checks in order:

1. If `path` is set, it reads that file. The error is "No skill file at ..." when the file is missing.
2. For a `name`, it removes a leading `ostra:`. It refuses a name that holds `/` or `..`.
3. It looks for the first existing `SKILL.md` in `.agents/skills/<name>/`, then `.ostra/skills/<name>/` (`find_project_skill`).
4. It looks for a custom skill that a workspace artifact holds.
5. It asks the embedded skill resolver. The only embedded skill is `meta-author`.
6. It returns the error "Unknown skill ...". The tool tells the agent to use the skill paths from the repo brief and not to guess a path.

### Instruction files

Instruction files are `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `AGENT.md` at the project root, in any letter case. `project_instruction_files` returns them in that order. Ostra reads them when it builds the first message of an execution. It appends their text under the heading `## Project instructions`. It skips a file that is empty, or that links to or copies a file that it already read, because repos often ship `AGENTS.md` as a link to `CLAUDE.md`. It cuts each file at 12,000 characters (`MAX_PROJECT_DOC_CHARS`). The agent reads the rest from disk.

The initializer treats instruction files as grounded facts. It uses their commands and conventions in detect. When it writes the `convention` skill, it points to the file for any rule that the file already states, because every agent already receives that file. The initializer never edits an instruction file.

## Skill archetypes and the meta-author standard

The generate-skill mode fills one of three templates from [`assets/refs/skill-archetypes.md`](assets/refs/skill-archetypes.md):

| Archetype | Use | Main rules |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A, creation | A recurring component type, for example entity, route, or handler. | Steps ordered by dependency. A template that compiles or parses after substitution. A checklist. Every section grounded in the exemplar. |
| B, convention | Rules for all edits. Exactly one for each repo. | Only rules that the repo follows consistently. Each rule shows a PASS and a FAIL example. No open-ended lists. |
| C, test | A recurring test type. The skill name is `unit-test-<component-type>`. | Grounded in a real test exemplar. When the repo has no tests, the skill is marked `convention-seeded` and takes the test convention of the stack reference. One test for each execution path. |

Creation and test skills come from two catalogs in the stack reference: the component catalog and the test component catalog. Each skill must also satisfy [`assets/skills/meta-author/SKILL.md`](assets/skills/meta-author/SKILL.md). That file is the one skill that Ostra embeds. It sets 16 writing laws for any file that a model reads one time and executes.

These are examples of the laws:

- Define a term before its use.
- Write one instruction in each sentence.
- Write ALL or ANY for each quantifier.
- Show a PASS and a FAIL example for each rule.
- Use one word for each concept.
- Write a plain statement instead of a metaphor.

The file also sets the rules for a subagent file and a system prompt. It adds a self-review checklist that the writer runs on its own output.

## Manage skills in the console and the API

The module [`crates/ostra-server/src/skills.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/skills.rs) backs the Skills screen. Users can read, write, delete, and adopt skills without a session.

### Routes

| Route | Function |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/skills` | `list`: every project with its skills and a `blocked` reason. |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/skills/{name}` | `get`: the `SKILL.md` text and its view. |
| `PUT /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/skills/{name}` | `save`: write the file and register it. |
| `DELETE /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/skills/{name}` | `delete`: remove the entry and the directories. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/skills/{name}/adopt` | `adopt`: copy a harness skill into `.agents/skills/`. |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/harness-skill?path=` | `get_harness`: read a harness skill that the user did not adopt. |

### What scan returns

`scan` builds the list of `SkillView` values in three passes:

1. Each entry in the `skills` list of `project.toml`, with `origin: ostra`. The `exists` flag is false when the named file is not on disk, or when its path leaves the project.
2. Each directory under `.agents/skills/` and `.ostra/skills/` that holds a `SKILL.md` and has no registration, with `origin: ostra` and no `entry`. It skips a directory whose path or name is already registered.
3. Each skill under a harness dir, with `origin: harness`. The harness dirs are `.claude/skills`, `.codex/skills`, `.grok/skills`, `.gemini/skills`, and `.ultracode/skills` (`HARNESS_DIRS`).

The description comes from the frontmatter. `frontmatter_description` reads a one-line value. It also reads a folded (`>`) or literal (`|`) block. Only registered skills reach agents, because Ostra builds the repo brief from `project.toml`. Agents do not load a skill that is on disk but not registered.

### Rules and errors

- **Name.** `check_name` allows letters, digits, `-`, and `_`, at most 64 characters, starting with a letter or a digit, because the name becomes a directory name. A bad name returns 400.
- **Kind.** `check_kind` allows `convention`, `creation`, `test`, and `other` (`KINDS`). Another value returns 400.
- **Content.** `SKILL.md` cannot be empty and cannot exceed `MAX_SKILL_BYTES` (512 KB). Both cases return 400. The limit exists because agents read the file whole.
- **Blocked project.** If `init_status` is `missing`, `list` returns no skills and a reason. If `init_status` is `initializing`, `save`, `delete`, and `adopt` return 409 with the reason "Wait for the init session to finish before you change skills, because the initializer writes them." A read needs only the project folder. It returns 404 when the folder is missing.
- **Broken profile.** A `project.toml` that does not parse makes `save`, `delete`, and `adopt` return 409 "Fix `.ostra/project.toml` first".
- **Write scope.** `save` writes to the registered path, or to the dir that already holds the skill, or to `.agents/skills/<name>/`. It resolves symlinks first. It refuses a file that is not under `.agents/skills/` or `.ostra/`, with 409 "Edit ... in the Files tab". A symlinked `.agents` dir therefore cannot carry a write out of the project.
- **Path from the profile.** `project.toml` can come from the repository itself, so `in_project` checks that a skill path stays inside the project. If it does not, `get` returns 409 "Move skill ... inside the project".
- **Register.** After `save`, `upsert_entry` sets the kind and the component type. A new entry gets `source: user`. An existing entry keeps its source.
- **Delete.** `delete` removes the entry and the skill directory in each skills dir, with every file in it. It returns 404 when neither exists.
- **Adopt.** `adopt` copies the harness skill directory to `.agents/skills/<name>/`. It skips symlinks, so a copy cannot reach outside the skill. It registers the skill with `source: adopted`. It returns 409 when the name is already a skill, and 404 when the `from` path is not a harness skill. The harness copy stays where it is.

### The Skills screen

[`web/src/screens/SkillsScreen.tsx`](web/src/screens/SkillsScreen.tsx) lists the projects as panels with the count of registered skills. The search box matches the name, the description, and the component type. A chip on each row shows the state:

| Chip | Condition |
| --- | --- |
| The first two path segments, for example `.claude/skills` | The skill is a harness skill. |
| `File missing` | `project.toml` names a file that is not on disk. |
| `Not registered` | The skill has no entry in `project.toml`. |
| The kind | The skill is registered and on disk. |

The editor has the fields Name, Kind, and Use for, and a `SKILL.md` text box. A new skill starts from a template with `name` and `description` in frontmatter. The save button reads "Create the skill", "Register the skill", "Write SKILL.md", or "Save", depending on the state. A harness skill is read-only and has the button "Adopt into Ostra". The `blocked` text disables every change.

## The lesson memory store

A lesson is one project fact that an agent or a user recorded, because it cost real effort to find. Examples are a constraint that the code does not state, a version-specific API detail, and how a build failure was fixed. The store belongs to one project. Its path is `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3` (`paths::project_memory_db`). The module is [`crates/ostra-store/src/memory.rs`](crates/ostra-store/src/memory.rs).

### Schema

The table `lessons` has the columns `id`, `area`, `lesson`, `source`, and `created_at`. The pair `(area, lesson)` is `UNIQUE`. A virtual table `lessons_fts` (FTS5) indexes `area` and `lesson`. Three triggers (`lessons_ai`, `lessons_ad`, `lessons_au`) keep it current on insert, delete, and update. The timestamps are UTC in RFC 3339 format with milliseconds.

The store has no size cap and no expiry. Nothing deletes a lesson except a user, because later sessions treat each lesson as fact.

### Operations of MemoryStore

| Method | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `open` | Creates the directory, the file, and the schema if they are missing. |
| `record(area, lesson, source)` | Inserts a lesson. If the pair exists, it updates `source` and `created_at`, so the newest record wins. It returns the total count. |
| `recall(area, query, limit)` | Returns lessons, best first. See the next part. |
| `list(query, limit, offset)` | Serves the memory browser. With a query, it ranks by `bm25`. Without a query, it returns the newest first. |
| `update(id, area, lesson)` | A user edit. It sets `source` to `user` and `created_at` to now. It returns a not-found error for an unknown id. |
| `delete(id)` | Deletes by id. It returns false when the id does not exist. |
| `forget(area, lesson)` | Deletes one exact pair. No code outside the tests calls it. |

Every method opens a new connection and sets a `busy_timeout` of 5,000 ms. Parallel executions therefore wait on the SQLite file lock and do not share a handle. If the lock is not free after 5 seconds, the call returns an error. `recall`, `list`, `forget`, and `delete` return an empty result when the file does not exist. A search must not write into a project, so the palette search skips a project whose store file does not exist.

## Recall rules

`recall` builds up to two buckets of lessons and then merges them. The function `fts_query_from_text` splits the query on every character that is not alphanumeric. It quotes each token and joins the tokens with `OR`. A lesson matches when it holds any token in its `area` or its `lesson`. A query without tokens, for example `::`, counts as no query.

| `area` | `query` | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| set | set | Bucket 1: lessons in the area or in `area::<sub>`, best `bm25` match first. Bucket 2: all lessons that match, best first. |
| set | none | Lessons in the area or its sub-scopes, newest first. No global fill. |
| none | set | All lessons that match, best first. |
| none | none | All lessons, newest first. |

The merge keeps the first copy of each `(area, lesson)` pair and stops at `limit`. Ostra trims the area, and an empty area counts as no area. The area scope `orders` also matches `orders::Service`, because the SQL tests `area = ?` or `area LIKE 'area::%'`.

The `MemoryRecall` tool wraps `recall`. Its `limit` defaults to `DEFAULT_RECALL_LIMIT` (8) and Ostra clamps it to 1 to 50 (`MAX_RECALL_LIMIT`). The result text reads "N lessons recalled, most relevant first", with one line for each lesson: the number, the area, the text, the source, and the date. The answer "No lessons recorded for this query." means that the store has nothing to return.

## How lessons are recorded and what guards them

Two actors write lessons: an agent through the `Memory` tool and a user through the Memory screen. Ostra blocks every other path to the file.

### The Memory tool

The tool takes `area` (required), `lesson` (required), and `source` (optional). It trims the values. An empty `area` returns "`area` is empty. Scope the lesson to a module, for example `orders::Service`." An empty `lesson` returns "`lesson` is empty." The default `source` is the agent name and the execution ID, for example `implementer x_test`. The result reads "Recorded the lesson under `<area>`. The store now holds N lessons."

The tool description tells agents what to record:

- A constraint that the code does not state.
- Behavior that contradicts a name.
- A version-specific API detail.
- An invariant that spans files.
- How a build failure was fixed.

It tells agents not to record what the code makes obvious or the task of the current run.

An `answer_only` run, such as a quick answer, cannot call `Memory`. The policy refuses it, because such a run must not write.

### Guard 1: only the tool writes the store

The state-ownership guard refuses a file tool or a shell command that writes the store. The message is "Record lessons with the Memory tool instead of writing ...: the lesson store is written only by that tool, because later sessions recall it as fact." A shell command that touches the store path with a program other than a plain reader gets the hint "Use MemoryRecall to read lessons and Memory to record one".

The sandbox adds a second barrier. It mounts the store file and its `-wal`, `-shm`, and `-journal` files read-only for agent commands. The rule is in [Policy engine: guards and permissions](policy.md) and [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md). The `Memory` tool is safe, because it runs in the Ostra process and not inside the sandbox.

### Guard 2: recall after a repeated build failure

The policy keeps a `Streak` for each execution. It counts consecutive failures of build or test commands. The policy inputs come from `policy_inputs` in [`crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs`](crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs) and in [`crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs). Both functions build the two command sets from `[commands]` of `project.toml`:

- `build_commands` holds `build`, `test`, `test_one`, `lint`, and `typecheck`.
- `test_commands` holds `test` and `test_one`.

Neither set reads `[test_types.*]`. The policy joins both sets to decide whether a command is a build command. If the project has no configured command, a built-in pattern for tools such as `cargo`, `mvn`, `npm`, and `pytest` applies. The streak reads a failure from the exit code, or else from failure markers in the output. A timeout or an interrupt gives no evidence and does not change the streak.

The streak also builds a diagnostic signature. The signature is the first output line of 12 to 400 characters that names a known error, such as `cannot find symbol` or `error[E...]`. Ostra normalizes the line in these steps: it removes the prefix, replaces paths with `<path>`, drops line and column numbers, replaces versions with `<v>`, squashes spaces, and cuts the text at 160 characters.

| Consecutive failures | Constant | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 or more | `RECALL_THRESHOLD` (2) | If a signature exists, Ostra recalls up to 5 lessons with the signature as the query and appends them to the tool result. A known fix therefore arrives at attempt 2. |
| 3 and 4 | `WARN_THRESHOLD` (3) | A note asks the agent to state the root cause and what will change. It does not allow a variation of the same edit. The note says how many failures remain. |
| 5 or more | `DENY_THRESHOLD` (5) | The `build-streak` guard refuses further build and test commands. The agent must call its submit tool with status `stuck`. |
| A pass | none | The streak resets to 0. |

### Guard 3: the lesson gate

A pass after 3 or more consecutive failures with a known signature is a verified recovery. The streak then adds the recovery to `pending` (at most 12 entries, `MAX_HISTORY`). It also appends a note that asks the agent to record what fixed the failure. When a recovery is pending, the `lesson-gate` guard refuses these calls:

- The `Report` tool without a `reason`.
- A write to the declared report file of the execution.
- A submit call with `status` `ok`.

Two actions release the gate:

- A successful `Memory` call clears every pending recovery.
- A `Report` call with a non-empty `reason` clears them. The reason must say why no lesson applies, for example when the fix was situational.

The gate does not refuse a submit call with status `stuck`. The gate exists because the same diagnostic recurs across sessions. A recorded lesson stops the next run from finding the fix again.

## The Memory screen and its API

Users manage lessons in [`web/src/screens/MemoryScreen.tsx`](web/src/screens/MemoryScreen.tsx). The screen shows one project at a time. It uses tabs when the workspace has 6 projects or fewer (`MAX_TABS`) and a select box when it has more. The search box waits 250 ms (`SEARCH_DELAY_MS`) after the last key and then queries. The table columns are Area, Lesson, and Recorded by, which shows the source and the time.

The URL `?project=<key>` selects a project. The anchor `#lesson:<key>:<id>` selects a lesson, scrolls to it, and flashes the row. The palette search produces such links. The function `rank_lessons` returns up to 20 lessons for each project (`LESSONS_PER_PROJECT`).

The route `/api/workspaces/{ws}/projects/{key}/memory` serves the screen:

| Method | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `GET` with optional `q` | Returns at most 500 lessons, ranked by the query or newest first. A missing project returns 404. |
| `PATCH` with `LessonEdit {id?, area, lesson}` | Trims the text. An empty area or lesson returns 400 "A lesson needs an area and text." With an `id`, it calls `update`. Without an `id`, it records the lesson with `source` `user`. |
| `DELETE` with `?id=` | Deletes the lesson and returns 204, also when the id does not exist. |

An edit that makes a lesson equal to another lesson in the same area breaks the `UNIQUE(area, lesson)` constraint, and the store returns an error. A user edit changes the source to `user` and the time to now. The delete dialog warns that later sessions no longer recall the lesson.

Edit or delete a lesson that is wrong or stale. Agents act on what they recall, so a wrong lesson misleads every later run in the project.

## Memory limits and defaults

| Name | Value | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DEFAULT_RECALL_LIMIT` | 8 | `ostra-store/src/memory.rs` |
| `MAX_RECALL_LIMIT` | 50 | `ostra-tools/src/misc.rs` |
| Lessons that a failure recall adds | 5 | `ostra-exec-native` and `bridge.rs` |
| `busy_timeout` | 5,000 ms | `MemoryStore::conn` |
| `RECALL_THRESHOLD`, `WARN_THRESHOLD`, `DENY_THRESHOLD` | 2, 3, 5 | `ostra-policy/src/build.rs` |
| `MAX_HISTORY` of pending recoveries | 12 | `ostra-policy/src/build.rs` |
| Lessons for each list request of the API | 500 | `memory_list` in `api.rs` |
| `LESSONS_PER_PROJECT` for palette search | 20 | `nav/search.rs` |
| Lesson count cap and expiry | none | `MemoryStore` |
