The lesson gate refusal text.
The Memory and MemoryRecall tools.
The Skills screen with the editor and the adopt dialog.
The Memory screen with search, add, edit, and delete.

sections.title: Storage: databases and data layout
sections.summary: How Ostra keeps state in three SQLite databases (registry, workspace, memory), how the event log relates to the materialized tables, how migrations run, and where each file lives on disk.
sections.body:
## Why Ostra uses three databases

Ostra must keep state across server restarts, and this state has three different owners. The machine owns the list of workspaces and the saved credentials. A workspace owns its sessions, executions, gates, and decisions. A project owns the lessons that agents learned about its code. Ostra keeps each kind of state in its own SQLite file, so a user can delete, copy, or back up one scope without the others.

The `ostra-store` crate owns all three databases. The `ostra-core` crate owns every path in [`crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs), so each reader and writer resolves the same file.

| Database | File | Scope | Rust type | Schema control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Registry | `<data dir>/registry.db` | The machine | `RegistryDb` | `MIGRATIONS` with 1 entry, tracked by `user_version` |
| Workspace | `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.db` | One workspace | `WorkspaceDb` | `MIGRATIONS` with 3 entries, tracked by `user_version` |
| Memory | `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3` | One project | `MemoryStore` | `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` on each open |

The page covers the three databases, the folder layout, and the session folders. Other pages own the topics that touch storage:

- The session events and the fold that reads them: [Sessions and the pipeline](sessions-and-pipeline.md).
- The code that appends events and recovers after a restart: [Engine runner](engine-runner.md).
- The master key and the sealed credentials: [Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md).
- The lesson recall rules and the Memory tool: [Project init, skills, and lesson memory](project-init-and-memory.md).
- The settings files in the data dir and the workspace: [Configuration reference](configuration.md).
- The tool output limits of the native tools: [Native tools](tools.md).
- The creation and the deletion of a workspace: [Workspaces, projects, and approvals](workspaces-and-trust.md).

## How every database file opens

The registry and the workspace database share one function, `open_connection` in [`crates/ostra-store/src/workspace.rs`](crates/ostra-store/src/workspace.rs). It does these steps in order:

1. Create the parent folder, and set its mode to `0700` on Unix.
2. Open the SQLite file.
3. Set `busy_timeout` to 5000 ms. A writer that finds the file locked waits up to 5 seconds, then returns `StoreError::Sqlite`.
4. Set `journal_mode` to `WAL`, so readers do not block the writer.
5. Set `foreign_keys` to `ON`.
6. Run the pending migrations.
7. Set the mode of the file, its `-wal` file, and its `-shm` file to `0600` on Unix.

The mode step exists for two reasons. The registry holds credentials, and the workspace database holds the text of sessions, including the tool output in the `activity` table. SQLite creates its side files with the umask of the process, so Ostra sets the modes after it opens the file. A side file that does not exist yet is skipped, because `restrict` ignores a `NotFound` error.

On Windows, Ostra sets no mode. A new folder or file inherits the access list of its parent. Under the profile folder of a user, that list grants only the user, SYSTEM, and administrators.

The `WorkspaceDb` and the `RegistryDb` each hold one `Connection` in an `Arc<Mutex<Connection>>`. A clone shares the connection. If a thread panics while it holds the lock, the next caller takes the lock anyway (`unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner())`), so one panic does not stop all storage.

The `MemoryStore` does not use `open_connection`. See [The memory database](#the-memory-database).

## Migrations

A migration is one SQL string in the `MIGRATIONS` array. The `migrate` function reads `PRAGMA user_version`, then runs each string from that index on. Each string runs in its own transaction, together with the update of `user_version`. If a string fails, its transaction rolls back and `user_version` keeps its old value.

These rules follow from that design:

- Add a change as a new string at the end of `MIGRATIONS`. Never edit a string that shipped, because `user_version` records only how many strings a file ran. An edited string does not run again on a database that already ran it.
- A new database runs every string. An old database runs only the strings that it lacks.
- Ostra has no downgrade. A database that a newer build migrated keeps its higher `user_version`, and the older build runs no migration on it.

The workspace database has 3 migrations:

| `user_version` after | Change |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Creates `meta`, `projects`, `sessions`, `events`, `executions`, `messages`, `activity`, `gates`, `decisions`, `tool_calls`, and their indexes. |
| 2 | Adds `sessions.title` and `executions.summary`. |
| 3 | Creates `search_docs`, the `search_fts` full-text table, the triggers that keep them in step, and a backfill of the existing sessions. |

Two tests in [`crates/ostra-store/tests/workspace_db.rs`](crates/ostra-store/tests/workspace_db.rs) show the rule. `a_version_one_database_gains_the_new_columns` builds a version 1 file and checks that the open adds `title`. `search_index_backfills_sessions_from_before_the_migration` sets `user_version` to 2 and checks that the open rebuilds the search index.

> Caution: `RegistryDb::open_in_memory` runs only `MIGRATIONS[0]`. If you add a second registry migration, change that function too. Otherwise the tests that use an in-memory registry run on an old schema.

## The registry database

The registry is the one database of the machine. `RegistryDb` stores its file at `registry.db` in the data dir. The server opens it with `open_registry` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs), which first calls `ensure_data_dir`. The offline command `ostra stop` also opens it, to find the workspace that holds a session.

The registry has 3 tables:

| Table | Columns | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `workspaces` | `id`, `name`, `root` (unique), `created_at` | The workspaces that the machine knows. |
| `push_subscriptions` | `endpoint` (key), `p256dh`, `auth`, `workspace_id`, `created_at` | The Web Push subscriptions. A `NULL` `workspace_id` means the subscription is for all workspaces. |
| `kv` | `key` (key), `value` (blob) | Small values: sign-in tokens, approval records, sealed credentials, and flags. |

### Workspace rows

`add_workspace` returns `StoreError::Invalid` when another workspace already uses the same root folder. `remove_workspace` deletes the workspace row and the subscriptions that name it in one transaction. It touches no file on disk. A subscription with no `workspace_id` stays, because it is not scoped to one workspace.

The delete flow of a workspace is a different action. The function `unregister` in [`crates/ostra-workspace/src/runtime.rs`](crates/ostra-workspace/src/runtime.rs) calls `remove_workspace`. Then it forgets the approval records of the root and deletes these files with `std::fs::remove_file`: `workspace.toml`, `workspace.db`, `workspace.db-wal`, and `workspace.db-shm`. A file that does not exist is skipped. Any other delete error goes to the log as a warning. [Workspaces, projects, and approvals](workspaces-and-trust.md) describes the flow.

### The kv table

The `kv` table maps a text key to bytes. The key prefix shows the owner of the value. The page lists the families that appear in the code:

| Key or prefix | Holds | Sealed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `vapid_private` | The private key for Web Push signing. | Yes |
| `provider_credentials:` | Saved provider API keys. | Yes |
| `git_credential:` | Saved Git credentials. | Yes |
| `mcp_oauth:` | OAuth state of an MCP server. | Yes |
| `mcp_secret:` | Secret values of an MCP server entry. | Yes |
| `auth:token:`, `auth:cookie:` | The sign-in token and cookie records. | No |
| `trust:` | The approval records for commands that folder files name. | No |
| `secrets:backend`, `secrets:check` | The place of the master key, and a check value for it. | `secrets:check` only |
| `onboarded_at` | The time of the first-run setup. | No |
| `secrets_vacuumed` | A flag that the registry file was rewritten after sealing. | No |

The constant `SECRET_KEYS` in [`crates/ostra-store/src/secrets.rs`](crates/ostra-store/src/secrets.rs) lists the sealed keys. An entry that ends in `:` is a prefix. Other entries must match the key exactly. Only `secret_get` and `secret_set` call `debug_assert!(is_secret_key(key))`, so a new credential key must go into `SECRET_KEYS` first. The assertion runs in debug builds only. The function `secret_scan` takes a prefix, calls `self.sealer()?`, and has no assertion.

`kv_replace(key, expected, new)` is a compare-and-set. It updates the row only when the value still equals `expected`, and it returns `false` otherwise. Two callers that both try to claim one value cannot both win. The sign-in code uses it to mark a one-time token as used. The test `kv_replace_lets_only_one_caller_claim_a_value` checks this rule.

`mark_onboarded` uses `INSERT OR IGNORE`, so a second call keeps the first time. The test `registry_onboarding_keeps_the_first_time` checks that the time survives a reopen.

### Sealed credentials

The registry file holds credentials, so Ostra encrypts them before it writes them. A `Sealer` encrypts each value with AES-256-GCM under the master key of the machine. It uses a new 12-byte nonce for each value, and it uses the row key as associated data. A sealed value starts with the prefix `enc:v1:`. Because the row key is part of the encryption, a sealed value that someone copies to another row does not open.

The master key lives in the system keychain or in an owner-only file. [Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md) describes how the server finds and stores it. This page covers only the effect on the registry:

- `RegistryDb::open` returns a registry with no `Sealer`. It sets `secure_delete` to `ON`, so SQLite zeroes freed pages and a replaced plaintext value does not stay in the file.
- A registry with no `Sealer` fails `secret_get`, `secret_set`, and `secret_scan` with `StoreError::Locked`. Each of them calls `self.sealer()?`. The message is: "the registry has no encryption key, so credentials cannot be read or saved".
- `with_sealer` adds the `Sealer`. The server calls it after it loads the key.
- If a value was sealed under another key, or if someone altered it, `secret_get` returns `None` and writes a warning to the log. The user must enter the credential again in the settings.

`seal_plaintext_secrets` upgrades a registry that held plaintext credentials. It does these steps:

1. Scan every `kv` row.
2. For each row that has a secret key and no `enc:v1:` prefix, seal the value and write it with `kv_replace`.
3. If it sealed a row, or if the `secrets_vacuumed` flag is missing, run `VACUUM` and `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)`. Then it sets the flag.
4. Return the number of sealed rows.

The `VACUUM` and the checkpoint remove the old plaintext from the main file and from the write-ahead log. The flag covers an earlier run that sealed the rows but stopped before the rewrite. At the next start, the missing flag makes Ostra finish the rewrite.

## The workspace database

The workspace database is `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.db`. The server opens it when it loads a workspace: `WorkspaceRt::open` in [`crates/ostra-workspace/src/runtime.rs`](crates/ostra-workspace/src/runtime.rs) calls `WorkspaceDb::open`, then `set_workspace_id`. The id goes into the `meta` table, because the file does not otherwise know which workspace it belongs to.

When `WorkspaceDb::open` runs, it also writes `<workspace>/.ostra/.gitignore` if the file does not exist. The file holds these patterns: `workspace.db*`, `sessions/`, and `uploads/`. A `git add -A` in the workspace root then cannot publish the database, which holds the text of every session. If a `.gitignore` already exists there, Ostra does not change it. The file `workspace.toml` is not in the list, so a team can commit its workspace settings.

The test `database_and_its_dir_are_owner_only` checks mode `0700` for `.ostra` and mode `0600` for the database and its side files. It also checks that the `.gitignore` contains `workspace.db*`. It does not check `sessions/` or `uploads/`.

### The event log is the source of truth

The `events` table is the record of what happened in a session. Each row holds `session_id`, `seq`, `type`, `payload`, and `at`. The primary key is `(session_id, seq)`. The `payload` is the JSON of one `SessionEvent`. The `type` column copies the `type` field of the JSON, so a query can filter without parsing the payload. The table holds `SessionEvent` payloads only. It does not hold tool output.

Ostra does not store the state of a session. It stores the events and folds them. The engine loads a session with `db.events(id)` and `SessionState::fold`. A restart rebuilds the same state from the same rows. [Sessions and the pipeline](sessions-and-pipeline.md) describes the events and the fold.

`append_event` does these steps in one `IMMEDIATE` transaction:

1. Read `MAX(seq) + 1` for the session. The first event gets 1.
2. Insert the row with the time in UTC, as an RFC 3339 text with 3 digits for milliseconds.
3. Set `sessions.updated_at` to the same time.
4. Commit and return a `StoredEvent`.

An `IMMEDIATE` transaction takes the write lock at its start. Two appends to one session cannot read the same maximum. The test `concurrent_appends_get_distinct_seqs` runs 8 threads with 10 appends each and expects the sequence numbers 1 to 80 with no gap. The `seq` counts are separate for each session: the test `events_are_sequenced_per_session` shows that a second session starts at 1.

`events_after(session, n)` returns the events with `seq > n`, in order. A client that already has the events up to `n` uses it to catch up.

#### The append path in the engine

The engine does not call `append_event` alone. Its private method `Inner::append` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs) keeps the log, the tables, and the memory state in step. The method `Inner::load` builds the state of a session from the log, and `Inner::materialize` copies events into tables.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Engine
    participant State as SessionState
    participant Db as WorkspaceDb
    participant Client as Subscribers
    Engine->>State: lock the state of the session
    Engine->>Db: append_event(session, event)
    Db-->>Engine: StoredEvent with seq
    Engine->>Db: materialize: upsert_gate, answer_gate, insert_decision
    Engine->>State: apply(stored)
    Engine->>Db: update_session(status, lane, stage_label, cost_usd, title)
    Engine->>Client: EngineNotice::Event and SessionUpdated
    Engine->>Engine: wake the driver of the session
```

The state lock makes the order of the sequence numbers equal to the order of the fold. The engine also refuses to start work after a session ended. While it holds the lock, it checks for a terminal state and rejects `ExecutionStarted`, `ExecutionResumed`, and `CommandStarted` with `EngineError::Ended`. This check cannot race a stop, because both use the same lock.

### The materialized tables

A materialized table is a table that holds data derived from events or written next to them, so the console can list and filter without a fold of every session. The log is the source of truth. A materialized row that is wrong does not change what happened.

| Table | Key | Holds | Written by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `meta` | `key` | Small workspace values: `workspace_id` and `ui_state`. | `set_workspace_id`, `meta_set` |
| `projects` | `key` | The path, `init_status`, and `stack` of each project. | `upsert_project`, `set_project_init_status`, `delete_project` |
| `sessions` | `id` | The summary row: kind, request, category, status, lane, `stage_label`, projects, `yolo`, `cost_usd`, `title`, and times. | `create_session`, `update_session` |
| `executions` | `id` | One row for each agent run: agent, purpose, stage, executor, model, spawn block, status, usage, `cost_usd`, `error`, `submit`, `final_text`, `summary`, and times. | `insert_execution`, `finish_execution`, and the setters |
| `messages` | `(execution_id, seq)` | The conversation of a native execution, as JSON. | `append_message` |
| `activity` | `(execution_id, seq)` | The stream of `ExecutionDelta` items that the console shows, including the tool results. | `append_activity` |
| `gates` | `id` | The open and answered gates. | `upsert_gate`, `answer_gate` |
| `decisions` | `id` | The judge decisions, with `overridden` and `can_override` flags. | `insert_decision`, `mark_overridden` |
| `tool_calls` | `id` (auto) | A table for tool calls, with the policy decision and the rule that decided. The method `record_tool_call` and the table exist, but no running server writes them. Only a test calls the method. | `record_tool_call` |
| `search_docs`, `search_fts` | `id` | The text search index. | Triggers and `index_artifact` |

The engine method `materialize` copies only 3 event types into tables: `GateOpened` (to `upsert_gate`), `GateAnswered` (to `answer_gate`), and `DecisionMade` (to `insert_decision`). The session row follows each appended event, through `update_session`. The other tables have their own write methods, and no event copies them.

Some facts about these tables:

- `upsert_gate` refreshes the title, the explanation, and the payload of an existing gate, and it keeps `opened_at`. Two events for one gate id give one row. The test `gates_open_and_answer` checks this.
- A gate is open while `answer IS NULL`. `SessionSummary.open_gates` is a count of these rows, which `session_from_raw` computes for each read.
- `mark_overridden` replaces the `output` and `reason` of a decision, and sets `overridden` to 1. It does not keep the old output in the row. The event log keeps the first `DecisionMade` event.
- `update_session` changes only the fields that are `Some`. For `category` and `title`, the type is `Option<Option<...>>`: `Some(None)` clears the value, and `None` keeps it. One transaction checks that the session row exists, then runs one `UPDATE` for each field that is `Some`. The function always sets `updated_at`.
- `list_sessions` returns the newest session first. `list_executions` returns the oldest first. `list_sessionless_executions` returns the executions that have no session (side-panel runs), newest first.
- `execution_from_raw` computes `can_resume`. It is true only for a harness execution that has a `native_session_id`.
- `reopen_execution` sets a paused execution to `Running` again and keeps its usage, messages, and activity, so the resumed run adds to them.

#### Where tool output lands

Live tool output goes to the `activity` table, not to the `events` table and not to `tool_calls`. The engine receives each `ExecutionDelta` from an executor. For the item `ExecutionDelta::ToolResult { output }`, the runner calls `append_activity` in [`crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs) (line 2883). `append_activity` applies no 8 KB cut of its own. The native executor can shorten a result before it emits it, with `EMIT_LIMIT` in `crates/ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs`. [Native tools](tools.md) describes that limit.

#### The unused tool call table

`WorkspaceDb::record_tool_call` cuts the `output` text to `TOOL_OUTPUT_LIMIT`, which is 8 KB (`8 * 1024` bytes). `truncate_utf8` moves the cut back to a character boundary and adds the line `[truncated: N bytes]` with the original size. The test `tool_calls_truncate_output` stores 20,000 bytes and expects fewer than 9,000.

The limit applies only inside `record_tool_call`. Nothing calls that method at run time, because its only caller is the test. A running server therefore never writes the `tool_calls` table, and `TOOL_OUTPUT_LIMIT` never cuts live tool output.

### Text search

The console searches sessions and artifacts with `search_text`. The index has two parts:

- `search_docs` holds one row for each searchable item: `kind` (`session` or `artifact`), `ref`, `session_id`, `label`, `body`, and `mtime`. The pair `(kind, ref)` is unique.
- `search_fts` is an FTS5 table over `label` and `body`. It uses the tokenizer `unicode61 remove_diacritics 2` and prefix indexes for 2 and 3 characters.

Triggers keep the parts in step. A new session inserts a `search_docs` row with the title as label and the request as body. A change to `title` or `request` updates that row. The index update for `search_fts` follows each insert, update, and delete on `search_docs`.

An artifact row comes from `index_artifact`. The server calls it from `index_artifacts` in [`crates/ostra-server/src/nav/mod.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/nav/mod.rs). The `mtime` (in milliseconds) lets the caller skip a file that did not change, and `indexed_artifacts` returns the stored label and `mtime` for each path. A new `index_artifact` call for the same path replaces the old text.

`fts_prefix_query` builds the query. First, it splits the text at every character that is not a letter or a digit, and it drops the empty parts. Then it wraps each word in double quotes and adds `*`. The words join with a space, so every word must match as a word prefix. The input `ord canc` becomes `"ord"* "canc"*`.

The split makes the query safe. A double quote is not a letter or a digit, so the split treats it as a separator and drops it. No word holds a double quote. The `replace` of `"` in the code therefore never changes a word. The same split removes `*`, `(`, `)`, and spaces from the words. The input `"zz*) OR (` becomes `"zz"* "OR"*`, so the text cannot act as FTS syntax. The test `text_search_over_sessions_and_artifacts` runs this input and expects an empty result and no error.

The results sort by `bm25(search_fts, 4.0, 1.0)`: a match in the label counts 4 times as much as a match in the body. A lower rank is better. The function returns an empty list when the query has no words.

### Cost queries

The `executions` table keeps `usage` as JSON and `cost_usd` as a number. Two functions read it:

- `spend_since(since)` returns the sum of `cost_usd` for executions that started at or after `since`. The settings that cap spending use it. [Model providers, tiers, and cost](providers-and-cost.md) describes those settings.
- `cost_report(since)` groups the usage 4 ways: by session, by stage, by agent, and by executor. It also returns a total. A side-panel execution has no session and counts under the key `side-panel`. An execution with no stage counts under `none`. Each list sorts by cost, highest first, then by key. The field `cache_reads_per_tool_call` is `cache_read_tokens / tool_calls`, or 0 when the count of tool calls is 0.

The time filter compares text. The stored times and the `since` value use the same fixed-width RFC 3339 form, so the text order equals the time order. `cost_report(None)` uses an empty text, which matches every row.

### What happens when

- **The server restarts while an execution runs.** At start, `Engine::recover` finishes each running execution of a session as `Interrupted` (or `Waiting` if it waited for an answer), appends an `ExecutionFinished` event, and denies the permission gates of dead executions. Then `mark_running_interrupted` sets any other row that is still `Running` to `Interrupted`. [Engine runner](engine-runner.md) describes the full recovery.
- **A database from an older build opens.** The pending migrations run before any query. A database with a newer `user_version` than the build knows is not changed.
- **Two threads append to one session.** The `IMMEDIATE` transaction serializes them, and the sequence numbers stay unique.
- **The database file is locked by another process.** The caller waits up to 5000 ms, then gets `StoreError::Sqlite`.
- **`update_session` names an unknown session.** It returns `StoreError::NotFound`. `finish_execution`, `reopen_execution`, and `answer_gate` do the same for an unknown id.
- **A stored timestamp does not parse.** `parse_time` returns `StoreError::Invalid` with the text of the bad value.
- **The code calls `RegistryDb::remove_workspace`.** The workspace row and its scoped push subscriptions go away. The call touches no file.
- **A user deletes a workspace, and the server runs `unregister`.** The function calls `remove_workspace`, then deletes `workspace.toml`, `workspace.db`, `workspace.db-wal`, and `workspace.db-shm`. Project folders, session artifact folders, and per-project `.ostra` files stay. [Workspaces, projects, and approvals](workspaces-and-trust.md) describes the flow.

## The memory database

The memory database holds the lessons that agents record about a project. Its file is `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3`, and `paths::project_memory_db` builds the path. The module comment in [`crates/ostra-store/src/memory.rs`](crates/ostra-store/src/memory.rs) says that the store uses the schema of Ultracode's `mcp/lib/memory.js`. The comment names these traits: dedupe on `(area, lesson)`, area sub-scopes (`area::sub`), `bm25` ranking, and targeted forget.

The table `lessons` has the columns `id`, `area`, `lesson`, `source`, and `created_at`. The pair `(area, lesson)` is unique. An FTS5 table `lessons_fts` indexes `area` and `lesson`, and three triggers keep it in step with inserts, updates, and deletes.

`MemoryStore` stores only the path. Each call that opens the database calls the private method `conn`. It creates the parent folder, opens a new connection with a `busy_timeout` of 5000 ms, and runs the `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` schema again. Two executions in parallel therefore wait on the file lock of SQLite and do not share a handle. The store has no `user_version` and no migration list, so a schema change must work with `IF NOT EXISTS`. The store does not set `WAL` mode and does not change file modes.

### Record, recall, and forget

- `record(area, lesson, source)` inserts a lesson. If the same `(area, lesson)` exists, the new call updates `source` and `created_at`. The newest record wins, and the table has no duplicate. It returns the total count of lessons.
- `recall(area, query, limit)` returns at most `limit` lessons. The constant `DEFAULT_RECALL_LIMIT` is 8. It builds up to 2 buckets and removes duplicates in this order: lessons in the area and its sub-scopes (`area` and `area::%`), then text matches in all areas. With an area and a query, the first bucket sorts by `bm25`. With an area only, it sorts by newest first, and no global bucket follows. With no area and no query, the result is the newest lessons of all areas.
- `fts_query_from_text` joins the quoted words with `OR`, so one matching word is enough. This differs from the search of the workspace database, where all words must match.
- `forget(area, lesson)` deletes one exact pair and returns `true` if it deleted a row.
- `list`, `update`, and `delete` serve the memory browser of the console. `update` sets `source` to `user`, so a lesson that a person edited is easy to see.

The store never caps the number of lessons and never expires one. Only `forget` and `delete` remove a lesson.

### When the memory file does not exist

The methods `open`, `record`, and `update` call `self.conn()`, and `conn` creates the parent folder and the file. The method `update` has no `path.exists()` check. On a missing store, `update` therefore creates an empty store and then returns `StoreError::NotFound`.

The methods `recall`, `list`, `forget`, and `delete` check `path.exists()` first. If the file does not exist, they return an empty list or `false`, and they do not create the file. The test `missing_store_recalls_nothing` checks this for `recall`.

### Who can write the memory file

The policy treats the memory file as engine state. Its guard `TOOL_OWNED` allows only the Memory tool to write `knowledge.sqlite3`, because later sessions recall its lessons as facts. [Policy engine](policy.md) describes the guard.

## Folder layout on disk

Ostra puts files in 4 places: the data dir, the global config folder, the workspace `.ostra` folder, and the project `.ostra` folder.

### The data dir

The function `data_dir` returns the value of `OSTRA_DATA_DIR` if the variable is set. Otherwise it returns the `ostra` folder in the local data folder of the user (on Linux, `~/.local/share/ostra`), or `./ostra` if the system gives no data folder. `ensure_data_dir` creates the folder and sets its mode to `0700` on Unix, so only the owner can enter it. It does this on each start, so it also tightens an older folder.

```text
<data dir>/
  registry.db, registry.db-wal, registry.db-shm
  master.key        (only when the system keychain does not hold the key)
  server.log        (the server appends to it; OSTRA_LOG sets the level)
```

No agent can read this folder. `secret_paths` lists it first, together with the file that `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE` names and the credential paths in the home folder. The policy and the sandbox use that list. [Policy engine](policy.md) and [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md) describe how.

The global config file `config.toml` is not in the data dir. `global_config_path` returns `OSTRA_CONFIG` if set, or `config.toml` in the `ostra` folder of the user config folder. [Configuration reference](configuration.md) describes all three config layers.

### The workspace folder

The function `workspace_runtime` returns `<workspace>/.ostra`. The constant `RUNTIME_DIR` holds the name `.ostra`.

```text
<workspace>/.ostra/
  workspace.toml        settings of the workspace (safe to commit)
  workspace.db          the workspace database, with -wal and -shm
  .gitignore            workspace.db*, sessions/, uploads/
  uploads/              staging area for uploaded files
    .gitignore          *
    <32-hex id>/<file>
  sessions/
    .gitignore          *
    <session id>/       the session root
```

The `uploads/` folder is the staging area. A user can upload a file before the session exists, so the engine writes it to `uploads/<id>/<name>` first. The module [`crates/ostra-engine/src/uploads.rs`](crates/ostra-engine/src/uploads.rs) sets these limits: `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` is 25 MB for one file, and `MAX_UPLOADS` is 20 files for one request. `safe_name` keeps only the last path segment, replaces `: * ? " < > |` with `_`, removes control characters and leading dots, and cuts the name to 120 characters. When the session starts, `claim` moves each file into `<session root>/uploads/`. If the name exists there, the file gets a number: `report (2).pdf`.

### The session folder

The function `session_root(workspace, id)` returns `<workspace>/.ostra/sessions/<id>`. The engine creates it when it starts a session, with one subfolder for each project key.

```text
<session root>/
  ostra-spec-*.md|json         the spec
  ostra-plan-*.md|json         the plan and its phase files
  ostra-session-context.md     request, artifact paths, and feedback rounds
  uploads/                     files that the user attached
  <project key>/               reports and research documents of that project
  .state/                      engine state
    harness/<execution id>/    hook config, MCP registration, terminal.log
```

The folders differ in who can write them:

- **The session root** holds the artifacts that cross projects: the spec and the plan. The guards allow only one agent to write each kind. `ostra-spec-*` belongs to `GenerateSpec`, `ostra-plan-*` to `Plan`, and `ostra-research-*` to `Explore`.
- **The project folder** (`session_project_dir`) holds the reports of the agents for one project.
- **The `.state` folder** (`session_state_dir`) belongs to the engine. No agent can write it. The guards treat the `.state` folder of any session as engine state. The sandbox mounts the state folder read-only, and it hides the `harness` folders of other executions, because each one holds the bridge token of an execution.
- **The `harness/<execution id>` folder** (`harness_execution_dir`) holds the files that a harness execution needs. `terminal.log` (`terminal_transcript`) keeps the raw bytes of the terminal, so the console can replay an ended run.

The workspace `.gitignore` files hide `sessions/` and `uploads/` from Git. The engine writes the one inside `sessions/` the first time it creates a session, and the staging code writes the one inside `uploads/` at the first upload.

### Report and artifact names

The module `paths::report` declares each report name, so that the engine, the agents, and the later stages predict the same file. The `phase` argument is the phase number in the plan.

| Function | File name | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `implementer(phase)` | `ostra-implementer-phase-<phase>.md` | The report of an implementer. |
| `implementer_progress(phase)` | `ostra-implementer-progress-phase-<phase>.md` | Only `Implementer` writes it. A re-run reads it to learn which steps succeeded. |
| `epa(phase)` | `ostra-epa-phase-<phase>.md` | |
| `write_test(phase)` | `ostra-write-test-phase-<phase>.md` | |
| `docs_request()` | `ostra-docs-request.md` | The stub that the engine writes for a documentation session when no implementer ran. |
| `docs_parts()` | `ostra-docs-parts.json` | The book parts of this session, for the architecture agent. |
| `prompt_gen(n)` | `ostra-prompt-gen-<n>.md` | |
| `completion()` | `ostra-completion.md` | |
| `test_request()` | `ostra-test-request.md` | |
| `session_context()` | `ostra-session-context.md` | In the session root. A revision reads files and not a conversation. |
| `review_ledger(phase)` | `ostra-review-ledger-phase-<phase>.md` or `ostra-review-ledger.md` | See below. |
| `security_sentinel()` | `ostra-security-block.json` | Only `CodeReviewer` writes it. It records findings of the level BLOCKER that nobody can waive. |

The `review_ledger` function reads the `Phase:` value of a loop. A value of `N` or `N-tests` (digits, then an optional `-tests`) gives `ostra-review-ledger-phase-N.md` or `ostra-review-ledger-phase-N-tests.md`. Any other value, such as `none`, gives `ostra-review-ledger.md`. `CodeReviewer`, `Implementer`, and `WriteTest` can write a ledger. The engine counts its iterations to cap the review loop, so no other writer can change it.

The constant `ARTIFACT_PREFIX` is `ostra-`. Every artifact name starts with it.

### The project folder

The function `project_runtime` returns `<project>/.ostra`. It holds the files that belong to one project:

```text
<project>/.ostra/
  INVENTORY.md                 the project inventory (project_inventory)
  project.toml                 the project profile (project_profile)
  memory/knowledge.sqlite3     the lesson database (project_memory_db)
<project>/.agents/skills/      the skills that Ostra writes (SKILLS_DIR)
<project>/.ostra/skills/       the old skills folder: read, never written
```

`SKILL_DIRS` lists both skill folders in lookup order, and `find_project_skill` returns the first `SKILL.md` that it finds. `project_instruction_files` finds `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and `AGENT.md` at the project root in any letter case, in that order. [Project init, skills, and lesson memory](project-init-and-memory.md) describes how Ostra uses them.

## Private files and folders

The module `paths` has helpers that give owner-only modes. Use them for any file that holds secrets:

| Helper | Effect on Unix | Effect on Windows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ensure_data_dir` | Creates the data dir, sets `0700`. | The folder keeps the inherited access list. |
| `create_private_dir_all`, `create_private_dir` | Create a folder with mode `0700`. `create_private_dir` succeeds if the folder exists. | Inherited access list. |
| `private_file_options` | Opens a new file with mode `0600`. | Inherited access list. |
| `restrict_to_owner` | Sets `0600` for a file or `0700` for a folder. | No change. |
| `link` | Creates a symlink. | A junction for a folder. For a file: a symlink, then a hard link, then a copy. |

### Compare paths and resolve links

The functions `is_inside` and `resolve` in [`crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/paths.rs) do different work. [Policy engine](policy.md) uses them for the write-scope and secret-read guards.

- **`is_inside(outer, inner)`** compares paths by text only. It calls `normalize`, which applies `.` and `..` lexically, and then `fold`. It does not follow links and does not read the file system. On Windows, `fold` removes the `\\?\` prefix, changes `/` to `\`, and ignores letter case. On Unix, `fold` returns the path unchanged.
- **`resolve(cwd, target)`** follows links. On Unix, `resolve_posix` walks one component at a time and follows a link before it applies a later `..`. It follows at most 40 links. A link therefore cannot make a path look inside a root when the write lands outside it.
- **On Windows,** `resolve_windows` first applies `..` lexically (`win32_lexical`), as Win32 programs do. Then it follows the junctions and symlinks in the result, and it returns the real letter case of the longest existing ancestor.

To test the real target of a path, call `resolve` first and then `is_inside`, because `is_inside` alone does not follow links. The function `dot_dot_after_link` reports a `..` right after a link on Windows. Win32 programs and POSIX-style programs open different files for such a path, so a guard cannot judge both.

## Limits and defaults

| Name | Value | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `busy_timeout` of the registry, workspace, and memory databases | 5000 ms | `open_connection`, `MemoryStore::conn` |
| `journal_mode` | `WAL` (registry and workspace only) | `open_connection` |
| `TOOL_OUTPUT_LIMIT` | 8 KB. It applies only inside `record_tool_call`, and nothing calls that method at run time. | `workspace.rs` |
| `EMIT_LIMIT` | 8 KB. The native executor applies it before it emits a tool result. See [Native tools](tools.md). | `ostra-exec-native/src/lib.rs` |
| `DEFAULT_RECALL_LIMIT` | 8 lessons | `memory.rs` |
| `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` | 25 MB for each upload | `uploads.rs` |
| `MAX_UPLOADS` | 20 uploads for each request | `uploads.rs` |
| Mode of the data dir and `.ostra` folder (Unix) | `0700` | `paths.rs`, `open_connection` |
| Mode of database files (Unix) | `0600` | `open_connection` |
| Search weights | label 4.0, body 1.0 | `search_text` |

The user has no setting for these values. They are constants in the code.

## Errors

Every function of `ostra-store` returns `StoreError`:

| Variant | Message starts with | Cause |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Sqlite` | `sqlite:` | SQLite failed, for example a lock timeout. |
| `Io` | `io:` | A folder or file operation failed. |
| `Json` | `json:` | A stored JSON value does not parse. |
| `NotFound` | `not found:` | The id does not exist. |
| `Invalid` | none | A rule failed, for example a duplicate workspace root or a bad timestamp. |
| `Locked` | `the registry has no encryption key` | A credential call on a registry without a `Sealer`. |

## What the storage layer does not guarantee

- The file modes protect the files from other users of the machine. They do not protect them from a process that runs as the same user.
- Tool output sits in plaintext in the `activity` table of the workspace database. Only the registry credentials are encrypted.
- The `.gitignore` files of Ostra help to keep the databases out of Git. They do not stop a user who force-adds the files.
- The memory database has no migration list and no file-mode step. It depends on the folder mode of the project.
- Ostra does not back up any database. A user must copy the files, with their `-wal` files, when the server is not running.

sections.title: Server, REST API, and WebSocket
sections.summary: How the ostra server starts, how `App` and `ServerServices` connect the engine to HTTP, every REST route by area, the `/ws` channels, the embedded web build, the Files view back end, the Sessions tree, search, and artifacts.
sections.body:
The `ostra-server` crate is the only process that a browser talks to. Without it, the web console has no way to reach the engine, the project files, or git. The crate starts the listener, checks every request, serves the REST routes and one WebSocket, embeds the web build, and gives each workspace an engine. This page covers these parts:

- the start sequence and the shared state (`App`, `Shared`, `ServerServices`)
- the request guard and the error shape
- the REST routes by area
- the `/ws` socket with its channels, `ClientMsg`, and `ServerMsg`
- the embedded web build
- the Files view back end: tree, file, save, diff, changes, and the write watch
- the git routes
- the Sessions tree, search, and workspace activity
- session artifacts and workspace artifacts

This page stops at the edge of other parts. [Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md) owns the cookie and the token. [The engine runner](engine-runner.md) owns the `Engine` and the `Services` trait. [The web console](web-console.md) owns the React app. [Code navigation](code-navigation.md) owns the code index behind the `/code/*` routes.

## Source files and what each owns

| File | What it owns |
| --- | --- |
| [`app.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/app.rs) | `ServeOptions`, `Shared`, `App`, `build`, `run`, `attach`, `delete_workspace`, `stop_offline` |
| [`services.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs) | `ServerServices`, the engine's view of the server |
| [`api.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs) | `router`, the `guard` middleware, `ApiErr`, and the REST handlers |
| [`ws.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/ws.rs) | The `/ws` handler and the channel routing |
| [`assets.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/assets.rs) | The embedded web build and its fallback rules |
| [`files/`](crates/ostra-server/src/files/mod.rs) | Tree, file reads, save, diff, changes, write watch, folder browser |
| [`nav/`](crates/ostra-server/src/nav/mod.rs) | The Sessions tree, search, and workspace activity |
| [`artifacts.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/artifacts.rs) | Workspace artifacts: list, upload, hide, move, delete, download |
| [`git.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/git.rs) and [`repo.rs`](crates/ostra-server/src/repo.rs) | Git credentials, clone, pull, and the Git dock commands |
| [`ostra-core/src/api.rs`](crates/ostra-core/src/api.rs) | Every request and response type, plus `ClientMsg` and `ServerMsg` |

The types in `ostra-core/src/api.rs` are the one contract between the server and the browser. The `ts-rs` crate writes the TypeScript types for `web/src/api/gen` from them when the Rust tests run. To regenerate them, run `cargo test -p ostra-core export_bindings`. No build step does it. See [the web console](web-console.md).

## Start the server

`app::run` is the entry point of `ostra serve`. It does these steps in order. The command line flags are in [Install, run, and the command line](install-and-run.md).

1. Read the global config. If the file is unreadable, use the default config.
2. Compute the listen address with `bind_addr`. The `--bind` flag wins over `server.bind`, and `server.bind` wins over `127.0.0.1`. The values `localhost`, `all`, and `*` mean `127.0.0.1`, `0.0.0.0`, and `0.0.0.0`.
3. Bind a port. If a port comes from `--port` or `server.port`, bind exactly that port. If no port is set, try `7878` (`DEFAULT_PORT`) and the next 19 ports. If all 20 fail, bind port `0` and let the OS choose.
4. If `auth::server_running` says no other server runs, stop the processes that earlier sandboxes left, remove stale egress sockets, and remove stale decoy files. A second server on the same data dir does not run this cleanup, because the cleanup kills the processes of the first server.
5. Call `build`, which creates the `App` (see the next diagram).
6. Write the server file, print the sign-in URL, and open the browser unless `--no-open` is set.
7. Serve the router. On `ctrl_c`, the server stops gracefully, removes the bridge socket, and removes the server file.

### What `build` does

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["validate global sandbox config"] --> B["open registry, unlock master key"]
  B --> C["materialize assets into data dir"]
  C --> D["build Providers and executors"]
  D --> E["Notifier with VAPID keys"]
  E --> F["detect harnesses: EnvStatus"]
  F --> G["HarnessRuntime with write sink"]
  G --> H["create Shared and App"]
  H --> I["bind code tools, management, coordination"]
  I --> J["start bridge socket and background tasks"]
  J --> K["attach each registered workspace"]
  K --> L["sweep caches of ended sessions"]
```

- `build` refuses to start when the `[sandbox]` section of the global config has an issue. It prints the path of the issue and the config file.
- If the sandbox does not protect agent commands, `build` logs a warning that agent commands run with the full rights of the user. See [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md).
- The stderr banner prints only when the sandbox status carries a message. In mode `off`, `build` only logs the warning.
- `open_registry` sets mode `0600` on the registry database and on its `-wal` and `-shm` files on Unix, because the registry holds provider keys, git credentials, and the push signing key.
- `ostra_agents::materialize_assets` writes the embedded prompt assets into `<data dir>/assets`, and the server reads them from there.
- The VAPID key for Web Push is the registry secret `vapid_private`. The server generates it once and reuses it. See [MCP servers and Web Push](mcp-and-notifications.md).
- On Unix, `serve_bridge_socket` creates the hook bridge socket. Sandboxed harness hooks use it. Unsandboxed hooks call `/internal/*` over loopback HTTP.
- Two background tasks start: `files::run_touches` and `nav::run`. Both hold a weak reference to the `App`, so they end when the `App` is gone.

### What happens when the server starts

- **A registered workspace has no `workspace.toml`.** `build` logs a warning and skips it. The server still starts.
- **A workspace fails to open.** `build` logs an error and continues with the other workspaces.
- **The global config has an error after start.** `Shared::global` logs a warning and returns the last good copy. See the next part.
- **The bind address is not an IP address.** `bind_addr` fails and the server does not start.
- **The server listens on a non-loopback address.** The server prints a warning that the traffic is plain HTTP. It prints the other LAN addresses when the machine has more than one.

## `App`, `Shared`, and `ServerServices`

`App` is the state that every handler receives. `Shared` is the part that every workspace uses.

| Field of `App` | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `shared` | The `Shared` state |
| `workspaces` | `RwLock<HashMap<WorkspaceId, Arc<WorkspaceRt>>>`, the open workspaces |
| `hub` | A broadcast channel of `HubMsg`: engine notices tagged with a workspace. Capacity 8192. |
| `push` | A broadcast channel of `Pushed`: messages that the server itself creates, with an explicit list of channels. Capacity 1024. |
| `auth` | The `Auth` state for sign-in |
| `files` | `Files`: tree, read, diff, caches, and write tracking |
| `code` and `code_tools` | The code index for the Files view and for the agent tools |
| `nav` | `Nav`: the Sessions tree, search support, and activity |
| `dev` | True when `--dev` is set |

`Shared` holds the global config path and its cache, the registry database, `Providers`, the `NativeExecutor`, the `HarnessRuntime`, the `Notifier`, the MCP gateway, the detected harnesses, the executable path, and the port.

`Shared::global` reads the global config file on every call. Because of this, an edit applies without a restart. If the file does not parse, or if the sandbox section fails validation, the function logs a warning and returns the last good copy. Settings are described in [Configuration reference](configuration.md).

`Shared::protected_paths` returns the executable, the global config, the data dir, and the assets dir. `ServerServices::protected_paths` adds the `workspace.toml` and the workspace database of the workspace. The engine passes these paths to the policy so that agents cannot write them.

### `ServerServices`

`ServerServices` implements the `Services` trait of `ostra-engine`, one value for each workspace. The trait is described in [The engine runner](engine-runner.md). `ServerServices` gives the engine these things:

- `global()` and `workspace()`. The workspace settings come from `workspace.toml` with the trust overlay (`ostra_workspace::trust::effective`). See [Workspaces, projects, and approvals](workspaces-and-trust.md).
- `executor(kind)`. The native kind returns the shared `NativeExecutor`. A harness kind returns the executor of the `HarnessRuntime`, or `None` when the harness is not available.
- `factory()`, which is `AgentsFactory`.
- `judge(...)`. It finds the provider for the routed model and calls `ostra_providers::structured`.
- `notify(notice)`. If `notifications.push` is off in the workspace settings, nothing is sent. Otherwise the server sends the notice to every push subscription of the workspace, or with no workspace. The notice URL gets the prefix `/w/<workspace id>`. If the push service answers `Gone`, the server removes the subscription.
- `command_approved(...)` and `add_allow_rule(...)`, which read and write the trust state.

### Open and close a workspace

`App::attach` opens a registered workspace. It does these steps:

1. Return the open workspace if it exists already.
2. Open `WorkspaceRt` with the shared state.
3. Call `engine.recover()`. This restarts the sessions that were running when the server stopped.
4. Spawn a forwarder task that reads the engine notices. For each notice the task calls `files.observe`, calls `nav.observe`, and sends a `HubMsg` to `hub`.

If the forwarder falls behind the engine channel, it logs `hub lagged by N notices` and calls `nav.lagged`. The Sessions tree then rebuilds every session on the next tick.

`App::delete_workspace` removes a workspace. It holds the write lock of the workspace map while it calls `rt.retire()`. Because of this lock, no request reaches the engine between the busy check and the removal. If work is running, the call returns `DeleteError::Busy`, which the route maps to status 409. After the removal the server forgets the navigation state and the MCP connections, and pushes `workspace_updated` to `workspace:<id>` and `home`. The project folders stay on disk.

## The guard: what every request passes

`api::router` wraps every route, the WebSocket, the `/internal/*` bridge, and the static fallback in the `guard` middleware. The guard answers before any handler runs.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  R["request"] --> H{"Host allowed?"}
  H -- no --> E421["421 This host is not allowed."]
  H -- yes --> P{"loopback IP host and not /internal?"}
  P -- yes, page --> T307["307 to the private name, keep the query"]
  P -- yes, API --> E421b["421 Open Ostra at the private name"]
  P -- no --> I{"/internal and remote peer or browser headers?"}
  I -- yes --> E403a["403"]
  I -- no --> A{"/api or /ws: Origin, Sec-Fetch ok?"}
  A -- no --> E403b["403 This origin is not allowed."]
  A -- yes --> C{"cookie valid, or /api/auth/exchange?"}
  C -- no --> E401["401 Sign in with the URL the ostra command printed."]
  C -- yes --> N["handler"]
```

The rules and their reasons:

- **Host check.** The `Host` header must pass `Auth::allowed_host`. A refused host gets status 421.
- **Private name.** A cookie that a page sets on `127.0.0.1` reaches every other local port. For this reason the app lives at its private name. A page load on the IP address redirects with status 307 and keeps the `?query`. The URL fragment `#token=` stays in the browser. An API call on the IP address gets 421.
- **`/internal/*`.** Only harness hooks and the MCP shim call these paths. The guard refuses a non-local peer and refuses any request with an `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site` header, because a browser page on this machine is a local peer too.
- **Origin and fetch metadata.** For `/api/*` and `/ws`, the `Origin` must pass `allowed_origin`. The `Sec-Fetch-Site` values `cross-site` and `same-site` are refused. The `Sec-Fetch-Dest` value must be absent, `empty`, `websocket`, or `document`. An image, script, or frame request is page content that reaches the API, for example a Markdown image that an agent wrote.
- **Cookie.** Every `/api/*` and `/ws` request except `/api/auth/exchange` needs a valid session cookie. The guard logs the request facts for a refusal, never the cookie value.
- **Not in `/api`.** The static files and `/mcp/oauth/callback` need an allowed host but no cookie. The OAuth redirect is a cross-site navigation, so the `SameSite=Strict` cookie is not sent. The single-use `state` value authenticates it. See [MCP servers and Web Push](mcp-and-notifications.md).

### Headers on every answer

`secure_headers` adds these headers to every answer, including a refusal:

- `content-security-policy` with `default-src 'self'`, `script-src 'self'`, `img-src 'self' data:`, `frame-ancestors 'none'`, and `object-src 'none'`. The `connect-src` directive names `ws://<host>` and `wss://<host>` only when the host passed the allowlist.
- `x-content-type-options: nosniff`, `referrer-policy: no-referrer`, and `x-frame-options: DENY`.
- `cache-control: no-store` for `/api/*` and `/ws`.

The policy allows no remote images. An injected agent can otherwise send data out through a Markdown image URL. The test `the_browser_boundary_refuses_page_content_and_other_sites` in [`tests/e2e.rs`](crates/ostra-server/tests/e2e.rs) checks these rules.

## The error shape

Every REST failure has a JSON body of the type `ApiError`:

```json
{ "error": "text for a person", "issues": [ { "path": "field", "message": "text" } ] }
```

`issues` is a list of `ValidationIssue` values. It is empty for most errors. For a 409 from `ApiErr::conflict_on` it holds one issue with the name of the field that no longer matches, such as `base_hash`, `path`, or `to`. For a 422 it holds one issue for each bad field.

| Status | When the server sends it |
| --- | --- |
| 400 | The request is not valid: a bad path, an empty question, an unreadable body, a bad `since` time |
| 401 | No valid session cookie |
| 403 | A path leaves its root (containment), a read-only file, or a refused origin |
| 404 | An unknown workspace, session, gate, execution, decision, project, or file |
| 409 | A conflict with the current state: a busy workspace, a changed file, an existing name, `EngineError::Invalid`, `EngineError::Ended`, `GitError::Busy` |
| 413 | A UI state patch is too large |
| 421 | A host that is not allowed |
| 422 | Settings or a new workspace, project, clone, or credential with problems. The `error` text also lists the issues, for clients that show only `error`. |
| 429 | Too many failed sign-in exchanges from one address |
| 500 | `EngineError::Store`, `StoreError`, or an I/O failure |
| 502 | `GitError::Git`: git ran and failed, or could not run |

If the engine returns `EngineError::NotFound`, the route sends 404. A request to an unknown `/api/...` path that passes the guard gets an empty 404 from the static handler.

On the socket, an error is a `ServerMsg::Error { message }` frame. The connection stays open.
