sections.title: MCP servers and Web Push
sections.summary: How Ostra connects to external MCP servers over stdio and streamable HTTP, signs in with OAuth, and serves their tools to every executor. Also how it encrypts and sends Web Push notices.
sections.body:
Agents need tools that Ostra does not ship, such as a GitHub server or a documentation search. Without one shared client, each executor needs its own connection code, its own sign-in, and its own policy check. A person who steps away from the console also needs a way to learn that a gate is waiting. This page covers both areas.

The page covers these parts:

- The MCP client in `ostra-mcp`: two transports, tool discovery, tool calls, and OAuth sign-in.
- The gateway in `ostra-server`: one connection for each server, token storage, and the tools that each execution gets.
- The REST routes that show MCP status and start a sign-in.
- The Web Push sender in `ostra-notify`: message encryption, VAPID, and the subscriptions.
- The browser code that subscribes, and the service worker that shows the notice.

The settings keys of `[[mcp_servers]]` and their validation rules are in [Configuration reference](configuration.md). The policy rules for tool calls are in [Policy engine](policy.md). The MCP shim that harness CLIs use is in [Executors](executors.md). The sealed registry and the master key are in [Sign-in, host checks, and secrets](auth-and-secrets.md).

## Where each part lives

Ostra is the only MCP client. It keeps one connection for each server of a workspace, signs in, finds the tools, and serves them to native runs directly. It serves them to harnesses through its own MCP server. Thus one policy and one allowlist cover every executor.

| Part | File | Job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Client, `Client`, `Endpoint`, `McpError` | `crates/ostra-mcp/src/lib.rs` | Handshake, `tools/list`, `tools/call`, timeout, cancel |
| Stdio transport | `crates/ostra-mcp/src/stdio.rs` | Child process with newline-delimited JSON-RPC |
| HTTP transport | `crates/ostra-mcp/src/http.rs` | One POST for each message, JSON or SSE answer |
| Result text | `crates/ostra-mcp/src/content.rs` | Turns a `tools/call` result into text |
| OAuth | `crates/ostra-mcp/src/oauth.rs` | Discovery, registration, PKCE, token requests |
| Names and checks | `crates/ostra-core/src/mcp.rs` | Tool names, server name rules, `${VAR}` expansion, `validate` |
| Gateway | `crates/ostra-server/src/mcp.rs` | `McpGateway`: connections, sign-in, tools for each execution |
| Tool traits | `crates/ostra-tools/src/mcp.rs` | `McpTools`, `McpConnector`, and `run` |
| Routes | `crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs` | `mcp_status`, `mcp_refresh`, `mcp_login`, `mcp_logout`, `mcp_callback` |
| Push sender | `crates/ostra-notify/src/lib.rs` | Encryption, VAPID, `Notifier::send`. `ServerServices::notify` in `crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs` calls it. |
| Browser push | `web/src/lib/push.ts`, `web/public/sw.js` | Subscribe, show the notice, open the deep link |

## Tool names inside Ostra

The name of a tool depends on who reads it. A tool `create_issue` of the workspace server `github` has three names:

| Name | Form | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bare name | `github__create_issue` | Ostra's own MCP server, which serves the tool to harnesses |
| Harness name | `mcp__ostra__github__create_issue` | The harness CLI, which adds the `mcp__ostra__` prefix |
| Canonical name | `mcp__github__create_issue` | The native loop, the policy, permission rules, and the Activity view |

The canonical name uses Claude Code's spelling. `canonical`, `bare`, `server_of`, `is_gateway_tool`, and `is_gateway_bare` in `crates/ostra-core/src/mcp.rs` convert between the forms. The separator is `__` (`SEPARATOR`). Ostra's own tools never contain `__`, so `is_gateway_bare` tells an external tool from an own tool.

A server name has at most 24 characters (`MAX_SERVER_NAME`). It uses lowercase letters, digits, and dashes, and it starts with a letter. The name `ostra` is reserved. `is_server_name` accepts any run of dashes and does not enforce single dashes. The `__` split of a bare name still holds, because `is_server_name` rejects underscores.

A bare name has at most 52 characters (`MAX_BARE_NAME`). Harnesses add the 12 characters of `mcp__ostra__`, and providers cap a tool name at 64 characters. `bare_name` uses `server__tool` when the tool name has only letters, digits, `_`, and `-`, and the result fits. Otherwise it replaces each other character with `_`, shortens the tool part, and adds `_` and an 8-digit hex hash of the original tool name.

The hash is FNV-1a with 64 bits, truncated to 32 bits. The code writes it as `{:08x}` of the value `as u32`. Two different tool names of one server can share one bare name when the 32-bit hashes collide and the sanitized parts match. A collision is possible but unlikely. The test `names` in the same file shows the result for `search.pages/v2` and for an 80-character name.

## Connect and run the handshake

`Client::connect(endpoint, timeout)` makes the transport that matches the `Endpoint` and then runs the MCP handshake:

1. The client sends `initialize` with `protocolVersion` `2025-11-25` (`PROTOCOL_VERSION`), empty `capabilities`, and `clientInfo` named `ostra`.
2. The client reads `protocolVersion` from the answer. If the version is not in `SUPPORTED_VERSIONS`, the client returns `McpError::Transport`. The list holds `2025-11-25`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26`, and `2024-11-05`.
3. The client tells the transport the negotiated version with `Transport::initialized`. The HTTP transport then sends it in the `mcp-protocol-version` header.
4. The client keeps `serverInfo` as the text `name version` in `server_info`.
5. The client sends the notification `notifications/initialized`.

Ostra declares no client capabilities. Thus it answers only `ping` when a server sends a request. For each other method, it answers with error code `-32601` and the text `Ostra does not support <method>` (`answer_server_request`). The client notes the notification `notifications/tools/list_changed` in a flag, and `take_tools_changed` reads and clears it.

### Timeouts and cancel

Each request goes through `Client::rpc`. It waits for the first of three events: the answer, the timeout, or the cancel token. After a timeout or a cancel, the client calls `Transport::abandon` for the request id. Then it sends `notifications/cancelled` with the id and the reason. The client skips that notification for `initialize`. The error is `McpError::Timeout(seconds)` or `McpError::Cancelled`.

The error type `McpError` has six variants:

| Variant | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `NeedsAuth { www_authenticate }` | The server answered 401, or 403 with `insufficient_scope`. The header text is kept for discovery. |
| `Transport(text)` | The process did not start, the network failed, the body is wrong, or the version is not supported |
| `Rpc { code, message }` | The server answered with a JSON-RPC `error` |
| `Timeout(seconds)` | No answer in time |
| `Cancelled` | The caller cancelled the request |
| `Closed(text)` | The server exited or ended the session |

## Discover and call tools

`list_tools` sends `tools/list` and follows `nextCursor`. It stops after 50 pages. Each page is one round trip, and a server can return a cursor on every page without end. For each tool, the client keeps:

- `name`. A tool without a name is skipped.
- `description`, or the `title` when the description is missing.
- `input_schema`. If the server sends none or sends a value that is not an object, the client uses an empty object schema.
- `read_only`, from `annotations.readOnlyHint`. The default is `false`.

`call_tool` sends `tools/call`. If the arguments are not a JSON object, it sends `{}`. The result is `Ok(Ok(text))` for a tool result and `Ok(Err(text))` when the server sets `isError`. The outer `Err` is a protocol or transport failure.

### Tool results become text

A tool result in Ostra is text. `result_text` in `crates/ostra-mcp/src/content.rs` joins the `content` items with a newline:

| Item type | Text that Ostra keeps |
| --- | --- |
| `text` | The text |
| `image`, `audio` | `[image image/png, 3 bytes, not shown because tool results are text]` (kind, MIME type, decoded size) |
| `resource` with text | The text |
| `resource` without text | `[binary resource <uri>]` |
| `resource_link` | `[resource <uri> <name>]`. When the item has no name or an empty name, the text is `[resource <uri>]`. |
| Other type | The item as JSON |

If every part is empty and the result has `structuredContent`, Ostra uses that value as pretty JSON. The text is cut at 100 KB (`MAX_RESULT`, 102400 bytes) at a character boundary, and it ends with `... (N more bytes cut)`. If `isError` is `true` and the text is empty, the error text is `The tool reported an error without a message.`

## The stdio transport

A local server is a child process that speaks one JSON-RPC message for each line (`crates/ostra-mcp/src/stdio.rs`). `Stdio::spawn` sets these properties:

- Ostra removes each name in `env_remove` from the child environment, then adds the variables of `env`. The working directory is `cwd`, which is the workspace root.
- The pipes for stdin, stdout, and stderr are open, and `kill_on_drop` is on.
- `ostra_core::proctree` puts the child in a process tree. Servers that start through `npx` or `uvx` run in grandchildren. When the transport drops, `Tree::terminate` ends the whole tree. On Windows, dropping the tree closes its job object, which kills the processes.
- `guard` is an opaque handle that the caller gives. It lives as long as the server, and it is dropped after the tree is ended. The gateway uses it to hold the sandbox members of the server.

One task reads stdout line by line. A line that is not JSON is skipped and logged at debug level, because some servers print logs on stdout. A line can hold one message or an array. A response goes to the waiting request through a `oneshot` channel that the `pending` map holds, keyed by id. A request from the server is answered on stdin. When stdout ends, the task sets `alive` to `false` and drops every waiting request.

Another task reads stderr and keeps the last 4096 bytes (`STDERR_TAIL`). If a request fails because the process is gone, `closed` waits up to 500 ms for stderr to end. Then it builds `McpError::Closed` with the text `the server exited: ` and the last 5 stderr lines, joined by ` / `. If stderr is empty, the text is `the server exited`. Thus the user sees why a crashing server stopped.

## The streamable HTTP transport

The HTTP transport sends each message as one POST to the server URL (`crates/ostra-mcp/src/http.rs`). It sends `Accept: application/json, text/event-stream`. The answer is either one JSON body, a JSON array, or an SSE stream. The transport reads only the message whose `id` matches the request. Each other message goes to `side_message`: a request from the server gets its reply as a new POST, and a notification sets the flags.

The transport keeps two header values:

- `mcp-session-id`. The transport stores the value from any successful answer and sends it in each later request.
- `mcp-protocol-version`. The transport sets it after `initialize`.

The client has a 15 second connect timeout and the user agent `ostra/<version>`. The request timeout comes from the caller of each call, not from the HTTP client. Header names and values from the settings must be valid HTTP, or `Http::new` returns `McpError::Transport`.

### Redirects stay on one origin

`same_origin_redirects` follows a redirect only if the scheme, host, and port equal those of the first request. It stops after 5 earlier redirects with the error `too many redirects`. A header with a secret, such as an API key or a bearer token, thus never reaches another host and never moves from https to http. The gateway uses the same policy for its OAuth requests.

### Status codes

The `send` method checks each answer in this order:

1. Status 401, or status 403 whose `WWW-Authenticate` header contains `insufficient_scope`: the transport asks the `TokenSource` to refresh the token with `refused`. If it gets a new token, it sends the request again, one time. Otherwise it returns `McpError::NeedsAuth` with the header text.
2. Status 403 without that challenge: a plain refusal. The transport returns `McpError::Transport` with the text `the server refused the request (403)` and the first 300 characters of the body.
3. Status 404 when the transport holds a session id: the server ended the session. The transport sets `alive` to `false` and returns `McpError::Closed` with `the server ended the session`.
4. Any other status that is not 2xx: `McpError::Transport` with the status and the first 300 characters of the body, or `no body`.

An SSE stream that ends before the response gives `McpError::Closed` with `the event stream ended before the response`.

## OAuth sign-in for remote servers

A remote server can answer 401 and ask for OAuth. `crates/ostra-mcp/src/oauth.rs` follows the MCP authorization specification with these standards:

- Protected resource metadata (RFC 9728).
- Authorization server metadata (RFC 8414) and OpenID discovery.
- Dynamic client registration (RFC 7591).
- PKCE with the `S256` method.
- The `resource` parameter (RFC 8707).

### Discovery

`discover(http, server_url, challenge)` finds the authorization server. It tries these resource metadata URLs in order and uses the first JSON that has `authorization_servers`:

1. The `resource_metadata` value of the `WWW-Authenticate` challenge, if the earlier 401 had one.
2. `<origin>/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource<path of the server URL>`, if the URL has a path.
3. `<origin>/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource`.

The `resource` value of the metadata becomes the resource indicator. If the metadata has none, the indicator is the server URL without its fragment. The first entry of `authorization_servers` is the issuer. A server without resource metadata is treated as its own authorization server, because older servers host it themselves.

The scopes come from the first source that has some: the `scope` of the challenge, `scopes_supported` of the resource metadata, then `scopes_supported` of the authorization server. The user can override them with `oauth.scopes` in the settings.

`authorization_server` reads the metadata of the issuer from these URLs: `oauth-authorization-server`, then `openid-configuration`, and for an issuer with a path, a third form that adds `/.well-known/openid-configuration` after the path. If the `issuer` field of the metadata differs from the issuer that Ostra asked for (a trailing `/` does not count), Ostra refuses the metadata. RFC 8414 section 3.3 requires this, because another server could otherwise hand out endpoints for this one.

If no metadata exists, the result depends on the resource metadata:

- No resource metadata and no authorization server metadata: Ostra guesses the 2025-03-26 defaults `/authorize`, `/token`, and `/register` on the server origin. The `Discovery` has `guessed` set to `true`.
- Resource metadata exists, but the authorization server metadata cannot be read: the error is `could not read the metadata of the authorization server <issuer>`.

### Endpoint checks

Ostra sends the browser to the authorization URL and sends codes and secrets to the other endpoints. A hostile server can name a `javascript:` URL in its metadata. The browser then runs that URL on the origin of Ostra. `check_endpoint` thus accepts only these URLs:

```rust
let ok = match u.scheme() {
    "https" => u.host().is_some(),
    "http" => is_loopback(&u) || server_origin.is_some_and(|o| o == origin(&u)),
    _ => false,
};
```

Plain `http` is allowed only on a loopback host (`localhost`, `127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`) or on the origin that the user chose for the MCP server. The check covers the resource metadata URL, the issuer, and the authorization, token, and registration endpoints. `authorization_url` checks the authorization endpoint again, because a saved record can come from an older version that did not check.

### Client registration

The client identity comes from one of two places:

- The user sets `oauth.client_id` in the settings, and optionally `oauth.client_secret_env`. Ostra reads the secret from that environment variable of the server process.
- Ostra registers itself with `register`. It posts the client name `Ostra`, the redirect URI, the grants `authorization_code` and `refresh_token`, the response type `code`, and `token_endpoint_auth_method` `none`. Thus it is a public client.

If the authorization server has no `registration_endpoint`, the error tells the user to set `oauth.client_id`.

### PKCE, tokens, and refresh

`pkce` makes a verifier from 32 random bytes in URL-safe base64 (43 characters). The challenge is the SHA-256 hash of the verifier in the same encoding. `random_token` also makes the `state` value. The authorization URL carries `response_type=code`, `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `state`, `code_challenge`, `code_challenge_method=S256`, `resource`, and `scope` when scopes exist.

`exchange_code` and `refresh` post a form to the token endpoint. Both send the `resource` parameter. The client authentication depends on the credentials:

| Case | Authentication |
| --- | --- |
| No client secret | `client_id` in the form |
| Secret, and the server lists `client_secret_basic` but not `client_secret_post` | HTTP Basic authentication |
| Secret, any other case | `client_id` and `client_secret` in the form |

The `Tokens` value holds `access_token`, an optional `refresh_token`, and `expires_at` in Unix seconds from `expires_in`. `Tokens::expired` returns `true` when the token expires within 60 seconds. If a refresh answer has no new refresh token, Ostra keeps the old one.

`parse_challenge` reads `resource_metadata` and `scope` from a `WWW-Authenticate` header. It matches the parameter name only at a word boundary, and it accepts quoted and unquoted values.

## The sign-in flow from the browser

The user starts a sign-in in Settings, MCP servers. The console opens a new tab before it sends the request, because browsers block a tab that opens after an `await`. The diagram shows the full flow.

### Diagram: OAuth sign-in for one server

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Browser
    participant API as Ostra API
    participant GW as McpGateway
    participant AS as Authorization server
    participant Reg as Registry
    Browser->>API: POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/mcp/{name}/login
    API->>GW: login(root, name, origin)
    GW->>AS: discover: well-known metadata, register
    GW->>GW: keep PendingLogin under state for 600 s
    GW-->>API: authorization URL
    API-->>Browser: McpLogin authorization_url
    Browser->>AS: open authorization URL
    AS-->>Browser: redirect to /mcp/oauth/callback?code&state
    Browser->>API: GET /mcp/oauth/callback
    API->>GW: callback(state, code)
    GW->>AS: exchange_code with PKCE verifier
    GW->>Reg: save OAuthRecord as mcp_oauth key
    API-->>Browser: HTML page Signed in
```

`McpGateway::login` runs these steps:

1. It loads the approved copy of `workspace.toml`. If the file waits for approval, it returns the pending message. Rule A1 requires this, because a sign-in sends `oauth.client_secret_env` to the endpoints of the server. See [Workspaces, projects, and approvals](workspaces-and-trust.md).
2. It finds the server by name. It fails for an unknown name, and it fails for a local server (`Sign-in applies to remote servers only: this one runs as a local command.`).
3. It takes the `WWW-Authenticate` header from the last `NeedsAuth` error of the connection, if one exists, and runs `discover`.
4. It builds the redirect URI: the browser origin plus `/mcp/oauth/callback` (`CALLBACK_PATH`).
5. It picks the client. For a configured `client_id`, it reads the secret from the named variable and refuses a variable that holds a provider key or a bridge token. Otherwise it reuses the saved client if the URL, the redirect URI, and the issuer are the same. If not, it registers a new client.
6. It makes the PKCE pair and the `state`, and builds the authorization URL. The scopes are `oauth.scopes` when set, else the discovered scopes.
7. It stores a `PendingLogin` under the `state` and drops every pending login older than 600 seconds (`LOGIN_TTL`).

If registration fails and the discovery was guessed, the error says that the server asks for a sign-in but publishes no OAuth metadata. It tells the user to give the server a token in a header, for example `Authorization: Bearer ${TOKEN_VAR}`.

`McpGateway::callback(state, code)` removes the `PendingLogin` first. Thus a `state` works one time, even if the exchange then fails. A missing or old `state` gives `This sign-in link has expired or was already used. Start the sign-in again from Ostra.` On success, the gateway saves an `OAuthRecord` and resets the connection, so the next use reconnects with the token.

The record holds the server URL, the `Discovery`, the client credentials, the redirect URI, and the tokens. It lives in the registry under the key `mcp_oauth:<workspace root>:<server name>`. The prefix `mcp_oauth:` is in `SECRET_KEYS` of `crates/ostra-store/src/secrets.rs`, so the registry seals the value with the master key. A record is used only when its `url` equals the current URL of the server. If the user changes the URL, Ostra never sends the old token to the new address.

### Token use and refresh

The `Stored` type implements `TokenSource` for the HTTP transport:

- `token()` returns the saved access token, or refreshes it when `Tokens::expired` is true.
- `refused(token)` runs after a 401. If the saved token already differs from the refused one, another call refreshed it, and Ostra returns the saved token. Otherwise it refreshes.
- A mutex allows one refresh at a time, because a refresh token can be single-use.
- If a refresh fails, Ostra logs it, clears the tokens in the record, and returns `None`. The server then shows the state `needs_auth`.

`logout` deletes the `mcp_oauth:` key from the registry and resets the connection.

## The gateway: one connection for each server

`McpGateway` in `crates/ostra-server/src/mcp.rs` holds the connections and the pending logins. The app creates it at start (`McpGateway::new` in `app.rs`). A connection has the key (workspace root, server name). Parallel executions share one connection and one connect attempt, because each connection has a mutex.

| Constant | Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CONNECT_TIMEOUT` | 30 seconds | Start of a server, the handshake, and each `tools/list` |
| `RELIST_AFTER` | 30 seconds | A tool list older than this is fetched again when an execution opens |
| `RETRY_AFTER` | 20 seconds | A failed server is not tried again sooner. Without this delay, each parallel execution starts the failed server again. |
| `LOGIN_TTL` | 600 seconds | How long a sign-in link works |
| HTTP timeout of the gateway client | 30 seconds | Discovery, registration, and token requests |

### A new connection when a setting changes

Each connection has a fingerprint: a JSON text of `command`, `env`, `url`, `headers`, `oauth`, and the workspace sandbox values `mode`, `network`, `allowed_hosts`, `loopback`, and `blocked_ports`. If the fingerprint of the current settings differs, the gateway makes a new connection and the old one is dropped. A dropped stdio connection ends its process tree. The settings `disabled_tools`, `agents`, `enabled`, and `timeout_secs` are not in the fingerprint. Ostra reads them from the settings file each time an execution opens, so they apply to the next execution without a reconnect.

### Diagram: how `ready` returns a client

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["ready(root, cfg, force)"] --> B{"force?"}
    B -- yes --> C["clear the state"]
    B -- no --> D{"client alive?"}
    C --> G
    D -- yes --> E{"list older than 30 s or tools changed?"}
    D -- no --> G{"failed less than 20 s ago?"}
    E -- no --> F["return client and cached tools"]
    E -- yes --> H["list_tools"]
    H -- ok --> F
    H -- error --> G
    G -- yes --> I["return the saved error"]
    G -- no --> J["connect with the approved copy of the file"]
    J -- ok --> F
    J -- error --> K["save the error and return it"]
```

The connect step has these parts:

1. The gateway loads the approved copy of `workspace.toml` and finds a server entry equal to the current one. If either fails, the error is `Approve the changed commands in settings, because they changed outside Ostra.` Rule A1: no server starts from a workspace file that waits for approval, and it starts from the approved copy.
2. `endpoint()` builds the `Endpoint`. For a URL, the headers are expanded and a `Stored` token source is attached. For a command, the program starts through `ostra_sandbox::host_command` in the workspace root, so it runs under the agent sandbox. See [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md).
3. `Client::connect` and `list_tools` run with `CONNECT_TIMEOUT`.
4. The gateway turns `McpError::NeedsAuth` into `ConnError::NeedsAuth` and every other error into `ConnError::Other`.

### Header and environment values

A value in `env` or `headers` is one of three kinds:

- The text `${ostra_secret}` (`SAVED_SECRET`). Ostra reads the real value from the sealed registry key `mcp_secret:...`. The key includes the server name and a hash of the URL and command, so a changed target never receives the old value. If the value cannot be read, the error says to enter the field again.
- A text with `${VAR}`. `expand_env` replaces each `${VAR}` with the environment of the Ostra server process. An unset variable gives the error ``set `VAR` in the Ostra server's environment, because `field` names it, then restart the server``. Here `VAR` is the variable and `field` is the setting.
- A literal. Ostra moves a literal into the sealed registry when it saves the settings, and leaves `${ostra_secret}` in the file.

Ostra refuses a `${VAR}` that names a credential that it keeps from MCP servers. `credential_env_names` builds the list: the provider variables, the bridge variables (`OSTRA_TOKEN`, `OSTRA_EXECUTION`, `OSTRA_URL`, `OSTRA_HARNESS`), and each `oauth.client_secret_env`. A stdio server also does not inherit these variables, because `env_remove` lists them.

## How an execution gets MCP tools

The engine gives each execution a `McpConnector`. `Connector::open(spec)` in the gateway returns the tools for that execution:

1. If the execution is an inspect resume (a read-only session), the result has no tools.
2. The gateway keeps the servers that serve the agent (`mcp::serves`): the server is `enabled`, and its `agents` list is empty or names the agent.
3. It calls `ready` for all those servers at the same time.
4. A server that fails adds one line to `notes`. The native loop and the harness path show each note in the Activity view as a status message. The other servers still work.
5. For each tool that is not in `disabled_tools`, it builds a `ToolDefinition` with the canonical name. A repeated canonical name is skipped. An empty description becomes ``The `<tool>` tool of MCP server `<server>`.``
6. If no tool remains, `tools` is `None`.

The tool list is fixed when the execution starts. `McpTools::read_only` returns the canonical names of tools with `readOnlyHint`. The policy uses it as `read_only_mcp_tools`.

### Call a tool

`ExecMcp::call` finds the tool by canonical name and uses the `timeout_secs` of its server (default 120, at most 600). If the client is no longer alive, the gateway runs `ready` again, so a server that exited since the execution opened starts one more time. Failures become text for the model:

- `NeedsAuth` gives the sign-in message: ``Sign in to MCP server `<name>` in Settings, MCP servers, or give it a token in a header, because it refuses requests without one.``
- Any other `McpError` gives ``MCP server `<name>` failed: <error>``.
- A server result with `isError` is a tool error with its text.

The tool run in `crates/ostra-tools/src/mcp.rs` calls `McpTools::call`. If the execution has no MCP tools, the tool name is unknown.

### The permission rules

The policy treats a tool of a workspace MCP server by Rule M1: it is allowed unless a rule says otherwise. In plan mode, only the tools with `readOnlyHint` are allowed. The rules are in [Policy engine](policy.md).

### The path for harness CLIs

A harness CLI lists the tools of Ostra's MCP server once at its start. The `Wrapped` executor in `crates/ostra-server/src/bridge.rs` thus opens the MCP tools before the harness starts. The shim reaches the server through `POST /internal/mcp`. For each call, `mcp_call` converts the bare name to the canonical name, runs the policy check, asks the user if the policy says ask, and then runs the tool through `ostra_tools::execute`. It records the call and the result in the execution log.

Rule M2: the hook of the harness passes a gateway tool without a check, because the MCP handler checks and logs the call when it runs it. Thus a call is checked one time. Harness-native MCP calls arrive as `Other:mcp__...` and do not count as gateway tools. For the shim and the hook, see [Executors](executors.md).

## Status and sign-in routes

The console reads and changes MCP state through five routes. The handlers are in `crates/ostra-server/src/api.rs`.

| Route | Handler | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/workspaces/{ws}/mcp` | `mcp_status` | A list of `McpServerStatus`, one for each `mcp_servers` entry. It connects to every enabled server at the same time. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/mcp/{name}/refresh` | `mcp_refresh` | One `McpServerStatus`. It clears the state and connects again. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/mcp/{name}/login` | `mcp_login` | `McpLogin` with `authorization_url`. The status is 502 when the sign-in cannot start. |
| `POST /api/workspaces/{ws}/mcp/{name}/logout` | `mcp_logout` | `McpServerStatus` after the saved sign-in is deleted |
| `GET /mcp/oauth/callback` | `mcp_callback` | An HTML page. The status is 200 with `Signed in`, or 400 with `Sign-in failed`. |

An unknown server name in `refresh` or `logout` gives 404 with ``This workspace has no MCP server `<name>`.``

The callback route is outside `/api`. The redirect of the authorization server is a cross-site navigation, so the browser does not send the `SameSite=Strict` cookie. The single-use `state` authenticates the request instead (test `mcp.rs` in `crates/ostra-server/tests` checks that the callback needs no cookie). The page escapes the server name and the error text with `html_escape`.

The `login` route builds the return address from the `Origin` header, if it starts with `http`, or else from the `Host` header with `http://`. The request guard has already checked both headers. If neither is present, the status is 400.

### The status values

`McpServerStatus` has these fields:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name`, `transport` | The server name, and `stdio` or `http` |
| `state` | `McpConnState`: `disabled`, `connected`, `needs_auth`, or `error`. The enum also has `idle`, but the gateway does not set it. |
| `message` | Why the server is not connected, or what to do |
| `server_info` | `name version` from `initialize` |
| `signed_in` | `Option<bool>`. The cases are in the list below this table. |
| `tools` | A list of `McpToolInfo`: `name`, `canonical`, `description`, `enabled` (not in `disabled_tools`), and `read_only` |

The gateway sets `signed_in` in `server_status` in these cases:

- Whenever a saved record exists for the current URL, `signed_in` is `Some(record.tokens.is_some())`. The gateway computes this value before it checks `enabled`.
- `Some(false)` also occurs when a failed refresh cleared the tokens of the record.
- `Some(false)` also occurs when the connection fails with a `needs_auth` error, even without a saved record.
- `None` occurs when no saved record exists for the current URL.
- `None` also occurs for every stdio server, because a stdio server has no URL.

A disabled server returns `disabled` and no connection starts.

### What the console does

`web/src/screens/workspace/McpSection.tsx` shows each server with a state chip and the buttons for reconnect, sign in, and sign out. After the sign-in tab opens, the screen calls `refresh` every 2 seconds. It stops when the state is `connected` or `signed_in` is true, or after 120 seconds (`SIGN_IN_WAIT_MS`). The screen refuses an authorization URL that is not `http` or `https`.

### What happens when (MCP)

- **A server answers 401 on the first connect.** The state is `needs_auth`. The user chooses Sign in. The failed `WWW-Authenticate` header guides the discovery.
- **An access token expires.** `Stored::token` refreshes it before the request. If the server still answers 401, `refused` refreshes once and the request is sent again.
- **A refresh fails.** The tokens are cleared and the state becomes `needs_auth`.
- **A server fails to start or to answer.** The state is `error` with the text. Ostra does not try again for 20 seconds, except when the user chooses reconnect.
- **A server process exits during a run.** The next tool call starts the server again. The call that was in flight returns ``MCP server `<name>` failed: the connection closed: ...``.
- **A tool call exceeds `timeout_secs`.** The client returns `no answer after N s` and sends `notifications/cancelled`.
- **The execution is cancelled.** The cancel token stops the wait, and the client sends `notifications/cancelled`.
- **The server says the tool list changed.** The flag is set. The next `ready` lists the tools again.
- **The workspace file changed outside Ostra.** No server starts until the user approves the change.
- **The user deletes the workspace.** `forget` drops every connection of that workspace.
- **A sign-in link is used twice, or after 600 seconds.** The callback returns status 400.
- **The authorization server names a different issuer.** Discovery fails with `refused the metadata at <url>: it names issuer ...`.

## Web Push: the problem and the parts

A session can wait for hours at a gate. Without a push notice, the user must keep the console open. Web Push lets the server send a notice to a browser even when the console tab is closed. The push service of the browser vendor delivers it, and a service worker shows it.

The crate `ostra-notify` implements the sender without OpenSSL. It follows three standards:

- RFC 8291: message encryption for Web Push.
- RFC 8188: the `aes128gcm` content coding for the body.
- RFC 8292: VAPID, which proves to the push service which application server sends the message.

The parts are:

| Part | Where | Job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `VapidKeys` | `crates/ostra-notify/src/lib.rs` | A P-256 key pair. It signs the VAPID JWT. |
| `encrypt`, `encrypt_with` | same file | Encrypt a payload for one subscription |
| `Notifier` | same file | Builds and sends the HTTP request |
| `push_subscriptions` table | `crates/ostra-store/src/registry.rs` | The subscriptions |
| `Services::notify` | `crates/ostra-engine/src/services.rs` | The method of the `Services` trait that the runner calls with a `Notice` |
| `ServerServices::notify` | `crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs` | The server implementation. It finds the subscriptions and sends one notice to each. |
| `push_for` | `crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs` | Chooses which session events send a notice |
| `push.ts`, `sw.js` | `web/` | Subscribe in the browser, and show the notice |

## Encrypt a message

The push service must not read the notice, so Ostra encrypts it with keys that only the browser holds. Each subscription has two values, both in URL-safe base64:

- `p256dh`: the public key of the browser.
- `auth`: a 16-byte secret that the browser makes for this subscription.

`encrypt_with(plaintext, ua_public, auth_secret, as_secret, salt)` runs these steps:

1. It rejects a payload longer than 3993 bytes (`MAX_PLAINTEXT`) with `NotifyError::TooLarge`. Push services accept at most 4096 bytes of body. The header takes 86 bytes, the tag 16 bytes, and the padding delimiter 1 byte.
2. It computes the ECDH secret between the sender key (`as_secret`) and the browser key.
3. It derives the input key material with HKDF-SHA-256. The salt is the `auth` secret. The info is `WebPush: info\0`, then the browser public key, then the sender public key.
4. It derives a 16-byte content encryption key and a 12-byte nonce with HKDF. The salt is the random 16-byte salt, and the info values are `Content-Encoding: aes128gcm\0` and `Content-Encoding: nonce\0`.
5. It appends the byte `0x02` (the delimiter of the last record) to the payload and encrypts it with AES-128-GCM.
6. It builds the body from the salt (16 bytes), the record size `4096` (4 bytes, big-endian, `RECORD_SIZE`), the key length (1 byte), the sender public key (65 bytes), and the ciphertext.

```rust
let mut key_info = b"WebPush: info\0".to_vec();
key_info.extend_from_slice(ua_public);
key_info.extend_from_slice(&as_public);
let mut ikm = [0u8; 32];
hkdf_expand(auth_secret, ecdh.raw_secret_bytes(), &key_info, &mut ikm)?;
let mut cek = [0u8; 16];
hkdf_expand(salt, &ikm, b"Content-Encoding: aes128gcm\0", &mut cek)?;
```

The message has one record, so one record holds the whole message. `encrypt` calls `encrypt_with` with a new random sender key and a new random salt for each message. The sender key for encryption is not the VAPID key. The test `rfc8291_test_vector` checks the output against the RFC 8291 Appendix A vector, and `round_trip_with_fresh_keys` decrypts a message with the browser key.

`b64_decode` accepts URL-safe base64 with or without `=` padding, because browsers produce either form.

## Prove the sender with VAPID

The push service needs to know which application server sends a message, so that it can limit abuse and contact the operator. `VapidKeys` holds one P-256 key. `jwt(audience, subject, expires)` builds an ES256 token (RFC 8292):

- The header is `{"typ":"JWT","alg":"ES256"}`.
- The claims are `aud` (the origin of the push endpoint), `exp`, and `sub` (the contact URI).
- The signature is 64 bytes in URL-safe base64.

`authorization(...)` returns the header value `vapid t=<jwt>, k=<public key>`. `public_key_b64url` returns the 65-byte uncompressed public point. The browser uses it as `applicationServerKey`.

The server makes the key pair at the first start and stores the private bytes in the registry under `vapid_private` (`vapid_keys` in `app.rs`). The prefix list `SECRET_KEYS` seals this key. If the stored bytes cannot be read as a key, the server makes a new pair and replaces the old one. The server gives the public key to the console in `GET /api/info` as `vapid_public_key`. The contact URI is `mailto:ostra@localhost`.

## Send a message

`Notifier::send(subscription, notification)` does the following:

1. It serializes the `Notification` (`title`, `body`, `url`, `tag`) as JSON and encrypts it.
2. It takes the audience from the endpoint with `origin_of`. Only `http` and `https` are accepted, and the audience is `scheme://host[:port]`.
3. It sets the JWT expiry to the current time plus 12 hours (`JWT_TTL`).
4. It posts the body with these headers: `Authorization` (VAPID), `Content-Encoding: aes128gcm`, `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`, `TTL: 86400` (`PUSH_TTL_SECS`, 24 hours), and `Urgency: high`.

The HTTP client has a timeout of 20 seconds. The result is a `SendOutcome`:

| Outcome | Condition | What `ServerServices::notify` does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Delivered` | Status 200 to 299 | Nothing |
| `Gone` | Status 404 or 410 | Deletes the subscription |
| `Failed { status, message }` | Any other status, or a network error | Logs a warning. The message is the first 500 characters of the body. The subscription stays. |

A bad key or an oversized payload gives `Err(NotifyError)`. The server logs `push error` and goes on.

## Subscriptions

A subscription is the endpoint of a browser's push service and its two keys. The registry stores it in `push_subscriptions` with the columns `endpoint` (primary key), `p256dh`, `auth`, `workspace_id` (can be empty), and `created_at`. See [Storage](storage.md).

- `POST /api/push/subscribe` takes a `PushSubscription` (`endpoint`, `keys.p256dh`, `keys.auth`). It refuses an endpoint that does not start with `https://` and answers 400 `Push endpoints must use https.` It answers 204 after it stores the row.
- `add_push_subscription` inserts the row, or updates the keys and the workspace when the endpoint exists. Thus one browser has one row.
- The subscribe route stores `workspace_id` as empty. An empty value means that the browser gets the notices of every workspace. The store also supports a row that is scoped to one workspace.
- `remove_workspace` deletes the rows that are scoped to that workspace.
- `list_push_subscriptions` returns the rows ordered by `created_at` and `endpoint`.

## Which events send a notice

`push_for` in `crates/ostra-engine/src/runner.rs` builds a `Notice` for these session events. The engine does not decide whether push is on.

| Event | Title | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GateOpened` | The gate title | `gate-<session>` |
| `SessionCompleted` | `Session complete` | `done-<session>` |
| `SessionFailed` | `Session stopped` | `done-<session>` |
| `PhaseBlocked` | `Phase <phase> is blocked` | `blocked-<session>-<phase>` |
| `ContainmentSignal`, when the count of signals for the contained execution reaches 3 (`PAUSE_AFTER`) | `Session paused` | `contained-<session>` |

A `GateOpened` event in YOLO mode sends no notice, except for a harness failure, because the user must log in to the harness. The body of a gate notice is `<Harness> needs you to log in.` for a harness failure, the reason for a permission gate, and `A step is waiting for your decision.` for other gates. Notices with the same tag replace each other in the browser, so a session shows one notice for its gate or its end.

The deep link is `/s/<session>`. `ServerServices::notify` in `crates/ostra-server/src/services.rs` adds the prefix `/w/<workspace>`. The `Services` trait in `crates/ostra-engine/src/services.rs` declares `notify`, and the runner calls it through the trait.

### Diagram: from a session event to a browser notice

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Runner as Engine runner
    participant Svc as ServerServices::notify
    participant Reg as Registry
    participant N as Notifier
    participant PS as Push service
    participant SW as Service worker
    Runner->>Svc: Notice from push_for
    Svc->>Reg: list_push_subscriptions
    Svc->>N: send(subscription, Notification)
    N->>PS: POST endpoint, aes128gcm body, VAPID header
    PS-->>N: 201 or 404/410
    PS->>SW: push event
    SW->>SW: showNotification(title, body, tag)
```

`ServerServices::notify` first reads `notifications.push` from the settings of the workspace. If it is `false`, it returns. The default is `true`. The setting applies to every subscribed browser, and a change takes effect for the next notice. Then it starts a background task, so the engine does not wait. The task sends to each matching subscription one after the other. A subscription matches when its `workspace_id` is empty or equals the current workspace.

## The browser side

`web/src/lib/push.ts` has the browser code, and `web/src/screens/workspace/SettingsSections.tsx` shows it in Settings, Notifications.

`enablePush` runs these steps:

1. It stops with a message if the browser lacks `serviceWorker`, `PushManager`, or `Notification` (`pushSupported`).
2. It asks for the notification permission. If the user does not grant it, the message is `Notifications are blocked for this site. Allow them in the browser's site settings.`
3. It reads `vapid_public_key` from `GET /api/info`. If it is empty, the message is `The server has no push key configured.`
4. It registers `/sw.js` and reuses the existing push subscription, or it subscribes with `userVisibleOnly: true` and the key as `applicationServerKey`.
5. It sends the endpoint and the keys to `POST /api/push/subscribe`.

`disablePush` calls `unsubscribe` in the browser only. It does not call the server. The row stays in `push_subscriptions` until the next send gets 404 or 410 from the push service, and then the server deletes it.

The service worker in `web/public/sw.js` handles two events:

- `push`: it reads the JSON payload. If the payload is not JSON, the body is its text. The title defaults to `Ostra`. It shows the notice with the tag, the icon `/favicon.svg`, and the `url` in its data.
- `notificationclick`: it closes the notice. If a window of the same origin is open, it focuses that window and navigates to the deep link. Otherwise it opens a new window.

### What happens when (push)

- **`notifications.push` is `false`.** No notice is sent for that workspace.
- **The push service answers 404 or 410.** The subscription is deleted.
- **The push service answers another error, or the network fails.** The server logs a warning, keeps the subscription, and sends the next notice to it again.
- **The browser sends the same endpoint again.** The row is updated. No second row appears.
- **The endpoint is not https.** The subscribe route answers 400.
- **The payload exceeds 3993 bytes.** `NotifyError::TooLarge`. The server logs the error.
- **The VAPID key cannot be read at start.** The server makes a new key. A browser subscription belongs to the key that created it, so users must enable push again if the push service refuses old subscriptions. The code does not delete such rows on a refusal other than 404 or 410.
- **The user disables push in the browser.** The server learns this only from a later 404 or 410.
- **The browser is closed.** The push service holds the message for up to 24 hours (`TTL`) and delivers it when the browser connects.

## What this design does not guarantee

- A tool of an MCP server is not safe because Ostra checks its name. The server decides what the tool does. Ostra allows it by default (Rule M1), and the user must write deny or ask rules for risky tools.
- A remote MCP server receives the headers and the tokens that the user gives it. The same-origin redirect rule protects against a redirect to another host, not against a server that is hostile on its own origin.
- A local server runs under the agent sandbox, but it can still use the files and the network that the sandbox allows. See [Sandbox and egress proxy](sandbox.md).
- The tool list is fixed for the whole execution. A tool that a server adds later is not available to a harness that already started.
- Push delivery is not guaranteed. The push service can drop a message, and the server does not retry a failed send.
- A push notice shows the title and the body that Ostra builds from session events, so these texts can include the gate reason or the session summary. The push service cannot read them, because the body is encrypted for the browser.
- Ostra sends a notice to every subscribed browser. It does not check which user owns the browser.
- Two tool names of one server can map to one bare name when their 32-bit hashes collide. The chance is small, but the code does not check for it.
