sections.title: The design system
sections.summary: The `design/` package: tokens, the seven component groups, the focus and keyboard helpers, the documentation renderer, the Gallery, and the rules for use from `web/`.
sections.body:
The `design/` package holds the tokens, the React components, the documentation renderer, and the Gallery that the web console uses. This page lists each part, its rules, and how `web/` uses it.

## Why the design system exists

The console needs one look and one set of interaction rules for every screen. Without a shared package, each screen picks its own colors, spacing, focus handling, and keyboard keys, and the screens drift apart. The `design/` package (`@ostra/design`) removes this problem. It holds the tokens (CSS variables), the React components that use them, a renderer for Markdown documentation, and a Gallery that shows every component.

The package has no server code and makes no network call. Each component gets data through props. The `FolderPicker` shows the rule: it does not call the server, it takes a `list` function from the caller. The `web/` package supplies the data. See [The web console](web-console.md) for the screens.

This page covers:

- The entry points of the package and its dependencies.
- The tokens: colors, spacing, typography, effects, and the base styles.
- The seven component groups: brand, core, data, feedback, forms, navigation, and pipeline.
- The shared focus and keyboard helpers.
- The documentation renderer: `Docs`, `Markdown`, and `Diagram`.
- The Gallery.
- The rules for use from `web/`, and the tests.

## Package layout and entry points

The package is private and has the version `0.1.0` and the license MIT. The file `design/package.json` sets `exports`, so a consumer imports only the names in this table. The package ships TypeScript source. It has no build step, and the consumer's bundler (Vite) compiles it.

| Import | File | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@ostra/design` | `design/src/index.ts` | Every component, type, and helper. It also loads `index.css` as a side effect. |
| `@ostra/design/index.css` | `design/src/index.css` | Fonts, tokens, base styles, component classes, and the brand styles. |
| `@ostra/design/gallery` | `design/src/Gallery.tsx` | The Gallery page (default export). |
| `@ostra/design/docs` | `design/src/docs/index.ts` | The documentation renderer: `Docs`, `Markdown`, `Diagram`, and helpers. |
| `@ostra/design/docs.css` | `design/src/docs/docs.css` | The styles of the renderer. |
| `@ostra/design/docs-standalone.css` | `design/src/docs/standalone.css` | The renderer styles with the color, type, and spacing tokens, and no fonts. |

The source folders are:

- `design/src/tokens/`: the CSS token files, the base styles, and the component classes.
- `design/src/components/<group>/`: one folder for each component group.
- `design/src/docs/`: the documentation renderer.
- `design/src/cx.ts`, `focus.ts`, and `keys.ts`: the shared helpers.
- `design/src/*.test.tsx`: the tests.

The runtime dependencies are `lucide-react` (icons), `@fontsource/ibm-plex-sans` and `@fontsource/jetbrains-mono` (fonts), `mermaid` (diagrams), and `mdast-util-from-markdown`, `mdast-util-gfm`, `mdast-util-to-string`, and `micromark-extension-gfm` (the Markdown parser). `react` and `react-dom` at version `^19.3.0` are peer dependencies.

The root `package.json` lists `design`, `web`, and `site` as npm workspaces. This checkout has no `site/` folder. The description in `design/package.json` says the console (`web/`) and the site (`site/`) share the package.

## Tokens and themes

A token is a CSS custom property on `:root`. The file `design/src/index.css` imports the token files in a fixed order: `fonts.css`, `colors.css`, `typography.css`, `spacing.css`, `effects.css`, `base.css`, and `components.css`. Then it imports `components/brand/brand.css`. The header of `index.css` says that the files under `tokens/` are copied verbatim from the Claude Design project, except `fonts.css`, which loads bundled fonts instead of Google Fonts.

### Themes

Dark is the default theme. The `:root` block in `colors.css` holds the dark values and sets `color-scheme: dark`. The block `[data-theme="light"]` overrides the semantic tokens and sets `color-scheme: light`. To switch to the light theme, set `data-theme="light"` on the `<html>` element. The value `dark` also works, because it matches no override. The effects file overrides `--shadow-popover` and `--shadow-dialog` for the light theme too.

### Colors

The color tokens have two layers:

- **Base tokens** hold raw values. They are the warm gray scale `--gray-950` to `--gray-10` and `--white`, the Ostra blue scale `--blue-200` to `--blue-950`, and four status hues (green, amber, red, and violet) with the steps 400, 700, 900, and 50.
- **Semantic tokens** name a role and point to a base token. A component uses only semantic tokens. The light theme changes the target of each semantic token.

The semantic groups are:

| Group | Tokens | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Surfaces | `--surface-chrome`, `--surface-panel`, `--surface-editor`, `--surface-raised`, `--surface-sunken`, `--surface-overlay`, `--surface-terminal`, `--surface-hover`, `--surface-active`, `--surface-selected`, `--surface-scrim` | Title bar and docks, sidebar, center pane, cards, code blocks and inputs, popovers and dialogs, terminal, and interaction states. |
| Borders | `--border-subtle`, `--border-default`, `--border-strong`, `--border-focus` | Dividers, outlines, and the focus color. |
| Text | `--text-primary`, `--text-secondary`, `--text-muted`, `--text-disabled`, `--text-on-accent`, `--text-link` | Text roles. |
| Accent and status | `--accent`, `--accent-hover`, `--accent-soft`, `--accent-fg`, `--ok`, `--warn`, `--bad`, `--info`, and the `-soft` form of each status | The one accent and the four status tones. |
| Code and diff | `--code-bg`, `--diff-add-bg`, `--diff-add-fg`, `--diff-del-bg`, `--diff-del-fg`, `--syntax-keyword`, `--syntax-string`, `--syntax-number`, `--syntax-fn`, `--syntax-comment` | Code views and diffs. |
| Terminal | `--term-bg`, `--term-bar`, `--term-border`, `--term-fg`, `--term-muted`, `--term-blue`, `--term-green`, `--term-red`, `--term-amber`, `--term-cursor` | The harness terminal. |

The `--term-*` tokens are always dark. The light block does not override them, because the terminal shows the raw output of a harness CLI in both themes.

### Spacing and sizes

The file `spacing.css` defines the scale `--space-0` (0px), `--space-0-5` (2px), `--space-1` (4px), `--space-1-5` (6px), `--space-2` (8px), `--space-2-5` (10px), `--space-3` (12px), `--space-3-5` (14px), `--space-4` (16px), `--space-5` (20px), `--space-6` (24px), `--space-8` (32px), `--space-10` (40px), and `--space-12` (48px). It also defines the control and chrome sizes:

| Token | Value |
| --- | --- |

### Typography

The file `typography.css` sets two font stacks: `--font-sans` (IBM Plex Sans, then system fonts) and `--font-mono` (JetBrains Mono, then system monospace fonts). The UI base size is 13px (`--text-base`) because the console is dense like an editor. Prose reads at 14px (`--text-md`). The scale is `--text-2xs` 10.5px, `--text-xs` 11.5px, `--text-sm` 12px, `--text-base` 13px, `--text-md` 14px, `--text-lg` 16px, `--text-xl` 20px, `--text-2xl` 26px, and `--text-code` 12.5px.

The weights are `--weight-regular` 400, `--weight-medium` 500, and `--weight-semibold` 600. The leading values are `--leading-tight` 1.25, `--leading-normal` 1.45, and `--leading-relaxed` 1.6. The file also defines six role shorthands for the CSS `font` property: `--type-ui`, `--type-prose`, `--type-title`, `--type-heading`, `--type-label`, and `--type-code`.

The file `fonts.css` declares the `@font-face` rules for IBM Plex Sans (400, 500, 600, and 400 italic) and JetBrains Mono (400, 500, 600). The fonts are bundled from the `@fontsource` packages as woff2 files, because Ostra runs offline and cannot load Google Fonts. Each subset has a `unicode-range`, so the browser fetches only the subsets that a page needs.

### Effects and motion

The file `effects.css` sets the radii: `--radius-xs` 3px, `--radius-sm` 4px, `--radius-md` 6px, `--radius-lg` 8px, and `--radius-pill` 999px. Its comment states the elevation rule: borders come first, and shadows appear only on floating layers. The floating layers use `--shadow-popover` and `--shadow-dialog`. The focus ring is `--ring-focus`.

The motion tokens are `--ease-out`, `--ease-in-out`, `--dur-instant` (60ms), `--dur-fast` (100ms), `--dur-base` (160ms), and `--dur-slow` (240ms).

### Base styles and animations

`base.css` sets `box-sizing: border-box`, the body font and colors, link colors, the monospace font for `code`, `kbd`, `pre`, and `samp`, the selection color, and the scrollbar. It also sets the global focus style: `:focus-visible` removes the outline and applies `--ring-focus`. Every focusable element therefore shows the same ring.

The file defines the keyframes `os-pulse`, `os-spin`, `os-fade-in`, `os-scrim-in`, `os-dialog-in`, `os-slide-in-right`, `os-slide-in-left`, and `os-rise`. When the user sets `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, the rule at the end of `base.css` sets every animation and transition duration to 1ms with `!important`.

### Component classes

The file `components.css` holds the CSS of every component. Each class starts with `os-` and follows the BEM pattern, for example `os-btn--primary` and `os-panel__head`. The React components render these classes. The header of the file says that plain HTML can use the classes too. The file has sections for buttons, kbd, inputs, checkbox and radio, switch, chip, status dot, spinner, banner, tabs, tree item, breadcrumbs, panel, table, the lane stepper, stage row, phase node, tool call, gate, decision, terminal, execution group, menu, dialog, stepper, folder picker, and code view. It ends with the step-transition classes `os-enter-forward`, `os-enter-back`, and `os-rise`.

## Component groups

Each component lives in `design/src/components/<group>/` and has an exported `...Props` type. The tables below list the public props that change behavior. Use the prop comments in the source for the full list.

### Brand

`LiveMark` draws the Ostra mark as an SVG: a rounded tile with eight arcs and a center pearl. The eight arcs stand for the board lanes from research to docs. The state is a `MarkState` value: `{ arcs: MarkArc[]; pearl: MarkPearl | null }`.

- An arc is `done`, `run`, `wait`, `fail`, or `off`. A pearl is `run`, `wait`, `fail`, `ok`, `rest`, or `off`.
- `MARK_ARCS` is `8`. `REST` is eight `done` arcs with a `rest` pearl. `IDLE` is eight `off` arcs with no pearl.
- When an arc leaves `off`, it draws clockwise over an `off` track. The prop `draw` sets the draw time of one arc. The default is `0.32s`.
- An arc or pearl in the `run` state uses the `done` color and pulses through the class `live-mark-pulse` (1.4 seconds). The rule in `brand.css` stops the pulse for `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`.
- `LiveMark` has `size` (default `16`) and `label`. With `label`, the SVG has `role="img"`. Without it, the SVG is hidden from assistive technology.

`markSvg(state, theme)` returns the mark as a standalone SVG string for a favicon. A favicon cannot read CSS variables, so this function uses literal colors for the `dark` and `light` themes.

`Dialog` has these rules:

- The dialog renders in a portal on `document.body`. When it opens, it moves focus inside. It keeps Tab inside until it closes. After it closes, it restores the previous focus (`useFocusTrap`).

| `Input` | A text field or, with `multiline`, a textarea (3 rows by default). Props `label`, `hint`, `error`, `icon`, `mono`, `size`, and `trailing`. When `error` is set, the border is red, `aria-invalid` is set, and the error text replaces the hint. |

The `Combobox` does not filter. The caller passes `items` that already match the query. The list shows only when the field has focus, the query is not empty, and there is at least one item or the `loading` prop is false. Arrow keys move the highlight, Enter picks the highlighted item, and Escape closes the list. When no item is highlighted, Enter calls `onSubmit`. The `empty` text defaults to `No matches`.

`FolderPicker` has two modes:

- **List mode.** The caller passes a `list` function of the type `FolderLister`. The picker lists the directory part of the typed path and waits `debounceMs` (default 120 ms) before each request. It aborts a request that a newer one replaces. The shape of a listing is `FolderListing`, which matches the response of `GET /api/fs`. See [Server, REST API, and WebSocket](server-and-api.md).
- **Controlled mode.** Without `list`, the caller passes `browsePath`, `entries`, `parent`, `missing`, and `onBrowse`, and the caller loads the listing.

In both modes, the path field is also the selection. A path with a trailing separator means that the user browses the folder. A path without one is the chosen folder. These keys apply: Tab completes the highlighted match, the arrow keys move the highlight, Enter uses the folder, and Backspace after a separator goes up one folder. A click opens a row, and a double click selects it. A name filter shows names that start with the typed text first, then names that contain it.

When the `mkdir` prop is set and the typed folder does not exist, the picker offers a `Create` row. This is like `mkdir -p`, because it also creates the missing parents. When the folder is missing, the picker shows an error row, disables `Use this folder`, and offers the nearest existing folder. When the typed text is not an absolute path, the field shows an error.

The file exports path helpers for POSIX and Windows paths: `isWindowsPath`, `isAbsolutePath`, `endsWithSep`, `trimSep`, `withSep`, `baseName`, and `splitPath`. A Windows path starts with a drive letter, or with `~` when the home folder is a Windows path. Both `\` and `/` separate its parts. A bare drive such as `C:` filters the list of drives.

| Component | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `Tabs` | A tab strip with the variants `underline` (default), `bar`, and `segmented`. |

`Tabs` rules:

- Only the selected tab is a tab stop. Arrow keys, Home, and End move the focus and select the tab. The movement wraps at the ends.
- The `italic` field of a tab renders the label in italic in every variant. The comment in the source calls an italic tab a preview tab.
- The `bar` variant makes editor tabs. Only this variant adds a close button (and the Delete key) with `onClose`, and a pin button with `onUnpin` for a pinned tab.
- Reorder works only in the `bar` variant with `onMove`. The tabs become draggable, and Ctrl+Shift+Left or Right (or Cmd+Shift) moves the focused tab. `onMove` gets the index where the tab must end.
- `revealSelectedTab(strip)` scrolls only the strip, not its ancestors, because `scrollIntoView` also scrolls every ancestor, including a page that frames the console.

`Menu` rules: place it in a `position: relative` wrapper next to its trigger. On open, focus moves to the first item. Arrow keys, Home, and End move the focus. Enter or Space selects the item and closes the menu. Escape and Tab close it. A click on the scrim closes it. On close, the menu restores the previous focus only if focus fell to the body, so it does not take focus back from a user who moved it. An item can have `checked` (a radio item), `danger`, `kbd`, `hint`, and `indent`. `ContextMenu` keeps the menu inside the viewport with an 8px margin. The default width is 220.

`CommandPalette` rules: the caller controls `open`. The palette renders in a portal and traps focus. The default filter keeps the items whose label, hint, or group contains the query, in the original order (`filterPaletteItems`). The caller can replace the filter with `filterItems` and can search a server with `onQueryChange`. Items must be sorted by group, because the palette prints a group header when the group changes. Escape or a scrim click closes the palette and returns focus to the previous element.

`TreeItem` indents each level by 14px. Pass `expanded` to show a chevron. The keys are Enter and Space (activate), Right on a collapsed row and Left on an expanded row (toggle), and Up and Down (move to the neighbor row in the same tree, without wrap). `FileTree` renders rows only. The caller puts it inside an element with `role="tree"`, loads each open folder, and answers `folder(dir)`. It lists folders before files and sorts each by name. When a folder loads, it shows `Reading…`. It supports drag and drop through `dropEffect` and `onDrop`, a context menu, and an inline field for a new file or folder (`NewEntryField`). In that field, Enter creates the entry, and Escape or an empty blur cancels. `fileIcon(path)` picks an icon by file extension, and `parentDir(path)` returns the folder of a `/`-separated path.

## Focus and keyboard helpers

Three small modules give every component the same keyboard behavior. All three are exported from the package.

| Helper | File | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cx(...parts)` | `design/src/cx.ts` | Joins class names and drops falsy parts. |
| `useFocusTrap(ref, active, initial?)` | `design/src/focus.ts` | When `active` becomes true, it moves focus into the container (the `initial` element, else the first focusable element, else the container). It returns a keydown handler that wraps Tab inside the container. When `active` ends, it restores the previous focus. |
| `focusables(root)` | `design/src/focus.ts` | Lists the focusable elements of a container and skips elements inside `[inert]`. |
| `arrowIndex(key, index, count, orientation, wrap = true)` | `design/src/focus.ts` | Returns the next index for the arrow keys, Home, and End. It returns `null` for any other key. |
| `activateOnKey(fn)` | `design/src/keys.ts` | Returns a keydown handler that runs `fn` on Enter or Space. It ignores events from child elements. Use it for a clickable element with `role="button"`. |

`Dialog` and `CommandPalette` use `useFocusTrap`. `Menu`, `Tabs`, `LaneStepper`, and `TreeItem` use `arrowIndex`. `StageRow`, `PhaseNode`, `ExecutionGroup`, and `ToolCall` use `activateOnKey`. The tests check these rules, for example that Tab stays inside a dialog and that focus returns to the opener.

## Documentation renderer

The books that Ostra writes are Markdown. The renderer in `design/src/docs/` shows them in the console and in an exported HTML file. It has three parts: the `Docs` class (the model), the `Markdown` component, and the `Diagram` component. The comment in `docs/index.ts` says that the site's docs and the console's documentation books share it. See [Documentation books](documentation-books.md) for how the server writes a book.

### Flow from sources to the screen

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["NavGroup list and sources"] --> B["new Docs"]
  B --> C["parseMarkdown"]
  C --> D["pickSection and build Page"]
  D --> E["indexAnchors and indexSearch"]
  E --> F["Markdown component"]
  F --> G["Diagram for a mermaid fence"]
```

### The `Docs` model

The constructor is `new Docs(nav, sources, fileUrl?)`. The `nav` is a list of `NavGroup` values (`{ label, pages }`). Each `PageDef` has an `id`, a `title`, a `file` (a key in `sources`), and an optional `section`. The `sources` object maps each file key to Markdown text. If a `file` is not in `sources`, the constructor throws an error.

The constructor works in these steps:

1. It parses each source file once with `parseMarkdown`. The parser is `mdast-util-from-markdown` with the GFM extensions.
2. For each page, `pickSection` selects the blocks. Without `section`, the page is the whole file. A `section` value selects one `##` part, by its number (`"8"` matches `## 8. The engine`) or by its exact text. An empty string selects the text before the first `##`.
3. If the first block is a heading, the model drops it. It becomes the page title, and its depth is `titleLevel`.
4. The model gives each heading an id with `slug`. A repeated id gets the suffix `-2`, `-3`, and so on. The headings one level below the title form the table of contents.
5. `indexAnchors` builds the global anchor map. The title of a page and its section heading come first, then each heading id. The first owner of an id wins.
6. `indexSearch` builds the search index with one entry for each page title, heading, and text block.

The model has these public methods:

| Method | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| `page(id)` | Returns the page or `undefined`. |
| `fromHash(hash)` | Reads `#page/anchor`, or a bare anchor from an older link. It decodes the escapes. An unknown value opens the first page. |
| `link(href, page)` | Resolves a Markdown link. See the next list. |
| `search(query)` | Case-insensitive substring search. See the next list. |

The link rules are:

- A link that starts with `http:`, `https:`, or `mailto:` is external.
- A link with any other scheme, such as `javascript:` or `data:`, gives `null`, and the renderer shows plain text.
- A link with a path resolves against the folder of the current page file (`resolvePath`). If the file is a page of the docs, the link goes to that page and the optional anchor. If not, the link uses `fileUrl(file)`. The default `fileUrl` returns `null`, so the link renders as plain text.
- A link with only an anchor first looks in the headings of the current page, then in the global anchors.

The search rules are:

- It makes one hit for each page section: a page title, a heading, or a text block under a heading.
- It sorts the hits by rank: titles first, then headings, then text. The limit is `MAX_HITS`, which is `80`.
- Each hit holds 48 characters before the match and 90 characters after it, with `…` where it cuts the text.
- Table cells are kept apart with ` · ` in the searchable text (`blockText`).

This search is a simple substring match in the browser. The server has a separate BM25 search for agents. See [Documentation books](documentation-books.md).

### The `Markdown` component

`Markdown` takes `docs`, `page`, `go`, `theme`, and an optional `images` map. It converts the blocks of the page to React elements: headings, paragraphs, code, quotes, lists (with task checkboxes), tables, footnotes, and rules. It uses the classes `md-*` from `docs.css`.

- **Headings.** The level is relative to the dropped title: the first level below it renders as `h2`, the next as `h3`, and deeper levels use `h4` styles. The tag never goes past `h6`.
- **Code.** A fence with the language `mermaid` renders as a `Diagram`. Other fences render as `pre` with `code`.
- **Raw HTML.** The renderer drops raw HTML, except `<br>`. The SVG that Mermaid draws is the only other markup.
- **Images.** Only an image in the `images` map renders. The key is the source path that `resolvePath` makes from the page file. Any other image becomes a link with the text `Image: <alt>`. This follows the console rule that pages load no image from another origin.
- **Links.** An internal link calls `go(target)` on a plain left click. A click with Cmd, Ctrl, or Shift, or with another button, uses the browser default. An external link opens in a new tab with `rel="noreferrer"`.

### The `Diagram` component

`Diagram` draws a Mermaid block as SVG. It loads the `mermaid` package with a dynamic `import`, so a page without a diagram does not load it. The component sets these options on each render:

- `securityLevel: "strict"` and `htmlLabels: false`, so labels are SVG text and a diagram cannot carry an image or HTML.
- A `secure` list (`secure`, `securityLevel`, `startOnLoad`, `maxTextSize`, `suppressErrorRendering`, `maxEdges`, and `htmlLabels`), so the directives and the frontmatter of a diagram cannot change these keys.
- The theme `dark` for the dark console and `neutral` for the light console.

After the render, the component replaces each link in the SVG with its children, so a `click` line cannot make a link. If a block does not parse, the component shows its source in a `pre` element. If the source or the theme changes during a render, the component ignores the old result. The page writers must keep diagrams within the size limits that [Documentation books](documentation-books.md) states.

### Styles of the renderer

`docs.css` holds the classes for the reader layout (`docs-nav`, `docs-article`, `docs-toc`, `docs-pager`, and `docs-hit`) and for the Markdown blocks (`md-*`). The file `standalone.css` imports `colors.css`, `typography.css`, `spacing.css`, and `docs.css`, and no fonts, because an exported HTML file loads nothing. The console inlines this file into an exported book with the `?inline` import.

## The Gallery

The Gallery (`design/src/Gallery.tsx`) is a page that shows every component in its variants. It is the visual check for a change to the package. Its header comment calls it a dev-only gallery, translated from the design's cards.

The page has a title, a segmented `Tabs` control that switches the theme between dark and light, and seven cards in this order:

1. **Core:** `Button`, `IconButton`, `Kbd`, and `Icon`.
2. **Forms:** `Input`, `Select`, `Checkbox`, `Switch`, and `FolderPicker`, with a fake file system for both picker modes.
3. **Feedback:** `Chip`, `StatusChip`, `StatusDot`, `Spinner`, `Banner`, and `Dialog`.
4. **Navigation:** `Tabs`, `TreeItem`, `FileTree`, `Breadcrumbs`, `Menu`, `ContextMenu`, `Stepper`, and `CommandPalette`.
5. **Data:** `Panel`, `SectionLabel`, `Table`, and `CodeView`.
6. **Pipeline:** `LaneStepper`, `StageRow`, `PhaseDag`, `ToolCall`, `GateCard`, `Decision`, `ExecutionGroup`, and `Terminal`.
7. **Icons:** every name in `ICON_NAMES`, with the count.

The theme control writes `data-theme` on the `<html>` element. For the light theme it sets `light`, and for the dark theme it deletes the attribute. The Gallery has its own `gx-*` styles in a `<style>` element. The web console serves the Gallery at the route `/_design`, only when `import.meta.env.DEV` is true. The route loads the Gallery with a lazy import of `@ostra/design/gallery`, so a production build does not route to it. Run `npm run dev` in `web/` (or `npm run dev:mock` for the mock API) and open `/_design`.

## Rules for use from web

The console imports the package as `@ostra/design`. These rules come from how `web/` and the package fit together.

- **Load the styles once.** `web/src/main.tsx` imports `@ostra/design/index.css`. The documentation screen imports `@ostra/design/docs.css`. Do not import a token file by path.
- **Import from the package entry.** Import components, types, and helpers from `@ostra/design`. Many files in `web/src` do this. A name that the entry does not export is not public.
- **Read colors from variables.** Use `var(--surface-panel)` and the other semantic tokens in a style. Do not write a hex color, because the light theme changes the semantic tokens and cannot change a literal color.
- **Set the theme on the root element.** `web/src/lib/theme.ts` calls `applyTheme`, which sets `data-theme` on `<html>` and stores the choice in `localStorage` under the key `ostra.theme`. `resolveTheme` follows the system setting when nothing is stored.
- **Pass backend values as they are.** `StatusChip` and `statusTone` take the raw status strings of the backend, so a screen does not repeat the mapping. A new backend status needs a change in `StatusChip.tsx`. Until then, it shows as a `neutral` chip.
- **Keep data out of the components.** A component gets props and callbacks. A screen loads the data, calls the API, and passes the result in.
- **Pass the theme to the renderer.** `Markdown` and `Diagram` take `theme` as a prop, because Mermaid sets its own colors.
- **Build from the root.** `build.sh` rebuilds `web/dist` when a file under `design/src` or `design/package.json` is newer than `web/dist/index.html`. The `Dockerfile` copies `design/` and `design/package.json`, because `web/` builds against the package.

When you add a component, follow the pattern of the existing code. Put the file in the folder of its group. Add the `os-` classes to `tokens/components.css`. Export the component and its `Props` type from `index.ts`. Add a case to the matching Gallery card. Add a test when the component has keyboard or focus behavior.

## Tests and commands

The package has its own scripts in `design/package.json`. Run them in the `design/` folder. The cargo commands do not run them.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run test` | Runs `vitest run` in a `jsdom` environment on `src/**/*.test.ts` and `src/**/*.test.tsx`. |
| `npm run typecheck` | Runs `tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.json`. |
| `npm run lint` | Runs `biome lint`. |
| `npm run check` | Runs `biome check`. The command `npm run check:fix` writes the fixes. |

The three test files cover behavior that a user feels:

- `forms.test.tsx`: `Switch`, `Checkbox`, `Input`, `splitPath` and the path helpers, `FolderPicker` in both modes, and `Combobox`.
- `feedback.test.tsx`: `Dialog` (close paths, no `onClose`, focus trap and restore, inline mode), the `StatusChip` mapping, and `Icon`.
- `navigation.test.tsx`: `CommandPalette`, `Tabs` (selection, arrows, close, reorder), `Menu`, and `TreeItem`.

The package has no test for `docs/`. The model of the book in `web/src/features/docs/bookModel.test.ts` tests the book pages that feed the renderer. See [Tests and evals](testing.md) for all test layers.

### What the package does not do

- It does not guarantee a safe diagram or Markdown source by itself. The safety comes from the renderer rules above: no raw HTML, strict Mermaid, and no image from another origin. The exported HTML file adds its own policy in `web/src/features/docs/exportHtml.ts`.
- It does not check that a screen uses tokens. A screen can still write a literal color.
- It does not load data and does not know the server API, except the listing shape of `FolderListing`.

The os- component classes for every component.

sections.title: Tests and evals
sections.summary: The test layers of Ostra, what each one proves, what it needs, and the command that runs it: cargo tests, conformance fixtures, e2e server tests, model evals, the browser security suite, Vitest suites, and the Windows probes.
sections.body:
Ostra has parts that one kind of test cannot check. The planner is a pure function of an event history. The server is a real HTTP listener with an engine behind it. The console renders text that an agent or a repository wrote. The sandbox depends on the operating system. The judges and agents depend on a live model. For this reason the repository has several test layers. Each layer answers one question and has its own cost, its own needs, and its own command.

This page lists the layers, shows how to run each one, and states what each one proves. The page also states what a layer does not prove. For the commands that build the project, see [install-and-run.md](install-and-run.md).

## The test layers in one table

| Layer | Where it lives | What it needs | Cost | Command |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cargo unit tests | `#[cfg(test)]` modules in `crates/*/src` | Rust toolchain | None | `cargo test --workspace` |
| Cargo integration tests | `crates/<crate>/tests/` | Rust toolchain, `git` for some | None | `cargo test -p <crate> --test <file>` |
| Engine conformance fixtures | `tests/conformance/main.rs` | Rust toolchain | None | `cargo test -p ostra-engine --test conformance` |
| E2E server tests | `crates/ostra-server/tests/e2e.rs` | Rust toolchain, `git` | None | `cargo test -p ostra-server --test e2e` |
| Model evals | `tests/evals/*.toml` and `crates/ostra-server/tests/*_evals.rs` | Model credentials | Paid model calls | `cargo test -p ostra-server --test <name> -- --ignored --nocapture` |
| Browser security suite | `tests/browser` | Node, Chromium, a built `ostra` binary | None | `cd tests/browser && npm test` |
| Web and design Vitest suites | `web/src`, `design/src` | Node | None | `cd web && npm test`, `cd design && npm test` |
| Windows sandbox probes | `tests/windows-probes` | A throwaway Windows VM | None | Manual, see below |

The command `cargo test --workspace` runs the first four layers. It also runs the offline checks of the model evals. It skips every test that carries `#[ignore]`, because those tests need a live service. The browser suite, the Vitest suites, and the Windows probes are not part of `cargo test`. The Windows probes are not even part of the Cargo workspace.

The format command is `cargo fmt --all`. Run it before you commit Rust code.

## Run the cargo tests

Run the whole Rust test set with this command:

```bash
cargo test --workspace
```

To run one crate, pass its name. To run one integration file, add `--test` and the file name without `.rs`. To run one test, add a name filter after `--`:

```bash
cargo test -p ostra-policy
cargo test -p ostra-server --test e2e
cargo test -p ostra-engine --test conformance -- d1_
```

### Unit tests

Unit tests sit in `#[cfg(test)]` modules next to the code they check. 105 source files under `crates/*/src` hold such a module. These tests need no network and no model. Crates that have no `tests/` folder, such as `ostra-tools`, `ostra-agents`, `ostra-notify`, `ostra-workspace`, `ostra-exec-native`, and `ostra-exec-harness`, have only unit tests.

### Integration tests per crate

An integration test is a file in `crates/<crate>/tests/`. It uses the crate through its public API. These files exist:

| Crate | Files | What they check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ostra-code` | `graph.rs`, `graph_ostra.rs`, `index.rs`, `lsp.rs`, `outline.rs`, `usages.rs` | The index, outlines, the dependency graph, usages, and the LSP provider against an in-process fake server over a pipe |
| `ostra-engine` | `conformance` (from `tests/conformance`), `pause.rs`, `recover.rs`, `runner.rs` | The planner, pause and resume, restart recovery, and the runner. See the sections below |
| `ostra-mcp` | `client.rs` | The MCP client against fake servers: stdio, streamable HTTP with JSON, streamable HTTP with SSE, and a full OAuth sign-in |
| `ostra-policy` | `policy.rs` | Guard cases (scope, bash scope, artifacts, ledgers, reports) and the permission model |
| `ostra-providers` | `anthropic.rs`, `openai.rs`, `common/`, `fixtures/*.sse` | The streaming clients against recorded SSE streams that a local server replays |
| `ostra-sandbox` | `env_scrub.rs` | `scrub_startup_env` against `sysctl(KERN_PROCARGS2)`. The test runs on macOS only, in its own process, because the scrub rewrites the whole environment |
| `ostra-server` | `e2e.rs`, `mcp.rs`, four `*_evals.rs` files | The whole stack, MCP servers through the stack, and the model evals |
| `ostra-store` | `workspace_db.rs` | The workspace database: events, sessions, gates, and push subscriptions |

The test `graph_ostra.rs` reads Ostra's own source tree. It checks the graph against the crate layout that the repository guarantees. If you move a crate or add a dependency between crates in the wrong direction, this test fails. See [code-navigation.md](code-navigation.md) for the graph.

### Ignored live tests

Some tests call a real service or a real tool. They carry `#[ignore]`, so `cargo test --workspace` skips them. Run them on purpose with `-- --ignored`:

| Test | Command | What it needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `live_smoke` in `anthropic.rs` | `cargo test -p ostra-providers --test anthropic -- --ignored` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`. `OSTRA_LIVE_MODEL` sets the model (default `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`). If no provider is configured, the test passes, but `OSTRA_LIVE_REQUIRE` makes that case fail |
| `live_smoke` in `openai.rs` | `cargo test -p ostra-providers --test openai -- --ignored` | `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Without the key, the test returns at once |
| `live_rust_analyzer` in `lsp.rs` | `cargo test -p ostra-code --test lsp -- --ignored` | `rust-analyzer` on `PATH` |
| `live_gopls` and `live_gopls_into_the_standard_library` in `lsp.rs` | same command | `gopls` and `go` on `PATH` |

The model evals use the same `#[ignore]` rule. See the section on model evals.

### Generated TypeScript types

The file `.cargo/config.toml` sets `TS_RS_EXPORT_DIR` to `web/src/api/gen`. Types with `#[ts(export)]` write their TypeScript form there when you run `cargo test`. After you change such a type in Rust, run `cargo test` and commit the changed files in `web/src/api/gen`. The web console owns the use of these types. See [web-console.md](web-console.md).

## Engine conformance fixtures

The conformance fixtures prove that the planner follows the pipeline rules. The planner is the function `next_steps` in `ostra-engine`. It reads a `SessionState` and a `PlanCtx` and returns the next `Step` values. The sessions page owns the rules. See [sessions-and-pipeline.md](sessions-and-pipeline.md).

The file `tests/conformance/main.rs` holds 126 synchronous `#[test]` functions. The file lives outside the crate folder. The manifest `crates/ostra-engine/Cargo.toml` registers it:

```toml
[[test]]
name = "conformance"
path = "../../tests/conformance/main.rs"
```

Run the fixtures with `cargo test -p ostra-engine --test conformance`. Add a name filter to run one rule family, for example `-- hard21_` or `-- p3_`.

### How a fixture works

A fixture needs no database, no executor, and no model. It builds an event history, folds it, and checks the steps that the planner returns. The helper struct `H` does the work:

1. `H::new` records a `SessionCreated` event and sets the format command of each project in `PlanCtx`.
2. `H::ev` appends one `SessionEvent` to the history as a `StoredEvent` with the next `seq`.
3. `H::decide` appends a `DecisionMade` event with a scripted judge output. `H::start` finds a spawn step and appends the matching `ExecutionStarted` event.
4. `H::steps` folds the history and calls the planner:

```rust
fn state(&self) -> SessionState {
    SessionState::fold(self.id.clone(), &self.events)
}

fn steps(&self) -> Vec<Step> {
    next_steps(&self.state(), &self.ctx)
}
```

5. The test asserts on `Step::summary()` strings or on the fields of a `SpawnRequest`. `H::spawn_step` finds a spawn by the prefix of its summary and panics with all summaries if none matches.

The reason for this design: the session is an event log, and the planner is a function of the folded log. A test can state any state by writing events. It does not need to run an agent.

### Rule families that the fixtures cover

The module comment says that the file has one fixture per rule ID of the pipeline rules. The test names start with the rule ID. These families exist:

| Rule IDs | What the fixtures check |
| --- | --- |
| D1 to D10, M2 to M6 | Research leads to a spec and never straight to a plan. The spec waits for every research run and for the sufficiency judge. Open questions come before the fact-check. The plan reads only the spec. The scheduler runs phases by their dependencies. A failed phase removes its dependents. A requirement change after the plan restarts at the spec |
| T1 to T7, A1 | Format once, one closing gate for each project, and tests and docs only after the closing gate. An unapproved format command is skipped once |
| C1, C2, P1 to P3 | Context files and context delivery, pause, resume, and the containment pause after 3 signals. A resume continues the same execution and counts signals from zero |
| Hard 4, 13, 15, 16, 21 | A missing submit is a failure. Phase spawns carry the phase file. A blocker finding has no cap and blocks docs |
| Review, HANDOFF, STUCK | The review loop splits autofix and fix and stops at 3 rounds. A stuck run goes to rescue and never to a plain retry |
| YOLO | The engine answers gates, and the review budget rises to 10 |
| B1 to B7 | Documentation books: writers fan out under a cap, the architecture run needs two or more projects, and a book update replaces the part of its project |
| Cost controls, tracks, F1, F2 | The session budget pauses spawning, and YOLO never raises it. The light track is the default for IMPLEMENT, and the track judge can escalate it. The user reviews a finished phase until they accept it |
| O2 to O6 | A project that the approved plan creates joins the session, is initialized before anything else runs in it, and gets an advisor look at a failed init step |
| H1 to H9 | Subagent coordination. See [subagent-coordination.md](subagent-coordination.md) |

When you add a pipeline rule, add a fixture. Name the test with the rule ID and write the rule in a comment above it. Then a reader finds the test from the rule.

## Engine integration tests

Three files in `crates/ostra-engine/tests/` run a real `Engine`. They use an in-memory `WorkspaceDb`, a scripted executor, and scripted judges. A test struct implements the `Services` trait and returns mock tiers, so no model is called. See [engine-runner.md](engine-runner.md) for the runner.

| File | Tests | What it proves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `runner.rs` | 5 | An IMPLEMENT session runs to completion under YOLO. Init sessions notify project changes. Subagents wake each other and pair loops continue. A pinned session holds only its pinned projects. A docs session writes the book into the workspace |
| `pause.rs` | 8 | Pause, resume, containment, and mid-session context. A `Hanging` executor runs until cancelled and spends 1 dollar, and the test records the id, the resume info, and the capabilities of each run |
| `recover.rs` | 2 | Restart recovery. A running execution becomes interrupted, keeps what it spent, and its step runs again with the same spawn block |

## E2E server tests

The e2e tests prove that the whole stack works together. The file `crates/ostra-server/tests/e2e.rs` starts a real listener on `127.0.0.1` and uses REST with cookie sign-in. It runs the engine, the native loop, the policy, the tools, and git staging. A scripted model plays each agent. The model writes its files with the `Write` tool and then calls its `submit_<agent>` tool. The file has 24 async tests. Run them with `cargo test -p ostra-server --test e2e`.

### How the test server starts

The function `boot` starts a server and signs in. These steps happen:

1. The test sets `OSTRA_CONFIG`, `OSTRA_DATA_DIR`, `OSTRA_MASTER_KEY_FILE`, and `OSTRA_SANDBOX_CACHE` to paths under a temporary folder. It sets `OSTRA_MODELS_DEV_URL` to an empty string, so the server downloads no price catalog.
2. The test writes a `GlobalConfig` in which every tier of the `native` table is `mock:m`.
3. The test binds `127.0.0.1:0`, calls `ostra_server::app::build`, and registers a `ScriptedProvider` named `mock` with the function `respond`.
4. `respond` reads the tool list of each request. A request with the single tool `decide` is a judge call, and `judge` answers it from the schema. Any other request is an agent, and the `submit_*` tool name tells which one.
5. The test reads the sign-in URL, takes the token after `#token=`, and posts it to `/api/auth/exchange`. The client keeps the cookie and the test expects status 204.

### What the tests cover

The long test `yolo_implement_session_end_to_end` runs a whole IMPLEMENT session and then checks many API routes. Other tests cover these areas:

- The setup wizard, the onboarding flag, UI state, and provider credentials that the browser saves.
- Skills, uploads, artifacts, and documentation books through their routes.
- Git: cloning and pulling with a saved git credential, and the git dock (stage, commit, push, switch branch).
- The terminal over the socket, and the setup terminal for a harness login.
- Folder commands that run only after approval, and the rule that a new workspace needs no approval for its own commands.
- Sign-in sessions that the user lists and revokes, and the browser boundary that refuses page content and other sites.
- Private host names for a loopback server, and the rule that live or starting work blocks removing a project or a workspace.
- A project that an approved plan creates, initializes, and builds.
- A server start removes the tool caches of ended sessions and keeps every other cache.

The file `crates/ostra-server/tests/mcp.rs` covers workspace MCP servers through the stack: settings, discovery, the status API, OAuth sign-in through the browser callback, and a native agent that calls a server tool. See [mcp-and-notifications.md](mcp-and-notifications.md).

### What happens when

- **Two tests run at the same time.** They cannot. The server reads its config and data paths from the process environment. Each test locks the static `SERIAL` mutex before `boot` and holds it while its server runs.
- **A session does not reach the wanted state.** `wait_for` polls `GET /api/sessions/{id}` every 100 milliseconds. After 60 seconds it fails and prints the last status and stage label.
- **The test runs on Windows.** Tests that need Unix sockets or a PTY carry `#[cfg(unix)]`. The test `the_bridge_socket_serves_only_harness_callbacks` and the harness login test are examples. The file allows unused imports on other systems.

## Model evals

The evals measure how real models behave in the roles that Ostra gives them. A unit test cannot do this, because the answer of a model changes from run to run. An eval calls the model several times for each case and reports pass counts and cost. There are four evals. The first three roles and the judges are in [gates-and-judges.md](gates-and-judges.md) and [subagent-coordination.md](subagent-coordination.md).

| Eval | Case file | Test file | Cases | What it scores |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Judge routing | `tests/evals/judges.toml` | `judge_evals.rs` | 83 | The answer of a judge call: classify (23), feedback (16), route_answer (25), stakes (3), sufficiency (2), track (14) |
| Advisor | `tests/evals/advisor.toml` | `advisor_evals.rs` | 13 | The advisor agent on a failed init step of a created project: its action (`retry` or `escalate`), the facts its text names, and a grader verdict |
| Subagent coordination | `tests/evals/coordination.toml` | `coordination_evals.rs` | 11 | Live agent runs in a real engine session on a snapshot of Ostra's own source: questions, answers, statuses, submits, files, and cache reads |
| Test stage | `tests/evals/test_stage.toml` | `test_stage_evals.rs` | 13 | The execution path analyzer and `write-test` on small projects from `tests/evals/test_stage/` |

A case in `judges.toml` has an `id`, a `judge`, a `workspace`, a `request`, and an `expect` table. The `workspace` value is one of three names:

- `one`: Ostra as the single project `ostra`.
- `split`: the two projects `server` and `web`.
- `triple`: the three projects `server`, `web`, and `site`. 3 cases use it, and `judge_evals.rs` builds it.

The judge test builds the session state that the judge sees. It uses the same fold and `judge_input` as the engine.

### Run a live eval

Caution: a live eval calls paid models. Set `OSTRA_EVAL_CASES` and `OSTRA_EVAL_RUNS` to small values for a first run. The eval spends money for each model, each case, and each run, and also for the grader.

The live tests carry `#[ignore]`, so you must pass `--ignored`. Use `--nocapture` to see the table:

```bash
OSTRA_EVAL_MODELS=anthropic:claude-opus-5-5,anthropic:claude-sonnet-5-5 OSTRA_EVAL_RUNS=3 \
  cargo test -p ostra-server --test judge_evals -- --ignored --nocapture
```

The test names are `judge_routing_evals`, `advisor_evals`, `coordination_evals`, and `test_stage_evals`. The test files are `judge_evals`, `advisor_evals`, `coordination_evals`, and `test_stage_evals`. Each eval needs credentials for every provider in its model list.

### The OSTRA_EVAL variables

| Variable | Meaning | Default | Used by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `OSTRA_EVAL_MODELS` | Comma-separated model ids, each as `provider:model` | Judge: `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5`. Advisor: Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5. Coordination and test stage: Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and `anthropic:claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` | All four |
| `OSTRA_EVAL_RUNS` | Runs of each case for each model | Judge 3, advisor 5, coordination 3, test stage 3 | All four |
| `OSTRA_EVAL_CASES` | Case ids to run. A case runs if its id contains one of the comma-separated substrings | Empty: all cases | All four |
| `OSTRA_EVAL_TIERS` | Eval tiers to run, for example `1,2` | Empty: all tiers | Coordination, test stage |
| `OSTRA_EVAL_JOBS` | How many sessions or runs go at the same time | Advisor 4, coordination 3, test stage 3 | Advisor, coordination, test stage |
| `OSTRA_EVAL_GRADER` | The model that grades the rubric of a case | `anthropic:claude-opus-5-5` | Advisor, coordination, test stage |

An eval tier is not a model tier. It is the difficulty level of a case, from 1 to 3. In the coordination eval, tier 1 is answering, tier 2 is deciding whether to ask, and tier 3 is loops of several live runs. The coordination file has 4, 4, and 3 cases in tiers 1, 2, and 3. The test stage file has 3, 4, and 6.

### How an eval scores a run

Each eval first selects the cases, then runs each case `OSTRA_EVAL_RUNS` times for each model. The scoring differs by eval:

- **Judge routing:** a run passes when the judge answer matches the `expect` table of the case. The report shows accuracy, consistency, errors, and cost. A case is consistent when all runs gave one answer and none failed.
- **Advisor:** a run passes when the action matches, the text names every required fact, and the grader finds the rubric met. Cases come in pairs with the same surface problem and opposite answers, so an advisor that matches only the problem text fails one of them.
- **Coordination:** a run passes when every code check holds and the grader finds the rubric met. A router executor sends the runs that the case lists as `live` to the native loop on the model under test. It plays every other run from the case. The report includes the share of live input tokens that the prompt cache served.
- **Test stage:** an analyzer run passes when its report is at the declared path, it changed no project file, the report holds each expected fact, and the grader agrees. A `write-test` run passes when its status is the expected one, it changed only test files and listed all of them, each expected level got a test, the project tests pass, every planted mutant fails them, and the files that must stay keep their text.

Each eval prints a table and writes a report file in `target/evals/`. The judge report is `judges-<timestamp>.json`. The evals call providers through the cached models.dev price catalog when the server has one, so the cost column uses real prices.

### What happens when

- **A model answers differently on each run.** The eval does not fail. It reports the spread of answers. You read the report to judge the result.
- **Calls fail.** The judge eval fails only when every call failed, with the message `every judge call failed; check the provider credentials`. The advisor eval fails when every run failed to finish. The coordination eval fails when no live run finished. The test stage eval fails when no live run happened.
- **A case is broken.** The offline tests find it for free. See the next section.

### Offline checks of the evals

Each eval has a test without `#[ignore]` that runs in `cargo test --workspace`. These tests make sure that a broken case does not cost money later:

| Test | What it checks |
| --- | --- |
| `eval_cases_build_their_sessions` | Every judge case folds into the state its judge expects, and the judge input holds the request and the named facts |
| `advisor_cases_build_their_spawns` | Ids are unique, the action is `retry` or `escalate`, and the advisor spawn builds with the lines `Failed step:`, `Problem:`, `Step inputs:`, `Step context:`, and `Repo root:` |
| `coordination_cases_run_dry` | Every case parses and has a tier from 1 to 3. A replay with stand-ins for the live runs reaches each live run and stops where the case says. The snapshot must not contain the eval expectations |
| `test_stage_cases_run_dry` | Every case lays out, the project's own tests let every planted mutant survive, and the golden tests kill every mutant |

The test stage eval file has the attribute `#![cfg(unix)]`, because the project test commands run through `sh`.

## Browser security suite

The suite in `tests/browser` proves that the browser-facing defenses hold in a real Chromium. The risk is this: the console shows text that an agent, a repository, or a user wrote. If one render path runs that text as script, an attacker controls the console. The suite checks the render paths, the terminal, the cross-origin boundary, the sign-in token, uploads, and browser storage. It checks the console and the site (homepage and docs).

Run the suite with these commands:

```bash
cd tests/browser && npm install
npm test
```

`npm test` runs `playwright test`. Playwright is pinned at version 1.63.0 in `tests/browser/package.json`.

### What a run does

The file `tests/browser/global-setup.ts` prepares the world before any spec runs. Nothing leaves the machine, because the model API is a local fake, the harness is a stub script, and the MCP server is a stub.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant G as "global-setup.ts"
    participant F as "fake model"
    participant O as "ostra serve"
    participant S as "specs"
    G->>G: "npm run build in web/, cargo build -p ostra-server"
    G->>F: "startFakeModel"
    G->>O: "spawn serve --no-open --port N --bind 127.0.0.1"
    G->>O: "POST /api/auth/exchange with the token from ostra url"
    G->>O: "POST /api/workspaces, /projects, /sessions"
    O->>F: "model calls of a YOLO session"
    G->>O: "GET /api/sessions/{id} until the session ends"
    G->>G: "write state.json and the test book"
    S->>O: "drive Chromium on the app origin"
    F-->>S: "a canary request fails the test"
```

These steps happen in order:

1. The build step runs `npm run build` in `web/` and `cargo build -p ostra-server` with `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` set to `target-browser`. The binary is `target-browser/debug/ostra`. `OSTRA_BIN` overrides the path.
2. The setup stops an old scratch server only if its command line holds `ostra` and `serve`. Then it empties `/tmp/pw-browser`. The setup refuses a scratch root that is not under `/tmp/`.
3. The setup starts the fake model, an attacker server on another port, and the site as plain files on `ostra-site.localhost`.
4. The setup writes a config and a git repository whose file names and contents carry test strings, and starts `ostra serve` with its own `HOME`, config, data dir, and master key file. `OSTRA_MODELS_DEV_URL` is empty, so no price download runs.
5. The setup signs in, creates a workspace and a project, and writes lessons, a skill, and uploads that carry test strings. It starts one YOLO session and waits up to 120 seconds. If the session does not complete, the setup prints a warning and renders what the session made.
6. The setup writes a documentation book with test strings in every field to `.ostra/docs/pw_book/book.json`.
7. The setup saves the state to `/tmp/pw-browser/state.json`. At the end it stops the server by pid.

### The guard fixture

Every test string sets `window.__pwned` or requests `<fake>/canary/<id>` if it runs or loads. The `guard` fixture in `tests/browser/lib/guard.ts` fails a test on any of these signs:

- `window.__pwned` is set.
- A request reaches the canary route of the fake model.
- A CSP violation occurs on the app origin. The message names the blocked URL, and its id names the render path.
- An unexpected dialog, popup, or navigation away from the app occurs.

### Specs

| Spec | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| `00-smoke` | The app loads signed in |
| `render` | Agent messages, tool output (Bash, MCP), artifacts as documents and Markdown, the completion report, session titles, repo file names and contents, branches and commits, MCP metadata, memory, skills, decisions, search, the quick answer |
| `mobile` | The same render paths in the phone layout (viewport 412 by 880) |
| `terminal` | OSC 52, OSC 8, title sequences, and device queries through xterm.js. The PTY input must match a run with no browser attached |
| `cross-origin` | Attacker pages on another localhost port and another site: forms, fetch, WebSocket, tags, frames, and a navigation to every GET route in `api.rs`. Also DNS rebinding and page content that reaches `/api` |
| `signin` | The token leaves the URL, no request carries it, and what the profile keeps is spent |
| `uploads` | SVG and HTML uploads never render inline, through chips, the artifact view, or raw links |
| `storage` | localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, and Cache Storage hold no transcripts, tokens, or keys |
| `shortcuts` | The web app manifest and icons load from the app origin under the CSP. A recorded shortcut stays in the workspace localStorage entry and runs |
| `site` | Docs Markdown with test strings, Mermaid diagrams with hostile labels, every docs page, search, the homepage and its console shot under their meta CSP, and storage |
| `books` | The test documentation book: the Docs list, each reader page, Mermaid diagrams, search, and the exported HTML file. The export must hold no script, carry its meta CSP, and render with nothing blocked |

The sign-in and the host checks that these specs test are in [auth-and-secrets.md](auth-and-secrets.md). The console and its render paths are in [web-console.md](web-console.md).

### Settings and options

| Name | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run test:fast` | Sets `PW_SKIP_BUILD=1` and skips the build. Use it to rerun after a spec change. The site pages still rebuild, because the test page names the port of the fake |
| `PW_SKIP_BUILD` | Skips `npm run build` and `cargo build`. Without a built `site/public/console`, the setup fails with `site/public/console is missing: run the suite once without PW_SKIP_BUILD` |
| `PW_KEEP_SERVER=1` | Leaves the scratch server running after the run. Its pid is in `/tmp/pw-browser/server.pid` |
| `PW_CHROME` | Path of the Chromium binary. The default is the cached `chromium-1217` under `~/.cache/ms-playwright`, a Linux path |
| `OSTRA_BIN` | Path of the `ostra` binary. The default is `target-browser/debug/ostra` |

The file `tests/browser/playwright.config.ts` sets `workers: 1` and `fullyParallel: false`, because one scratch server and one PTY serve the whole run, and specs that type into the PTY must not overlap. The test timeout is 90 seconds. The `expect` timeout is 15 seconds. The browser maps the host `evil-ostra.test` to `127.0.0.1` with `--host-resolver-rules`, so the attacker pages have a second site name. The suite keeps a trace for a failed test, writes `test-results/`, and writes an HTML report to `playwright-report/`.

Note: the site specs build the `site/` folder with `npm run build:console` and `vite build`. The root `package.json` lists `site` as a workspace. This checkout has no `site/` folder, so the setup of the suite fails at the site build until that folder exists.

## Web and design Vitest suites

The console and the design system have unit and component tests with Vitest and jsdom. Install the packages once at the repository root, because the root `package.json` defines the workspaces `design`, `web`, and `site`:

```bash
npm install
cd web && npm test
cd ../design && npm test
```

Both `test` scripts run `vitest run`. To run one file, use `npx vitest run <path>` in the package folder.

| Package | Config | Test files | What the tests cover |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `web` | The `test` block of `web/vite.config.ts`: `environment: "jsdom"`, `env: { VITE_MOCK: "1" }`, files `src/**/*.test.ts` and `src/**/*.test.tsx` | 48 | App routes and shell, screens (session, workspace, project, setup, execution, artifact), the mobile shell and its logic, the API socket, the stores and libraries under `src/lib` (palette, shortcuts, events, tabs, gate answers), the Markdown renderer, and terminal safety |
| `design` | `design/vitest.config.ts`: the React plugin, `environment: "jsdom"`, files `src/**/*.test.ts` and `src/**/*.test.tsx` | 3 | The component groups `feedback`, `navigation`, and `forms` |

The setting `VITE_MOCK=1` makes the web tests use the mock API instead of a server. A web test needs no running Ostra server and no model. The design test files `feedback.test.tsx`, `navigation.test.tsx`, and `forms.test.tsx` match only three of the seven component groups, so a change in `brand`, `core`, `data`, or `pipeline` has no group test file.

Both packages also have a type check and a Biome check:

| Command | Package | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `npm run typecheck` | `web`, `design` | Runs `tsc --noEmit` with the package `tsconfig.json` |
| `npm run check` | `web`, `design` | Runs `biome check` |
| `npm run check:fix` | `web`, `design` | Runs `biome check --write` |
| `npm run lint` | `web`, `design` | Runs `biome lint` |

The Vitest suites do not prove the security of the render paths in a real browser. The browser security suite does that. jsdom does not apply a CSP.

## Windows sandbox probes

The folder `tests/windows-probes` holds `winprobe`, a standalone program. It checks the assumptions of the Windows sandbox design on a real Windows machine, before the sandbox code relies on them. A unit test cannot do this, because the assumptions are about the behavior of Windows itself: users, ACLs, tokens, Job Objects, and the firewall. The sandbox page owns the sandbox. See [sandbox.md](sandbox.md).

The probes are not a cargo test. The root `Cargo.toml` excludes `tests/windows-probes` from the workspace with `exclude`, so `cargo test --workspace` never builds it. The program has no Ostra code. Its `.cargo/config.toml` sets `-C target-feature=+crt-static`, so the single exe runs on a bare VM without the Visual C++ runtime.

Caution: run the probes only on a throwaway Windows VM, and run `winprobe cleanup` when you finish. The `setup` role creates local users, a password file, and ACL grants. The `run` role creates firewall filters. A host that you use for other work keeps these changes until you run `cleanup`.

### Run the probes

1. Build the crate in `tests/windows-probes` for Windows. Copy the exe to the VM, for example with `scp`.
2. On the VM, run `winprobe setup` as an administrator. It creates the users `OstraProbeA` and `OstraProbeB`, the folders `C:\ostra-probe` and `C:\ostra-probe\out`, and the password file `C:\ostra-probe\pass.txt`. It also sets the ACL grants and builds a test repository tree (`build_repo_tree`). It creates no firewall rule.
3. Run `winprobe run`. It starts confined probes as the probe user and runs the checks of the host side. It writes `C:\ostra-probe\results.md`. The network probe (`net_probe`) creates the firewall rules `OstraProbeInAllow` and `OstraProbeOutBlock`.
4. Run `winprobe cleanup`. It deletes both users and their profile folders, removes the firewall rules named `OstraProbe*`, and deletes `C:\ostra-probe`.

The other roles, `asuser`, `markself`, `medspawn`, `sleeper`, `openone`, `spinjob`, and `netfilter`, are helpers that `run` starts. Do not start them by hand.

### Read the results

Each finding has a verify number, a status, a check name, the expected result, and the observed result. The status is one of four values:

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `PASS` | The assumption of the design held |
| `FAIL` | The assumption broke. The sandbox code must handle the gap |
| `INCONCLUSIVE` | The VM cannot decide the check, for example because a tool is not installed |
| `NEEDS_CLIENT` | The check needs a Windows 11 client or a machine with other antivirus software |

The committed file `tests/windows-probes/results-full.md` is the record of one run on Windows Server 2025 build 26100. It has 54 findings in 17 verify groups: 43 `PASS`, 3 `FAIL`, 4 `INCONCLUSIVE`, and 4 `NEEDS_CLIENT`. The three failures are these:

- The Windows Firewall cannot limit loopback traffic to the proxy port, because it does not filter loopback. A raw WFP filter is the planned fix.
- A process of the sandbox user can open a sibling process of the same user with a plain token.
- A restricting SID set cannot isolate same-user siblings. Isolation must come from one user for each execution slot.

The file is a record of a past run. It does not change when the code changes. Run the probes again after you change a Windows assumption, and update the file.

## What the tests do not prove

- The conformance fixtures prove the planner only. They do not run an agent, so they cannot find a fault in a prompt or an executor.
- The e2e tests use a scripted model. They prove the wiring, not the quality of model answers. The evals measure answer quality.
- The evals measure models at the time of the run. A pass rate is a sample over `OSTRA_EVAL_RUNS` runs, and the evals do not fail on a wrong answer.
- The browser suite runs one Chromium on the scratch server. It does not test Firefox or Safari.
- The Windows probes ran on a headless server VM. Checks of desktop isolation, ConPTY, Git Bash, and toolchain compatibility need a Windows 11 client.

## Limits and defaults

| Item | Value | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E2E wait for a session state | 60 seconds, polled every 100 milliseconds | `wait_for` in `e2e.rs` |
| Browser session wait | 120 seconds | `global-setup.ts` |
| Browser server wait | 60 seconds, polled every 200 milliseconds | `waitFor` in `global-setup.ts` |
| Playwright test timeout | 90 seconds | `playwright.config.ts` |
| Playwright `expect` timeout | 15 seconds | `playwright.config.ts` |
| Playwright workers | 1 | `playwright.config.ts` |
| Eval runs per case | 3 (advisor 5) | `OSTRA_EVAL_RUNS` |
| Eval jobs at the same time | 3 (advisor 4) | `OSTRA_EVAL_JOBS` |
| Eval report folder | `target/evals/` | the `*_evals.rs` files |
| Browser scratch root | `/tmp/pw-browser` | `tests/browser/lib/env.ts` |

The trait that serves the tools of external MCP servers for one execution.
The SQLite file `<project>/.ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3` that holds the lessons of one project.
The SQLite store of lessons at .ostra/memory/knowledge.sqlite3, with FTS5 search.
A build mode with `VITE_MOCK=1` in which the console uses fixtures and needs no server.
The public JSON price and limit list that Ostra caches in models-dev.json and uses to price each response.
The executor that calls a model API with an API key and runs the tools itself in a turn loop.
The 16 language ids that the index parses and that a `language_servers` entry can name.
The saved sign-in of one remote server: URL, discovery result, client credentials, redirect URI, and tokens. The registry seals it.
A random 64-character hex value in the sign-in URL fragment that the server accepts for one exchange within 15 minutes.
An environment variable that sets the `tracing` filter for the server log. The default level is `info`.
The function that replaces the safety fields of a loaded workspace file with the registry values.
A loop of two agents that work in rounds, such as a spec author and a fact checker, or an implementer and a reviewer.
The function that checks a spawn block against the contract of one agent and returns the values by parameter id.
The overview and the sections of one project inside a book.
A small piece of the text of a unit that the search ranks and shows.
The commands of a folder file whose hash differs from the approved hash. Ostra removes them from the effective settings.
The default answer of layer 2 for a call that no rule matches: `default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, or `bypass`.
One unit of a plan with steps, requirements, constraints, complexity, test policy, and depends_on. It has its own JSON and Markdown file pair.
A sign-in method in which the client proves with a random verifier that it started the authorization request.
The facts from outside the log that the planner needs: `format_commands` and `budget_usd`.
The function `next_steps`. It reads a `SessionState` and a `PlanCtx` and returns the list of `Step` values.
The component that checks each tool call with layer 1 guards and layer 2 permissions before the tool runs.
A tab in italics that the next list row replaces. At most one preview tab exists.
The exact hosts named by `WebFetch(domain:...)` rules, which WebFetch can reach even when they resolve to private addresses.
A random host name `ostra-<16 hex>.localhost` that scopes the cookie to Ostra and not to other local ports.
The description of the boundary of one execution, without a backend name: mounts, environment, egress policy, forwarded ports, and decoys.
The short name of a project in a workspace. It matches `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*`.
The machine-readable summary of one project that the initializer writes to `.ostra/project.toml`.
The paths in `ExecContext::protected_paths`: the Ostra executable, the global config file, the data dir, the assets dir, `workspace.toml`, and the workspace database.
The trait that gives the agent loop and the judge calls one interface to a model API.
The ordered list of `code_provider` program, language servers, and the built-in provider that `Code::ask` builds for each request.
A pseudo terminal in which Ostra runs a harness CLI and mirrors its screen to the browser.
The endpoint of a browser's push service plus its `p256dh` and `auth` keys, stored in `push_subscriptions`.
A message that the server creates itself, such as `project_fs_changed` or `tree_patch`, sent on the `push` channel with an explicit list of channels.
One open question of an agent, with options, a recommended option, and a multi-select flag.
The one SQLite database of the machine, with workspaces, push subscriptions, and the `kv` table of sealed credentials.
The permission mode, YOLO, limits, tool enforcement, and sandbox choices. They live in the registry under `workspace_access:<root>`, never in a folder file.
The part of the first message that gives the stack, commands, and module map of the project, cut at `MAX_BRIEF_CHARS`.
The function that turns a route key and a phase complexity into an executor, a model, and a tier.
A string such as `session:<id>` that names one thing the console can open in a tab and maps to one URL.
The backoff rule for provider requests: 4 retries, a 1000 ms base delay, and a 60 s cap.
The rule for review after a work pass: `Always`, `IfCodeChanged`, or `Never`.
The decision of `SessionState::route` for a question to a subagent: `WakeInPlace`, `Consult`, `Pending`, or `Failed`.
The name of an agent or `judge` that the `[routing]` tables use to choose an executor, a model, and an effort.
The rule that safety settings live in the registry and never take effect from `workspace.toml`.
The label of a decision that names its layer (`guard` or `permission`) and the guard id, rule text, or mode label.
The effect of a coordination call on the run: `Continue`, `Wait`, or `Finish`.
A file such as `.mcp.json` or `.envrc` that makes a tool run a program the next time someone opens the project.
The kernel boundary under agent commands, with an egress proxy for network access.
The hidden argument of the `ostra` binary. It starts the helper inside a bubblewrap sandbox, before the runtime starts.
The marker that replaces a literal MCP header or env value in the workspace file and in the browser view.
A provider for tests that replays queued responses and makes no network call.
The names of environment variables that Bash, PowerShell, and Cmd remove from the child process.
The type that encrypts registry credentials with AES-256-GCM under the master key.
The macOS sandbox. Ostra writes a policy in SBPL and runs the program with `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec`.
A token that names a role, such as `--surface-panel`, and points to a base token. The light theme changes its target.
A file in the data folder that records the port, the URL host, and the process ID of a running server.
The message type that the server sends over `/ws`, either JSON or, for terminal output, a binary frame.
The per-workspace value that implements the `Services` trait of the engine and gives it config, executors, judge calls, notifications, and trust state.
The trait through which the engine reaches settings, executors, judges, and notices. The server implements it as `ServerServices`.
One run of the pipeline for a user request, stored as an append-only list of events.
A file that an agent wrote in the session folder, such as a spec or a report.
A Markdown index of the session that `context::render` writes so that a revision reads paths and summaries, not the whole conversation.
The `ostra_session` cookie that the server sets after a token exchange and that proves a sign-in for 30 days.
The folder `<workspace>/.ostra/sessions/<id>` that holds the artifacts, uploads, and engine state of one session.
An agent that the write-scope guard confines to the session folder and the OS temp folder, as `is_session_only` marks.
One fact in the session log, such as `ExecutionStarted` or `GateAnswered`.
The state that `SessionState::fold` computes from the stored events of one session.
A class that gives many components one REST fetch and one socket subscription for each key.
A build mode with `VITE_SHOT=1` that shows the console in an iframe on the project homepage.
The registry row that holds the id, times, user agent, and address of one sign-in, stored under the hash of the cookie.
A link of the form `http://<host>/#token=<token>` that signs one browser in. The token works once.
One command of a parsed shell line, with its words, assignments, and redirects. Layer 2 matches each rule against each simple command.
A directory with a SKILL.md file that teaches one recurring task. Ostra writes new skills under .agents/skills/.
One unit of parallel scouting, usually one module or one top-level source dir of the repo.
A value that counts one running execution against the limit `limits.max_parallel_executions` and gives the count back on `Drop`.
The first message of an execution: a list of `Label: value` lines that `SpawnParams::render` builds.
The trait that builds the prompt, the spawn block, and the effort for one agent spawn.
The trait that each typed spawn struct implements to render its spawn block and its JSON record.
The data that the spawn factory needs to start one agent execution.
One node of the pipeline, named by `StageKind`.
A file that the engine stored under a hex id in the workspace staging folder before a session claims it.
The judged risk of a change: `Low`, `Medium`, or `High`. `Low` skips the plan stage.
A pool entry whose server failed to start or died, and whose age since its creation is at least `RETRY` (30 seconds).
A chip that maps a raw backend status string and a kind to a tone and a label.
One action that the planner asks the runner to do, such as `Spawn`, `Judge`, or `OpenGate`.
A block of a Stop event that tells the agent to call its submit tool. The bridge allows at most `MAX_STOP_NUDGES` of them.
A `SessionEvent` with its sequence number `seq` and its UTC time `at`.
The policy counter of consecutive build or test failures in one execution. It triggers recall, a warning, a denial, and the lesson gate.
One key press written as `ctrl+alt+shift+meta+<key>`. A shortcut binding has one or two strokes.
One conversation of one agent in a session, named by the execution ID of its first run.
The tool `submit_<agent>` that an agent calls once as its last action to return its typed result to the engine.
The part of a book of two or more projects that describes components, links, failure recovery, and scaling.
A name such as `tool_read` in a prompt that `Mapping::context` replaces with the tool name of the executor.
The phase field with the value Required or Skip. It tells the engine whether a requested test run covers the phase.
A phase field with the values `Required` and `Skip`. It decides if the test stage covers the phase.
A name for a class of model: fast, balanced, advanced, or frontier. A tier table maps it to a model for each executor.
A CSS custom property on `:root` that holds a color, size, font, radius, shadow, or timing value.
The setting `tool_enforcement` that turns on the guards that check where a call writes: `write-scope`, `report-path`, and the `self-protection` checks.
The file `assets/tool-mapping.toml`, which gives the tool name of each capability for each executor table.
The section that Ostra puts at the start of a harness prompt to list the tools of the agent with their harness names.
The canonical form of a tool call, with a `tool` name and a JSON `input`, that every executor passes to the policy.
The per-execution state that tools share: working directory, files read, HTTP client, private hosts, scrub list, and sandbox.
The result of one tool call: text, error flag, exit code, duration, optional diff, and the run end marker.
A record that a tool wrote a file. The Files back end uses it to drop caches and push `project_fs_changed`.
The choice between `Light` and `Full` for an `IMPLEMENT` session.
One node of the Sessions tree: a session with its groups, runs, and artifacts. The server pushes a whole node in a `tree_patch` message.
A host rule that the user chose, in `allowed_hosts` or in a base URL of a harness launch. It can resolve to any address.
One request to the model and its response in the native loop.
A research document, spec, or plan that an agent writes as validated JSON, with Markdown that Ostra renders from it.
A part of a book that a search hit points to, such as a section or a glossary term.
One refused setting, with a dotted `path` and a `message`. A save with an issue writes nothing.
A signed token (RFC 8292) that shows the push service which application server sends a message.
A run that asked a question and waits for the answer. A native run ends with status `Waiting`. A harness run keeps its process.
A browser service that delivers an encrypted notice from a server to a browser through the push service of the browser vendor.
A standalone program that checks the assumptions of the Windows sandbox design on a real Windows machine.
The `RwLock<bool>` in `WorkspaceRt` that makes a busy check and a removal one step. The bool is true after delete.
The number of work executions that started in a loop. `on_started` adds 1 for each start that is not resumed.
The reason a work execution ran: `Initial`, `Fix`, `BlockerFix`, `Resume`, `Rescue`, or `Rerun`.
The state of one implementer or write-test sequence for one phase, with its reviews.
A file that the user keeps for all sessions of a workspace. It is not a typed document.
The SQLite file `<workspace>/.ostra/workspace.db` with the event log, the materialized tables, and the search index.
The trait that gives a workspace the registry, the global config, machine facts, provider status, and engine services.
One open workspace in a running server: its settings, database, engine, host, clone list, and work lock.
The settings type for one workspace, stored in `.ostra/workspace.toml` and in the registry.
The planner step that makes the runner merge the parts into the book and write the files.
A session mode in which the planner answers gates by itself. Guards and security blocks still apply.
A session mode in which the engine answers gates and the policy allows permission asks without a person.
